title: Version History says who changed what, read from the document's own marks
entry:
**An assembled entry's links point where the text went.** A changelog fragment is written in `changelog.d/` and a pending decision in `docs/decisions/pending/`, and their links are written from there; the assembler moved the text one directory and left the links behind, so `lint:doc-links` refused every rendered file for a mistake nobody made, and the pre-push hook refused every branch with it. `parseFragment` now rebases a fragment's links to the file the text lands in (the root changelog, or the public changelog under `docs/`), `rebasePendingLinks` rebases a numbered decision's links one level up and repoints a sibling link at the sibling's numbered file, and `rewriteReferences` repoints a path link to `decisions/pending/<slug>.md` anywhere under `docs/` at the numbered file alongside the `ADR-<slug>` token it already rewrote. The rendered files on `main` are repaired in the same change, and the 25 baseline entries the repair made stale are deleted.

**Version History says who changed what, read from the document's own marks.** `readTrackedChanges` in `@magna-carta/document-assembly` (`./ooxml-read-tracked-changes`) walks the same tree the accept pass resolves and reads every revision element as a mark: kind (insertion, deletion, formatting), the author as the document names them, the instant, the words (a paragraph break as a newline, a deleted row's words, a reformatted run's words), the part and the paragraph; one act of typing split across runs folds into one mark. The marks are read when a version's export copy is made (`apps/api-worker/src/exports/record-version-changes.ts`), the one moment the document is in hand off the request path, and the rows ride the batch that records the copy. A version records only the marks no earlier version of the file did, identified by what the document holds rather than the editor's renumbered ids; the author's name resolves to a member through the version's participants first and the firm's roster second, and a name two members share resolves to neither. `file_version_change` is keyed by version and document order, the words capped at 2000 characters and the rows at 5000 per version; the member reference is pseudonymized on erasure like the participant row.

`GET /api/v1/files/{id}/versions` rows carry `changes`, one entry per author with counts, from one grouped read per page; `GET /api/v1/files/{id}/versions/{versionId}/changes` (`files.versionChanges`) lists a version's changes in document order, bounded by construction. Version History shows the per-author summary on each row and opens a version's changes by author: additions underlined, removals struck through, formatting marked.

title: Every number the firm issues is the firm's to shape, and Settings › Numbering fits on one screen without a second scrollbar
entry: **Every sequence the platform draws is now shaped by a scheme, and the numbering screen is eight folds instead of one long menu.** The register's `fixed` formulation is retired (`packages/sequence-numbering/src/purposes.ts`): `invoice`, `time_entry` and `communication` join the five already scheme-shaped, so `SchemeNumberingPurpose` is `NumberingPurpose` and a new run is a row rather than a renderer. Three additions made that reach without changing an issued number. `month`, `day` and `matter_number` join `NumberSegment`, its zod union and `renderNumber`, so the day-scoped call number and the matter-prefixed entry number are templates rather than special cases. `scopeSource: "segments" | "owner"` on the register says whether the counter scope is derived from the template's scoping parts (the collision-proof general case) or passed by the domain — a time entry counts within its matter's handle, an invoice within the letterhead chosen at finalize — and `schemeSchemaFor` refuses a scoping mark on an owner-scoped run, since the switch would do nothing. `scopeDistinguishedBy` names the part such a scheme must carry (time entries: `matter_number`); the invoice run's is conditional and `finalizeInvoice` refuses `unknown-number-scope` by name for a bill drawn under a scope its scheme cannot render. Its mirror, `invoice-numbering-needs-letterhead`, refuses a firm-wide bill once the scheme prints the office code, where the bill would otherwise have reached the renderer and failed as a server error. `renderInvoiceNumber`, `renderEntryNumber`, `renderCommunicationNumber` and their start-value constants are gone; `planSchemeDraw` gained `{ scopeKey, count }` and returns a `SchemeDrawPlan` carrying every number of a block, over the new `guardedAdvanceStatement(…, by)`. The call counter's scope keys are re-keyed by `20261002T192145_communication-number-scope-parts.sql` from `2026-09-08` to the `2026:09:08` the scoping parts derive. On the web surface, `settings/numbering/+page.svelte` is an `Accordion.Root type="multiple"` with the current example on each heading; `numbering-scheme-editor.svelte` puts reorder and delete at the row's end, sizes cells to content, states `preview.parts[index]` in a cell the purpose cannot customize, and offers the starters as "Load an example" in the table's last row. `tooling/lint-settings-scroll/` walks all 27 settings routes through their component graph and fails a nested scroll region, with 15 stated allowances. Two defects the static scan cannot see were found by rendering the page: the parts table was still 1038px in an 848px column because each `ChoicePicker` asked for a text input's default width, which a content-sized table takes as a column floor (the picker gains `fillsCell`, Part alone takes the spare width, the long heading wraps, the row controls are `icon-sm`; `apps/web/test/numbering-parts-table.test.ts` pins it), and `NavigationLayout`'s content-box navigation column was `h-full`, so its gutters overshot the row by 48px and scrolled the canvas on every settings page (it is `self-stretch` now, and the layout's Storybook story measures that neither column passes the layout's bottom).

title: Meetings: a room of three hundred with a host, a waiting room, chat on the record relayed live, a raised hand and reactions, and a socket that spends from a budget
entry:
**A second person on a guest's link no longer walks into the room under the first guest's name.**
An arrival on a link whose stay is already open still returns that stay, but now puts it back at
the door under the name just typed, so a host sees who is arriving and admits them deliberately.
The room drops the earlier holder's tile and socket at once. The name the stay carried before, and
who admitted it, stay on the arrival's audit row.

**Sending a fresh link closes the stay the old one held**, in the same write, and the fresh link
arrives at the door. Withdrawing a link and replacing one both close the stay `left` rather than
`removed`, so inviting the person again brings them back instead of telling them they were put out.
A fresh link, whether rotated or re-sent, also starts its arrival count again, so a guest whose
connection kept failing is never sent a link that is already used up.

**A link says why it stopped working.** An expired link this deployment signed is answered
`410 guest-link-expired` with no database read, instead of the flat 404 a guessed token gets, and
it is counted under its own reason. An arrival whose link changed under it is told whether it was
withdrawn, replaced, used up or expired. A link whose person has been taken off the event is refused
as withdrawn, and the refused arrival is recorded.

**The meeting socket takes a guest's grant as a WebSocket subprotocol** (`meeting-guest`, then the
grant), and answers with the bare protocol name, so the credential stays out of the socket's
address. The `guest` query parameter is still accepted, on the socket route alone; the messages and
departure routes now refuse it even on an upgrade.

**An invitation whose e-mail could not be sent is no longer remembered as sent.** Nothing is stored
under the request's idempotency key until the mail has gone, so the host's retry sends a fresh link
rather than replaying a success the guest never received.

**Six corrections to hosting and the door, found in review.**

**A hand-over leaves the outgoing host a co-host.** `grantHosting` now inserts a co-host grant for
the person stepping down, in the same batch as the revocation, so there is no instant in which they
hold nothing. Handing the room over is not leaving it: dropping the outgoing host to an ordinary
member took the mute, the spotlight and the door away from somebody who had been hosting a second
earlier, with nothing on any screen to say so. `revokeHostGrantStatement` takes an optional `role` for
the same reason — a batch that closes one grant and opens another for one member is the only place
"whatever they hold" stops being one row, and the hand-over now names the grant it is closing so a
race is caught by the guard rather than by a raw constraint one statement later.

**A co-host may stand down.** `POST /api/v1/meetings/{meetingId}/hosts/{userId}/revoke` naming
YOURSELF is a resignation and is anybody's to make; the one refusal is the sole grant-holder, because
a host resigning out of a room where nobody else holds anything leaves a running meeting with nobody
running it. Its own audit event, `meetings.meeting.hostingResigned`, because both rows carry the
caller as the actor and one name would make "did somebody stand down or were they stood down" a
question you answer by comparing identifiers.

**Two co-hosts and an absent host no longer leave a room permanently hostless.**
`countOtherHostsPresent` counted every live grant, so each co-host saw the other and neither could
claim a room nobody was holding. It now counts a live HOST grant whose holder is in the room. A
co-host does not prevent the claim; the host does.

**The door is now shut in the same statement as the arrival.** The join path read the lock and the
lobby a round trip before its insert, so a host shutting the door in that instant had the arrival
land in a locked room — and a host turning the LOBBY on in the same instant put somebody straight
into a discussion the door was opened to keep them out of. Both conditions are now predicates on
`insertAttendanceUnderCapStatement` and, inverted, on the waiting insert, so the guarded write rolls
the whole batch back rather than half-landing a stay in a room that is shut.

**Removing somebody who was still at the door leaves no key behind.** The room's release only knew
the `participant:` keyspace, so a removal from the lobby closed the stay in the record and left a
`waiting:` key — the host's own panel went on offering to admit somebody the record says is not in
the meeting, and the key kept arming the door's grace deadline.

**A lock or lobby write that changed nothing no longer disturbs the room.** Both routes now skip the
room call when the service reports nothing moved, rather than spending a room-state broadcast on
every socket to restate what each of them already draws.

**A raised hand and six reactions, relayed by the room and stored nowhere.** `RosterParticipant`
gains `hand` and `handRaisedAt` — two wire fields over ONE stored fact, projected in
`room/room-roster.ts` and nowhere else — and the client `presence` frame gains an optional `hand`.
The browser decides the boolean and the room stamps the instant, for the reason a chat message's
instant is the server's: a queue ordered by what each person's machine said is not one ordering. A
host lowers one hand or all of them with `lower-hands { participantId | null }`, authorized from the
STORED participant record like every other host frame and refused `not-host` otherwise; nobody is
spared by "lower all", including the host who pressed it. A lowered or raised hand travels on a
ROSTER change rather than a frame of its own, which is what keeps a host's queue right for the
browser that joined a minute after the hand went up.

**`MEETING_REACTIONS` is a closed vocabulary of six** — `thumbs-up`, `thumbs-down`, `heart`, `laugh`,
`applause`, `celebrate` — named by meaning rather than by the glyph that draws them, so upgrading the
icon package is not a change to the meeting protocol. A `reaction` naming anything else does not
parse.

**The room coalesces above `ROSTER_DELTA_THRESHOLD`, which is the whole design.** Three hundred
people applauding one sentence is three hundred inbound frames and, relayed one by one, ninety
thousand outbound inside a second. At or below the threshold the room sends `reaction
{ participantId, name, at }` and leaves the sender out; above it, reactions accumulate into a
per-name count flushed as ONE `reactions { counts, at }` frame per second for the whole room, driven
by the next frame with the room's own alarm as the backstop. The branch is counted over the WELCOMED
SOCKETS rather than over the roster: it is choosing a fan-out, and a roster read there would spend
three hundred keys on every reaction in exactly the room the coalescing exists for. The load harness
now drives a second of applause and measures it at **one frame per socket and zero roster reads per
reaction**.

**A new refusal reason, `rate-limited`, and it is the first throttle here that refuses rather than
drops.** Every other one discards a frame inside its window, which is safe because those frames
restate themselves. A hand may be the last thing somebody does for ten minutes and a reaction is a
single act with no later frame to carry it, so both answer to `SIGNAL_INTERVAL_MILLISECONDS` —
exported from the protocol package, because a client that paced itself by a different number would be
refused for behaving correctly — and the frame inside the window is refused with the socket kept
open.

**Nothing reaches the record.** No table, no migration, no audit row and no personal-data
registration: a hand and a reaction are transient room state on the terms the roster already is,
deleted when the stay ends and when the meeting does. One event,
`meetings.room.reactionsRelayed`, carrying the count and whether it was coalesced, and no field for
which reaction it was.

**The browser is asked for a treated microphone, and the room says what it got.** `publish()` in
`apps/web/src/lib/meetings/client/meeting-client.svelte.ts` captures through the constraint builder
in `client/media-effects.ts`: noise suppression, echo cancellation and gain control asked for as
plain booleans, never `{ exact: true }`, because an exact constraint a device cannot meet rejects
the whole capture and a member with no microphone is worse than one with an untreated microphone.
`readAudioTreatment` reads back from the track what the browser actually applied, three-valued
(true, false, or not reported), and `readBlurCapability` probes the platform's own background blur
and answers controllable, platform-controlled or unavailable. The `MediaEffects` seam sits between
capture and publish with a pass-through stage, so the picture and sound slices swap in one place.
The preference is remembered per member. The Effects popover in the control bar draws no control
that cannot act: where the browser offers no blur, one sentence says so.

**Polls and a question queue, on the record on chat's own terms.** Six per-firm tables by one
additive migration — `meeting_poll`, `meeting_poll_option`, `meeting_poll_respondent`,
`meeting_poll_answer`, `meeting_question`, `meeting_question_upvote` — the poll and question trios in
`@magna-carta/meetings`, and twelve routes in `routes/meeting-polls.ts` and
`routes/meeting-questions.ts`. Every act is a route with an audit row of identifiers and instants;
opening, closing, reading who answered what and marking a question answered are host acts that ask
the GRANT on the meeting through `requireHostGrant`, so an Attorney holding `meetings:host` and no
grant is `403 meeting-not-host`. Answering, asking and upvoting need an open stay, as posting a chat
message does.

**Anonymity is two tables that cannot answer each other's question.** `meeting_poll_answer` holds what
was chosen and, on a poll that shows no names, a participant pair of literal NULLs written by a
statement that has no argument for them; `meeting_poll_respondent` holds that a stay answered, the one
instant, and nothing about what. The answer names its option as the pair `(poll_id, option_id)`
against the option table's own unique pair, so an answer to another poll's option fails at the
foreign key. One participation per member per poll — the respondent insert refuses a later stay of the
same member, not only the same stay — and no audit row ever carries the question, a label or which
option was chosen.

**Six room frames and no client frame.** `poll-opened` and `question-asked` carry the row whole so
three hundred browsers are not sent to the read at once; `poll-closed` carries the final tally;
`question-updated` the new state, with an empty body for a redaction; `poll-tally` and
`question-tally` go through the reactions' per-second bucket, extracted to
`room/room-coalescing.ts` and now shared, holding the latest count the route read rather than a sum.
A guest's socket receives every frame with its user identifiers nulled. Two telemetry events,
`meetings.room.pollRelayed` and `meetings.room.questionRelayed`, carry socket counts and nothing a
person typed. Every participant CHECK accepts `attendee` beside `member` and `guest`, and a poll and a
question carry a nullable `breakout_id` by value, both while the migration is unlanded.

**A meeting can now be asked about after it has ended.** The room holds no rows, deletes its own
state as it goes and hibernates between frames, so a three-hundred-person meeting that went wrong
left attendance and an Error ID on whichever refusal a member happened to see. `meetings.room.*` in
`@magna-carta/telemetry`'s catalog is now the durable trace: one allowlist builder per act — joined,
welcomed, published, subscribed, layer changed, presence relayed, refused, socket lost, swept,
superseded, admitted, denied, muted, removed, locked, ended, the alarm and what it found due, a
frame's storage spend, and a browser's own report — each correlated by firm, meeting and, where the
act is about a person, stay. `apps/api-worker/src/meetings/room/room-diagnostics.ts` is the room's
one emitter and nothing may throw out of it; every other module reaches it with one call.

**The redaction is structural, not a rule at the call sites.** There is no declared field for a
display name, a track name, a session description or a chat line, so an edit cannot add one without
adding it to the catalog first, where it would have to be argued for. A test reads the whole emitted
set back as text and fails on any of them. What is left is identifiers the platform minted, counts,
closed enums and instants — the posture the custody and asset registers take, for a sharper reason:
the metadata of a law firm's meetings is a disclosure with no transcript attached.

**A refusal is sent and recorded in one call**, because a refusal recorded and not sent — or sent and
not recorded — is exactly the drift the Error ID exists to close: the member ends up holding a handle
the record does not know, and the support search the field exists for finds nothing.

**Two things are deliberately not recorded per occurrence**, because they are the frames a large room
sends most. Presence is one event per coalesced flush carrying the count it covered. What a frame
spends in storage is sampled, one frame in twenty, and is approximate under concurrency — a budget,
never a ledger, and the catalog says so.

**A browser now tells the room what its connection is doing.** `diagnostic-report` is an additive
client frame carrying quality, round trip, loss fraction, jitter, the outbound layer and the count of
inbound streams. Every field is optional — an absent measurement is "not taken", never "none" — and
every one is bounded in the schema, because it is the one frame whose whole content is an
unverifiable claim about the sender and telemetry aggregates these. The room takes one per
participant per five seconds and drops the rest in silence, keeps the last sample on the participant
record for the inspect call, and acknowledges nothing.

**`GET /api/v1/meetings/{meetingId}/inspect` reads one live room**, behind the platform-operator
guard. It is the only meeting route that names the firm in the query rather than addressing the room
by the session firm, and the reason is structural rather than convenient: its caller belongs to no
firm, so there is no session firm to read. A firm permission was rejected — a member who could read
the room's internals could read a colleague's connection quality and their place in the meeting. It
answers with the roster (role, presence, track and subscription counts, last sample), the door, the
open sockets and which stay each carries, the alarm and which of its deadlines are pending, the
storage key count and approximate size, the routing sessions and the ended marker, and it changes
nothing. A room nobody has ever addressed answers with empty lists, because that is itself the
finding.

**The room's fan-out cost is a number now.** `apps/api-worker/test/support/meeting-room-load.ts`
drives real socket pairs against the real object: everybody arrives, everybody publishes, everybody
talks at once, the gallery turns a page, a tenth of the room reconnects, the host ends it. Forty
clients run in the ordinary suite as an assertion on the two bounds; three hundred run by hand
(`VITE_MEETING_ROOM_LOAD_PARTICIPANTS=300`). At three hundred: one frame per join per socket exactly,
0.4 storage lists per frame, 414,180 frames delivered, 1,500 on the busiest socket, in twenty
seconds.

**It falsified a design claim on its first run, and found a bug.** Every deferred presence transition
armed the alarm through the full reconciliation, which reads the whole roster AND the whole door to
find the nearest deadline — two roster-wide reads on the frame a room of three hundred sends most,
measured at 1.2 storage lists per frame against a design that claims one. The deadline is already
known where the transition is deferred, so `relayPresence` now answers with it and the caller arms
for that instant; the same pass fell to 0.4. Separately, the room's direct replies to one socket
called `send` unguarded, and `send` on a closed socket throws — and a throw out of `webSocketMessage`
resets the Durable Object, dropping every socket in the meeting. A supersede, a leave or the end of a
meeting racing a queued frame would have ended the meeting for everybody in it. The room-wide
broadcast had swallowed that since it was written; every direct reply now goes through the same
`trySend`.

**A member given a grant mid-meeting is now told who is already at the door.** Every other `waiting`
frame goes out because the queue moved; this one goes out because the audience did. A co-host
appointed at the twentieth minute learned the roster had changed and nothing at all about the people
standing outside, so their lobby panel stayed empty until the next knock — which, in the case that
matters, is a meeting where the person who could let somebody in has just been appointed. An empty
door is stated rather than left silent.

**The event form can open a meeting with its lobby on.** `CalendarEventMeetingInput` takes an
optional `lobby`, read on the create path exactly as the medium beside it is. Omitted means off,
which is what every meeting scheduled before the door existed was — a form that did not ask must not
quietly put a firm's own colleagues in a queue.

**Twenty import cycles left the API worker.** Every one of them ran through `authForEnv` living in
`app.ts`, which imports every route module — so a route-specific guard that has to resolve a session
for itself (the platform-operator lane, which the per-firm chokepoint cannot serve because its caller
belongs to no firm) closed a cycle, and a second route in that lane added two more findings. It moved
to `src/auth-instance.ts`, which takes only the `Bindings` type from `app.ts`. The `import/no-cycle`
ratchet drops from 36 to 16.

**A meeting can have a guest from outside the firm, on a signed link.** Two additive per-firm tables
join the lineage (`meeting_guest_invitation`, `meeting_guest_stay`, migration
`20260924T090000_a-guest-holds-a-signed-link-and-a-stay-of-its-own`). An invitation is one row per
Directory person or organization per meeting, holding only the SHA-256 of the link's secret; a stay
is the guest's own presence in the room, beside `meeting_attendance` rather than a nullable column on
it. The in-the-room and waiting predicates are now unions over both tables, composed in one place
(`MEETING_STAY_TABLES`), so a guest counts against the room's and the door's ceilings exactly as a
member does.

**The chokepoint has a guest lane.** A route declaring `guestLane: "invitation" | "grant"` is
admitted by a signed credential in the `x-meeting-guest` header — or, on the socket upgrade alone,
the `guest` query parameter — in place of the session, member-active and permission steps. The
handler gets a firm and the credential's names and never a user id. Registration refuses a guest
route that names a permission or is authenticated, and a guest credential sent to any other route is
answered the reserved 404. The credential shares the support session's signed format
(`src/signed-token.ts`) under its own `typ`.

**Ten routes.** A host (`meetings:host` and a grant on the meeting) invites, lists, rotates and
withdraws links under `/api/v1/meetings/{meetingId}/guests`; the invitation is mailed after its batch
commits and the token is never returned, stored or logged. A guest reads a reduced summary
(`GuestMeetingSummary`, a schema of its own with no matter or event field), arrives at the door,
opens the socket, reads and sends chat once admitted, and leaves, under `/api/v1/guest/*` with no
meeting identifier in any path. Opening the link spends nothing; an arrival does, up to twenty.

**The room redacts per viewer.** `welcome`, `roster`, `roster-delta` and `message` frames are built
for the socket they go to: a guest's copy carries `userId: null` for everybody. Roster entries and
the hosts' `waiting` list gain `kind` (`member` | `guest`), and a waiting guest's entry carries the
name the link was minted for (`invitedName`) beside the name typed at the door.

Host controls for meetings, as far as the server goes: who is running a room is a grant on the
meeting rather than a permission key half the firm holds.

`meetings:host` says a firm lets a member convene meetings. It could never say who is running THIS
room, because that changes while the meeting runs — hosting is handed over, co-hosts are named and
withdrawn, and the member who opened the room may have been called away an hour ago. So the meeting
record carries the answer in a new `meeting_host` table: the starter gets a grant in the same batch
as the room, a co-host is another under the same meeting, and a hand-over closes one and opens
another at one instant. A grant is CLOSED and never deleted, because the question a firm asks months
later is who was hosting when something happened, which is a question about an interval.

**Hosting does not pass on its own.** A host whose tunnel drops for ninety seconds has not stopped
hosting, and a room reassigned on a socket loss would hand a client meeting to whoever happened to
be next in the roster. What replaces it is a claim: a key-holder may take a room nobody is running,
refused the moment anybody else holding a grant is in it and audited as a claim rather than as a
hand-over, because nobody gave it.

**Ending a meeting narrows.** It was gated on the key alone, so any Attorney in the firm could close
any meeting they could see the event for, from anywhere, without being in it. It now needs a grant
like every other act here; the ordinary case is unchanged because the starter holds one, and a
key-holder closing an abandoned room claims it first, which leaves a record of exactly that.

The acts split by whether somebody could later ask who did it. Removing a participant, locking the
room and changing who is hosting are routes with audit rows; muting one person, muting the room,
asking somebody to unmute and spotlighting a participant are frames on the signaling socket, because
each is about this moment and an audit row for each would fill a matter's log with the mechanics of a
conversation. A mute closes the target's audio at the routing service rather than asking their
browser nicely — a mute the browser could decline is not a mute — and asking somebody to unmute is a
request their screen answers, never a microphone opened for them.

The room authorizes every host frame from the STORED participant record rather than from the socket's
attachment, so a co-host whose grant was withdrawn ten minutes ago stops on their next frame instead
of when their socket happens to close. No new permission key: the authority is in the grant, and the
key is narrower than it was.

**Scheduling a meeting is recording a calendar event with a medium on it.** The event form — the one
form, for a matter's event, the firm's, or one member's — gains a **Meeting** choice on its Where
tab: None, Video meeting, Audio call. Answering it writes the meeting row at save time through
`createMeeting`, so the entry window offers **Join** from the moment the event exists rather than
from the moment somebody presses Start. There is no second record and no second form: a meeting has
never carried a title, a time or a participant list of its own, and a scheduling feature that minted
its own invitation record would have been minting a second answer to when the meeting is and who is
at it.

**The room opens after the event commits, and that ordering is forced rather than chosen.**
`createMeeting` reads the event through the visibility predicate before it writes, so a meeting
composed into the batch still inserting the event it hangs on would be refused by its own gate. What
makes the second write safe is the property the create path already had: one meeting per event, held
by a partial unique index rather than by anything the caller passes — so the step carries no
idempotency key of its own, a retried save finds the room the first attempt opened and writes
nothing, and the response carries the same identifier on a replay as on the first commit.
`POST /api/v1/matters/{matterId}/events` and `POST /api/v1/firm-events` take
`meeting: { medium: "video" | "audio" } | null` and answer `{ id, meetingId }`; the two `PATCH`
routes take the same field and answer `{ ok: true, meetingId }`.

**An edit keeps the meeting; a cancellation settles it.** Moving an event's day or hour touches
nothing on the meeting, which carries no time of its own — and `meeting` on a correction can only
ADD a room, never take one away, because ending a gathering is an act with its own route and its own
audit row. Cancelling an event ends a **scheduled** meeting in the same batch as the cancel, so a
room nobody entered cannot outlive the setting it was for. Cancelling an event whose meeting is
**live** is refused, `409` with the new `meeting-in-progress` problem type naming the remedy: ending
a live meeting as a side effect of a calendar edit would take a room away from the people in it on
somebody else's click, and cancelling while leaving it running would have the record say the setting
is off while the product says it is happening.

**The colleagues on the event are told, through the notifications subsystem and nothing else.**
`calendar.event.meetingScheduled` is an outbox row in the same atomic batch as the room it announces
— so a batch that rolls back leaves no message, and a message that exists is proof the room was
opened. It carries identifiers, the medium, and the member handles named on the event at the write,
and no title, description, location or participant name. The new `named-members` audience is the
plural of `named-recipient` and resolves on its reasoning: the people to invite are the people who
were on the event when it was recorded, not whoever happens to be on it when the queue drains.
Directory-entity participants get nothing, and the form says so under the choice rather than leaving
a member to discover it from a client who never arrived. Firm events do not raise the invitation
yet: `notification_event.subject_kind` is a SQLite `CHECK` with no `firmEvent` value, and widening
one rebuilds a table `notification_recipient` points at — the firm meeting is scheduled, created and
joinable, and it is the notification alone that waits on that migration.

**Who is already busy is read, never refused.** Where the form lists colleagues, each one's own
calendar is read for the day being booked — the member filter the server already resolves in SQL —
and what it finds at the chosen hour is stated beside their name. It states and never blocks: two
things at once is routinely correct, and a scheduling form that would not let a member book over a
colleague is a form people stop using. What it prints is what the grid paints and never a title: the
federated read declares non-privileged labels by contract, so a matter event reads as its type, and
printing one matter's content on another matter's form would be a disclosure.

**The Meetings page schedules.** It gains the product's one create control, which opens the same
event form with the meeting choice preset to Video meeting, over the same `calendarContext` every
other calendar surface reads — a second assembly of the roster, the type catalog and the firm's
rooms would be a second answer to what the form is offering.

**A meeting now says why a tile is poor, from the browser's own connection.**
`apps/web/src/lib/meetings/client/connection-quality.ts` is a pure module that reads one
`RTCStatsReport` against the reading before it — packets lost, jitter, bytes, frames and the
outbound camera's resolution and simulcast layer, with the round trip taken from the candidate pair
actually carrying the media — and turns the connection's climbing counters into rates over the
interval. `qualityOf` judges three dimensions against stated thresholds and lets the worst one
decide; nothing measured is `unknown`, which is deliberately not `good`.
`client/diagnostics.svelte.ts` samples every five seconds through an injectable timer while a
meeting is live, keeps five minutes of samples and the last sixty wire events, and answers the
quality of the local uplink and of each other participant — traced from a media section back to its
owner through the mapping the subscriptions module already keeps.

**Nothing it holds is recorded.** The samples live in the tab, go when the meeting does, and never
reach the meeting's record, which stays who was in the room and for how long. `report()` assembles
the redacted snapshot a periodic post will one day carry — participant handles, qualities, the
uplink's numbers, the event ring — and a test reads it as text to hold that no session description,
display name or track name is in it. `sendReport` is a no-op until the room has a frame to receive
it on.

**The events come through a seam, not a reference.** Signaling and subscriptions emit through a
small `DiagnosticsSink` that defaults to a no-op, so neither has to know diagnostics exist and both
still run under a test with nothing listening.

**Three room-facing fixes found in review, each with a case that fails without it.** A `subscribe`
and a `close` are now chunked at the protocol's `MAX_SUBSCRIBE_TRACKS` / `MAX_CLOSE_MIDS` the way
`layer` already was — the room refuses an over-large frame whole, so every track it named would have
stayed black. A simulcast layer is recorded as settled only when the room's `layered` names the
media section, with what the plan wants held separately, so a `layer` frame the room's window drops
is asked for again rather than leaving a tile at the wrong size. And a `sync` the room never
answered no longer latches the socket shut for the rest of the meeting: the latch lets go after two
seconds, so a later gap can ask again.

**A roster row is authoritative the moment it arrives.** The presence map is kept beside the roster
and used to be never overwritten by one, so a rejoin delta saying "not speaking" — which is what the
room sends, because it resets deferred presence on a rejoin — was ignored, and a stale speaking mark
held that person at the front of everybody's gallery with their microphone pulled. Rows a frame
actually carried now overwrite the map; rows merely carried forward in a delta's merged list do not.

**Every frame a meeting socket sends now spends from a budget.** The room throttled a `sync`, a
layer change, a hand and a reaction, and nothing else — so `publish`, `subscribe`, `renegotiate`,
`close` and the speaking half of `presence` could each arrive as fast as a browser could write to a
socket. The first four are a billed call to the routing service apiece, presence writes the
participant record, and every refusal emitted an unsampled telemetry event, so the cheapest thing to
send was the most expensive thing to serve. A per-socket token bucket —
`FRAME_BUDGET_PER_SECOND` (20) and `FRAME_BUDGET_BURST` (40) in `@magna-carta/meeting-protocol`,
on the wire because a client has to know the pace it is held to — is now spent in
`dispatchClientFrame` ahead of the parse, so a frame the room will not read costs it no parse
either. Over budget is `refused: rate-limited` with the socket kept open, host frames included.

Underneath it, the four acts that reach the routing service carry per-participant windows on the
existing `syncAt`/`layerAt` pattern (`publishAt`, `subscribeAt`, `renegotiateAt`, `closeAt`),
claimed past every refusal the roster can decide and ahead of the session, so a frame the room was
never going to act on spends nothing. They are refused rather than dropped because the browser is
waiting on an answer to each of them. A request to unmute carries a window kept on the member being
ASKED — two hosts taking turns would otherwise each stay inside a budget of their own — and the
budget's own refusals are sampled into telemetry on the terms the storage budget is, because a flood
recorded frame-by-frame costs more than the flood. The load harness sends six frames per socket
across a whole pass, so its pace is unchanged and its counts are unchanged.

**A room is claimed from inside it.** `claimHosting` asked only whether any OTHER grant-holder had
an open stay, so a member holding `meetings:host` who had never joined could take a live meeting
sixty seconds after the host's tunnel dropped, from outside it — and the record would show a host
nobody in the meeting had met. Nobody hands this grant over, so being in the room, or standing at
its door, is the whole of what makes taking it an act of the meeting rather than of the permission
key. Refused `meeting-not-joined`; the door case is unchanged and the claimer is still admitted by
the same batch, which is how a lobby-on meeting whose host has gone gets a host at all.

**Two smaller ones from the same review.** A reconnect no longer hands back a grant that was
withdrawn while the socket was being opened — an existing participant record keeps its own
`hostRole`, and the routes' `hostingChanged` stays the only writer of truth after the first welcome.
And the platform operator's read into a live room (`routes/meeting-inspect.ts`) is `audited: true`,
writing the operator, the firm and the meeting to the control plane's `auth_audit` before the room
is read.

**The room now relays a chat message as it is said.** `MeetingRoom` gains two RPCs the chat routes
call AFTER their own writes commit, on the `participantLeft` / `end` precedent: `messageSent`
broadcasts a `message` frame carrying the whole record the list route returns, and `messageRedacted`
broadcasts `message-redacted { messageId, redactedAt }`. The route is still the record and stays the
record — the frame is a copy of a row that is already committed, the write never goes through the
socket, and a browser that misses one is caught up by the read. Both frames reach every WELCOMED
socket and never the lobby, which is structural rather than filtered: a waiting socket is never
welcomed and the broadcast skips everything that is not. **The room stores nothing about a
message** — no key, no count — and a room nobody holds a socket on is a no-op.

**And the read converges what the relay cannot.** A poller walks forward on `(sent_at, id)`, and a
redaction moves no row's position in that ordering — so a message already handed to a browser could
be taken back somewhere the poll would never look again, which the frame closes for a socket that is
open and nothing closed for one that reconnected. `GET /api/v1/meetings/{meetingId}/messages` now
carries a second array beside the page, **`redacted: [{ id, redactedAt }]`**: the messages taken back
since the caller's own `since` instant. It is populated only for a caller that says where it read to,
because a first page already carries whatever the record holds.

**One event, `meetings.room.messageRelayed`**, carrying the socket count and which of the two acts it
was. There is no declared field for the message handle and none for its body: what was said is the
transcript's to hold, under the matter's own retention, and the telemetry stream has different
readers.

**`MAX_MEETING_PARTICIPANTS` moves from twelve to three hundred**, and the guarded insert that
actually holds the ceiling is unchanged — it binds the number as data, so the cap moved by moving one
constant. What had to be built is on the two ends of the connection rather than in the routing
service, which forwards whatever it is asked for.

**The room sends what changed.** Above `ROSTER_DELTA_THRESHOLD` (sixteen participants) every
broadcast is a new `roster-delta` frame — `{ joined, left, updated }`, with `left` carrying handles
rather than whole entries — because a full roster to three hundred sockets on every one of three
hundred arrivals is ninety thousand frames of the whole list for three hundred facts. At or below the
threshold the full `roster` frame is still sent, where the list is smaller than the bookkeeping a
difference costs. `welcome` always carries the whole roster, since a socket that has just arrived
holds nothing to apply a difference to, and a new `sync` frame is the way back to the truth for a
client that suspects a gap: the room answers that one socket with one full `roster`. Every path that
changes the roster knows who it changed, so the difference is built at the call site rather than by
comparing two lists — and a frame costs **at most one** `storage.list`, asserted in the room suite
against a three-hundred-participant roster seeded directly into the object.

**Cameras publish three layers and subscribers choose between them.** `subscribe` tracks take an
optional `preferredRid` (`f`, `h`, `q`) and a new `layer` frame changes the choice for tracks that
are already flowing — `PUT tracks/update` upstream, answered with `layered`. It is deliberately not a
second `subscribe`: the media is already arriving, and asking for it again would build a second media
section and renegotiate the connection, so a gallery page turning would cost every tile on the page a
renegotiation. Both fallbacks are `asciibetical` because the layer names sort in size order, so "the
next one along" means "the next size down" without the service being told what the names mean. A
`layer` naming a pair this room is not carrying is `refused` with `unknown-track` through the same
check a `subscribe` answers to — one function, so the two cannot drift.

**Who is talking is relayed, not measured by everybody.** A browser measures its own microphone and
sends `presence { speaking, muted }` on transitions; the room stores both on the participant, relays
a `presence` delta `{ participantId, speaking, muted, at }` to everybody else at most once per second
per participant, and carries the two booleans on `RosterParticipant` so an arriving browser sees who
is talking immediately. A transition inside the window is **dropped rather than deferred** — the
stored state stays current either way, and a presence frame carries the whole of what it is about, so
an unsent frame loses nothing a later one does not restate. Deferring would mean arming this object's
one alarm at sub-second range on a room that otherwise sleeps between a minute-long grace and a
day-long marker.

**The meeting screen pages a large room rather than drawing all of it.** What a browser pulls is now
decided by one pure function over the roster, the presence facts, the pins and the gallery page
(`apps/web/src/lib/meetings/subscription-policy.ts`): at most sixteen cameras, at most one screen
share, at most twenty-four microphones, ordered pinned first, then whoever is sharing, then the most
recent speakers, then roster order. It is a function rather than a method on the client for one
reason — the case that matters is three hundred participants, and three hundred browsers cannot be
stood up in a test.

**The client makes the plan true and nothing more.** `reconcile()` asks for what the plan names and
is not already coming in, closes what the plan no longer names by its media section, and moves a
simulcast layer where the plan changed it; a burst of `roster-delta` frames costs one pass rather
than one pass each, because reconciliation acts on the first change and folds everything inside the
next quarter second into one. Cameras publish three layers (`f`, `h`, `q`) and a subscriber asks for
the full picture on a page of four tiles, half on a page of nine and a quarter beyond — a screen
share still publishes one layer, because a quarter-size document is unreadable. A `roster-delta`
naming somebody this browser has never heard of is a gap, and the answer is one `sync`, not a guess.

**Every voice is played once, apart from the tiles.** The people a browser hears and the people it
shows are different sets, ranked differently on purpose, so playback moved out of the tile into one
component over the pulled streams. Sound coming through the tiles is how a room goes quiet the
moment somebody turns a page.

**Participants open their media sessions at the same time rather than one behind another.**
`sessionFor` in `apps/api-worker/src/meetings/room/room-media.ts` held `blockConcurrencyWhile`
across the call that opens a Cloudflare Realtime session, so every arrival waited for the one before
it and one slow upstream answer stalled every frame in the room. The lock now covers storage only:
a per-stay map of openings in flight makes two frames from one participant share one call while
other participants proceed, the session is written onto the record together with the first publish
or subscribe (a first publish still costs five reads), a failed opening is retried on the next frame
with the same refusal and Error ID, and a browser that reconnects or leaves mid-opening is handled
rather than merged into a record it no longer owns. The load harness gains a per-frame-type count of
storage reads beside its count of lists.

The second wave of Meetings came back from review with seven defects that share one shape: a decision
made from a read that was already stale by the time it was acted on, or a frame nobody was counting.

**A held-back presence transition is now relayed, not dropped.** The room throttles how often one
person's speaking and muted state is relayed, which is what makes a room of three hundred
affordable — but the transition inside the window was discarded outright, and the last transition of
a burst is the one that is still true. A one-word answer left somebody `speaking: true` on every
other screen until they next spoke; a quick mute and unmute left them shown muted for the rest of the
meeting. A suppressed transition now raises `presenceDirty` and arms the room's alarm for the end of
its window, and the alarm relays what is stored. The room's one alarm reconciles three deadlines
where it reconciled two.

**A cancelled event can no longer end a meeting somebody is in.** The cancel read the meeting a round
trip before it committed, and the statement it composed matched `status <> 'ended'` — so a member who
joined in between had the room closed under them by somebody editing a calendar, with the room itself
never told, and a host who ended it in the same window turned the cancel into a server error. The
closing now carries its own precondition (`status = 'scheduled'`, no open stay) and its own guard
label, so the batch rolls back whole and the route answers the 409 it answers from the pre-read —
or, when the host got there first, treats the closing as a no-op and lets the cancellation through.

**Opening a room from the event form asks for `meetings:host`.** The four event mutations ride
`calendar:manage`, which is the key for keeping a diary; a `meeting` field on the form convenes a
gathering, which is a meetings act by another door. Refused with a 403 about that field alone — the
event still records. Cancelling stays on the diary key, because after the fix above a cancellation
can only ever close a room nobody walked into.

**A poller following a chat no longer loses a message to a tie.** `since` was a strict comparison on
an instant, so the second of two messages stamped the same millisecond was gone for that reader
permanently. The continuation is now the `(sent_at, id)` keyset every other list walks: the read
takes `sinceId` beside `since`, and the last page carries a `nextCursor` as a POSITION rather than a
has-more flag, which is what a screen following a live meeting actually needs.

**The words of a chat message are no longer stored in the idempotency record.** That row is replayed
verbatim to whoever retries the key and is not part of the record a redaction reaches, so a retried
send would have served text a member had already taken back. The record's own fields are stored and
the words are not; a first answer is read back off the row.

**Two members taking the same message back together are both answered.** The loser of the race met
the redaction's guard and was handed an Error ID for a message that is, in fact, gone.

**And three costs nobody was counting.** `sync` and `layer` are now throttled per participant, the
way presence is — one whole-roster answer a second and one layer change a quarter second, because a
browser can send either as fast as it can write to a socket and each costs the room a read of every
key it holds or a call to the routing service. A layer change is refused unless it names a media
section the room actually subscribed for that browser, which the roster check it passed never
constrained. A broadcast skips a socket that has been accepted and not yet welcomed, so concurrent
arrivals no longer set every new browser asking for the whole roster at once. And resolving who is
connected walks the sockets once a pass rather than once a participant — ninety thousand attachment
reads per alarm in a full room, before.

The protocol package's frames-have-handlers scan was reading for the frame's name anywhere in a
side's sources, which passes for six frames whose names appear in a type alias or a meeting state; it
now parses the dispatch on each side and compares the set both ways.

**A meeting can hold arrivals at a door.** `meeting.lobby` is `'off' | 'on'`, chosen at Start beside the medium and — unlike the medium — changeable by a host afterwards: a medium is what the people already in the room agreed to, and a lobby is a standing decision about who may come in. One lobby per MEETING and never one per firm, on the owner's ruling of 2026-09-20: a firm runs several meetings at once, so a firm-level door would queue the people arriving at a partner's deposition behind the people arriving at a staff briefing, in front of a host who is in neither.

**A waiting arrival is a stay from the moment it reaches the door.** `meeting_attendance.waiting_from` and `admitted_at` are additive on the existing row rather than a second table: the socket upgrade's ticket is an open stay and a waiter needs a socket, the signaling room's own storage is transient and is deleted when the last socket closes, and the record has to be able to say who waited and was never let in. `joined_at` therefore widens to mean "when this stay began", at the door or in the room, and the read carries all three instants so nothing downstream has to infer anything.

**"In the room" and "has an open stay" stopped being the same sentence, so both are single exported fragments.** `IN_THE_ROOM_PREDICATE` and `WAITING_PREDICATE` in `packages/meetings/src/meeting-statements.ts` are composed by the live count, the capacity guard, the roster and the lobby list, so the four cannot drift into disagreeing about who is present.

**The capacity guard moved from the door to the ADMISSION.** `MAX_MEETING_PARTICIPANTS` counts admitted open stays only, which is what the room actually holds, so the arrival insert cannot be the statement that holds it. `admitAttendanceUnderCapStatement` carries the count in its own `WHERE` and is `guarded()`, and the door gets its own much smaller ceiling — `MAX_MEETING_LOBBY` (100), refused as `meeting-lobby-full`, because a queue is not somewhere a firm should be able to accumulate ten thousand rows and the guest door lands on this path next.

`POST /api/v1/meetings` takes `lobby`; `POST .../join` answers `{ waiting, participantId, displayName, iceServers }` and mints the relay credentials either way — they last an hour, which covers any wait anybody will sit through, and minting at admission would need a second round trip at the exact moment somebody is being let into a meeting that has started without them. Four new routes on `apps/api-worker/src/routes/meeting-lobby.ts`, all of them host acts including the read: `POST/GET /api/v1/meetings/{meetingId}/lobby`, `POST .../lobby/admissions`, `POST .../lobby/denials`. The read is the one in this family that the people inside the room may not make — it is a list of people a host has not decided about yet.

**There is no server-side "admit everyone".** Admit all sends the identifiers the host's panel was showing, because a server-side "all" would admit whoever arrived in the millisecond after the host looked at the list — precisely the person the host did not decide about. The response reports one outcome per identifier (`admitted`, `not-waiting`, `room-full`), so a host admitting five people into two free seats learns which three did not get in.

**On the wire:** a waiting socket is stored under `waiting:<attendanceId>` and never under `participant:`, so `storedParticipants()` — the one read every roster, delta, subscription check and broadcast is built from — cannot include them; a waiter is not omitted from the roster by a filter somebody has to remember. It receives `lobby { position, waiting, at }` instead of a welcome, `admitted { at }` followed by the ordinary welcome, `refused: denied` with a 4000 close, and `ended`. Every other frame from it is refused `not-admitted` with the socket kept open, decided before the routing client is even resolved. Hosts receive `waiting { participants }`, whole, and nobody else does. `room-state` gains `lobby`, and `welcome` gains the lobby list — empty for everybody who is not running the meeting.

**Barred entry is one rule with two labels.** A stay closed `removed` or `denied` bars that member from this meeting while it runs; only the sentence differs (`meeting-removed`, `meeting-not-admitted`). A denial that did not bar would be a button that does nothing.

**Turning the lobby off admits nobody**, and the lock beats the lobby. A setting is not a decision about a named person, and somebody may be waiting precisely because the host intends to deny them; a locked room is shut to everybody, so there is nothing to queue for. A host or co-host of the meeting never waits, and holding `meetings:host` is deliberately not enough — a paralegal with the key walking past the door of a confidential matter discussion is what a host turns the lobby on to prevent.

**The lobby's one deadlock has an exit.** A lobby-on meeting whose host has gone leaves everybody queued for somebody who will never admit them; a key-holder claims the hostless room from inside the lobby, and a grant written for a member whose stay is waiting admits that stay in the same batch — so there is no instant in which somebody is hosting a room they are not in. That admission carries no capacity count, deliberately: refusing the claimer for a full room would restore exactly the deadlock the claim exists to end.

The screen is the web half and is not built: the waiting state, the host's lobby sheet with its badge, and the lobby switch at Start.

The frames a meeting's two ends exchange are now one package — `@magna-carta/meeting-protocol` — imported by the `MeetingRoom` Durable Object and by the browser client alike, with the signaling room and the client each split into the concerns they had grown.

They were declared twice, and had to be: a browser bundle cannot import from a Worker, so the room stated the wire with zod and the client re-stated it by hand. Three slices added frames to both ends by prose agreement, and the drift that produces does not fail a build — it shows up as somebody's tile staying black.

The package holds the schemas, the builders, the refusal vocabulary, the version and the caps, and a fitness function asks four questions of every frame in it: the room has somewhere to put each one a browser may send, a browser sends each of them, the browser has somewhere to put each one the room may send, and the package builds each of them. Its first run found `renegotiated` — the room's acknowledgement of a browser's answer — had no handler in the browser at all, falling through the receive switch's `default` since the day it was added.

Beside it, the room is now an orchestrating Durable Object over six modules (state, roster, presence, media, lifecycle, frames), each taking the object's context explicitly so it can be driven without the runtime; the SFU client and the relay credentials moved under `meetings/sfu/`; and the browser client is the same split (signaling, negotiation, subscriptions, capture, presence) with the media-effects stage seamed in at capture as the identity. Mechanical throughout — every test passed with its assertions unchanged.

**In-meeting chat, kept on the record** — the owner's ruling of 2026-09-20, and it makes `meeting_message`
the meeting subsystem's first stored content. Everything the record held until now was identifiers
and instants, because the audio, the video and the screen share are routed between browsers and
reach no storage here at all. A chat message is a thing somebody said, so it carries what a filed
message carries: it is retained under the matter, it is registered as personal data, and it can be
taken back.

**A message hangs from the STAY, not from the member.** Being in the room is what made it sayable,
so the row names the stay it was said from and the member is resolved through it — which means
somebody whose connection dropped and who dialled back in has each message attributed to the stay it
was actually said in, rather than to a person who was present through a gap they were absent for.
The stay is named BY VALUE (`participant_kind` + `participant_id`, no foreign key) because a
member's stay is a `meeting_attendance` row and an external guest's will be a `meeting_guest_stay`
row: `meeting_attendance.user_id` is NOT NULL, so a foreign key onto it here would have barred every
guest from chat, and relaxing that afterwards is exactly the table rebuild this schema refuses on a
table anything references. `@magna-carta/meetings` writes the literal `'member'`; nothing writes
`'guest'` yet, on the call and text log's reasoning for its own producer column.

**Taking a message back is not a delete.** `redacted_at` and `redacted_by_user_id` blank the body and
keep the row, held from both sides by a CHECK — a redacted row's body is empty and a live row's is
not — so the transcript says a message was there and that somebody removed it. A second removal
answers with the row as it stands rather than moving an instant somebody's record already carries.
The author may take back their own words and a member holding `meetings:host` may take back
anybody's, and both stay possible after the meeting has ended: the words outlive the gathering.

**Three routes** — `POST /api/v1/meetings/{meetingId}/messages` (idempotent, 201),
`GET /api/v1/meetings/{meetingId}/messages` (cursor-paged, oldest first, with `since` for a poller)
and `POST /api/v1/meetings/{meetingId}/messages/{messageId}/redact` — all on `meetings:join`, with
the host question asked inside the redaction handler because the AUTHOR may do it without holding
`meetings:host`. Every one reads the meeting through the same visible-matter gate the rest of the
subsystem composes, so a walled matter's transcript is as absent as its room. The room will later
relay a `message` frame so a message reaches the other browsers as it is said; the route is the
record either way, because a write through the socket would put the firm's record in a Durable
Object's transient storage, which empties when the room does.

**The audit rows carry identifiers, instants and a character COUNT** — never the body, and least of
all on the redaction, where an audit row recording what was removed would be the one place the
removed words survived.

title: Live mode streams the remote browser: frames out, pointer and keyboard in
entry: Live mode in the Safe Website Viewer streams the remote browser instead of returning a screenshot per step, on the owner's ruling that live websites should be streaming. `GET /api/v1/safe-browse/live/stream` upgrades to a WebSocket (same-origin only, through the chokepoint on `tools:safeBrowse`) and hands it to the member's `SafeBrowseSession` object, which holds the socket and a CDP connection to their browser: `Page.startScreencast` JPEG frames go out one in flight at a time, paced by the page's acknowledgements, and pointer, wheel, key and pasted-text input comes back through one shared, bounded protocol (`@magna-carta/safe-browse/live-stream-protocol`). The SSRF guard now covers every document the browser requests for the whole session through CDP's Fetch domain, not one navigation at a time. Popups fold into the visible tab, downloads are denied, the file chooser is intercepted, dialogs are dismissed and reported. A second tab opening Live takes the browser over; idle is now three minutes without input. `POST /api/v1/safe-browse/live/navigate` is retired. The cross-origin upgrade check the meetings socket carried moved to `chokepoint/same-origin-upgrade.ts` so both sockets share it.

title: A direct load of an account page no longer throws
entry:
**A direct load of an account page no longer throws.** The Secure Shell captured Close's destination
with `navigation.from?.url.pathname`, and on a full page load SvelteKit's entry navigation carries a
`from` whose `url` is null — although `NavigationTarget.url` is typed as always a `URL`. Every direct
visit to `/account/*` logged a `TypeError` from `afterNavigate`. Close still went Home, because the
default was already right; the error was the only symptom. The decision now lives in
`apps/web/src/lib/components/secure-shell-return.ts`, which answers an `enter` navigation by its type
before reading `from`, and `apps/web/test/secure-shell-return.test.ts` pins it.

title: A firm can connect its postage account and buy, print, track and void a label, and the gate says when a check never finishes
entry:
**A literal U+FFFD in a `u`-flagged regex hangs the linter, and the file carrying it is silently
un-lintable.** `packages/magnus/src/limits.ts` cut a UTF-8 prefix on a character boundary and stripped
the replacement character the cut can leave behind, writing that character as itself. Oxlint never
returns on it. Not slowly — a seventy-line file, no output, still running after two minutes.

The trigger needs three things at once, and the third is the surprising one: a **raw** U+FFFD (the
escape never triggers, and CJK, Latin-1 and emoji never do either), the `u` flag (`/…/` without it is
fine), and the regex being **consumed** — matched, tested, replaced with, or passed through a const
into one. A regex literal that is assigned and never used parses and lints clean. So this is not the
parser; it is the analysis that runs once a pattern is known to be used. Anchors are irrelevant.

The failure is bad out of proportion to its cause because of where it lands. Nothing reports it —
no error, no timeout, no named file, only a pass that does not finish, which reads as a slow machine.
The whole-repository lint died at the same step five times running and was each time put down to
container uptime. Every scoped lint in between passed, because `pnpm check:scoped` lints the diff and
nothing had touched this file since it landed. The gate of record was unrunnable end to end for six
days while every local signal stayed green.

The character is now written as the escape `\uFFFD`, which is the same character to the regex engine.
The whole-repository lint completes in 31 seconds over 4,278 files; magnus's six test files and
fifty-six tests are unchanged, `cutToByteLength("日本語", 4)` among them, which is the mid-character
cut this strip exists for. It was the only raw U+FFFD in first-party source.

Two things this does NOT do, both deliberate. It does not stop the character coming back — nothing
yet rejects a raw U+FFFD on the way in. And it does not fix the linter, which still hangs on this
input for everybody; the escape is a local workaround for an upstream defect that wants reporting.
What would actually pay is neither: a check that cannot finish should fail loudly and name what it was
reading, so the next one of these costs minutes rather than six days.

**`pnpm gate` gives every step a time budget, and reports a step that exceeds it as `NO END` rather
than as a failure.** A check that never returns is indistinguishable from a slow machine: no error, no
exit code, no file named, only a command that has not come back. That ambiguity cost six days in
September 2026 — one character in one seventy-line file made the `lint` dimension non-terminating, it
was put down to container uptime five separate times, and the gate of record could not be run end to
end the whole while. The character was a one-line fix. Finding it was the entire cost.

A timeout is its own outcome and never folded into `FAILED`, because a dimension that did not finish
reached **no verdict**: the change is unverified rather than bad, and the next move is different. The
message says so, and says what to do — halve the step's inputs, keep the half that hangs — rather than
leaving a reader to conclude their machine is tired.

Budgets are per **step**, not per dimension: the step is what hangs and what can be named, and capping
the dimension would kill honest work in a long one to catch a hang in a short one. They are set well
past the slowest legitimate run, because what they catch does not terminate at all — any finite budget
detects it, and the only way this can do harm is by firing on real work. The test battery's budget is
deliberately the same 90 minutes the test lock already treats as past the slowest run; a test asserts
the two never disagree. `MAGNA_CARTA_GATE_TIMEOUT_SCALE=2` doubles them, `=off` removes them, and a
value it cannot read is an error rather than a quiet fallback to unscaled.

**The teardown is the half that is easy to get wrong.** The gate never holds a handle on the process
doing the work — under `vp` sits the lint or test CLI, and under that the worker threads and esbuild
services — so killing the direct child orphans the rest onto init with the CPU and the caches still in
hand. `spawnSync`'s own `timeout` does precisely that, and it is not theoretical: the morning this was
written, two `vp check` processes from the previous day's killed runs were still resident, and a fresh
lint that should have taken three seconds sat at 0.1% CPU behind them. Steps therefore lead their own
process group and are torn down through the bounded ladder the test guard already proved. A test spawns
a parent that spawns a grandchild and asserts the grandchild is gone; it fails when group-leading is
disabled, so it is testing the thing it claims to.

**The per-firm credential read is built, and the five shipping operations that answered 501 now run.** A connected integration's credential lives in its own per-firm `integration_credential` table under a new `integrations:useConnection` permission, rather than in `firm_secret` under `firm:manageSecrets`. That separation is the whole change: a protected column carries exactly one declaration and that declaration's permission IS the decrypt gate, so while the two shared a column the routes gating on `shipping:manage` would either refuse the member they had just admitted or be fixed by granting that member read access to every secret the firm holds. `firm_secret` keeps its administrator gate untouched. A store may now raise exactly one error, `CredentialAccessForbiddenError`, which the registry turns into a `credential-forbidden` dispatch outcome, so `resolve` keeps its promise never to throw and the route answers 403 naming the grant instead of a 500. The shipping end-to-end test drives the real store rather than a fake; disconnect clears the credential in the same batch as the connection row. Reasoning: `docs/decisions/pending/a-credential-used-on-a-members-behalf-is-not-a-secret-they-may-read.md`.

**Shipping's `matterContext` moves from `none` to `optional`, and the buy flow gained a matter picker.** Until now the wizard never sent a `matterRef`, so every shipment was created with a null matter — and `chargeToCaptureInputs` treats a null matter as a firm-administrative charge with nowhere to disburse and emits nothing. The whole cost-recovery path was built, tested and structurally unable to fire: `packages/costs`, the outbox event, the adapter and the per-line idempotent capture, all correct, and nothing ever gave them a matter.

`optional` rather than `required` because the schema already says so — `shipment.matter_ref` is nullable, and a firm posts plenty of mail to a bank or an insurer with nothing to bill. The picker offers "No matter" as a real answer rather than treating an unfiled shipment as an omission, and the step says what the choice decides.

The consumer's own suite already covered the null-matter case; what had no test was a matter reaching a shipment at all, so the round trip — draft, register row, shipment read — is now asserted, along with the no-matter case beside it.

Unchanged and deliberately so: whether the platform's service fee is billed on to the client. That is already a per-firm setting defaulting to off (`cost.recover_platform_fee.shipping_service_fee`), and postage as a pass-through is always recovered regardless.

**The fourth surface: a shipment opens in a record window over the register.** `/shipping/[id]` survives as its address and redirects into it, the same shape as a directory record's former address and for the same reason — a record opened in place needs no way back. The route is registered in `STANDING_EXEMPTIONS` as declining a back affordance, beside the directory's, because nothing ever renders there.

`RecordWindow` rather than the modal design's `reading` kind, settling **D4**: a shipment has a history and two acts, and one of them voids a bought label, which is destructive and about money. Tracking is asked for rather than fetched on open — the tracking route is a live carrier call, so a reader clicking through ten rows would otherwise be ten calls nobody asked for — and the tab states when it was last asked, because an event list with no timestamp beside it reads as current forever.

The label is fetched through the generated client and opened as an object URL rather than linked to by address: the contract's paths live in the client, and the bytes are behind the session anyway, so a blob the browser already holds beats a second authenticated navigation a pop-up blocker could lose. Which shipment is open comes from the URL rather than a local variable, so the browser's own back button closes the window — the gesture a reader reaches for whether or not the window offers one.

**Three of the four shipping surfaces.** `/shipping` is the register (the product's grid over declared columns in `shipment-columns.ts`, so the reader chooses between the "where is my letter" columns and the "what have we spent" ones); `/shipping/new` is the stepped buy flow; `/settings/shipping` is the postage account, and the first occupant of the `integrations` settings group, which had been declared and empty since the group list was written. The tool's maturity stage moves from `soon` to `alpha`, which is what turns its dead rail row into a link. The shipment window that opens over the register — and the `/shipping/[id]` address that redirects into it — is the remaining surface.

Two seams were corrected mid-build rather than worked around. Writes carry their Idempotency-Key from a `WriteIntent`, because the generated mutation options have no notion of one and a second click is otherwise a second label. And `shipping-api.ts` calls the generated client's own functions rather than spelling `/api/v1/...` paths: `lint:screen-data` holds that count down and it only falls, so a new hand-written transport module would have been the wrong direction even though it compiled. Amounts print through `@magna-carta/money`; nothing divides minor units by a hundred, and a currency the package does not yet register is stated plainly rather than thrown over.

Eight failures the scoped gate never sees, found by the full test battery on the shipping branch.

Four were pinned state that the shipping work deliberately changed, each mechanism working as designed: the Owner/Admin permission list in `me.test.ts` and `auth-provisioning-e2e.test.ts` (which gained `integrations:useConnection`), the back-navigation exemption register — pinned by name precisely so a new exemption cannot be added without a second person reading its reason — and `tool-destinations`, which used shipping as its example of a `soon` tool. Shipping is `alpha` now; the case is about the STAGE, so it follows one of the three tools that still has it.

Two were real mistakes. A bare `window.open(url, "_blank")` in the shipment window bypassed `$lib/navigation/open-beside`, the one helper every new-tab opening goes through so the isolation a second tab gets is decided in one place rather than per caller. And the object-dimension scan read `credentials.put(...)` as a bucket write; it is the integration credential store and reaches no object storage at all, so it carries the sanctioned marker with that as its reason.

Two were one obsolete file: `shipping-unbuilt-credential-seam.test.ts` asserted that connect, rate, purchase, track and refund all refuse with 501 "because the per-firm credential read is still a seam". That read is built, so the file's premise is gone and the file with it.

Not fixed here, and not from this branch: `discovery-routes.test.ts` > "converges rather than duplicating when the same selection runs twice" fails with 409 where it expects 202. Verified against a clean worktree at `origin/main` — identical failure, same assertion — so it is pre-existing and belongs to whoever owns that lane.

**`pnpm run lint:control-characters` now also rejects a raw U+FFFD.** The replacement character is
written `\uFFFD` or not at all.

It rides the existing scan rather than a new one, because the argument is the same one that scan was
already making: a character whose raw form a reader cannot recognise makes source that reads as one
thing and means another. U+FFFD is what a decoder emits for bytes it could **not** read, so a literal
one is indistinguishable from a file that was itself mangled in transit — nobody can tell a deliberate
one from damage. It has a second reason of its own: inside a `u`-flagged regular expression that is
actually used, it hangs the linter with no error and no file named.

The two findings are reported apart. The remedy is identical and the reasoning is not, and a reader
handed the wrong reason for their finding argues with the rule instead of fixing the line.

The scan's self-test gains the new cases, including the code points either side of U+FFFD — a botched
comparison that swallowed the whole range would otherwise pass as a tightened rule. It found a real
offender on its first run: a changelog entry that meant to quote the escape and contained the character
instead, written by someone who had spent that morning on this exact problem. Which is the argument.

Three reads the shipping surfaces need and the subsystem never had: `GET /api/v1/shipments` (the firm's shipments, newest first), `GET /api/v1/shipments/{id}` (one shipment in full), and `GET /api/v1/integrations/shipping/connection` (whether an account is connected, and its health).

The eight routes built in June were all writes or live carrier calls. There was no way to ask what a firm had sent, which is why the register could not be built over them — `selectShipmentStatement` reads one shipment by id and nothing listed them.

The list pages on a keyset over `(created_at, id)` rather than an offset, because a register is read while shipments are being created and an offset skips or repeats rows as the page moves under the reader. It reads one row more than asked for, so whether another page exists comes from the read itself rather than a count that could disagree with it, and a cursor the register did not issue is a 422 rather than a silent first page — which would read as the register having reset.

Two projections are deliberately narrower than the row. A list item carries the recipient's name and not their address, so a list of a firm's mail does not send every recipient's street address to the browser; and the detail says `hasLabel` rather than the storage key the label lives at.

title: Two-factor can be set up from Account · Security, every fixable npm advisory is cleared, and a forked snapshot chain fails its own check
entry:
**`check-snapshots` fails on a forked snapshot chain instead of reporting "nothing to do".** Merging
two branches that each added a per-firm migration leaves two snapshots naming one parent, and
drizzle refuses every `generate` against that lineage — but the pinned drizzle-kit reports the
refusal as an `Error:` line and **exits 0**, so `refresh-snapshot.mjs`, which read the status alone,
took a refused generate for "the schema matches the snapshot". It passed through two such merges on
one branch.

Two layers now. `refresh-snapshot.mjs` looks for the fork itself before generating — any two
snapshots sharing a `prevId` — and names the files and the repair: keep the one already on main,
delete the branch's, refresh, then let `generate` report "No schema changes". And any `Error:` line
drizzle-kit prints is a failure whatever its status, which covers the failures that are not forks.
Both are proven against the real pre-repair commit and a stub that errors at exit 0.

The broader gate was not blind: `tooling/migration-integrity`'s lineage check does catch the fork
(checked against the same commit). What it could not do is stop a person who ran the snapshot check
alone — which the repair message itself told them to re-verify with. That message now names the
generate as the proof.

**Every npm advisory with a fixed release is cleared. The only npm findings left are the two the
`osv-scanner.toml` header already names as out of reach.** Ten advisories had opened since the last
