Outside-month days now carry a wash on the cell rather than only paler text: the small month under the calendar rail draws six fixed weeks, so as many as eleven of its days belong to a neighbouring month, and colour alone left the reader counting columns to find where the month began. A new dev-only gallery at `/developer-console/calendar-day-states` holds every day state on one screen — including the today-and-selected pair, which was previously reachable only on the one day a month it happens, which is why it survived every review. `packages/design-system/test/calendar-day-states.test.ts` pins the scope, the declaration order, and the wash; a jsdom render could not have caught any of it, because the defect lived in the cascade rather than in any one declaration.

title: The quality gate is a command, not a runner: pnpm gate replaces the GitHub Actions workflow
entry:
**The whole-repo quality gate is `pnpm gate`, run on the machine that made the change, and the GitHub
Actions workflow that used to be it is gone.** The account's Actions minutes ran out on 2026-08-05,
again on 2026-09-03, and each time the required `gate` status stopped reporting: every pull request
wedged behind a check that had not run and merged on an administrator override, so the gate failed
closed on the budget and open on the code. `tooling/gate/index.mjs` now runs the same dimensions from
one command — format, governance, the pinned osv-scanner audit over both supply chains, the WASM
artefacts, the type-check, the four contract-drift checks, the type-aware lint over the affected
closure (sinks included, nothing deferred), the Rust and container gates where the change reaches
them, the test-collection floor and the full `pnpm test` — with the workflow's own path classification
deciding which have an input, `--plan` printing the decision, and a summary block the pull-request
template now asks for in place of the label. `gate.yml`, `seed-caches.yml` and `lint:cache-keys` are
deleted; `assemble-docs.yml` no longer dispatches a gate onto its assembly branch;
`lint:test-collection` keeps its collection floor and drops the partition proof that only a sharded
split needed; `lint:lints` reads the fitness-sweep step off the gate's own step list instead of YAML;
`lint:affected-scope` drops its verbatim-invocation check because the gate calls the classifier
directly. One owner step remains and is on the deploy queue: remove `gate` from the `main` ruleset's
required status checks, or GitHub keeps waiting for a check nothing will report.

title: The grip grips, and a sub-menu steps far enough to read as one
entry:
**Two corrections from the owner's pass over the deployed rail.**

The Customize row's **grip was inert**. `onpointerdown` sat on the row's label button and the grip
was its sibling, so the one thing on the row that says "move me" was the one thing that would not.
The press is caught on the row now — grip, glyph, name and badge all start the drag — with the
trailing eye/star/lock let out by `event.target.closest(".mc-sidebar-row-control")` rather than by a
handler on each, so a control added to that row later is covered without anybody remembering to. The
row takes `role="presentation"`: it is a layout box, and the accessible path is the button inside,
which keeps its role, its `aria-roledescription` and the Alt+Arrow it announces.

The **sub-menu step was too shallow to read**. The rail's rows carry an 8px inset of their own, so a
24px indent put a child's glyph barely a glyph's width right of its parent's and a cluster read as a
flat list with a hairline through it. It is 32px now — 20 of margin, which the hairline sits on, and
12 of padding, which keeps the rule off the rows.

title: A race is tested by choosing the interleaving, and five that were not
entry:
A shared harness for concurrency verifiers, `@magna-carta/data-access/interleave`: it runs a competing writer at a named point inside the operation under test — before its nth commit, or once a named read has resolved — so the window between a precondition read and its commit is opened deliberately instead of depending on how two promises happened to interleave. Its `runInterleaved` entry point throws when that point was never reached, so a concurrency test whose competing writer never ran fails instead of quietly passing as a single-caller test. Replaces the per-package copy in the matters tests, and is applied to the fee ledger's freeze, the cost ledger's billing lock, and the retroactive re-rate.

**Browser-side race safety, plus the Durable Object gate and two property verifiers.** `LatestOnly` (`apps/web/src/lib/api/latest-only.ts`) replaces five hand-rolled stale-answer counters; `pnpm run lint:stale-response` fails a sixth and is what found the fifth. `WriteIntent` holds one idempotency key across every attempt at one intent, so a retry after an ambiguous failure replays rather than duplicating — the double-click that `writeKey`'s comment claimed to cover is already handled by any synchronously-set in-flight flag; the comment is corrected in all four modules. `pnpm run lint:durable-object-gates` scans for a Durable Object deciding across a non-storage await and found `BundleBuildCoordinator.requestBundle` HEADing R2 mid-decision, so two requests for one expired bundle each enqueued a full rebuild; fixed with `blockConcurrencyWhile`. Property verifiers for the number draw (correctness absolute at every N; convergence bounded at five by the retry budget, now pinned) and for concurrent ledger postings against the domain's own fitness queries.

**A guarded write refuses its batch instead of being reported on after it commits.** A statement whose WHERE repeats the precondition its caller read is marked `guarded(statement, label)` in its effect; affecting no rows now raises from inside the transaction, so the audit row and outbox message riding the same batch roll back with it. Previously the WHERE clause protected the row and nothing else — `batch()` surfaces no per-statement row count, `commitEffectBatch` returned void, the route answered 200, and the unguarded audit statement recorded the refused edit. Both SQLite adapters enforce it, the Durable Object returns it as a typed `unaffectedGuard` outcome beside `uniqueConstraint`, and `commitEffectBatch` refuses a guarded effect handed to an adapter that has not declared `enforcesGuardedWrites`. The fee and cost ledgers adopt it and map the refusal onto the 409 they already return, so no contract moves. `pnpm run lint:guarded-writes` holds the line.

**All 134 guard-shaped statements triaged; the lint is now a hard gate.** Fifty-one are `guarded()` — discovery's document claim and terminal writes, the custody destruction decisions and status fences, matter hold/release, the deadline and conversation transitions, the trust reconciliation freeze, the folder-move cycle check, the time-entry draft edit and refile. Eighty-nine carry `fitness:unguarded-write` with a stated reason, in seven recurring shapes (at-least-once replay, claim-or-nothing, mirror columns, set-shaped updates, riding a guarded sibling, probes that match nothing in the happy case, partial progress by design). `GuardedWriteRefusedError` maps centrally to a 409 in the telemetry error handler, so every marked write answers sensibly without per-route wiring; the fee and cost ledgers still catch it first for their own refusal. Three chokepoint bypasses were found and closed — two in notifications, one in the conflicts recheck sweep — where `database.batch()` was called directly and would have dropped a guard silently.

title: The editor trusts its WOPI host through the channel that works, and the editor worker reports its failures through the standard pipeline
entry:
**The editor refused its own WOPI host, because the allow-list was being set through a channel the image does not reliably read.**

Once the frame loaded and the WebSocket connected, coolwsd answered "Unauthorized WOPI host": the WOPISrc host `wopi.magna-carta.internal` was not in its allow-list, even though the container's `aliasgroup1` environment variable named exactly that host. That variable is read by coolwsd itself, and only when the image's entrypoint passes `--use-env-vars`; and the mode switch it writes lands on the key `alias_groups[@mode]`, without the `storage.wopi.` prefix that `parseAliases` reads, so a group defined that way sits under the template's default mode `first`, which is the one state parseAliases refuses. The variable was set, the socket was up, and the host was still rejected.

The allow-list is now three `--o:` overrides in `extra_params` — the group's host, its allow flag, and the mode spelled `storage.wopi.alias_groups[@mode]=groups` — which the entrypoint expands onto coolwsd's command line and coolwsd folds into its highest-priority configuration layer. It is the channel every other setting in that file already uses, and the one this deployment proves works: `ssl.enable=false` from the same string is why the editor serves over HTTP behind the edge at all. It reaches coolwsd whether or not a given image version's entrypoint reads environment variables.

Recorded beside it: the editor worker gains its area note (`apps/edit-worker/CLAUDE.md`), the home for the container's operational knowledge — how the allow-list is set, what "Unauthorized WOPI host" means, and the three coolwsd log lines that decide it.

**The editor worker reports its failures through the standard pipeline, and the scrubber recognises a bearer token.**

`magna-carta-edit` had no error boundary. A throw anywhere on the path between the browser and a document's container reached the runtime unhandled: a bare error page, no Error ID, no structured event, and nothing to correlate but a raw exception line in Workers Logs. A WebSocket the container declined was worse — it was silent, because the browser reports every failed handshake as "closed before the connection is established" whatever the server answered, so a container answering 502 and a worker throwing mid-proxy read identically from outside. That is the defect [#633](https://github.com/Phauks/magna-carta/pull/633) fixed, and it took a round trip of guesswork to name; the boundary added here (`apps/edit-worker/src/diagnostics.ts`) would have named it in one log line.

A thrown fault is now a 500 carrying `X-MC-Error-Id` and one `error.captured`; an upgrade the container did not accept is passed through as answered and recorded as one `operation.failed` naming the status — the only record of that status anywhere. The route logged is always the pathname, never the URL: every request the browser makes to this worker carries the WOPI access token as a query parameter, so a quoted URL is a quoted credential. The worker gains the `TELEMETRY` binding the app worker already carries, against the same dataset.

The scrubbing backstop in `@magna-carta/telemetry` now recognises a bearer token in both shapes it travels in — `access_token=…` as written on the wire, and the bare three-segment base64url token an error message carries once something has unpacked the URL. It covered emails, identifiers, cards and phone numbers, and not the one credential this surface puts in every URL.

**A fleet-wide gap, recorded rather than fixed here.** `createWorkersLogger` is used by the app worker and, now, the editor worker. The other five extracted workers — scan, convert, search, OCR, discovery — carry no boundary of this kind either, so golden rule 4 holds for the request path and the WOPI host and not for the Containers fleet. Each wants the same ~60 lines; none is done in this change, because each fronts a different engine whose declining answers mean different things.

title: The list holds one line per file, the scale reaches it, and a modal holds still
entry:
**The file list's geometry, the scale control, and two panels that grew when they were pressed.** Six defects from the owner's round of 2026-09-16, five of them in one screen and one of them in two.

The grid reserved its row-mark slot as an inline box in every first cell. Every surface that composes a first cell out of an icon and a name composes it with flex — which is block-level — so the mark took a line of its own above the content: a band of empty space over every file name, a name reading low in a row whose other cells were still centred in a row a line taller than it should have been, and a list a third taller than the density asked for. The slot is now the cell's own leading padding with the pin painted into it (`data-table.css`), so the cell holds exactly one in-flow child whatever the surface renders there. The reservation is unchanged: a table that can mark a row still reserves the width on every row, so pinning moves nothing.

`DataTable.Grid` takes a `frame` of `card` or `flush`. A card's last row drops its hairline because the card's own bottom rule runs a hairline below it; a flush grid has no card — the file manager's toolbar and counts strip are its frame — so the rule left the last file as the one row in the list with nothing under it. Flush keeps the hairline and fills the frame. It replaces the `rounded-none border-0` incantation four file-manager grids and five money ledgers were each spelling out, which is the right trade: giving up the card changes three things that have to move together.

The scale control now scales the list. It moved one thing in list view — a single flip between two densities, at one threshold in the middle of a ten-step range — so nine of the ten steps changed nothing a reader could see. The grid reads `--mc-table-grid-scale`, a multiplier defaulting to 1, for its text, its row height and the glyphs inside its rows; the file manager publishes it once on the file area, so every view including the inside of an archive takes it. The header band and the counts strip do not scale: they are the frame around the list, and growing them pushes the rows a reader asked to see more of off the screen.

Location leaves the file list's browse columns, where a folder listing already answers "where is this" in the path above it and the tree beside it — it had to ship hidden for exactly that reason. It stands in Search Results and File Analysis, where rows come from different folders. File Type gives up the monospace face and reads in the table's own.

The Change Status panel is two sides: the steps down the left, and the step under discussion — what it does to the record, what it requires, and the field it asks for — down the right. It opens on the step the lifecycle runs toward, so `Choose a step first.` is struck along with the state that produced it.

title: The rail regroups, the tools become top-level abilities, and a page can be a favorite
entry:
**The `/tools` area is gone — the layout, the index, the catalogue projection and the `/tools/<id>`
addresses with it.** `toolRoute()` is `/<id>`, `ToolManifest.route` is deleted (nothing needs to
declare an exception to a prefix that no longer exists), and the five tool routes moved out of
`(app)/tools/` to the top level.

What replaced the index is what was already better at its job. Its two worthwhile parts were the
descriptors and the search, and neither belonged to it: the descriptors are the presentation layer's
and the search net is `toolSearchKeywords()`, both of which the command palette has rendered all
along — over every destination at once, from one keystroke, with no navigation first.

Three registries shrank with it. `tool-catalogue.ts` is deleted; `SUBJECT_GROUP_LABELS` moved to
`navigation/clusters.ts`, where a cluster's name sits beside its glyph and the group it folds inside;
and the eight catalog subject groups became four (`records`, `internet`, `mailing`, `files`) — eight
headings over nine tools is a heading per tool. `toolsByGroup()` sorts a cluster alphabetically by
name, because catalog order is a fact about this repository rather than about the firm.

The shared catalogue framework (`$lib/catalogue`) stays, with Reports as its one consumer. One screen
using a shared shape is not a reason to un-share it.

**`Sidebar.MenuTrigger` + `Sidebar.MenuSub` — the rail's second level**, and a general cluster
mechanism over them (`navigation/clusters.ts`). A destination names a `cluster`, the render tree
folds it there, and a cluster holding a single row is seated as a plain row instead. A cluster is a
fold and never a screen: it has no address, and pressing it opens the rows. The collapsed icon rail
draws every row flat, folds and all, because a rail with no labels has nothing to fold by.

**`navigation/favorites.svelte.ts` — the member's own shortcuts**, as the rail's first group. A
favorite is any pathname plus the title the screen had when it was saved; the glyph is resolved at
render time from the area the address sits under, so nothing has to be kept in step. The gesture
lives in `screen-header.svelte`, which is the one component every screen builds its title from, so it
reaches every page in the product without a screen opting in (`favoritable={false}` opts out).

**`Destination.permission`** — the gate a few destinations carry now that Firm Usage is one of them,
applied in the rail and in the palette alike. **`Sidebar.MenuButton`'s `trailing` snippet** — a grid
column sized to its contents that never shrinks, which is what stopped a long label clipping its own
maturity badge.

**Dragging a sidebar row to reorder it stuttered, and it was three faults stacked.**

The slot size came from the pressed element's own height, but rows are separated by a gap, so every
slot was measured short and travel of two rows read as travel of two-and-a-bit. `Math.round` flipped
the landing index at exactly half a row, which is precisely where a hand rests while it is deciding,
so the whole list reflowed on every tremor. And each `pointermove` wrote state — several times per
frame on a high-rate mouse — reflowing the list between two paintings of it.

`DragReorderController` measures the real PITCH from two rows marked `data-reorder-row`, moves the
landing index only once the pointer is six tenths of a row past the boundary (and four tenths back,
so a boundary is crossed once), and coalesces the offset into one write per animation frame. The rows
also carry a grip now: the grab cursor only answers once the pointer is already on the row, which is
an answer to a question nobody asked.

**The rail regroups on the owner's direction of 2026-09-16.** Six groups, each answering one
question: `favorites` (member data, not registry), `desk`, `work`, `money`, `firm`, `tools`. Home,
Notifications, Tasks, Calendar and Magnus left the old fourteen-row `top` group for My Desk — that
group had "your morning" in the same list as "the firm's evidence", and the split is what says so.

The tool rows are the catalog projected into the Tools group and folded into subject clusters; Firm
Usage left the catalog for a hand-written Firm destination at `/firm-usage`, keeping the
`tools:firmUsage` key through the new `Destination.permission`; the File Workbench went the other way
and is a catalog tool again, in the Files cluster.

title: The calendar stops waiting for every matter the firm has ever opened
entry:
**The calendar no longer waits for every matter the firm has ever opened before it paints.**

`calendar-context.svelte.ts`'s `ready` included `firmMatters`, and `calendar-controller.svelte.ts` refuses to issue the calendar's own reads until `contextReady()`. `FirmMatters` walks the whole matter listing — up to ten pages, and `listEveryMatter` issues two requests per page because the numbered and consultation streams are separate — one page after another, because each needs the previous cursor. So up to twenty requests across ten serial round trips completed before the grid's rows were even requested. Time to first paint scaled with how many matters the firm had ever opened, which is the wrong thing for it to scale with and gets worse every year a firm uses the product.

**What that walk contributes to the grid is a matter NUMBER on a chip** — the one thing on a chip that does not come back with its own row. Everything else a chip says (its kind, its type's name, its hour, its tone) is in the entry's own read.

So `ready` now waits for exactly what a chip cannot be painted without: the event-type catalog and the firm's week start, two parallel reads of fixed size. The matters are still read, in parallel, off the critical path — and `numbered` in `calendar-entries.ts` fills the number in from the controller's existing `visibleEntries` derived when they arrive. **Nothing is read a second time**: the chips re-label from state that is already in the browser.

`detailIsMatterNumber` on `CalendarEntry` is what makes that safe. Without it a later pass cannot tell a detail that WANTED a number from one that was complete as it stood, and would overwrite "Hearing · Department 12" on a matter's own calendar — where every row shares the matter, so the number is the one fact worth saying nowhere. `numbered` returns the same object where nothing changed, so a grid never re-renders a row nothing happened to.

**One consequence had to be handled rather than accepted.** A record form can now open before the matters land, and `MatterPicker`'s empty state said "No matters were read, so there is nothing to file this on." — which would have been false for a second on a large firm. An empty list means two different things and they look identical from inside the picker, so the caller, which holds the read, now says which: `reading` renders "Reading the firm's matters" instead. It defaults false, because a caller handing over a list it already has is never in that state.

Unchanged: the walk itself, its bound, and the Time Sheet's use of it. A firm past the bound still gets a capped list — and a chip whose matter is beyond the cap simply keeps no number, which is what it did before.

title: Every attorney-license register is on one screen, not behind a picker
entry:
**Attorney License Lookup lists all fifty-one registers instead of asking which one you want.** The
state `ChoicePicker` and the single revealed register card are gone; the screen is now
`DataTable.Grid` over `attorneyLicenseRows()`, one row per state, sorted by state name. Every answer
the tool could ever give is a hyperlink and there are only fifty-one of them, so the picker was
hiding fifty links and, with them, the two questions a list answers for nothing: is a state covered,
and which registers are not encrypted.

`attorney-license.ts` keeps its DOM-free split and swaps its API — `licensingStateChoices()` and
`registerForState()` out, `attorneyLicenseRows()` and `attorneyLicenseColumns()` in. The columns are
State (anchored, carrying the link), Code, Register, Connection, and Address hidden by default. The
plain-HTTP caution stops being an `Alert` that appears only for a state already chosen and becomes
the Connection column: a `set` filter over the declared `CONNECTION_STANDINGS`, so narrowing to the
unencrypted two is one gesture and the filter offers both values whatever the rows on screen hold.
Encrypted reads as quiet text; the two that are not carry the warning badge with what it means.

A register opens two ways, per the table's own convention: the row's gesture (`onActivate` →
`openBeside`) and the state's name as a link, which is what buys the browser's new tab and copied
address.

title: Retire the calendar round's active-work note
The calendar round: repeats, a folding rail, one record form, spans that span, and one way to hold a room
entry:
**A form that refuses now points at the field.** The commit's refusal has always been one sentence at the weak end of the bar — "A date is needed." — which says what is wrong and leaves the reader to find what it is about. On a short form that is a glance; on the record form, which asks about a matter, a title, a type, two dates, two times, a zone, a repeat, a location, a court reference, a link, a description and a list of people, it is a hunt (owner, 2026-09-16: "We need better visual language to showcase what is still required when the item cannot be saved").

Every calendar draft's shortfalls are now `Shortfall[]` — a field and a sentence — rather than bare strings (`apps/web/src/lib/calendar/shortfall.ts`). The bar shows the first sentence, unchanged, and the field it names carries the SAME sentence beneath it with `aria-invalid` on the control. One wording, written in the draft and rendered twice, so the bar and the field cannot drift. `shortfallSentences` is what a caller that only wants the bar reads, which is how the existing assertions stayed meaningful rather than being loosened.

**Nothing is marked before a save was asked for.** A form that opens with every unanswered field already marked has told the reader they are wrong for not having typed yet, so the marks appear together the moment a commit is pressed and refused, and clear on a save that lands. `field-refusal.svelte` renders in the design system's own `mc-form-errors`, so a refused field here and a refused field on a superforms-validated form read the same — there is one answer to "what does a refused field look like", not a second invented on the calendar.

The pattern is deliberately not lifted into the design system yet. It is a type, two helpers and three lines of markup over a recipe that already exists; a component would be a second name for it. The second surface that wants it is the moment to move it, and the module says so.

**And the rail answers whose calendar, so the toolbar now answers what kind.** `schedule-narrowing.ts` narrows the window to case settings, deadlines, firm events or dates. It filters what was already read and makes no request, so it reaches exactly as far as the window on screen — which is why it sits beside the window's own navigation rather than beside a search that would imply the whole record. A narrowing is never a read: turning a calendar off in the rail stops a request, turning a kind off does not, and keeping the two apart is what stops a reader thinking they have made the screen cheaper when they have only made it shorter.

An untouched control means EVERY kind, so the first press removes one rather than isolating one — pressing Deadlines means "not deadlines". Turning every kind off shows the whole window rather than an empty grid, because an empty answer to "show me nothing" is technically right and useless, and the one thing a calendar must not do is look empty when it is not.

**A calendar setting can carry a repeat rule.** A new `recurrence_rule` column on `matter_event` and `firm_event` (migration `20260916T000000_event-recurrence`), threaded through both statement modules, both services, the shared `event-shape` asserts, and the create/update/detail contracts on both scopes. The record forms and the entry window edit it through one `recurrence-field.svelte`, over the rule the draft holds.

**One row carries the series; nothing writes an occurrence.** A weekly status conference is one record with a rule on it, not fifty-two records. A row per date would multiply a firm's calendar by the length of its longest series before anybody looked at it, make "move the series" fifty-two writes, and make a correction a reconciliation. The dates are read back from the rule, inside the window somebody asked for — a year at most, which is the platform's own cap — so the work is bounded by what is on screen rather than by how far the rule runs.

**The grammar lives in `@magna-carta/civil-time/recurrence`, which both sides depend on.** The form writes a rule and the calendar service has to refuse one it could not itself have written; the web app does not depend on `@magna-carta/calendar` (a backend package carrying SQL), so a grammar held in either would have been copied into the other, and two readings of "what is a valid rule" disagree the first time one of them is corrected. A rule this platform cannot read back is a series nobody could edit again, so it is refused at the write (`calendar-invalid-recurrence`) rather than stored.

**RFC 5545 is the storage, and it is deliberately read narrowly.** `FREQ`, `INTERVAL`, `BYDAY`, `COUNT`, `UNTIL`, and `BYSETPOS` only in the one spelling this product writes. `parseRecurrence` answers null for anything else — a real answer the surfaces treat as one: the event still reads and still paints, and the form states that the rule was recorded elsewhere rather than half-showing a simplified version that saving would make true. The standard is stored rather than a private shape because a firm exporting its calendar should not find this product's dialect in it.

**Expansion walks civil days, never instants.** A weekly nine o'clock setting is nine o'clock on both sides of a daylight-saving change, which is true only because the walk counts days and the wall clock rides along untouched. A month with no such date — the 31st in February — is skipped rather than pulled back to the 28th: a firm that said the 31st did not mean the end of the month, and inventing a date it did not choose is worse than a month with no occurrence in it. A `COUNT` is counted from the series' own beginning, so occurrences before the window still count against it.

**A continuance does not inherit the series.** Continuing a hearing moves one setting to a new date; carrying the rule across would make the replacement repeat, which nobody asked for.

Nothing here generates deadlines. A recurring event is not a docketing rule, and the no-arithmetic position on deadlines is untouched. The occurrences are not painted on the grid yet — that is the next slice, along with the this-occurrence-or-series question an edit has to ask.

**A three-day trial is on all three days.** It was on the first one, and every other day it covered read as free (owner, 2026-09-16: "multi-day events are not showcasing through multiple days"). Two independent faults, either of which alone was enough to hide it.

**The READ windowed on the start alone.** `civilDateWindowConditions` compares both bounds against a source's sort column, and for an event that is `starts_on` — so a row running the 12th to the 16th was outside every window that did not contain the 12th. `spanningCivilDateWindowConditions` is the shape a spanning row needs: it starts before the window closes AND ends after it opens. `COALESCE(ends_on, starts_on)` makes a one-day row behave exactly as it always did, because its end IS its start, so the predicate collapses to the plain one for almost every row the calendar holds. Applied to the `matterEvent` and `firmEvent` timeline sources and to `selectFirmEventsStatement`. This does not widen what a source may return beyond its window — it returns rows the window always should have held.

**The TIME GRIDS placed by `entry.date === key`.** The month never had the fault, because `placeEntries` walks every day of a span; the week and the day could not use it, because a span on an HOUR axis is not the same entry repeated — it is a different piece of the day on each of its days. `day-segments.ts` cuts it: the first day runs from the start hour to midnight, a day in the middle is the whole column, and the last day runs from midnight to the end hour. Each piece carries its own id, because two pieces of one record are two things to render and a grid keyed on a repeated id drops all but one, and `continuesBefore` / `continuesAfter` are what let a block reaching the top of a column say it began yesterday rather than at midnight.

All-day entries never reach that module: they have no `startMinute`, they belong in the band above the hours, and both time grids already banded and spanned them correctly.

**Correcting where a setting is held now moves the room booking with it.** Booking the room a location names landed at the RECORD on 2026-09-14 and was never done at the CORRECTION — so an event moved from the Boardroom to Conference Room B kept the Boardroom held and never held Conference Room B. After one edit the two room calendars disagreed with the record and with each other, and Location and Book a Room still read as two features (owner, 2026-09-16: "booking a room and location should be consolidated. remove book room feature? or better implement together?").

`reconcileRoomBooking` in `room-location.ts` is the pure answer, and what it does NOT do is the load-bearing half: it releases a booking for a room the location no longer names, books the one it now does, and touches nothing else. A pool car, or a second room somebody held by hand from the Rooms tab, was never named by this field and is not swept away by an edit to it. Where neither the old nor the new location names a room — one courthouse to another — it moves nothing, which is what makes it safe to run on every save rather than only when somebody remembered to.

It runs AFTER the record saved, because the location it reconciles to is the one that landed. A booking it could not move does not unwind the correction: the correction is a real change the reader asked for, so the window states which half did not happen and leaves the record as saved — exactly the rule the record form already keeps.

**The Book a Room verb has left the entry window's action bar.** A second control for the act the Location field performs is the duplication itself. The Rooms tab keeps the control, because a second room is a real thing to hold and nothing else can hold it, and the tab is still where what an event has booked is read and released.

**There is one record form for an event, and its first question is who the event belongs to.** `record-firm-event-dialog.svelte` is deleted; `record-event-dialog.svelte` is the only one.

Two forms meant a reader had to know, before opening anything, whether the thing they were about to record was firm business — and had to close one panel and open the other on finding out they had guessed wrong. They asked nearly the same questions in nearly the same order and drifted anyway (owner, 2026-09-16: "firm events and events should be the exact same").

**Two choices and no third** (owner ruling). Matter writes a `matter_event`; Firm writes a `firm_event`. There is no None, because there is no third table for one to land in, and inventing a third word for the same row would put two records on the calendar that nothing could tell apart afterwards. A personal appointment is a firm event with only the one person on it, which is what the `participants` audience already means.

**What the choice reveals is only what genuinely differs.** Matter reveals the matter picker beside it, on the same line — "a matter" and _which_ matter are one answer given in two presses. Firm reveals the audience (everyone at the firm, or the people listed) and the office, which is a real foreign key on a firm event because it is what says which rooms are nearby; and it hides the court reference, which a firm meeting has no court for. An all-members firm event hides the participant list too, because that list is one the record ignores.

The `Record` menu offers two kinds rather than three. A third item would be a second way to open one panel, and the reader would still have to decide before opening anything — which is the thing that was wrong.

This supersedes the 2026-09-14 arrangement, where leaving the matter picker empty was what made the record a firm event. That was the right shape for the data and the wrong shape for the reader: an absence answered a question nobody had been asked.

**The calendar's rail folds, keeps a month in view, and the screen's name spans it.** Three corrections from the owner's 2026-09-16 pass, and one of them widened a shared component.

**A folder folds.** The disclosure is the folder's NAME — chevron and name are one button at the full width of what is left after the checkbox, the shape the application sidebar's own groups take. It is deliberately not the `Accordion` component: that component's trigger IS its whole header, and this header already holds the three-state checkbox, which cannot be nested inside a button. What folds is the LIST, not the head, so the folder's own switch stays reachable whether it is open or shut and folding hides no calendar a reader could otherwise turn on. A shut folder states how many of its calendars are on, because that count is the one fact its hidden rows were carrying. Held per browser beside the colours, and stored as a DEPARTURE like everything else in `calendar-preferences.svelte.ts`, so a folder shipped later arrives open rather than shut because a stored list predates it.

**`NavigationLayout` gained a spanning `header` and a pinned `navigationFooter`.** Both optional; giving neither leaves the DOM byte-identical for Settings, Magnus, Tools and Reports. Neither is calendar-specific — a title naming the SCREEN belongs over the whole canvas rather than over one column of it, and a rail with a picker under it is the shape of every navigation whose last element must stay in view while its list scrolls. The header sits inside the cancelled canvas inset and puts the gutter back itself; `navigationFooter` moves the scroll region and its reserved gutter off the `<nav>` onto an inner stack, because a pinned footer cannot sit inside the thing that scrolls past it. The landmark stays the `<nav>` either way, so what a screen reader announces does not change.

**The masthead spans and the date controls take its old place.** `CalendarView`'s `header` is now a plain `Snippet` that hands nothing back, and the view switch and window navigation sit at the top of the content column in every arrangement. That replaces the 2026-09-14 ruling, which seated them in the masthead's actions beside New — right while the masthead sat over the grid's own column, and wrong the moment it spanned both. One place instead of two, and no host decides.

`calendar-month-picker.svelte` rides the new footer. It moves the ANCHOR and never the view: somebody reading a week who presses a Thursday means that Thursday's week, so it calls `goToDay` rather than `showDay`, and its week begins on the day the firm chose so its columns and the grid's are the same seven days.

title: An upgrade is handed back, not rebuilt, so the editor gets the socket that carries the document
entry:
**The browser editor loaded its shell and never its document, because the worker in front of it rebuilt the WebSocket upgrade.**

The editing session rides a WebSocket. `allowAppFraming` added the app origins to the Content-Security-Policy on the way out of the container, and it decided whether a response needed that by looking at the policy header first — so a response carrying one was rebuilt with `new Response(body, { status, headers })`. For the upgrade, that is fatal twice over: the runtime refuses to construct a response with status 101 at all, so the handler throws and the handshake dies, and a reconstruction drops the `webSocket` the upgrade carries even where it would not throw. The editor's own page and assets are ordinary HTTP and loaded fine, which is why the shell drew and the document never arrived.

The upgrade is now handed back untouched, and that is checked BEFORE the policy header rather than after. The ordering is the fix: the previous arrangement was correct only while coolwsd never set a security header on its own upgrade, which is an assumption about somebody else's server that a version bump is free to falsify — and the cost of it being wrong is every editing session in the product rather than one stray header.

title: The enforcement surface audits itself: the sweep CI never called, and twelve gates that did not exist
entry:
**New dependency versions wait three days before they can be resolved.** `minimumReleaseAge` in `pnpm-workspace.yaml`. A version published minutes ago is the shape a compromised release arrives in: the attacker publishes, the weekly automated upgrade opens its pull request, and the package is in the tree before the registry has heard the report. Every recent npm compromise of this kind was caught in public within days, by other people, at no cost to us — the cooldown is how that work gets used.

It applies at resolution, so nothing already in the lockfile moves, and it is a floor rather than a wall: a security fix that has to land the day it ships is `pnpm add <package>@<version> --config.minimumReleaseAge=0`, a deliberate act with a reason.

**`pnpm run lint:money-arithmetic` — the money gate.** `@magna-carta/money` has been the one place an amount is added, rounded and split since it was built, and nothing enforced it. The scan looks for three things outside that package: arithmetic on a money-shaped name (`*Minor`, `*_minor`, `*E4`), a hard-coded minor-unit conversion (`/ 100`, which floats a currency value and fixes the exponent at two digits for every currency that will ever register), and a float escape (`toFixed`, `parseFloat`, `Number`) on a money expression. Comments, strings and template text are blanked by a state machine before any rule runs, with offsets preserved, so a reported line is the real line.

It landed against **152 findings across 73 files**, in a debt register that may only shrink. The classification is the useful part:

- **26 are display**, and one signature causes all of them: `formatMoney` takes a major-unit amount, so every surface divides on the way in — the same line copy-pasted into twelve Svelte surfaces. A minor-unit entry point that reads the exponent off the currency retires them mechanically.
- **69 are real arithmetic**, worst first: `document-assembly`'s expression evaluator is a **second money engine** — add, multiply, remainder, divide, an exact-division refusal and its own safe-integer guard, with an oracle test deriving the answer a third way in BigInt. `billing/contingency.ts` derives entitlement and residual in bare numbers. `trust/three-way-proof.ts` derives the whole reconciliation in raw numbers, which is the one place in the product where a cent of drift is a bar-compliance event. Twenty-seven findings are a hand-written `reduce` that is exactly `sum`, and "unpaid" is written out as `totalMinor - appliedMinor` in eight files.
- **The rest are tests and fixtures**, where the test re-computes the formula it is testing — and twelve conversions that look like display and are not: five feed a data-table column accessor whose totals row then **sums the divided floats**, so the conversion became arithmetic one layer down where the call site cannot see it.

**One finding the scan cannot see, recorded in `invariants.md` instead:** `billing/fitness.ts` computes the contingency entitlement in SQL as a float divide with hand-rolled half-up rounding, while `contingency.ts` computes it in TypeScript. Two answers that can round apart — and the fitness check meant to catch a divergence is one of the two.

**`lint:secrets`, `lint:containers` and `lint:native-builds` — the supply-chain family this repository had none of.**

There was **no secret scan of any kind**, on a platform that holds firm credentials, the root key that wraps every per-firm data key, and privileged client documents. A credential is compromised the moment it is pushed and stays compromised in the object database after the commit that removes it, so the only cheap moment to catch one is before it lands. Eleven rules over 7,111 tracked files, in-house for the same reason the license gate is: a hosted scanner is handed, by construction, exactly the bytes it is looking for. Findings never print the value. The tree is clean — and `apps/api-worker/.dev.vars` passes because the scan **decodes** its values and finds the placeholder inside, not because its path is allowlisted, so the file stays under the rule forever. The scan does not skip its own directory either: every pattern is written so its own source cannot satisfy it.

The container gate holds the Dockerfile properties that matter for images built here — an explicit tag, never `latest`; no `ADD` from a URL; no disabled certificate verification, in ten spellings; no credential baked into a layer. Two properties are ratchets rather than bans, with the measurement that made them so: **no** base image is digest-pinned (five distinct bases, each recorded with its reason, keyed by image so a new container reusing a known base needs no edit), and **1 of 11** runtime images drops privileges. What it leaves to review is stated rather than implied — whether a pinned hash is the right hash, and the sandbox properties that live in the Containers configuration rather than in a Dockerfile.

The native-build gate gives golden rule 14 a mechanism instead of a habit, across four surfaces: the `onlyBuiltDependencies` grants, the build scripts pnpm has blocked, the platform binaries in the lockfile, and every `-sys`/`cc`/`cmake`/`bindgen` crate in fifteen `Cargo.lock` files. It does not fail on what is already here — a gate that does gets switched off — it fails on what is **new**, and prints everything that is not memory-safe on every run with its language and its consumer. It refuses to pass when it reads nothing: a consent gate that silently scans an empty set is the one failure mode it must not have.

What that surfacing shows is worth reading: clamd is the one consented C engine, and beside it sit `onig_sys` (a C regex engine, in the OCR container's job path), `ort-sys` and `vectorscan-rs-sys` — sandboxed, but with no ruling on record the way clamd has. `openssl-sys` reaches three workspaces only through `ureq`'s `native-tls` default feature, which is a default rather than a decision. And `sharp` — libvips, the one C library the npm graph installs — is not ours: it arrives under miniflare, and so under wrangler and the Workers test pool every worker package carries.

**`pnpm run lint:hard-rules` — the linter rules this repository can enforce now, in a pass that can fail.** The Oxlint ruleset is almost entirely advisory by design (`suspicious` and `perf` warn, `correctness` keeps its inherited severity), and the consequence nobody chose is that the gate's most expensive job — a whole-repo type-aware pass measured at about forty-five minutes — can fail on exactly one rule, `oxc/no-barrel-file`. Everything else it finds is a warning in a list of roughly eight hundred.

Three rules move out of that list and into a pass that fails:

- **`import/no-cycle`**, held at 36 and falling only. Nothing in the repository looked for a cycle before this: the project-reference check verifies that references exist, not that they form a directed acyclic graph, and a bundler resolves a cycle silently by handing one side a half-initialised module. The thirty-six sit in twenty-nine files, concentrated in the worker's route graph and the web app's calendar and directory screens.
- **`vitest/no-focused-tests`** and **`vitest/no-disabled-tests`**, held at zero, which is free because the tree is already clean. A stray `.only` is green, silent, and takes the rest of its file's coverage with it — and it can ride a whole review here, because the battery is asked for rather than automatic.

Six seconds over about 3,900 files, no type-aware pass, so it sits in the always-on governance tier. It **proves its own invocation**: every rule is run against a fixture written to trip it before its count on the repository is believed, because a wrapper whose plugin flag was renamed reports a clean tree forever.

The `import` and `vitest` plugins deliberately stay out of the shared ruleset. Enabling a plugin switches on everything it carries at its category severity, which adds warnings to the forty-five-minute pass and moves nothing from advisory to enforced.

**Rust gets a lint floor, and `unsafe` is forbidden while the door is still shut.** `vp run rust-check` has always been `cargo fmt --check && cargo clippy -- -D warnings && cargo test`, on clippy's default lint set. There was no `[workspace.lints]` table anywhere, so nothing enforced the property the platform actually rests on: that Rust reading an opposing party's PDF, an unknown sender's `.msg` or a custodian's 7z stays memory-safe and does not abort on bytes it was handed.

`unsafe_code = "forbid"` rather than `deny`, so no crate, module or expression can take it back — the only way to reintroduce unsafe Rust is to edit the table, in a diff somebody reads. The crates workspace is unsafe-free today, which is exactly what makes it free to impose and exactly why now is the moment. `non_ascii_idents` goes the same way: a homoglyph pair reads as one word to a reviewer and is two symbols to the compiler. Two container workspaces do carry `unsafe` (the LibreOfficeKit error callback; two memory maps in the scan spool) and each omits the rule in its own manifest with the site named, so the gap is recorded rather than excused.

Panic-class clippy lints — `unwrap_used`, `panic`, `panic_in_result_fn`, `todo`, `unimplemented`, `mem_forget`, `dbg_macro` — are denied where the tree is already clean of them, and `print_stdout`/`print_stderr`/`exit` in the crates workspace, where every site was an evaluation harness. Those three are deliberately absent from the container tables: a container's binary **is** the process, so a startup diagnostic on stderr and a non-zero exit on a fatal boot failure are correct rather than a smell.

**Every level was measured first,** because the gate runs `-D warnings` and there is no level here that means "tell me later". What stayed out is recorded with its count: `clippy::indexing_slicing` at **361 sites**, clean in exactly one member so there is nothing to scope it to — the headline burn-down — and `clippy::arithmetic_side_effects` at **416**, whose real home is the byte-offset arithmetic derived from file headers. `clippy::expect_used` is four library sites away from landing.

Six source lines changed rather than watering a rule down: without them, `recovery-core` and `pdf-core` — the two crates the unwrap rule matters most for — would each have needed a crate-wide allow and lost it entirely. Test code is exempted through `clippy.toml` instead of attributes scattered through the suites.

Also fixed while in the area: the gate's cargo cache listed eight container workspaces and there are nine. `containers/discovery` rebuilt its whole dependency graph from cold on every run, silently, and that list is hand-written so nothing said so.

**Svelte accessibility findings fail the build.** `svelte-check` exits zero on warnings, and every accessibility rule the Svelte compiler carries reports as a warning — so for as long as both `check` scripts ran bare, nothing enforced them. The Storybook axe pass is real, but it sits in the test battery, which a pull request has to ask for.

Both packages now run `svelte-check --threshold warning`. The adoption cost was one suppression: the design system was already at zero warnings over 3,145 files and the SPA at one over 3,949. That one was `state_referenced_locally` in the matter's activity register, where the variant is a literal at both call sites and reading it once is correct — so it took the documented `svelte-ignore` the catalogue screen already uses, with the reason written beside it, rather than a change in behaviour.

**`pnpm run lint:lints` — the gate over the gates.** Thirty-eight governance lints, and until now nothing asked whether any of them could still fail. The argument is `lint-control-characters.mjs`'s own, one level up: a check that never fires is indistinguishable from a clean tree, and that hazard applies hardest to the checks nothing checks.

Four rules, all deriving their subject from the `lint:*` scripts in the root `package.json` rather than a roster:

- **Every lint can fail** — it has a fixture test beside it, or a self-test that runs on every invocation. Twenty-five can today; thirteen are carried on a register in `tooling/lint-lints/rules.mjs` that may only shrink, and deleting a name is the whole procedure for tightening it. A name on the register that has since gained a test is reported too, so the debt cannot quietly outlive its payment.
- **Every lint is documented** — named somewhere a reader can find it, so a failing run leads somewhere. All thirty-eight are.
- **Every lint command the conventions cite exists** — the reverse direction, which nothing checked after a rename.
- **The fitness sweep's environment variable is pinned** — the gate's `MAGNA_CARTA_FITNESS_SCOPES` held identical to `FITNESS_SCOPES_ENV`, the way `lint:cache-keys` holds the two cache-key expressions identical. A rename on one side would leave the sweep on its default scope, covering half of what the step claims, and say nothing.

It states its own limits: it proves the machinery is present and wired, not that a fixture is meaningful, and one stale sentence naming a lint counts as documented.

**The license gate reads the Rust supply chain, and its SPDX classifier is now a parser.** `pnpm run lint:licenses` read `pnpm licenses list` and nothing else, so ten Cargo lockfiles — the crates workspace plus every container, 866 crate versions — were vulnerability-scanned by osv-scanner for a year and license-checked by nobody, against a deny-by-default policy whose whole reason is that AGPL or SSPL would force a source offer.

The policy is now one thing in `tooling/license-policy/`, read by two gates: the npm one, unchanged in behaviour, and `pnpm run lint:cargo-licenses`, which discovers every `Cargo.toml` workspace rather than listing them, so a new container joins the gate the day it is added. It runs in the gate's `rust` job, where the toolchain and a warm cargo cache make it a second or two; on the slim runner it would have paid a rustup install and a 163 MB cold fetch for an answer only a lockfile can change.

**Extracting it surfaced a real hole.** The old classifier stripped parentheses and split on the operators, so `(MIT OR GPL-3.0) AND AGPL-3.0` came out **allowed** — it found a permissive disjunct and never saw that the AGPL conjunct binds the whole work. The replacement tokenises and parses the expression at its real precedence (`OR` loosest, then `AND`, then `WITH`), which also stops it denying three forms the Rust tree genuinely carries: `Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception`, the legacy `MIT/Apache-2.0` slash form, and lowercase identifiers. Anything it cannot parse is denied.

The Rust tree is clean: no AGPL, no SSPL, no GPL, no crate without a license. Six permissive identifiers the npm-era list had never met were added with their reasoning — `Unicode-3.0`, `CDLA-Permissive-2.0`, `BSL-1.0`, `MIT-0`, `NCSA`, `zlib-acknowledgement` — and they now bind both ecosystems.

**The repo-wide fitness sweep reaches CI.** `tooling/check-scoped/repo-wide.mjs` has always defined the repo-wide set as two halves — the `lint:*` scripts, and the Vitest checks that self-register with an `@repo-wide-fitness` directive — and the gate's `governance` job called only the first. The second half is where the encryption chokepoint scan (`no-plaintext-escape`), the telemetry console ban, the design system's off-token and `bits-ui` boundary scans, the PII registry coverage check and the schema conformance checks live; twenty-six members in all.

They were not unenforced, exactly: each runs under its own package's Vitest project. But the test battery is asked for on a pull request rather than automatic — the `run-tests` label, always on a queued merge — so on an unlabelled pull request nothing looked at them and the first report came from the merge queue, which is the most expensive place to learn that a protected-field read escaped its chokepoint.

The sweep is now a step of its own in `governance`, both scopes, unconditional: about four seconds for twenty-six read-only scans in one un-isolated process. Deciding whether to run it would cost more than running it. `lint:lints` holds the workflow's `MAGNA_CARTA_FITNESS_SCOPES` value identical to `FITNESS_SCOPES_ENV` in the module, so a rename cannot quietly halve what the sweep covers.

The derivation was never the problem and is worth restating: neither half has a roster, and adding a check to either is a line in `package.json` or a comment in the check's own header. A derived set still has to be called, and this one was half-called for as long as it existed.

**`lint:doc-links`, `lint:changelog-coverage` and `lint:active-work` — two gaps `documentation.md` named itself, and one rule held up by memory.**

**Dead links.** 1,734 relative links across 1,051 documents; every one now has to resolve, and an anchored link has to name a heading that exists (GitHub's real slug rules — punctuation deleted rather than replaced, emphasis unwrapped, duplicate numbering). External links stay out of scope: a gate must not depend on the network. Building it was mostly learning what a false positive looks like here — a decision fragment's prose is authored at three depths, because the same body lives at `docs/decisions/pending/`, at `docs/decisions/NNNN-`, and rendered into `docs/Decision-Log.md`, so a link is sound if it resolves from any home the prose actually has. That removed 65 of the first pass's 102 findings.

**The 37 that were real say something worth acting on.** Thirty are in numbered decision records and all have one cause: a link that was correct in the pending fragment climbs one directory too many when the assembler numbers the file, so `../conventions/invariants.md` lands at the repository root. The repair belongs in the assembler as a link rewrite on promotion, not in thirty files. Three more are in `CHANGELOG.md` and genuinely dead — `apps/worker` became `apps/api-worker`, `ci.yml` became `gate.yml`, a fixture baseline is gone. One spec points at a design that was deleted rather than moved. One was unambiguous and is fixed in place; the rest are a register that only shrinks.

**Changelog coverage.** A change touching `apps/`, `packages/`, `crates/` or `containers/` source brings a fragment. The carve-outs are a positive list, not a negative one, so a new directory is silent by default and must be added deliberately. Tests are deliberately in scope — they are the largest class of small change, and carving them out would leave the floor holding almost nothing. `tooling/` and `.github/` are out: the custom of changelogging them is worth keeping, but a gate firing on every lint tweak gets routed around in a week. **The gate holds the floor; the custom holds the ceiling.** Manifests and lockfiles are named in the source as the real remaining hole rather than hidden. On `main` and in the merge queue it stands down and prints why, rather than passing silently.

The escape hatch is `changelog.d/exemptions/<slug>.md` with a `reason:` in words — in the diff, where a reviewer reads the claim beside the change it excuses, and counted only as part of that change.

**The stream registry.** Every note under `docs/active-work/` has to sit at a branch-shaped path and carry the four keys the registry reads, with a status from the documented set. `vp run worktrees` only warned, and the root `CLAUDE.md` compensated by telling people to remember to run it. One note declared a status the registry does not document, which is exactly the shape that makes a note invisible.

**`pnpm run lint:area-notes` and `pnpm run lint:catalog-coverage` — two rules the repository states and nothing held.**

Every code area is supposed to carry its own `CLAUDE.md` for local rules and the invariants that bind there. 55 of 85 workspace packages do. The 30 that do not are now a register that only shrinks, and it includes `packages/data-access` — the home of the firm-scoping golden rule — and `apps/web`. The gate also checks what the existing notes do, and they all pass: each opens with a title naming its own area (so a note copied from next door is caught) and says what the area is before anything else. What it deliberately does not require is the template's full section list: `## Local conventions` appears in 9 notes of 55, so requiring it would mint 46 headings reading "None."

The design system's coverage rule — catalog entry, behaviour test, visual regression — is held at the **component family**, the directory the package's `exports` map names one subpath each, not the file. The per-file version was measured first: 229 of 235 `.svelte` files under `src/lib` are exported, because a compound component exports its parts by design, and only 56 are imported by a story directly. That opens a 173-entry register of parts the family's own story already photographs — a form to fill in rather than a debt to pay. At family level the number is 79 of 83, and the four missing entries are the register: `field-label`, `folder-glyph`, `record-reference`, `service-marks`.

Coverage counts the story an entry is **about**, never a component that merely renders inside someone else's story: rendered-somewhere is enough for a screenshot to move and not enough for a person to find the component, and not finding it is how the second implementation gets built. The behaviour leg is clean from either side (87 of 91 stories carry `storybook/test` assertions). The visual-regression leg is not per-component checkable and is not pretended to be — `catalog.spec.ts` holds no component list at all, deriving its matrix from the built catalog at run time, so the gate asserts that derivation instead and leg three follows from leg one.

title: A policy that could never have named the app refused every editor frame, and nothing said a document was opening
entry:
**An office document could not open in the browser editor, and the screen never said it was trying.**

Two defects, found on one real open, that compounded into a blank frame.

coolwsd composes its `frame-ancestors` from the two origins it knows — its own, and the WOPI host it was configured with — which is correct for the ordinary integration, where the WOPI host is also the page doing the framing. It is wrong for this topology by construction: the WOPI host here is `wopi.magna-carta.internal`, a non-routable name the container reaches only through outbound interception, and the page doing the framing is the firm's own app origin, which coolwsd is never told and cannot derive. The policy it sent named the editor origin and an internal host, the browser found the app origin missing, and refused. No document could have opened through this path.

The app origins are now added to that policy by the worker in front of the container (`apps/edit-worker/src/embedding-policy.ts`), not by coolwsd's own configuration. `net.frame_ancestors` is obsolete and ignored from CODE 24.12.4.1 onward, and its replacement `net.content_security_policy` is truncated at the first space when passed through the image's `extra_params` — which a list of origins always contains. Beyond that, who may embed the editor is a fact about this deployment's app domain rather than about the editor image, and nothing in this repository can exercise the container's configuration, where the rewrite is a pure function with tests beside it. The sources coolwsd put there are kept, because the editor frames pages of its own. Widening costs no tenancy: the access token names one version of one file in one firm and is re-verified on every callback, so the framing origin was never the gate.

The waiting state ended at the wrong moment. Opening is two waits — the launch call, which answers at once, and the editor container, which starts on first address — and the screen fell quiet between them, exactly when the long wait began. It now runs until the editor itself reports the document on screen, through the frame message protocol, and states it with Retry when the editor stays silent past a budget that allows for a cold start. For the editor to speak at all the host must tell it where: the launch now carries the origin that asked for it in the signed token, and `CheckFileInfo` returns it as `PostMessageOrigin` — carried rather than configured, because per-firm subdomains mean there is no one app origin a deployment could name.

**A developer-console gallery of three candidate headers for the document editor, for the owner to choose between.**

The direction is to take the app's rail and top bar off the editor screen and replace both with one band that carries what each of them was carrying. Which band that is, is not obvious: the rail and the bar between them hold a way home, a way back to the matter's files, search, the build chip, notifications, the Time Sheet handle, two transfer registers and the profile menu, and a header thin enough to be worth the change cannot hold all of it.

So the three candidates are rendered rather than described, at `/developer-console/document-editor-headers`, from the shipping components and over a stand-in document canvas at a fixed frame height — the band's cost in canvas is the visible difference between them. **Continuous chrome** seats the document in the app's own ink bar and gives nothing up. **Document masthead** keeps the header the document already has and folds what survives of the app into its action row. **Path bar** makes the path itself the header, every rung from the docket to the document on one row. Each renders four states — editing, saving, read-only, and an editor that has lost its connection — each measured, so a band that grows when the document turns read-only is a number rather than a squint.

Nothing about the editor changed. The real edit route, the app shell and `ScreenHeader` are untouched, and the only file outside the new directory is the fixtures registry that makes the surface findable. Two limits are stated on the page itself rather than left to be discovered: the save readout is driven by a prop, because the editor does not report its save state to the host at all yet, so what is under review is a shape and not behaviour; and the product's one back control has no register for an ink band, which is a design-system gap the first variant would have to close.

title: Repair the .dev.vars guard, and retire the transfer-register stream's note
entry:
**The `.dev.vars` placeholder guard was red on `main`, and with it the standing merge bar.**

`apps/api-worker/test/dev-vars.test.ts` pins the tracked `.dev.vars` byte-for-byte against a literal in the test. The two had disagreed since the header comment in `.dev.vars` was rewritten without the literal being updated in the same commit — which that test's own docstring asks for. Every key and value matched; the difference was one sentence of prose about which firm-provisioning adapter runs locally. So `pnpm test` failed for every branch, on a file most branches never touch, and the failure said nothing about the branch that ran it.

The literal now carries the file's current header word for word, and the test says out loud why the prose is pinned at all: a byte-for-byte guard cannot tell a rewritten explanation from an inserted credential, so it refuses both and a person decides which it was. That is the guard working, not a flaw in it — the cost is exactly this, and it is the right trade for a file whose whole job is to never hold a real secret.

title: The transfer registers become one shape, the tools leave their sub-page, and the sidebar folds
entry:
**The build panel's copy control is the copy symbol, and its repository link is GitHub's mark.**

Copy carried Lucide `clipboard-copy` — a clipboard with an arrow into it, which is the picture of PASTE — so the one control a person reaches for during an incident was drawn as its opposite. It is Lucide `copy`, the two-sheets glyph, everywhere else in the industry.

The repository link carried `git-branch`, which names a git concept rather than the service on the other side of the link. Lucide has no GitHub mark and could not: brand marks are not iconography. So the mark follows the brand-asset track instead of the icon rule — `@magna-carta/design-system/service-marks` is a new, deliberately quarantined home for a third party's own published mark, self-hosted and unaltered, taken in `currentColor` as the monochrome use GitHub's guidance provides for, with a row in `docs/conventions/third-party-trademarks.md` recording whose it is and on what terms. `lint:one-ui`'s hand-drawn-glyph rule learns the second exemption beside the brand mark's, with the reasoning on it.

**Counsel sign-off is outstanding** on that register row (policy 5, the ADR-0090 legal track) — the mark ships behind that flag rather than ahead of it.

**Every tool is a row in the left sidebar, and a tool opens onto the whole canvas.**

The Tools area was a two-sided screen: a navigation column of every tool on the left, the chosen tool beside it. The owner's direction of 2026-09-16 ends it for two reasons, and the second decided it. The tools are not a family — a postage rate, a WHOIS record, a county recorder's site and a bandwidth measurement share a sentence in the catalog and nothing else, so a column listing the other eight beside the one you opened is a column of things you are not doing. And it cost every tool the width of that column permanently, which the surfaces that will carry the most use — mailing and postage first, where a label, a rate table and an address want to sit side by side — can least afford.

`navigation/tool-sidebar.ts` projects the tool catalog into sidebar rows, so nothing about a tool is restated: the catalog still owns identity, subject group and the permission that gates it, the presentation layer the descriptor, stage and glyph, and `toolRoute()` the address. The registry gains a `tools` group headed by the index row (now "All Tools", and `exact` so it no longer lights up under every tool beneath it); `/tools/<id>` is unchanged, because that address is the catalog's and breaking saved links to shorten a URL is not a trade. `/tools/+layout.svelte` is a passthrough. A tool's rail row is `pinned`: what a member sees there is what they are permitted to run, and a star beside it would be a second, inert answer to a question access control has settled — which is also why Customize mode leaves the group out.

Sidebar groups fold, in the same pass: Workspace, Money, Firm and Tools each carry `Sidebar.GroupTrigger` — the heading itself, with a chevron and the full width as its target — and the fold is remembered per browser. The collapsed icon rail never folds, because a rail with no visible heading has nothing to fold by and nothing to press to bring the rows back. Folding is the sidebar's alone: every destination in a folded group is still one Ctrl+K away.

**Uploads and Downloads are one frame rendered twice**, and the upload half now has a memory.

`$lib/transfers/` is the shared half: `transfer-tray.svelte` is the top-bar frame both registers render through — the tooltip and the popover sharing one button, the attention dot that takes the maturity dot's corner while it is raised, the titled panel, the way to the full surface — and `transfers.ts` holds the words neither is allowed its own copy of. The Upload control had never named itself on hover, which made the one control in that band that starts a transfer the one a reader could not identify; it does now, because the frame does it for both. The tables stay apart on purpose, and the module's header says why: a download is a stored document any format can be taken from, an upload is a file on a matter.

`upload-history.svelte.ts` is the new half. A transfer still dies with its tab — the files are the browser's own handles — but what a finished batch DID is a list of names, a matter, a folder and the file each one became, none of which needs a handle. That record is kept per browser (the shared persisted-preference primitive, bounded at 50 batches and 250 files each), so the Uploads screen answers "where is the thing I sent yesterday" instead of "nothing uploading", and every file that landed carries a Download straight to its own route on the matter. Nothing privileged is kept: no bytes, no digests.

Both empty states are two words now — "No Uploads", "No Downloads" — which is the standing empty-state ruling (`docs/conventions/design-corrections.md`) reaching two screens that predated it with a paragraph each about the mechanism.

title: The schema row answers for the lineage, not for two head tags
entry:
**The Database section reported `Schema: Up to date` for a firm database that was refusing every request because of its ledger.**

The schema check compared two head tags and nothing else. The runner rejects a ledger holding a tag it cannot place _before_ it applies anything, so the tags already there are untouched and the ledger can sit exactly at the expected head — which read as health. The panel then showed `Firm database: Not answering` and `Schema: Up to date` together, two rows describing one subsystem contradicting each other, with the reassuring one wrong. That is the reading the section exists to prevent, and it shipped in the section's own worst case.

`migrationState()` was already returning the fault; `readSchemaState` read the object and used two fields of it. The schema state gains `refused`, read from the fault first, and the row says `Not applied` with the count and head the database does have — the refusal's own sentence stays on the firm database row rather than being copied into a second place free to drift from it.

**Two signals the firm database computes and sends were being dropped in the same function.** `outOfOrderArrivals` names migrations that reached this database behind its own ledger head, which has no other symptom — everything is applied, but this database ran the pair in an order a newly provisioned firm will not, and for dependent migrations those orders do not reach the same schema. `restorePoint` names the instant the object can be restored to and the migrations it sits in front of, which is the question a database broken by a migration raises next. Both now appear as lineage notes beside the row, on the same "said only when there is something to say" rule as the provisioning backlog, and both travel in the copyable report — a pasted report is how a diagnosis reaches anyone who can act on it.

The restore point's Cloudflare bookmark is deliberately not on the wire: restoring is an operator's act with dashboard access, and the opaque handle does nothing for the member reading the panel.

title: A stream note retires with the merge that lands it
entry:
**`vp run retire-note <branch> --with-merge` retires a stream note in the pull request that lands the work, instead of a second merge afterwards.**

`main` is production, so a follow-up pull request whose only content is deleting one file is a production deploy to delete one file. Four of the last ten merges were exactly that.

The landing check that made the second merge necessary is the right guard for the workflow it was written for — retiring on `main` after the fact, where the deletion takes effect the moment it merges, so removing a note early really does erase the one collision warning other worktrees get. It is the wrong question for a deletion committed on the branch: that reaches `main` when the branch does and not a moment sooner, so `main` keeps the note for as long as the pull request is open. And it cannot be satisfied anyway, because a branch has not landed while the pull request landing it is still open. What `--with-merge` checks instead is that HEAD is on the branch whose note it is, which is what makes "the deletion travels with the merge" true rather than asserted.

It does the paperwork only — clearing every `status.d/` pointer at the note, re-rendering `STATUS.md`/`STATUS.json`, deleting the note. Removing a worktree and deleting a branch cannot happen from inside that branch, so that half stays a later local `vp run retire-note <branch>` and keeps its landing check. The command no longer refuses that pass: a workspace with no note left is exactly what a landed `--with-merge` leaves behind, and it used to be told there was nothing to retire by the retirement that had worked.

The guard moved out of the runner into `retirementRefusal` in `tooling/retire-note/dependents.mjs`, on the same pure-rules / impure-runner split the migration gates keep, so the decisions now have tests — they had none before.

title: The calendar's rail is the one two-sided screen, its week and day answer time, and a setting can repeat
entry:
**A conference room is offered under the office it is in, and named by it where the firm has more than one.** The owner's shape: "A location may be Office 1, Room 1; Office 2, Room 2. Where offices are distinct addresses, but rooms are not."

The location picker listed every room under one "Rooms" heading, so a firm with three offices saw three "Conference Room 1"s and no way to tell them apart. It now draws a group per office, in the order the offices come, with rooms belonging to none under a final heading; an office with no bookable rooms is left out rather than drawn as an empty heading. What the field WRITES is the room's own name while the firm has one office, and "Main Office — Conference Room 1" once there is more than one.

Both spellings match back. A location recorded before this, or typed from memory, is a bare name and still finds its room and books it. A bare name that two offices both answer to matches **neither**: booking one of two rooms a person did not choose between is worse than booking none.

The grouping and the written name live in `room-location.ts` beside the matcher, because the module that writes a location is the one that reads it back to book the room — two answers to "what is this room called" would drift within a round.

`firm_resource` still has a firm-wide unique index on `name`, so two offices genuinely cannot hold rooms of the same name yet. That index, meeting links as bookable places with a concurrency ceiling, participants by tag, recurrence and a separate end zone are all specified in `docs/specs/2026-09-15-calendar-places-people-and-recurrence-design.md` and unbuilt.

**The foundation for a setting that repeats, and for saying what one would collide with.** The owner: "start recurrence… check conflicts."

**The rule and its expansion** (`apps/web/src/lib/calendar/recurrence.ts`). A repeating setting is ONE row with a rule, expanded across the window a read asks for — the alternative multiplies a firm's calendar by the length of its longest series before anybody looks at it, and turns "move the series" into fifty-two writes. The stored form is an RFC 5545 `RRULE`, because it is what every calendar product reads and writes and a firm exporting its calendar should not find this product's dialect in it. What the form offers is narrower than the standard allows, and `parseRecurrence` returns null for a rule it cannot present rather than half-showing one it would silently rewrite.

Two decisions worth stating because they are the ones a reader would argue about. **The expansion walks civil days, never instants** — so a weekly nine o'clock setting is nine o'clock on both sides of a daylight-saving change, where an instant-based walk would move half a firm's Tuesdays by an hour twice a year. And **a month with no such date is skipped, not pulled back**: a firm that said the 31st did not mean the end of the month, and February gets no occurrence rather than an invented one on the 28th.

**The schema** gains `recurrence_rule`, `recurrence_parent_id` and `recurrence_occurrence_on` on both event tables. An exception — one occurrence moved, renamed or called off — is a REAL event that knows which date of which series it replaces, so every read that already understands an event understands it, including the rule that a cancelled setting stays visible and struck. An exclusion list would have needed a second mechanism to say "and this one was cancelled".
