The added columns carry their own CHECK rather than the table being rebuilt, on the mechanism the task-rungs migration proved against real durable-object storage: a rebuild drops the table it replaces, and `matter_event` is a parent three tables reference.

**What a setting would collide with** (`schedule-conflicts.ts`). Recurrence is why it exists: one hearing at a bad hour is visible in the day schedule the form already draws, but a weekly setting for a year is fifty-two chances to collide and nobody scrolls a year to check. A double booking is never refused, only stated — two things at once is not something the platform knows to be wrong. Civil days and wall clocks, never instants; back-to-back is not a collision; a vacated hearing competes for nobody's Tuesday; and a series reports DAYS rather than collisions, because "three of the twelve dates" is the question a person asks.

**Not yet wired.** No service reads or writes a rule, no route carries one, no form offers one, and no read expands one — so nothing in the product repeats yet. The arithmetic and the storage are in place and asserted; the service, the contract and the form are the next slice.

Also withdrawn in the same round, before anything was built: the separate zone for a setting's END. The owner: "only have one field for time zone. always the same for start and stop." The forms already ask once, and no `end_time_zone` column exists or should.

**An event held in one of the firm's rooms now appears on that room's calendar.** The owner: "when i set an event to be in a location, it did not populate in to that locations calendar" — and, separately, "location and booking a room seem duplicative of what should be the same functionality". They are the same defect seen from two sides.

The Location field stores TEXT, deliberately: a courthouse, a department number and opposing counsel's office are none of them records this product holds, so the picker offers the firm's offices and rooms and keeps anything else that is typed. A room's own calendar, meanwhile, reads BOOKINGS. Nothing joined the two, so choosing "Boardroom" from the picker wrote the string "Boardroom" and the Boardroom's calendar stayed empty — while Book a Room, on the event's Rooms tab, did the real thing. Two ways to say one thing, and only one of them true.

`room-location.ts` matches the location text back to an active resource of the `room` kind, and the two record forms book it. The column stays free text — nothing dangles when a room is renamed, and a place the firm has no record of is still just typed — so what changed is only that where the text does name a room the firm has, the booking is made.

The match is exact on a trimmed, case-folded name, which is what the picker actually writes. Anything looser books a room off a guess: "Boardroom 2" is not "Boardroom", and a courthouse whose name happens to contain a room's name has not booked that room.

The booking is a second write, because it needs the event's id. So it can fail after the event has landed, and the form says so rather than closing on a room somebody believes is held: the event is never unwound, and the notice names the room and points at the Rooms tab.

Still open from the same round: the wider location model the owner described — offices carrying addresses with rooms inside them, and Zoom or Google Meet as bookable places with their own concurrency ceilings — which is a spec rather than a patch.

**Who is at a setting can be changed after it is recorded.** The owner: "in the modal it doesn't allow me to set new participants."

The entry window's Edit deliberately never re-sent participants — "a window that did not touch who is at a setting cannot change it" — which was a safety property while the window had no participant control, and became the reason there was no way to add somebody to a setting already recorded. The contract never had this limit: supplying participants replaces the list, omitting them leaves it alone.

The Participants tab now renders the same `ParticipantPicker` the record forms use while the window is editing, over the draft's own list, and the change rides the window's own Save rather than landing as you type — the pane says so above the field.

The invariant survives in the half that mattered. The window SAYS whether the pane was touched rather than the projection comparing lists: a draft's participants carry local keys and display names the server never sent, so any comparison would report a change on every open. A correction that never opens the tab still sends no participants at all. An edited list is sent whole, **empty included** — taking the last person off a setting is a real correction, and dropping an empty list would make it the one edit that silently does nothing.

Adding people by role, by matter, or by a firm-defined tag — the rest of the owner's ask — needs storage and a settings surface, and is specified in `docs/specs/2026-09-15-calendar-places-people-and-recurrence-design.md`.

**Four corrections on the calendar surface, from the owner's 2026-09-14 round.**

**Whose calendar left the toolbar.** The Mine / Everyone pair and the colleague dropdown beside them are gone: "remove colleague, mine, everyone buttons since that is covered by leftside bar functionality". They were a second mechanism for a question the rail already answers a calendar at a time — a reader wanting their own day turns their own calendar on. The address's `scope=` key is still read, so a link somebody was handed still opens where it says, and `chooseScope` survives for the host whose scope changes under it.

**The event type is a typeahead, sorted.** It was a plain select over a catalog that runs to dozens of hearing, conference and deposition kinds, in whatever order the read handed them over. It is now the same combobox the zone field and the member pickers are, and the list is alphabetical.

**The record form's timing fields are two identical lines and one zone control.** Three defects in one region, all reported: the zone sat in a 40-pixel slot, so its list of continents and cities opened into a field too narrow to read; the Ends line stated the same zone as a *sentence* where Starts offered a dropdown; and both lines were built from fitted controls, so an empty time field and a filled one were different widths and the two lines drifted out of alignment the moment somebody answered one of them. Starts and Ends are now the design system's `FieldRow` — equal tracks, which cannot do that — and the zone is its own full-width control beneath the two moments it qualifies. `TimeZonePicker` lost its `compact` mode with the slot that needed it; the list still reads by code and name both, because CST is three different zones.

Still open from the same round, and larger than a screen: a separate zone for the end of a setting (one `time_zone` column today), events reaching the calendars of their location and their participants, participants editable in the entry window and addable by tag, one location model over offices, rooms, places in town and meeting links, and recurrence.

**The firm calendar's rail of calendars moved onto `NavigationLayout`**, the design system's one shape for a screen with a navigational column on the left and content on the right.

It had drawn its own: a `<nav>` at `w-3xs` with a scroll region and a gutter of its own beside the grid — a sixth width and a sixth scroll treatment for the shape the owner ruled on 2026-09-11 is one component. Settings, Magnus, Tools and Reports were already on it; the calendar was the screen nobody had come back to.

`CalendarView` renders the layout where the rail stands — a firm-side scope with calendars to list — and keeps the plain full-height stack everywhere else, so a matter's calendar, a room's grid, Home's card and the record forms' day schedule are untouched. The screen's masthead is handed DOWN as a `header` snippet and drawn at the top of the content column: the layout takes the full height under the top bar and cancels the work canvas inset, so a masthead above the tag would sit above the whole canvas. The Magnus workspace already does this, for the same reason.

The rail's rows stay checkbox rows rather than becoming `NavigationLayout.Row`. The shared row renders its own anchor or button and lights the one the reader is standing on; every row here is a switch with a control already inside it, which cannot be nested in another. What the two columns share is the frame and the indent stagger — the folder heading its group at the column's cap-line, its calendars one step past it — which is precisely what "the layout imposes no structure on what the navigation holds" is for. A calendar's name now wraps rather than truncating, as every other navigation column's does.

**The entry window's Relate button says Link, and names what it links.** The owner: "Not sure what the relate button means."

One act had two names. The tab is called Links, the model calls them links (`entry-links.ts`, `createEventLink`, `RelatedLink`), and the button alone said Relate — so the word a reader met first was the one the rest of the product never used, and a bare verb with no object told them nothing about what it would act on.

It reads **Link Settings** on a matter's setting and **Link Events** on a firm event, matching the action bar's own verb-and-noun grammar (Continue Setting, Book a Room, Cancel Event). The dialog is "Link Two Settings" / "Link Two Events", its commit reads Link, its refusal says which choice is missing, and the tab's own heading and empty line read Linked rather than Related.

Nothing about the records or the contract changed: a link is the same link, written the same way.

**The week and the day are time grids, and a setting is a block from its start to its end.** The owner's 2026-09-14 round on the calendar, in four parts.

**An entry stretches.** "Start and end time need to properly show themselves on the calendar, not just on the start, should stretch accordingly." The day grid used to park a chip in the row of the hour a thing began in and say how long it ran in words, on the argument that a two-pixel sliver for a fifteen-minute call is unreadable. The sliver is now answered by a MINIMUM block rather than by refusing to stretch: a block is never shorter than one that can hold a line of text, and an entry that outgrows its true duration says so by overlapping what follows it, which is the truth about a day with a fifteen-minute call in it. An entry with no end — half of what a firm calendar paints, since the federated read declares a time of day and no duration — gets that minimum rather than a guessed hour.

**The week is one.** "Week view should be taller since we can include time." It was seven civil-day cells in the month's grammar, each holding a list of chips, which answers none of what a week is read for: who is where on Wednesday afternoon, what Thursday morning still has room for. It is now the day's shape with seven columns — hours down the leading edge, a day across the top — with a band above the hours where what is true of a whole day sits, and where a multi-day run is still drawn across its days and marked at each end.

**What runs at the same time is the reader's call.** "There should be a setting to allow for overlapping events on one calendar, or showing them next to each other." Side by side divides the column between the things in a cluster, so nothing hides; overlapping steps them over one another, so each block keeps more of its width. The choice is held per browser beside the calendar colours, and offered on the toolbar only where there is an hour axis to be concurrent on — the month and the agenda are lists of days, and a list has no concurrency to present.

**The view switch and the window sit beside New.** "Move month view controls to next to the new event button." `CalendarView` hands its action row UP to the host's `header` snippet, so the screen seats the controls on the masthead's own line; a host that ignores the snippet still gets the row above the grid.

Two pure modules carry the arithmetic, asserted without a browser: `time-placement.ts` (the span an entry occupies, the clusters it falls in, the share of the column it takes) and `time-blocks.ts` (which cell it renders in, and the style that draws it there). The block lives in the DOM cell of the hour it begins in — where a screen reader reading the table row by row should meet it — and is positioned out of that cell over one hour step, so the grids stay real tables.

title: A renamed migration tag is reconciled, not a database recreated
entry:
**A firm database that applied a migration under its pre-rename id now reconciles itself on wake, instead of refusing to start.**

The 2026-09-15 re-stamp of `20260911T000000_office-email-address-lines-and-firm-brand-images` and `20260914T090000_event-conference-link` was taken on the premise that no database could have applied either id — no firm onboarded, both per-firm pools empty and recreatable. A firm database had applied the first of them. From the moment the rename deployed it refused to wake, because the applied-ledger records the TAG and that id named a migration the lineage no longer contained. Every route that needs firm data answered with the build panel's `Firm database: Not answering`, and the runner's sentence for it — `deploy mismatch (code older than schema)` — pointed at the opposite of the truth: the deployment was newer than the rename, not older.

`packages/database/src/re-stamped-migrations.ts` records a rename as data, and `runPendingMigrations` consults it before it refuses. A re-stamp moves the id and not the SQL, so the schema the database has is already the schema the new id names, and the ledger row is rewritten through the `supersedeAppliedMigrations` seam the baseline collapse already uses — one transaction, no schema SQL, resumable if it is interrupted part way.

Three shapes are still refused, each in its own words: a ledger holding both ids of one re-stamp, which the rewrite cannot express and should not guess at; a deployment older than the rename, which is told to roll forward rather than sent hunting for a schema change nobody made; and a genuinely unknown tag, which is the deploy mismatch the original sentence was written for.

The immutability gate reads the registry directly, the way it already reads `LEGACY_BASELINES`, so a rename is recorded once and the gate and the runner cannot drift into disagreeing about which tags a database may still be holding. `tooling/migration-immutability/allowed-changes.mts` is correspondingly narrowed: it is for a tag going away with nothing standing in for it, and the 2026-09-15 rename is now its worked example of an entry that should not be written there — an allowance asserts nothing needs repairing, which is a claim about the fleet that is easy to believe and hard to check.

title: Retire the migration-hardening stream's active-work note
Retire the file-workbench stream's active-work note
The journal decides the lineage, and a migration that has deployed is history
entry:
**A migration lineage now defends its own apply order, its own bundle and its own history — three tools, all running on every pull request.** Apply order is by TAG, and a branch cut before another one lands keeps its earlier timestamp while drizzle renumbers its `idx` to the end. A fresh database then applies it before the migration it was written on top of, building its schema in an order no existing firm ever used. Nothing about the merge looks wrong afterwards and every firm that already exists keeps working, which is why two of them reached `main` in September 2026.

**The worker's tag-to-SQL bundle is generated from the journal** (`tooling/migration-bundles`). `apps/api-worker/src/per-firm-migrations.ts` and its control-plane sibling were a hand-kept map of forty lines that had to gain an entry every time the journal did, and it lost one three times — a merge resolves the journal cleanly, because its entries are adjacent lines, and drops one branch's import in the same conflict. `migrationsFromJournal` throws on that, but only inside a Durable Object on wake, so it surfaced as a twenty-second route timeout rather than as a missing import. `pnpm run lint:migration-bundles` now fails when a module and its journal disagree. The emitted text is a fixed point of the repo formatter, so the generator and `vp check --fix` cannot undo each other.

**A conflicted `_journal.json` is resolved by a command** (`node tooling/resolve-journal/index.mjs`), not by hand. What decides the answer is not "ours" and "theirs" — which of those is the branch depends on which direction the merge ran — it is `main`, which is production here, so a tag on `main` has deployed and is immutable and a tag that is not can still move for free. Trunk entries keep their tags and their order; everything else is appended in the order it was integrated and re-stamped above the head, its `.sql` renamed to match and the bundles regenerated. It reads git's conflict stages during a merge and the journal on disk otherwise, so it repairs an inversion that already landed as readily as it resolves a live one. `timestamp-latest-migration.mjs` shares its tag arithmetic: two implementations of "a tag that sorts above the head" is the shape of the bug both exist to prevent.

**A migration that has deployed can no longer be changed** (`pnpm run lint:migration-immutability`). The applied-ledger in every database records the tag, not the SQL behind it, so an edit to a deployed migration is never seen by the databases that already ran it, and a rename leaves them holding a tag the runner cannot recognise — which blocks every later migration for the life of that database. Neither is fixed by deploying again. The check measures from where the branch left `main`, not from `main`'s tip, so a migration that landed while the branch was open is not mistaken for one the branch deleted. Deliberate exceptions are recorded with the reason no database could have applied them; a baseline collapse is not one, because `LEGACY_BASELINES` reconciles those at runtime and the gate reads that list rather than asking for the same fact twice.

title: Retire the workspace-search stream's active-work note
The File Workbench is a place in the sidebar, not a tool inside Tools
entry:
**The ten standalone file-utility rows leave the tool catalogue.** File Converter, Metadata Scrubber, File Hash & Integrity, File Decryption, File Type Verifier, AI-Text Detection, File Repair, OCR, Email Inspector and Malware Scan were each a File Workbench capability tab under another name, so the catalogue promised ten screens that do not exist and never would. The `files` subject group is now the workbench alone, and `test/catalog.test.ts` fails on a new row there.

Two things had to outlive the rows, neither enforced by a type. Their permissions: every capability module is gated on the key its sibling manifest declared, and `grantedPermissions()` built its set from `CATALOG`, so the deletion would have emptied the tab strip silently — `tool-permissions.ts` names all nine explicitly now, held to the capability registry by a test. And their search vocabulary, which moved onto the workbench's synonyms in `tool-presentation.ts`. The access-control registry entries and `role_permission` seeds are untouched and still used.

**Two guards on the migration lineage, both closing gaps the audit found rather than suspected.**

`tooling/migration-integrity/` now diffs each lineage against the schema it claims to build: it applies the whole chain to node:sqlite and compares the result with `src/declared-tables.ts`, naming the table or column that disagrees. The package's own notes already prescribed exactly this comparison as something to do BY HAND when a divergence was suspected, which means it ran after the damage rather than before it.

The gap was wide open rather than theoretical. Hand-written migrations are the normal case here, so most of the lineage is authored beside the schema rather than derived from it — and the check that looks like it would catch a divergence does not, because `refresh-snapshot` re-derives the snapshot FROM the TypeScript, leaving snapshot and schema agreeing with each other and disagreeing with every database. Measured on the way in: 201 declared tables against 206 live, the five extras being the FTS5 virtual table and its shadow tables, and zero column drift. The discipline was holding; nothing was enforcing it. The FTS5 extras are enumerated by exact name in `UNDECLARED_BY_DESIGN`, not matched by prefix, so the next undeclared table is a finding rather than something the rule swallows.

`runPendingMigrations` now reports **out-of-order arrivals** — a pending migration whose tag sorts before a tag the database has already applied. Apply order is tag order, but the chain grows from parallel branches, and two merging can seat a migration behind one that already shipped: a database that woke in between applies the pair in the order it met them, while one provisioned afterwards applies them in tag order. Independent migrations reach the same schema either way; ones that touch the same objects do not, and that divergence is otherwise silent, because the ledger is a set of tags with nothing recording which arrived late.

It reports rather than refuses: the migration is genuinely pending and genuinely needed, and stranding a database over a usually-harmless condition would be worse. The report carries `outOfOrderTags` and `ledgerHead`, measured before the batch lands; a firm database holds it for its diagnostic read and the control-plane pass emits one `migration.arrivedOutOfOrder` event per tag.

The two migrations that prompted this were checked: they are independent, and both orders produce byte-identical schemas.

**Five user guides caught up with where the file tools actually are.** Four told the reader to open the Tools sidebar and pick a standalone tool that is now a File Workbench tab (Hash, Metadata, Unlock), and the workbench's own guide still routed through Tools rather than the sidebar. A guide that sends somebody to a screen that no longer exists is worse than no guide.

`attorney-license-lookup.md` is new, and carries the two things the screen cannot say at length: why Magna Carta sends you to the state's register rather than answering for you (standing is exactly the fact that changes after you look, so a stale copy would be worse than none), and what an unencrypted register means for the name you are about to type into it.

**Attorney License Lookup has a screen** — the fourth tool page, and the first of the five the catalogue still owed. Pick a state, get that state's official attorney register, open it beside your work. It reads nothing back and stores nothing: the tool is a link generator (`backing: library`), and the registers are the authority, so a copy of one of their answers held here and going stale would be worse than no answer — a suspension is exactly the fact that changes after you look.

The branching lives in `$lib/tools/attorney-license/attorney-license.ts`, DOM-free and tested, the same split the WHOIS tool keeps. The state list comes from `@magna-carta/government-links`, whose licensing registry gained the state's own `name`: it was previously recoverable only by taking a suffix off the site's display label, and the alternative was a second hand-written list of the fifty states. The screen imports the `/licensing` entry point rather than `/registry`, so rendering a state picker does not ship fifty states of county assessor tables to the browser.

Two of the fifty-one registers are served over plain HTTP (Rhode Island's judiciary search and Washington's). That is a fact about US government portals rather than a transcription error, and the screen says so before the link instead of after it: on such a page the lawyer being asked about, and the answer, are readable by anything on the path. The link is still offered, because the register is the authority whatever it is served over.

The catalogue entry's description changed with it. It said the tool would "check a lawyer's bar standing and discipline history", which promised an answer this platform never sees.

**The File Workbench becomes a sidebar destination in the Firm group, at `/file-workbench`, starred by default.** The tool catalogue had it inverted: of its twenty manifests, eleven are the `files` subject group, and ten of those eleven map one-to-one onto the workbench's own capability tabs, so the listing offered eleven doors into one room with the room filed alphabetically between two of its own doors. Firm rather than Workspace on a scope test rather than an importance one, since nothing brought here is filed, versioned, or remembered.

The route moves off `/tools/` because destination currency is a path-prefix match, so a workbench still under `/tools/` would light up the Tools row alongside its own. The manifest row stays, since contextual surfaces query the catalogue by context tag, so `ToolManifest` gains an optional `route` and `toolRoute()` becomes the one derivation every link-builder goes through. The palette's tool provider skips a promoted tool, which the destination registry already lists. `FILE_WORKBENCH_BACK` is deleted and the screen header drops its `back="tools"`: a top-level destination has no way back.

**Three fitness tests were red on `main` and are green again.** All three came from the merge window's own commits, and none of them was a defect in the code they guard.

`schema-conformance` did not know `magnus_conversation_attachment`. It is a composite-key join table, which the test allows as a documented exception; the exception was never registered.

`schema-name-sync` did not know the alias `m`. The upload-attribution work joined `member` to resolve an uploader's display name and never added the table, its alias, its columns or the `uploaded_by_name` projection to the allow-list.

`generated-migrations` asserted that lexical tag order matches the journal's dense `idx` order, and two migrations from parallel branches merged out of that order. The assertion was wrong rather than the migrations: apply order IS tag order (`src/migration.ts` sorts the journal by tag, never by `idx`), chosen precisely so parallel branches merge without a shared counter, and `idx` is read only by the authoring scripts to find the entry drizzle just appended — the highest one whatever the tags say. It now asserts what the journal actually needs: a gapless `0..n-1` range, and a total tag order.

Renaming a migration to satisfy the old assertion would have been the real damage, which is worth recording. The applied ledger is keyed by TAG, and a tag a database has applied but the code no longer knows is a hard refusal on wake ("deploy mismatch") — so renaming either of those two would have taken down every firm that had already applied it.

Two of the three were invisible locally: the fitness sweep only runs when `packages/database` changes, so a branch that touches neither never sees them.

title: Only the file list scrolls, a file is filed by dragging it, and the status seal is a pillbox again
entry:
**The file manager's rename field opens with the cursor in it, and does not move the row.** Three
defects with one field between them. The list's in-place field was never focused and never
selected, so making a folder put a name field on screen that nobody was typing in — the reader had
to find it, click it and click away again before it looked right; `beginRename` now focuses it and
selects the stem, the same gesture `file-inspector.svelte` already made for the panel's own field.
The field also pushed its row taller, which is arithmetic rather than styling: `.mc-table-cell` in a
grid is `block-size: var(--mc-control-sm)` with `padding-block: var(--mc-space-4)`, and `.mc-input-sm`
asks for that same full control height, so it could not fit in the box it was in. It gives up the
control's own minimum and takes the cell's content box. A refusal still grows the row, because the
reason has to be readable.

**A table's row mark keeps its space whether or not the row is marked.** `data-table-grid.svelte`
drew the pin in the first cell only while the row was pinned, so pinning shifted that cell's text by
the glyph and its gap — the reader saw the list twitch at the moment they acted on it. Any grid
given a `rowMark` now keeps the slot on every row; a grid that never marks a row reserves nothing.
The condition is the capability, not the current state, because a condition that changes when the
first row is pinned reflows at exactly the moment the reflow would be seen.

**One rename path, two places to say no.** `renameTo` answers with the sentence that refuses rather
than posting it itself, so the list's field sends a refusal to the screen's failure band while the
details panel keeps its own field open with the reason beneath it. The two halves of that seam were
built in parallel and disagreed about the answer's type; the panel's half is the one that was right.

**A file or a folder is filed by being dragged, everywhere the matter's file manager shows one.** A row in the list, a tile in the icon grid and a folder row in the rail are sources; a folder row in the rail, a folder row or tile in the list, and every crumb in the path including home are destinations — a crumb is how something comes back OUT of a folder, since every ancestor of where the reader is standing is already on the strip in front of them. Dragging one row of a selection carries the whole selection and the drag image says how many; dragging a row outside the selection carries that row alone.

It is ONE component rather than four copies of the same five handlers. `packages/design-system/src/lib/components/item-drag/` owns the payload, which destination is under the pointer, the mark drawn on it, the refusal and the clearing on `dragend` however the gesture ended; the surface owns only what may be dragged, what may accept it and what a drop means. The folder rail's own handlers were the first copy and were rewritten onto it rather than left as the fifth.

An upload and a move are now the same event on the same square inch, and the PAYLOAD tells them apart rather than the target: a transfer carrying `Files` came from the desktop, one carrying our own vendor media type came from a row on the page. Our own type is excluded from the file question explicitly rather than by omission, because a browser is free to add `Files` to a transfer we also wrote to.

A refusal is the pointer, not a banner — a destination that will not take the drop never prevents the event's default, so the cursor says no before the reader lets go. Four refusals, in `apps/web/src/lib/file-manager/file-drag.ts` with a test each: a destination that is not a folder, a folder into itself, a folder into its own descendant (the one that actually loses documents, by detaching the branch from the matter), and anything into the folder it already sits in. A mixed selection is not refused for its worst member — the rows that can land, land.

The drop runs `moveRows`, the path the clipboard's paste already took, so it is the same write, the same refusal and the same step on the undo stack. Cut and Paste are untouched and are not a fallback: every drag has a keyboard equivalent that already worked, which is why no second "move to folder" picker was added.

**The file manager's details panel renames what it is showing, in the panel.** Pressing the name called `onRename` back into `file-manager.svelte`, which set `manager.renamingKey` — so the field opened on the ROW, which may be scrolled out of view or in another folder. The reader pressed a name and watched a selection happen somewhere else. The panel now hosts the field itself: `file-inspector.svelte` keeps its own editing state, seeds the draft through `renameFieldValue`/`renameSelectionEnd` so only the stem is selected, commits through `committedRename` so a hidden extension reattaches, and takes one seam from the host — `onRenameCommit(name)`, answering null or the sentence that refuses. The behaviour is Magnus's `conversation-name.svelte`, which had already settled it: Enter commits, Escape abandons, blur commits, and a refusal keeps the field open holding what was typed with the reason beneath it, because a name that collides is fixed where it was written. The field takes the resting control's own height (`mc-input-sm` and `mc-button-sm` are the same `--mc-density-control-sm`), so opening it moves nothing else in the header. Six mounted tests in `apps/web/test/file-inspector-rename.test.ts` — the claim is about a rendered panel, so a source scan could not make it.

**A safety check says what it ran under, and a request that never ran says so.** Three facts the platform already recorded and did not show. The re-scan route audits `enqueued` on every request, and nothing read it back: a request that reached no queue — no engine recorded, or none bound — showed as "Check requested" and the reader waited for a verdict that was never coming. It now reads **Not queued** in the warning register with the reason beside it, derived from the second unread fact, the engine recorded at the moment of asking (`currentEngineVersion` in the same metadata, which `scanFactsFromMetadata` dropped). Third, the firm's own scan settings: the history response carries the four the File Safety page writes, so the Safety tab states the engine decomposed into its three parts beside the depth, the threshold, the treatment and the re-authentication choice — and says, in its own last row, that only the ENGINE is recorded per check. What a check ran under, when somebody has since changed the depth or the threshold, is recorded nowhere; stating that is more useful than a number that might describe a different configuration.

`FileScanEvent` gains `queued`, `FileScanHistory` gains `scanSettings`, and the reading of the policy on this route is deliberately open to any member who can read the file — reading a verdict means reading what it was looked for with, where CHANGING the policy stays behind `firm:manageScanPolicy`. The four settings' words moved into `scan-policy-words.ts` so the settings page that writes them and the Safety tab that reads them cannot name one setting two ways.

**The matter's file list is the only part of that screen that scrolls, and undo reaches the acts a reader performs on it.** Five corrections to the file manager, from the owner's walk of the deployed screen.

Scrolling a long folder used to scroll the whole page: the matter's title, its row of sections and the folder path all left the top of the screen while the counts strip walked off the bottom. The cause was one utility and it reached every working surface in the product. A screen of this shape renders inside a column whose height is a minimum over an auto height — deliberately, so an ordinary document section can still grow past the fold — and the section inside it asked for its share with `flex-1`, whose zero basis is a PERCENTAGE. Against a column sized by its content that resolves to the item's own content, so the section reported the whole table as its base size, the column grew to meet it, the minimum never applied, and nothing was ever capped. A definite basis gives the column its minimum back. The four money ledgers take the same fix.

Undo and redo were wired to one act out of five. A move between folders was recorded; renaming, deleting and pinning were not, so the controls sat disabled through most of a session and read as broken — the stack and the pair of controls were never the defect. Each of those acts now records a step with a real inverse, and each says what it will take back ("Undo renaming Motion.pdf to Answer.pdf"). A move records only what actually moved, which it did not before: an origin written before the write meant a refused move still landed on the stack, and undo would have offered to put back something that never left. Deleting a folder has no restore behind it, so it records nothing and the screen says so instead, naming Deleted Files, where the documents it held can still be recovered one by one.

In the left rail, a chosen folder and a chosen view now look like one state rather than two. The view rows wore the ordinary selected surface, which on that sunken rail is very nearly the rail's own colour, so the open view read as barely marked beside a folder that was plainly lit.

In the icon layout, a long file name used to run over the tiles beside it and both became unreadable. A name now wraps onto a second and a third line and then ends in an ellipsis, with the whole name on the tile's hover; the pin's space is held open on every tile, so pinning lights a glyph and moves nothing.

The details panel's rename commits through the panel now and runs the list's own path — the same collision check, the same write, the same undo step.

**The matter status seal is a pillbox again, and one control changes the status.** The dropdown of lifecycle steps that shipped three days earlier is gone: `matter-status-dialog.svelte` renders the Badge inside a plain button that opens the status window, and the window's status row carries one `Change Status` beside the seal. That opens `matter-status-change-dialog.svelte`, an `ActionDialog` of `ChoiceRow`s — one per step the lifecycle allows from where the matter stands, each carrying the block sentence or the standing line, with the chosen step's consequence and requirement rows beneath and the footer commit reading that step's own verb.

The checks moved with it. The close, open and graduate readiness reads, their requirement lists and the hold's reason field are in the change panel; the number, the engagement and the paper file stay in the window, because they are standing facts about the record rather than anything a step does. `matterStepStanding` in `matter-lifecycle.ts` answers where any step stands from one readiness record, so the panel renders one structure where the window rendered three shapes, and every step gained a `consequence` sentence while `takenFrom`/`confirmation` went with the separate confirm panel. The lifecycle contract is untouched.

title: The migration tag is the apply order, and a gate holds it on every pull request
entry:
**Two per-firm migrations were applied in an order no already-migrated firm ever used.** `20260911T000000_office-email-address-lines-and-firm-brand-images` and `20260914T090000_event-conference-link` were each cut on a branch before the migration they were merged after, so drizzle gave them the later `idx` while their timestamp ids still sorted earlier. Apply order is by TAG, so a freshly provisioned firm ran them first and an already-provisioned one ran them last. They are re-stamped to `20260911T120001_…` and `20260914T120001_…`; the schema outcome was identical either way, because the four migrations involved touch disjoint tables — this was a live tripwire, not a live defect.

**The belief that caused it was written down in three places.** `migrationsFromJournal` sorts the journal lexically by tag, and that is the order every database applies in; `idx` is drizzle's dense counter and names the snapshots. The integrity checks said "apply order is by idx", the bundle test said "the runner applies in journal ORDER", and the database `CLAUDE.md` called `idx` the apply order. All three are corrected, and `migration.ts` now carries the statement the others defer to.

**Why nothing failed before it landed.** The ordering assertion lived only in a Vitest fitness function, and the gate runs its test battery under the `run-tests` label. A migration pull request without the label never checked. `applyOrderViolations` moves the assertion into `tooling/migration-integrity`, which the gate runs on **every** pull request — the window in which a tag still costs nothing to change, because a migration nobody has applied can be renamed and one that has reached a database cannot.

**And the repair is now one command.** `scripts/timestamp-latest-migration.mjs` re-stamps a migration that sorts below the lineage head, not just a freshly generated `NNNN_` one — the case that arises every time `main` is merged into a branch carrying a migration. It is idempotent, steps one second past the head when wall-clock "now" would not clear it, and prints the old and new tags because the worker bundle keys off the filename.

A tag is immutable once a database has applied it, so the rename is only free while no firm is onboarded. `docs/deploy-queue.md` records what must be recreated and the point after which this remedy is gone.

title: Retire the modal-header stream's active-work note
A modal names the record it acts on, and every rung of a matter's life draws a number
entry:
**`pnpm run lint:modal-headers` — the scan that reads a panel's two lines.** The sibling of `lint:screen-headers`, built the same way: pure rules in `modal-headers.mjs`, the filesystem in `index.mjs`, fixtures beside both.

Every rule it asserts was already written down — in the shells' own prop documentation, and in the owner's rulings of 2026-09-08 — and none of it held. A rule recorded in a ledger binds the people who read the ledger; a rule with a gate binds the diff.

- **`heading-act`** — an acting panel's heading names the act in the imperative. A panel that makes a record says "New <Noun>"; a reading panel and a record window name the thing they show, and are asked nothing. The verb vocabulary is a closed set, so a new act is one reviewed line rather than a noun quietly becoming a heading.
- **`heading-question`** — no heading ends in a question mark. The panel is what makes it a question: a destructive kind already takes the `alertdialog` role and traps the decision.
- **`heading-case`** — interior articles and short prepositions stay lower case.
- **`subject-not-prose`** — no fact, and no subtitle snippet, is sentence-shaped.
- **`reference-shown`** — a panel handed a record's number as a prop names it in its heading or its subtitle. The registry of what counts as a record number is read out of the schema's own `*_number` columns, so a record kind that grows a number is asked this question the day its column lands; the eleven columns that are numbers of something else — a telephone, a vehicle, a parcel of land, a row in an import — are recorded with the reason each is not a record's own name. The scan exits non-zero if it can no longer parse the schema, because a rule that finds nothing passes vacuously.
- **`allowance`** — every recorded allowance still describes a real violation, on `lint:one-ui`'s discipline. The list is empty today, which is the honest state: the nine violations the first run found were fixed rather than recorded.

**A panel's second line is the record it is acting on, by the number somebody quotes.** The subtitle slot on `ActionDialog` and `RecordWindow` was contracted to name what is being acted on and to carry the record's own reference, and the owner ruled on 2026-09-08 that it is not the place for a paragraph about what a subsystem is for. Nothing enforced either, and the slot was typed `string`.

**A slot typed `string` accepts a paragraph.** Across 82 panel openings, 18 of 54 subtitles were prose about the subsystem, four billing panels put a number and a sentence in one interpolated string behind a middle dot in three places and an em dash in a fourth, `tabular-nums` was hand written 138 times, and the preview-before-save the owner asked for had reached exactly one file.

**So the slot takes a `RecordSubject` and the design system renders it.** An optional `RecordReference` — `kind`, `number`, and a `standing` of `drawn`, `tentative` or `preview` — plus short facts about that subject. The three standings are the domain's own: a matter number is drawn, a consultation number is tentative and outlives the matter opening, and a preview is what the next record would take. `RecordSubjectLine` states the preview's own wording in one place instead of one file, renders "A number is drawn when this is saved." rather than silence where no number exists yet, and owns the separator so no call site chooses one. The bare `string` arm is gone, which is the mechanism rather than a side effect: a sentence about the act has nowhere left to go, because the heading names the act.

Every panel that carried prose lost it — deleted where it restated the heading, moved beside the field it explains where it was load-bearing. Panels that held a record's number and showed something else now show the number: the two queue acts on a call or text state that message's own reference, the three custodian panels state the packet's custody number, and bill review states the invoice number.

**The preview-before-save leaves the call log.** The owner's ruling of 2026-09-08 — where a record carries a reference number a person reads back, the panel states the number the next one would draw while it is still being filled in, and says that it is a preview rather than a reservation — was written generally and reached one file. The call log had the effect, the wording, the racing-reads guard and the reset, hand-written; every other panel that mints a number showed nothing.

`PreviewedNumber` (`@magna-carta/design-system/record-reference`) holds it once. Each domain keeps its own endpoint and its own scope key — a call's number is scoped to the UTC day it happened on, a matter's to the firm's numbering scheme, a packet's to the custody register — and folding those into one route would put every domain's numbering rules in one handler. What is shared is the shape of the answer, the guard against a stale read landing after a newer one, and the words the reader is told: the parts that were drifting. It knows nothing about how the answer is fetched, so the app's transport and failure model stay in the app.

Two creation panels state the honest half now. **New Matter** says which number the save will draw and that it will — a consultation draws its own tentative number, an open matter draws the matter number, and an intake draws neither, because no number of any kind exists before a matter is at least a consultation. **New Packet** previews the custody number, except where the packet was carried in from a paper deeds register, in which case the number already written on its physical label is the packet's real number and the save only records it.

**An intake is numbered the moment the enquiry is written down.** The lifecycle ruling of 2026-09-06 said no number of any kind existed before a matter became active. The consultation sequence reversed half of that on 2026-08-31; the owner reversed the rest on 2026-09-14: "everything should have a number, intake would have a number as well."

An intake was already work — somebody took the call, a person is named responsible for it, a conflicts check may have run, procedure steps are being cleared against it — and the only name the platform had for it was its handle, which is what the platform joins on and what nobody can read back down a telephone.

**A third run, not a number moved earlier.** `matter.intake_number` is drawn at creation from a scheme whose `purpose` is `intake`, rendering `I2026-0001` until a firm configures its own. Drawing the consultation number at intake instead would have been cheaper and is the wrong shape: most enquiries are declined, so the consultation run would fill with numbers issued to nothing and stop being readable as a run of consultations — the same defect the consultation sequence was created to avoid on the matter run.

**Nothing is replaced.** Graduation adds the consultation number beside the intake number and opening adds the matter number beside both, so a file that came the whole way answers to three names and a note filed under any of them still resolves. Every surface that quotes a matter falls through to the newest number it has drawn; the matter list, the communications log and the intake desk search all of them.

The draw rides the existing `matter_number_counter` / `matter_number_allocation` mechanism under an `intake/` scope prefix rather than a third pair of tables. What each sequence IS — its prefix, its label, its retryable collision, whether a built-in default exists — moved out of the service's conditionals into `numbering/sequences.ts`: two sequences were two branches and read fine, three made the shape visible, and a fourth run is now one row rather than four edits. The migration backfills every row currently at status `intake` and seeds the counters to match.

title: Every Workspace screen searches itself through the one control, and a gate that keeps it there
entry:
**Every shipped Workspace screen searches itself through `ScreenSearch`, in the screen header's `actions` snippet, or records why it does not.** The Matters docket, the Directory and a matter's Notes each carried their own search — a `type="search"` field beside a Lucide search glyph, its own debounce, its own toggle behaviour on a live query — so both 2026-09-02 corrections against the shared control (the clear glyph, collapse-on-click-away) had reached the component and none of the three. All three now use the control. Downloads and Uploads gained one; both hold their whole list in the browser, so they narrow on `searchOn="keystroke"` with nothing leaving the machine.

**Four screens gained a search by gaining a query on their read**, which is where the work was. Notifications, the Conflicts Check log, Magnus and the Calendar were first recorded as declining on the grounds that their reads took no search parameter; that is a reason to add one.

- **Magnus** matches the conversation title and what was SAID in it — nothing generates a title, so a transcript search is the only way a conversation is found again. Content is in scope only for a member's OWN conversations; the firm-wide administrative read matches titles alone, because `packages/magnus/CLAUDE.md` holds that transcripts may not be swept across the firm's records until the discovery surface owns an include-or-exclude control for it. `searchesContent` is the one place that boundary is decided.
- **Conflicts Check** matches the matter a run was made against and the NAMES it surfaced, through `directory_name.normalized_display` so a term normalizes the way the corpus did. The closed labels stay with the column filters, which match them exactly. "Has this firm ever checked this person" is now one question rather than a walk through the log.
- **Notifications** carries no sentence in the record by design, so the client resolves the term into the kinds and categories whose WORDS match (`kindsMatching` / `categoriesMatching`) and sends those with it; the server OR-s them against the matter number. An empty `kinds` means the term matched no kind, never "match no row". The unread badge is deliberately not narrowed.
- **The Calendar** narrows the window on screen, because its three reads cap their horizon server-side and refuse a wider one rather than clamping it. The view states how many entries in the named window match and that other dates were not searched, so the control never implies a reach it does not have.

`@magna-carta/data-access/like-search` is the new one home for escaping a reader's text into a `LIKE` pattern. Two copies of that rule already existed (the discovery review reads and the communications log), agreeing by luck; a third was about to be written here. A test caught the bug that makes it worth having: `normalizeName("%")` strips to the empty string, and a contains-pattern built from an empty term is `%%`, which every stored name matches — a reader typing one stray character would have been handed the whole conflicts log.

`pnpm run lint:workspace-search` is the new fitness function. It reads the Workspace group out of `navigation/destinations.ts` and the pages out of the route tree — no roster kept by hand — and refuses four things: a Workspace screen that neither searches nor declines, a control seated outside the header's action row, a decline left standing after its screen got a search, and a second implementation of a search box anywhere beneath a Workspace destination. Coverage follows the render rather than the file, walking each page's `$lib` component imports, so Tasks passes on the search `TaskList` owns. Thirteen of the fourteen shipped Workspace screens now search; Home declines, being a summary of other screens rather than a list.

title: The issue report outlives the panel that opens it, and the panel links its source
entry:
**Report an Issue from the Build Information panel now stays open, and the panel links the
repository its commits belong to.**

**A dialog cannot be a child of the surface that dismisses it.** The panel mounted the issue
reporter inside itself, and the panel is the body of the chip's popover: pressing Report an Issue
closed the popover (correctly — a popover cannot be read from under a modal) and the popover's exit
then unmounted the dialog it had just rendered, about a second after it appeared. Both surfaces went
at once, which read as the report refusing to open. The flag and the diagnosis it carries now live
in `$lib/components/issue-report.svelte.ts` and the shell mounts the one dialog — the same move
`build-panel.svelte.ts` makes for the panel's own open flag, and for the same reason.

**One dialog, one draft.** The profile menu and the command palette each mounted a copy of the
reporter too. Those two worked, because a menu that closes does not own the dialog's DOM, but three
mounts meant three drafts: a half-written report begun from the palette was invisible from the
profile menu, and the other door opened on an empty field. All three doors now open the shell's one
dialog and contribute nothing but the gesture.

**The panel links its own source.** `repositoryUrl()` joins the commit and dashboard links in
`$lib/versions/deployment-links.ts`, and the panel's header carries it at the end of the control
cluster so the three controls beside it keep their seats. It is `BUILD_IDENTITY.sourceRepository` —
resolved at build time from the git remote, the same value every commit link is already built on —
so a build that resolved none renders no link rather than a dead one, and it is signed-in only by
the same rule the commit and Worker links keep.

title: Three defects that merged behind a gate that was not running, the matter's paper-file office, and one navigation row
entry:
**The matter's paper file is kept at one of the firm's offices, and the status window states which.**
`matter.physical_file_location_id` is a new nullable per-firm column pointing at `location`, set
through `PATCH /api/v1/matters/{id}` (`matters:edit`) and answered by the matter detail read as
`physicalFileLocationId` plus a resolved `physicalFileLocationName` — `selectMatterDetailStatement`
now joins `location` twice under two aliases, because a matter names two different offices.

It is deliberately not `matter.location_id`. That column says which office RUNS the matter and is the
citation on the matter header; this one says where its folder is KEPT, and a folder travels. One word
("Location") on two screens was hiding two facts.

The status window's Physical File renders the row through `$lib/offices`' `OfficeLink` and sets it
through `OfficePicker`, reading the matter itself when the window opens so a file moved elsewhere
between two openings does not leave the window stating where it used to be. Held In and Destroy After
keep the Soon mark: what a folder sits inside is a record that does not exist yet, and there is no
retention clock anywhere to derive a destruction date from. `MATTER_PHYSICAL_FILE_FACTS` carries a
`served` flag so which rows are real is one list with one test.

The New Matter dialog's Location moved from `vocabulary-picker.svelte` to the same `OfficePicker`,
which reads the firm's offices through the shared store; the dialog's `locations` prop is accepted and
no longer read, and nothing imports `VocabularyPicker` now.

**The navigation column's row is one design-system part, and the catalogue column has its own home.** `NavigationLayout` gained a `Row` export (`packages/design-system/src/lib/components/navigation-layout/navigation-layout-row.svelte`, recipe `mc-navigation-layout-row`): the control-height rounded row, the quiet hover tint, and the lit row's selected fill with the gilt start-edge bar drawn as an inset box-shadow. Three places had written that treatment out by hand — the settings layout, the catalogue column Tools and Reports share, and the inline `style` strings in both — with the file manager's folder tree already foreseen as the fourth. All three now compose the part, and `apps/web/test/{settings,tools,reports}-navigation.test.ts` each fail if a row grows a class list or an inline style of its own again.

Two judgments moved into the part. The element follows from `href` and nothing else: a string is an anchor, omitting it is a button, and `null` is an entry designed with nowhere to go yet, which stands unlinked and quiet with its Soon mark rather than dressed as a disabled control — the same spelling `CatalogueEntry.href` already used. And a name wraps rather than truncating: the control height is a `min-block-size` and the recipe carries no `white-space` or `text-overflow`, because a row reading "Property Listin… Soon" has stopped naming the thing, which is a navigation row's one job. The layout still imposes no structure on what the navigation holds; taking the row is a choice.

`catalogue-navigation.{svelte,ts}` moved from `apps/web/src/lib/tools/` to `apps/web/src/lib/catalogue/`. It serves Tools and Reports equally, so Reports had been importing a column out of the Tools directory; the catalogue framework's third view now sits beside its list and tiles views, and `apps/web/src/lib/catalogue/CLAUDE.md` says so.

**The matter status window's "read again on every opening" only ever read once.** The engagement read
was an `$effect` guarded by a plain `arrangementAsked` flag that `reset` — the shell's `onOpen` —
cleared. `ActionDialog` calls `onOpen` from an effect of its own, and a child component's effects run
after the parent's, so the guard was read before it was cleared: the window read the fee arrangement
on its first opening and never again for the life of the component.

Both facts the window re-reads (the engagement, and now the office the paper file is kept at) are
read from the opening transition itself rather than from an effect. The readiness reads stay effects
deliberately — they ask about the matter's own status, which only this window changes, so once per
visit is the whole of it.

title: The calendar becomes many calendars, in folders, with a day of columns
entry:
**The calendar's sixth round: many calendars in folders, a day of columns, and a form that asks where.** The owner walked the deployed calendar and issued eleven corrections; this is all of them, and the rulings are in [`docs/conventions/design-corrections.md`](docs/conventions/design-corrections.md).

The firm calendar stops being one undifferentiated grid. A CATALOG of individual calendars (`apps/web/src/lib/calendar/calendar-sources.ts`) stands over what the calendar context already read: the firm's own two (matters and deadlines, firm events), a folder per role the firm handed out holding the members who hold it, the rooms, everything else that is booked, and the dates. Each row turns on and off on its own; each folder's own control carries the third state and completes a part-filled folder. The folders are the firm's own vocabulary — nothing here decides who counts as support staff — and a member holding two roles is filed under the first, because a calendar listed twice reads as two calendars and toggles as one. File-destruction dates are listed, marked Soon and refused, because a retention schedule is the one date calendar nothing serves yet.

**A calendar that is on is a read; a calendar that is off is no read at all.** The read plan is a plan per calendar (`readOneCalendar`) rather than one read narrowed afterwards: a member calendar is the member filter the server already resolves in SQL, a room calendar is the availability read, a date calendar is the federated read narrowed to that layer's own sources. The reads are made together, fail independently, and a failure now names WHOSE calendar it was. The same record arriving from two of them is merged into one row that knows it is on both.

**`CalendarGrid.Day`** is the fourth presentation and the only one with a time axis: an hour per row, a CALENDAR per column, which is what makes a Tuesday six attorneys spend in four places legible. A record on two calendars is drawn in both their columns on purpose. An entry with no hour sits in a band above the hours, where a filing belongs. The hours are the working day, widened without asking by anything outside it.

The firm-wide federated read carries **the hour**. `TimelineEntry` gains `timeOfDay` and `timeZone`, declared per source (`timeOfDayExpression` on the two select builders) and set on matter events, deadlines and firm events. It is the same class of fact as the sort key — when a thing happens, said in the record's own terms, never converted — and it is what lets a day grid put a hearing on the ten o'clock row without the projection ever naming it. Before this the firm calendar painted no times at all.

**One palette, one home.** The eleven colours the file manager's folders offer moved to `packages/design-system/src/lib/palette/`, with their fills as `--mc-palette-*` on `:root`; `FOLDER_COLORS` re-exports them unchanged and the folder recipe aliases the shared properties. A calendar offers the nine that read on a chip, and wears its colour as a rule down the chip's leading edge — the status register keeps the fill, so a cancelled setting on the blue calendar is still visibly cancelled. `PaletteSwatches` is the one control both surfaces pick from. An unchosen calendar is dealt a colour by position.

**Double-clicking an empty day or hour** starts a record on it, with the day and the hour as the form's opening answers. It is an accelerator, never the only path, and it never fires from a press on a chip.

The record forms change with the same round. **Where is Location**, and it is the product's dropdown-with-add over the firm's own offices and rooms, still keeping a courthouse nobody has a record of. **A conference link** is its own field and its own column — a nullable `conference_url` on `matter_event` and `firm_event` — because a deposition can be in a conference room and on a call at once. **The times are time fields** with the zone beside them as a shortcode, worked out on the record's own day (`formatTimeZoneAbbreviation`, in the design system's display vocabulary); a record has one zone, so the ends line states the same code rather than offering a second control. **The day being booked stands in the panel's context pane**, as the product's own calendar with a day view and no toolbar. And **the matter is no longer required**: no matter is a choice whose row says what it writes, and the form writes a firm event instead — which is the shape the data already had.

Two lines come off. "A matter is needed." is gone with the requirement. "Nothing recorded in September 2026." is gone from every grid: a month that is empty says so by being empty. The agenda keeps its sentence, because an empty list is a blank rectangle.

title: Screens read through the generated client, and start reading on hover
entry:
A screen starts reading before you click it, and an empty list stops explaining itself.

Every screen used to fetch after it had mounted, which put a whole round trip after the click: chunk, parse, mount, and only then ask the server anything. `app.html` has set `data-sveltekit-preload-data="hover"` since it was written, meaning to spend the 200–400 ms between the pointer settling on a link and the click landing — but that preload runs a route's load function, and 93 of 98 screens had no load that read anything, so it bought the JavaScript and nothing else. Reads move into the load, where they start on hover and resolve out of a shared cache by the time the component mounts.

The same cache ends the re-reads. `/api/v1/me` was being read on every navigation by the (app) guard and again on mount by 38 surfaces, and it is not a cheap call — a control-plane read, a firm Durable Object wake, a permissions join, the channel and flags, the firm name and the membership state. It is now read once and shared, as are the firm's practice areas, its Locations and its roster.

What the screens read through is `@magna-carta/api-client`, the generated client ADR-0066 chose and CI has been regenerating and diff-gating all along while the app hand-wrote 12,389 lines mirroring the same contract beside it. `/matters` is migrated; the rest follow behind a ratchet that can only fall.

Empty lists now say **No Results** — two words, whether the record holds nothing or a filter excludes everything. They used to open with a definition of the domain term ("A packet is the physical thing the firm holds and moves: an envelope, a deed box, a sealed wallet…"), which is the explanatory prose the no-info-lines ruling already forbids everywhere else and whose home is the user guides. Where a filter is what emptied the table, the way back is still there — as the Clear All Filters control, not as a sentence about it. The table no longer accepts an empty state from the surface above it, so there is nothing to get wrong rather than a rule to remember.

The lint cost proxy stops counting work nobody does.

CI does not lint the whole repository on a pull request. It lints a computed scope, and it defers the one package whose lint is effectively a whole-repo lint — `apps/api-worker` — to the post-merge pass. Which package that is gets decided by a cost proxy: the number of lintable files the type-aware linter has to pull into a type program.

The proxy counted every file in a package's dependency closure, tests included. A dependency's tests are never pulled into a dependent's type program, because nothing imports a test — so across api-worker's 61-package closure that was 609 phantom files, 30% of the one number the rule is decided by. Its weight falls from 2022 to 1413 once they are dropped. A package's own tests still count, because linting a package does lint them.

The share that selects a sink moves from 0.50 to 0.35 in the same change and not independently of it: on the honest numerator, api-worker is 46% of the workspace rather than 65%, so at 0.50 it would have stopped being selected and the deferral would have become a silent no-op. The new share is set from measured lint time rather than from the proxy that was in question — api-worker takes 11.7s against 2.6s for `apps/web` and 1.4–2.1s for a typical domain package, and its per-file cost is superlinear, so a file-count proxy understates the outlier it is picking.

Two guards that compared a sink against its neighbour, or against how far past the bar it sat, are gone. Both fired on ordinary growth in `apps/web` rather than on anything about the deferral, and one could have deselected the expensive package while keeping a cheaper one. Selection is already the outlier test; what is left asserts the two failure modes worth failing on — no sink selected, so the deferral does nothing, and more than two, so it has stopped being about outliers. Simulated against this dependency graph, the rule now stays green from today through +1200 files in `apps/web`, while `apps/web` joins as a genuine second sink and api-worker eventually ages out of one.

Separately: a package with no lintable files of its own can never be a sink. `apps/web-worker` has zero and depends only on `apps/web`, so it carried `apps/web`'s weight exactly and forever — deferring it would defer no work while spending one of the two sink slots.

title: The Build Information panel says it once, files it, and links what it names
entry:
**The header's Build Information panel now says what it knows in one grammar, files what it is
showing, links what it names, and reports what a probe cost.** Its paste, the issue reporter's trace
and the panel's four sections were each built by hand; they are now one report model, one section
component and one registry apiece.

**One grammar for every diagnosis in the app.** `$lib/diagnostics/diagnostic-report.ts` owns the
shape — a row is `key: value`, a group indents under its heading — and both the issue reporter's
trace and the panel's paste render through it. They had invented their own formats independently
(`key: value` against `Label: commit · committed …`), so a reader who received both parsed two
documents; and each carried what the other lacked, the trace all the browser facts and none of the
fleet, the paste the reverse. The trace's output is byte-for-byte what it was — its own test pins
every line — and it now shares its environment block with the panel.

**A failed read is in the paste, which is the case the copy control exists for.** The panel's copy
was a single function inside the deployment model, which could not import the database or the
readiness models without a cycle, so both reached it as one pre-joined opaque string — and a section
whose value was `null` vanished silently. Somebody looking at "The version read failed · Error ID
error\_…" copied a report that never mentioned it. The assembly is now a list of contributors over one
state object (`$lib/versions/panel-report.ts`): each owns a section, states its own failure with its
Error ID, and returns null when it has nothing. A fifth section appends one function instead of
gaining a sixth parameter.

**A refused clipboard says so.** The three copy paths each called `navigator.clipboard.writeText`
inside a `catch { return }`, so on an insecure origin or under a managed-browser policy the control
did nothing at all and said nothing at all — and the fallback that works in exactly those cases
already existed in the design system. All three now go through `copyText`, which falls back to the
selection route and reports which happened; a copy that did not happen puts a line on the panel.

**Four hand-written sections became one component.** `version-panel-section.svelte` owns the heading,
the fold, the failure block and the loading region; each section still decides its own name, pills,
skeleton, failure sentence and rows. The wording had already started to drift between the four
copies. The folds are a registry too, keyed by section id — the fourth section had arrived without
the doc comment the other three carried and without the file's own header sentence being updated.

**Rows link to the things they name.** A Worker's name links to its Cloudflare dashboard page through
the account-agnostic `?to=/:account/…` form, so the link embeds no account identifier and works for
every member of the account. A commit links to the commit, on the parts a reader actually reads a
diff for — this build, the API, and the Worker serving this page — and the Update Available block
links to the diff between the running bundle and the one being served. Nothing is linked that cannot
be verified: a placeholder commit or an unresolved repository renders as plain text. The repository is
resolved at build time from the git remote (`resolveRepositoryUrl` in the shared commit-identity
script), so a fork links to itself.

**`GET /api/v1/meta/versions` reports what each probe cost.** The number was being paid for and thrown
away. Every probe is raced against a fixed timeout, so "reported" and "unreachable" are two ends of
one measurement with nothing between them — a Worker answering just inside the timeout read as
perfectly healthy until it flipped. Rows carry their latency and a slow one is marked.

**The panel can file what it is showing.** Report an Issue opens the same dialog every other surface
uses, carrying the panel's whole diagnosis; `POST /api/v1/incidents` accepts it as a bounded,
optional `context.deployment`, redacted by construction like every other field there. Previously the
only route was copy, close, find the profile menu, paste — four steps during an incident, each of
which can lose the paste.

**The panel is reachable from search, and so is the next tool of its shape.** The command palette
renders registries and never hand-lists an item, but every registry it had described a
_destination_ with an href. A surface that opens in place had no registry to join, so
`$lib/developer/diagnostic-actions.ts` is the one for that shape — an id, a label, the words it
should be findable by, whether this build offers it, and the function that runs. The panel's open
state moved out of the component (`build-panel.svelte.ts`) so a registry entry can reach it.

**The chip says which build mode it is, outside production.** Two screenshots of one commit, one from
a preview deploy and one from the real site, were indistinguishable.

**And the panel is finally tested in a browser.** Its component rules are asserted by regex over its
source, because the node pool cannot mount a design-system component — the right trade for what those
rules pin, and unable to tell you the panel opens at all. `e2e/build-panel.spec.ts` drives the real
thing: the sections settle, a fold survives a reload, the palette opens it, and a signed-out panel
issues no authenticated request.

**Merged onto the report extraction, not around it.** `main` split the panel into a shared
`version-report.svelte` rendered by both the chip and the new Settings · Versions page while this
branch was open. Everything above is applied to that component, so the page gets all of it too: the
same paste, the same links, the same latency, the same failure blocks. The chip keeps what is the
chip's — the build environment badge, and the popover state the palette opens. One regression from
that extraction is repaired on the way past: the health row had lost its `badgeVariant` passthrough,
so a readiness check reading "Not applicable" was rendering green rather than neutral.

title: A task is read and changed in one window, and moves along four rungs
entry:
**A task is read and changed in the product's one record window, and a new one is that same window
with nothing in it yet.** `task-record-window.svelte` carries the fields, the attachments tab, the
print sheet and the acts; `task-list.svelte` keeps the rows, the search, and the one act a list is
for. Everything that used to unfold inside the list is gone with it — the composer above the rows,
the row that turned into fields, the attach picker, the cancel-reason form and the per-row assignee
select — because each was a second place to learn where a task's fields live.

Two things fell out of it. `note-attachable-documents.ts` becomes
`record-attachable-documents.ts`, typed on the shape a document association has rather than on a
note's name for it: a note and a task attach a matter's files identically, and a second copy would
have been six lines free to drift. And the reason the firm is not doing a task is asked for in its
own action panel (`task-not-doing-dialog.svelte`) whose commit says "Record the Decision" — every
panel in the product leaves through a control that says Cancel, so a commit that also said it would
be two controls with one word and opposite meanings.

The owner's ruling was on the books for records that already had a window. A task had none, and the
tempting half-step — an action dialog for making one, the row still editing it — produces exactly
the defect the ruling names, with the panel and the row free to disagree about the record's own
fields. That half-step and its correction both happened here; only the second was the fix.

**A task's state becomes four rungs — To Do, In Progress, On Hold, Done — and cancelling is replaced
by archiving.** The rungs are one control group in the record window's action bar; beside them sit
the only two other things that happen to a task, and they differ in one thing: archiving keeps the
data, deleting takes it. Archiving is orthogonal to the rungs — a task is archived FROM where it
stood and comes back there — so the list's foot now offers **Show Done** and **Show Archived** as two
questions rather than one. The archive reason is optional, which is the whole lesson of the state it
replaces: cancelling required one, and nobody used it.

**The schema route is the finding, not the change.** `matter_task.state` is a CHECK-constrained enum
on a table `time_entry`, `matter_task_document` and `matter_task_external_link` all reference — plus
its own `blocked_by_task_id`. SQLite cannot alter a CHECK, and the rebuild that would has to drop the
table, which a durable object refuses at the commit for every child row: the migration applies to an
empty database and takes every real firm's offline on wake, which has happened here before. Six
mechanisms were probed against real durable-object storage and all six fail — including
`PRAGMA writable_schema`, SQLite's own documented way to change a constraint with nothing dropped,
which workerd's authorizer answers with `SQLITE_AUTH`.

So `state` narrows to the one thing the database pairs it with by CHECK — is the work finished — and
the three open rungs arrive as an added `progress` column, with `archived_at`/`archived_by`/
`archive_reason` beside it. `ALTER TABLE … ADD COLUMN` drops nothing, so it lands on a parent, and the
same probe file proves the three properties the route rests on: an added column may carry its own
CHECK, that CHECK may name a second column, and existing rows take the default. The reader's four
rungs are reassembled from the two columns in exactly one function. Recorded as
ADR-a-vocabulary-on-a-parent-table-grows-by-adding-a-column, which is the general answer for this
fleet rather than a note about tasks.

`20260914T120000_task-rungs-and-archive` carries every cancelled task onto the archive columns with
its reason intact, and `packages/database/test/task-rungs-migration.test.ts` runs it over rows rather
than over an empty database — the gap both of this repository's migration outages came through.

title: docs: the handover records that every round is on the stream branch
The owner's rounds of 2026-09-09 to 2026-09-14: settings, conflicts, the Upload dialog, the money screens, Magnus, the matter seal, and one component for a two-sided screen
entry:
**A conflicts check is a numbered record with runs under it, opened at once and searched after the response; the walk goes to closure and nothing a firm sets limits it.** `conflicts_numbered_check` and `conflicts_check_run` (per-firm lineage, `20260911T120000_conflicts-check-numbers-and-runs.sql`, with a backfill so every existing `conflicts_check` row becomes run 1 of a numbered check) sit beside the append-only log; `packages/conflicts/src/check-run.ts` draws the number (`CC-` and four digits, `MAX + 1` under a unique index), opens runs and settles stale ones, and `apps/api-worker/src/conflicts/check-run-executor.ts` executes a run after the response through `runInBackground`, reporting its stage and counts on the run row. `POST /api/v1/conflicts/checks` answers 202 with the id, number, run id and ordinal; `GET .../checks/{checkId}?run=` carries the runs and the selected run's record; `POST .../checks/{checkId}/runs` re-runs; `PUT .../checks/{checkId}/matter` files; `GET .../checks/next-number` previews. The hop budgets, default depth, closure cap and candidate cap are gone from `ScopeRequest`, `ConflictsPolicy`, the draft and the settings page — `expandGraph` walks to closure under `WALK_CEILING`, and `CANDIDATE_WRITE_CEILING` is the most one batch can carry, both stated on the record when reached; stored JSON keeps its key names so old rows read under the budgets they ran with.
