The web surface: the New Check panel's right pane is two tabs (Locations by place over `SEARCH_LOCATIONS`; Advanced Settings with name matching as a `ChoicePicker`), the matter field offers a chosen party's matters through `matter-choice.svelte`, the check screen is titled by its number with input and output in separate cards, a `ProgressSteps` reading of a run in flight (`run-progress.ts`), the run history, Run Again, File on a Matter, and exactly Print Report and Download Report (`report-download.ts` projects the sheet through the export renderer). The seam left behind: execution rides the request's background allowance with a two-minute stale rule; the executor is queue-ready once the per-firm dispatch table can take it.

**A consultation can be put on hold or closed, and the status seal is a menu of the steps a matter
can take.** The lifecycle graph gave `consultation` one edge, Open Matter, and the hold route
refused anything but an open matter. Now `holdMatter` and its in-batch guard accept `open` or
`consultation`; `releaseMatter` returns the matter to where the hold found it, reading `opened_at`
as the one honest signal rather than assuming `open`; and the close, which the service already
accepted for a consultation, is offered from the consultation's own seal as Close Consultation. A
closed or held consultation keeps its tentative number and draws no matter number. The seal on the
matter header is a `DropdownMenu` over the Badge listing the steps available from where the matter
stands (never the five statuses; the "steps, never a picker" comment in `matter-lifecycle.ts` now
says why a dropdown of steps is not a picker), with the status window as its last item. Each step
declares how it is taken (`takenFrom`): the hold, the close, the open and the intake's completion
open the window at the step; the release and the reopen ask once in the confirm panel and run. The
seal reads the session through the shared `sessionPermissions` store as the pointer reaches it.
Route descriptions, the OpenAPI snapshot and the generated client are updated.

**The floating surfaces share one alignment, one width rule and one stacking layer — settled in
the design system, not at each call site.**

A listbox, a menu or a popover now opens aligned to the right-hand edge of the control that opens
it and grows leftward, never extending past that edge and never wider than the room the screen has
for it: a long option wraps inside the panel instead of running the panel off the screen. Before
this, the components set no default of their own and the alignment was written by hand at
ninety-five call sites, with a settings row's listbox — its control pinned to the right of the
row — running off the right-hand edge of the screen. The Combobox now anchors its list to the
whole field a person sees rather than to the text box inside it, so the list's edge sits on the
field's. A caller whose control is left-anchored still says `align="start"` and wins.

The two context-menu parts move to the layer every other floating surface already sat on, above
the modal layer, so a right-click menu raised inside a dialog — the Upload dialog's queued files —
renders above the dialog and can be used, instead of painting underneath it.

**Magnus sorts its rail, keeps a conversation on a matter, attaches a matter's files, and the firm
chooses its model.** The conversation listing (`GET /api/v1/magnus/conversations`) takes a `sort`
of `date`, `name` or `matter`, honoured over the whole record with a cursor that pages within that
order; the rail carries the control in its empty state too. A conversation is renamed where its
name is read (Enter commits, Escape cancels, blur commits; a refused rename keeps the old name and
says so). `PATCH .../conversations/{id}/matter` keeps a conversation on another matter or on none,
refusing a closed matter and auditing both matters, because which matter a transcript is kept on
decides who may read it. `POST .../conversations/{id}/attachments` attaches one of the matter's
files BY REFERENCE (`magnus_conversation_attachment`, a new per-firm table); on each later question
the file's current version is read, its text taken through the platform's own extraction port, and
sent ahead of the question under a heading naming the file within a 64 KiB budget, and the row
records whether the model saw it whole, cut, or not at all. Nothing of a file is copied. The
disclosure moved to version 2 (what Magnus can see changed), so every member is re-prompted.
Settings · AI and the Assistant gains the model control: `inference.primaryReasoningModel` is
chosen from the catalog's verified reasoning entries through the product's combobox, or returned to
"the platform's current model" (which DELETES the firm's row rather than pinning today's default);
the page states each entry's retention posture and verification dates and the catalog's version and
effective date. `magnus-surface.svelte` is split into the rail, the transcript and the composer, and
the composer names the model that answers.

**Settings · Offices, the firm's brand images on Firm Profile, and the office family under `apps/web/src/lib/offices/`.**

The whole locations backend had no screen. It now has one: a `DataTable.Grid` register over `GET /api/v1/locations` (which now joins each office's addresses, its staffing count, whether it prints its own logo and whether it is the firm's default), and one `RecordWindow` for entering, reading and correcting an office, with the entry segmented into Office, Addresses and Letterhead tabs on the left and the acts that commit on their own (members, the letterhead logo) in tabs on the right. `?office=<id>` opens a record on arrival, which is what `OfficeLink` links to.

The contract grows `location.email` (one per office; a telephone belongs to each address), the four international address lines and the country on `location_address` so the design system's `AddressFields` writes an office's address the way it writes anybody's, `PUT|DELETE /api/v1/locations/{id}/members/{userId}` composed onto the per-member replace-set, `PUT /api/v1/locations/{id}/firm-default` (without which the close refusal on the default office was unrecoverable), and `GET /api/v1/locations/{id}/letterhead-logo`, which streams the office's own mark or the firm's primary brand image. `firm_brand_image` is a new per-firm table, content-addressed by the bytes' SHA-256, behind `GET|PUT /api/v1/firm/profile/brand-images`, `PATCH|DELETE .../{sha256}` and `GET .../{sha256}/content`, all under `firm:manageProfile`. The office picker (`OfficePicker`), the link (`OfficeLink`) and the shared `firmOffices` read are the modular pieces the matter status window's Location consumes next.

**One layout for a screen with a navigational column beside its content — `NavigationLayout` in
the design system.**

Settings drew a two-column canvas by hand (a nav at the popover measure plus its gutters, inside a
negative-margin full-height row with its own scrollbar) and Magnus drew the same shape a second way
(a rail at an off-token container width, a different scroll treatment). The owner's ruling is that
this is one shape, so it is now one component: `@magna-carta/design-system/navigation-layout`
provides the `<nav>` landmark with a required accessible name, two token-derived widths (`standard`
— the settings measure — and `narrow`, which lands on the global sidebar's width), two independent
scroll regions wearing the house scrollbar with a reserved gutter so nothing shifts when a scrollbar
arrives, and the canvas geometry (the full height under the top bar, the work canvas's inset
cancelled) that consumers stopped needing to repeat. What the navigation holds is the consumer's
snippet — grouped section links, a control over rows, a grouped list of tools — so the component
imposes no list structure and takes no `items` prop. Below the `lg` viewport the navigation stacks
above the content and the layout scrolls as one. Settings and Magnus adopt it in their own rounds;
Tools and Reports can take the same shape as list-left, chosen-thing-right.

**The settings surface consolidates: one page shape, one choice field, one table, one version report.** The owner's first Settings round (`docs/conventions/settings-rulings.md`, R1). The hand-rolled scroll region twenty pages carried by copy is one component (`settings-scroll-region.svelte`); the standard page (`settings-page.svelte`) is rewritten around the server-backed draft every firm page actually holds, and Billing, Calendar, Reports and File Safety render it; a plate's closing line is a component of its own. `SettingsRow`'s `select` kind renders the product's combobox, and every hand-placed `Select` under Settings (the notification matrices, the catalog dialogs, Matter Plans, Intake Procedures, the numbering editor, the Text page's Soon seams) is that same field, with sentinel values where "none" was an empty string. The five settings tables are `DataTable.Grid` over column models in `catalog-columns.ts`, so they sort, filter from their headers, offer their column roster and count themselves. The version chip's popover body is `version-report.svelte`, rendered by the chip and by the Versions page alike; the page's histogram workaround is gone. The Beta Access switch is bound to the session's channel through a getter/setter so a cancelled consent leaves it off, and its plate reads "Beta Branch". The scan depth options read "Core", "Extended", "Full", with the engine's reading and the chosen depth's meaning beneath them on File Safety. The matter numbering editor is a table of parts inside the settings anatomy, arrows leading the row.

**The firm's Time, Fees, Costs and Billing screens lose their header controls, and their column filters reach the server.** Each carried a period dropdown (worded three different ways), a billing or status dropdown, and a meta line beneath the title that no other main screen has (`docs/conventions/time-tab-rulings.md`, round twelve). The screens now open on their whole record and the table is the only thing that narrows them; the Date, Status, Billable and Timekeeper filters are sent to the listings as `from`/`to`, `status`, `billable` and `timekeeperUserId` (`apps/web/src/lib/money/listing-scope.ts`), so a filter holds across every page rather than over the page in hand, and the same choices ride the address. The three listings take either date bound alone or neither — nothing named is the whole record over the date index, where they used to answer empty — every one of the four takes a status LIST given repeatedly (`status=draft&status=submitted`), and every one gains a `search` (`packages/timekeeping` and `packages/billing` took the predicate for time and invoices), so all four screens carry the live `ScreenSearch` and a multi-state Status filter reaches the server whole. Billing gains "+ Bill": the draft dialog the matter register already uses grew a matter-first shape, resolves the client from the party record (`client-party.ts`), and goes to the matter's Billing section with the draft open. The messaging screen's four scope tabs are gone for the same reason; the Matter column's filter reaches the server as the listing's scope, and the count waiting to be filed stands in the counts strip.

**The Upload dialog holds one height, tabs its intake, states every file's readiness, names what
failed, and no longer asks whether to send files the firm already holds.** The source pane pins the
frame's height (`upload-dialog.svelte`, the record windows' own measure), so tabs, folders and rows
scroll inside it; the intake is `Tabs` — Location, Advanced Settings — in place of the accordion; Add
is one secondary button wearing the dropdown menu, with File and Folder as its items. The digest
register (`upload-digests.svelte.ts`) now asks the firm the moment a hash is in and reports each file
as reading, ready, held or not read, the batch starts every item from that readiness
(`UploadBatchPlan.readiness`), and `checkDuplicates` is gone from the plan: the hash is always read.
A failed item carries a one-line `failure` (the server's problem detail, or the transport class)
beside its full `reason`; the row and the top-bar tray both show it. On the server,
`purgeableVersionObjects` in `@magna-carta/file-manager` is the one door to destroying a version's
bytes, and it refuses while any other version row, live or soft-deleted, holds the same content or
key; the DELETE route's contract says so.

**Tools and Reports are two-sided screens on the design system's `NavigationLayout`.** Each area's routes now render inside a layout (`apps/web/src/routes/(app)/tools/+layout.svelte`, `apps/web/src/routes/(app)/reports/+layout.svelte`) that draws the catalogue as a navigation column on the left and the chosen tool or report on the right, on the same component Settings adopted first — the owner's 2026-09-11 ruling that a screen with a navigational menu and a content area is one component, and that it reaches Tools and Reports.

The column is `$lib/tools/catalogue-navigation.svelte`, one component for both areas, and it reads the same projection each landing index renders (`tool-catalogue.ts`, `report-catalogue.ts`), so a registry entry reaches the column, the index and the command palette with no edit. The current entry is decided by `catalogue-navigation.ts` on the path boundary, so the workbench's password-recovery screen still lights the File Workbench. A soon entry stands in its group unlinked with its mark and its dependency on the hover title, never omitted. The landing route keeps its catalogue index in the content column, so the column is never beside nothing.

The content column is the page's scroll region unless the page claims it: the File Workbench and the Safe Website Viewer stage their own full-height frames and say so through their route data (`content-column.ts`), and the Tools layout hands them a bare column. Every tool and report keeps `back` on its own header; the column is a finding aid beside it, not a replacement for it.

**Where data will arrive, the structure that will hold it renders first, empty.** The owner's
ruling of 2026-09-14: a screen that puts a sentence where its table, list or rail will stand
prepares nobody for what is coming and hides the shape a reader would use to spot a gap. The words
about the emptiness now live inside the structure's own empty state, and the structure stands from
the first paint.

Three design-system changes carry it. `EventRail` draws its frame with zero events — one hollow,
dashed marker where the first event will land and `emptyMessage` in the body beside it — and takes
a `note`, the one line a caller may hang beneath the events inside the frame for what the history
does not yet carry, instead of a paragraph loose on the canvas. `DefinitionList` is new: named
values, framed, with `DefinitionList.Row` drawing the table's empty-cell mark for a value not known
yet and `DefinitionList.Empty` as the row beneath the terms that the words about why go in.
`DataTable.GridFigures` takes a per-figure `scope`: a `whole-record` figure (a server-side count of
what is waiting, a total the loaded rows do not add up to) stands before the "In view:" sentence in
its own group, so a filter on the loaded rows never presents it as narrowed.

The gate is `pnpm run lint:structured-empty` (`tooling/lint-structured-empty/`), which reads a
Svelte file's markup tree for the two shapes the ruling named: a prose branch opposite a structure
in one conditional (and its `{#each}` and `{#await}` cousins), and a muted paragraph immediately
beneath a structure in the same block. It fires only where the prose branch's condition speaks of
absence, treats a non-breaking-space spacer as no prose, and takes an inline
`<!-- structured-empty-allow: <why> -->` whose reason sits beside the code it excuses; an allowance
that excuses nothing is itself a finding. The rule is recorded in `docs/conventions/ui-design.md`.

What it found, and what changed: the file inspector's Hashes tab, the speed test's server facts and
sample table, the matter status window's engagement list, the bill window's history and delivery
tabs, the trust-transfer dialog's ceiling, and the developer console's resource meters.

title: A document's details panel reads as tables, and a safety check can be run again
entry:
**The details panel's version history and safety history are `DataTable` grids, the Hashes tab
computes on entry for a chosen version and compares against a given digest, and a file can be
checked again.** `GET /api/v1/files/{id}/scans` reads a file's safety history off the audit log;
the commit, re-scan and quarantine audit rows now carry the verdict, engine and detail they
recorded, so each line keeps the engine that ran it. `POST /api/v1/files/{id}/rescan` enqueues a
`FileRescan` message the ingest consumer runs regardless of engine staleness and without the dedup
cache, keyed on the request's audit id, which its result row carries back. `fileIntegrity.verify`
accepts an optional `versionId`; `FileVersionItem` carries the scan facts. `safetyKeyOf` no longer
grades a missing document type as `info`, and the `untyped` issue kind is gone.

title: An upload is attributed to the member who made it
entry:
**Created By is no longer blank.** The file table's Created By column read from a resolver that
returned the empty string for every file (`file-manager.svelte`), because the file summary carried
no uploader at all — `file_version.uploaded_by` was written at reserve and never read back. The
list, the single-file read and the version history now project `uploaded_by` with the member's
display name off a `LEFT JOIN member` (`uploadedBy` / `uploadedByName` on `FileSummary` and
`FileVersionItem`); the column reads the name, the inspector gains a Created By row, and a departed
member's uploads keep their id and lose only the name.

title: A file the firm already holds is still filed, and a taken name is the reader's call
entry:
**A file the firm already holds is still filed, and a taken name is the reader's decision.** The
upload's hash check used to answer "the matter already holds these bytes" by filing nothing —
`already`, "Nothing was sent" — which turned an economy (do not send bytes the firm has) into a
policy (do not file what the reader chose). Owner ruling: the check is for storage and speed, never
a substitute for the upload. A match on the matter now takes the same path a match elsewhere did —
`uploads.duplicate` makes the new file server-side from the held version, `copiedFrom: "matter"` —
and the `already` outcome and stage are gone. What a duplicate does ask about is its NAME: a file
whose name is taken in the landing folder is filed under a numbered name by default, or, as the
reader chooses for the batch or per file, as the next version of the file that has the name
(`fileId` on the reserve, no hash question) or skipped (a `skipped` stage; nothing read, nothing
sent). The intake table gains a Name Taken column and menu, mirroring the document-type ones;
the queue resolves the clash against the destination's files before the digest is read.

title: An upload's safety check no longer waits on a cold scan instance
entry:
**An upload's safety check no longer waits on a cold scan instance.** The first real upload after the
readiness work landed, then sat at "Checking the file" for minutes: the scan worker picked a random
one of five container shards, four of which had scaled to zero, the engine answered 500 until clamd
had loaded its signatures, and the ingest queue's three immediate retries met the same cold shard
three times and dead-lettered the file until the five-minute redrive. Four changes: the scan
worker's warm-poke cron is on (the first firm is onboarded, which the config comment named as the
condition); a keyless scan routes to the warm primary shard, and the interactive ingest lane sends
no key (the bulk lane keeps its per-file key for the fan-out); the interactive queue waits one
second to batch rather than five and carries ten retries; and the consumer retries with a growing
delay rather than at once. The upload dialog says when the check is still running past the time it
waits, instead of reporting a finished upload the matter does not list yet.

title: The upload readiness report is the version panel's fourth section, not a modal
The mint-failure line names both tokens, and the runbook records what to do when a merge lands with no build
A queue id is the same queue with or without its hyphens
Retire the tasks stream's note
Retire the documentation-review stream's note
A refused notification rule names what the bucket holds
The documentation says what the repository does, and every finished stream's note is retired
entry:
**The documentation says what the repository does.** A review pass over the root and conventions
docs, changing only what could be verified against the code, the account or the git history: the
README's quickstart now gives the install order the root `CLAUDE.md` insists on (`pnpm install`
first, because `vp` is a devDependency) and the single-flight `pnpm test`; `CLAUDE.md` says that
`pnpm install` activates the tracked hooks through `postinstall` and that four packages, not three,
carry git-ignored WASM output; the maintenance runbook stops claiming the per-merge docs assembly
keeps the changelog current minutes after a merge (GitHub Actions has been blocked account-side since
2026-08-05, and 401 changelog fragments and 171 pending decisions are waiting) and stops saying the
docs-sync Routine has not been created (it was, twice); the documentation standard names the lint
rules that exist instead of a link checker and a changelog gate that do not; the conventions index
lists the four rulings ledgers and the engine-host seam it omitted and no longer calls `code-style.md`
and `typescript.md` stubs; the gate workflow's and the pre-push hook's comments stop describing
`git push main:release` as the only deploy; the roadmap stops placing the file-manager primitives on
a branch that no longer exists and stops saying Directory pronouns await a pull request; and the
relative links that broke when `apps/worker` became `apps/api-worker`, when decision fragments were
numbered, and when the calendar's time-zone module moved to `@magna-carta/civil-time` point at the
files again. Fifty-two `docs/active-work/` notes whose branches had landed are retired, with their
`status.d/` pointers cleared — twenty-seven of them the registry itself could not call landed from
the shallow clone a cloud session starts with, and could once the history was fetched in full —
along with the two July notes (`file-surface-web`, `slice-0-7b-app-shell`) whose streams the
notes themselves or the later auth-interface pull requests had superseded. The firm-usage stream's
one document that never reached `main`, the per-firm R2 bucket-isolation options brief that
`docs/specs/2026-09-01-per-firm-r2-bucket-isolation-review.md` reviews by path, is landed at the
revision that review read, and the download register's ledger evidence names the save-target seam
that is already on `main`.

title: The upload readiness check runs from the version panel, and a rule already in place is no longer called a fault
An upload that storage refuses can be diagnosed from one button, and a deployment cannot run the development adapter
entry:
**The deploy gate requires the Cloudflare provisioning credentials, and a firm's upload path can be checked from the server.** `wrangler.jsonc` adds `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN_FIRM_PROVISIONER` and `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` to `secrets.required`, so a deployment can no longer run the development provisioner (which records a bucket name and creates no bucket) or the development presigner against real firms. `apps/api-worker/src/files/upload-readiness.ts` verifies the six preconditions of the browser's direct-to-storage write in order — bucket recorded, bucket exists, ingest notification, expiry rules and CORS policy (each re-applied as a whole-set PUT), and a signed HEAD proving the S3 credential is honoured by the bucket (a 403 names the token scoped to one bucket and the re-mint) — and `POST /api/v1/firm/upload-readiness` runs it for the session's firm, audited, on `firm:manageScanPolicy`. The provider interface carries `kind` and `bucketExists` so the report states which adapter ran rather than inferring it. `GET /api/v1/meta/database-health` gains a `fileStorage` block — the upload path, the provisioning adapter, and the last readiness check read back from its audit row, never run — and the version overlay's Database section shows it as a fifth row. The first draft's deployment-mode object, startup refusal, daily sweep and firm-row cache were cut on the owner's ruling that best means easy to diagnose and not overcomplicated.

**Two defects found by reviewing the provisioning work against a fresh firm that still could not upload.**

**The runbook told the operator to create the R2 S3 token scoped to the platform bucket.** That
instruction is from 2026-06-22; per-firm buckets began being signed with "the same account-scoped
credential" on 2026-09-03, and nobody reconciled the two. A key scoped to one bucket cannot sign a
valid request for any other, so a token made to the runbook's instruction refuses every per-firm
presigned PUT with 403 — after the reserve has succeeded, which is exactly the shape the owner has
been seeing. The row now says "Apply to all buckets in this account", and says why.

**The reset script treated a bucket that was never created as a failure to delete**, which would have
blocked the whole reset behind every firm provisioned under the dev adapter (which records a bucket
name and creates nothing). A 404 on the listing now counts as already gone.

title: The front door asks less, and confirming is the way in
entry:
**The account door asks for an address and a password, and confirming mints the session.** The owner's 2026-09-09 pass over the deployed sign-in surface, recorded in `docs/conventions/design-corrections.md`.

`register-account-screen.svelte` drops the first and last name fields — `name` is now optional on `POST /api/v1/registrations` and the address is filed as `registration.display_name` where none is given, never a guess split out of the address — and gains a verify-password field gating the submit.

The confirmation handler in `routes/registrations.ts` now hands back a session: it inserts the `user` row unverified and calls Better Auth's own verify-email endpoint with a freshly minted token, under the new `emailVerification.autoSignInAfterVerification`, forwarding that endpoint's `Set-Cookie` onto its own 200. `next` gains a third value, `signedIn`, so the contract snapshot and the generated client move with it. A mint that does not happen flips `email_verified` directly and answers `signIn` — the credential is already committed, so the front door opens first try, and the account is never left in the one state `requireEmailVerification` refuses. Reasoning: `docs/decisions/pending/confirming-a-registration-is-a-sign-in.md`.

Around them: the persistent-session prop is `rememberMe` and reads "Remember Me"; `AuthPanel`'s `backLabel` names the destination rather than prefixing "Back to"; `check-email-screen.svelte` and `confirm-registration-screen.svelte` take that control instead of a foot button and nothing respectively; `reset-password-request-screen.svelte` loses its meta line; and `joining-choice-screen.svelte` loses its `name` prop with the greeting that used it.

title: Platform reset, a firm-resource manifest, and an object plane that stops carrying an account-wide key
entry:
**`reset-platform.mts` — the pre-launch clean slate, ordered so it cannot strand a resource.**

Destroying a firm's resources is not a fan-out, it is a sequence, because nothing outside the control
plane can enumerate what a firm owns: there is no API that lists Durable Object instances, and
`ai_search_instance` is deliberately the only index of the managed search instances
(control-plane-schema.ts: "Nothing ever calls the service's list operation"). Empty the control plane
first and every bucket and every search instance survives with nothing able to name it — still
running, still billed, against an account ceiling of 5,000 for the instances. So the control plane
goes last, and the script refuses to touch it while any search instance is still live, or if any
bucket failed to delete.

Three details worth keeping: the table list is read from `sqlite_master` rather than written down, so
a table added later cannot silently survive the wipe; each firm's key is crypto-shredded first,
because it is the one step whose value survives a later failure; and the firm databases themselves
are left unaddressed rather than wiped, since clearing Durable Object storage needs a route that
would outlive its one use. Dry run unless `--destroy` is passed AND the account id is typed out.

**A firm's objects are reached with a credential scoped to that firm's bucket, not one that reaches
every bucket in the account.**

A firm's bucket cannot be a binding, so the Worker signs S3 calls — and until now it signed them with
the parent R2 key, which addresses every bucket in the account for as long as it exists. That is
wider than the work: a request serving one firm's file has no business being able to address another
firm's bucket at all. `firm-bucket-credentials.ts` mints a credential derived from that parent,
scoped to one bucket, with a lifetime, and `object-read-write` rather than any admin permission — so
it cannot touch the bucket's own configuration either. A leak on the object plane now exposes one
firm for a window, where it used to expose the account.

The credential is a RESOLVER on `createS3FirmBucket`, not a value, which is what lets it be re-minted
mid-life without anything reconstructing the handle — and costs nothing, because every call there was
already awaiting a signature.

**The rule that is not obvious:** a presigned URL dies with the credential that signed it, whatever
its own `X-Amz-Expires` says, and R2's mint response carries no expiry at all — only the `ttlSeconds`
asked for. So the expiry is computed at mint time and every hand-out re-checks that the credential
outlives what is about to be signed with it, with margin. Skip that and a member gets an upload URL
good for an hour that stops working in four minutes, which reads exactly like the storage refusing
the upload and is diagnosed the same slow way.

Selection is by the presence of the provisioner's existing token — no new secret, and no code path
that only runs in production. Until it is set this behaves exactly as it did. A minting failure is
never answered with the parent key: falling back would make the narrowing decorative.

Still on the parent key: the PRESIGNER, which signs the URLs the browser follows. Same treatment,
plus `appendSessionToken` so the query-signed URL carries `X-Amz-Security-Token` — a separate change
because it is the browser-visible surface.

**`firm-resources.ts` — the one declaration of what a firm owns, because it cannot be discovered.**

A firm's record spans four things created at different moments by different code: control-plane rows,
a SQLite Durable Object, an R2 bucket, and possibly a managed natural-language search instance. None
of them can be enumerated from outside. There is no API that lists Durable Object instances, none
that maps a bucket back to its firm, and `ai_search_instance` is deliberately the sole index of the
instances. So the set can only be DECLARED, and anything missing from the declaration is invisible to
everything that walks it.

That is not hypothetical: writing the platform reset by hand missed the search instances entirely.
They would have been left running and unnameable against an account ceiling of 5,000.

Ordering is part of the declaration rather than a detail of any one caller. `destroyOrder` puts the
control plane last because it is the index of everything above it, and the tests pin the properties
that make a walk safe — control plane last, every orphanable resource strictly before it, positions
unique — so a caller that walks the list in order is correct by construction. Offboarding, a
data-subject export and the reset script read one list instead of three drifting copies.

What is not built yet, and is named in the file: a fitness scan that fails a per-firm resource
provisioning creates and the manifest never hears about, on the model of the PII/erasure registry's
attribution function.

title: Discovery searches its record and creates what it lists
entry:
**Discovery's three screens take the product's search and create controls, and the search is a real
one.** The register, a review set's document list and its Loads screen each shipped without
`ScreenSearch`; Loads carried a button per act — "New Custodian of Record" beside "New Load" — which
is the shape the standing list-screen ruling names outright, and the register listed corpora with no
way to start one.

**Every one of the three searches on the server, over the whole record.** A field that narrowed the
rows already fetched would have answered about the first page of a cursor-paged listing and read as
the whole of it, which on a corpus a firm certifies the contents of is the most expensive kind of
wrong. So the reads gained the parameter instead: `ReviewDocumentListFilters.search` over
`source_name` and `source_path`, the two review-set listings over `name`, and the loads listing over
`source_description`. Each is a LIKE scan placed AFTER every clause that can use an index — the
review-set predicate, the access predicate and the equality filters — so what it walks is one corpus
the member may see, stopped by the page limit; `likePattern` escapes the reader's own `%` and `_`
once, in one place, so a production whose files are named `100%_final` does not silently match
everything.

**The cost is measured rather than argued.** The load-profile harness runs both cases
(`discovery-review.list-page-by-name-search` and `-no-match`), and at the 250,000-document ceiling a
search that matches costs 0.4 ms — flat against the unsearched page, because the LIMIT ends the walk
— while one that matches nothing costs 62 ms, the pass over the review set. The plan is an index
search with no temporary sort at both volumes, which the existing fitness assertion there now holds
for the search too. Both numbers sit in the read that pays them, so the day one of them stops being
acceptable the answer is visible: the review set's own search index, not an index on a column a
leading wildcard cannot use.

**On the document list the search is a CRITERION, not a control beside them.** It is a built provider
in `criteria.ts` like every other narrowing, so it rides the address — a searched queue is a link a
supervising attorney can send — it composes with the Custodian, load, family, state and exception
filters as an intersection, and a bulk coding act over the result works unchanged, because what it
holds is a criteria set rather than a page of identifiers. Providers gained `setFrom` for the two
whose control is not the popover (the family, named by opening a document; the search, set in the
action row): they still render there, saying where they are set and offering the way to clear them,
because that popover is the one control answering "why is this list short".

**Keyword stays a separate criterion, and the difference is now legible on screen.** Searching what a
document is CALLED composes into this listing; searching what is INSIDE it composes into the review
set's own index, is still `soon`, and sits next to the name search in the Narrow control so a reader
choosing between them can see which is which.

**Loads' two buttons are one `CreateControl`** reading the bare "New", each choice carrying its own
refusal, and its "Each Load" panels follow the table rather than the read. **The register creates
too**: it shipped read-only on the reasoning that a create control would have to ask which matter
and would therefore be the matter's screen in disguise, which the Conflicts Check ruling settled the
other way a day later — `NewReviewSetDialog` now takes `chooseMatter` and asks, over the caseload,
exactly as the conflicts composer does from its own two doors.

title: A firm can say yes to a model, and mean two things by it
entry:
**The assistant has been reachable since the interface landed, and every firm's copy of it said the
same thing: one of two gates is shut. Nothing could open either one. `magnus.enabled` and
`inference.aiProcessingEligibility` had a reader, a fail-closed resolver and a re-read before the
model call, and no writer but the settings write path — so the honest closed state the surface
renders was also a state a firm could not leave.** Settings · AI and the Assistant is that writer:
`apps/web/src/routes/(app)/settings/ai` over `GET`/`PATCH /api/v1/firm/ai/settings`
(`apps/api-worker/src/routes/firm-ai-settings.ts`), audited on the write.

**Two switches, because they are two questions, and the page refuses to collapse them.** The outer
one asks whether this firm's content may be sent to a third-party model at all; the inner one asks
whether the free-form assistant is one of the things that may send it. A firm that enabled inference
for drafting has not consented to an assistant, and a firm that switches the assistant off has not
withdrawn consent for everything else — `apps/api-worker/src/magnus/consent.ts` has always read both
and failed closed on either, and the screen now asks both in the same shape. It also states the
**effective** answer over the staged values, in a sentence: an assistant switched on above a closed
processing gate does nothing at all, and a screen that showed only "Magnus: On" would be telling an
administrator it works.

**`firm:manageAiSettings`, Owner/Admin alone, and deliberately not `magnus:converse`.** The
conversation key already seeds to Attorney and Paralegal, because asking the assistant a question is
ordinary work. Deciding for the whole firm that privileged client content may leave the platform is
not, and reusing the work key would have let any seat that can ask decide that asking is allowed. The
route test seeds exactly that member and asserts 403 on the read and the write alike — the same
bracket, and the same test shape, that `firm:manageScanPolicy` and `firm:manageReportPolicy` sit in.

**The model is stated and cannot be selected, and that is the design rather than the unfinished part
of it.** Consenting to third-party processing without being told which model receives the content,
what it retains, and whether it trains on it, is consent to nothing legible — so the page reports
`inference.primaryReasoningModel` with its pinned snapshot and both confidentiality facts, as
reported facts in the Versions page's definition-list voice, never as dead controls. The route accepts
no model field. A dropdown would have cost something invisible: an unconfigured firm follows the
platform's reasoning tier and moves forward with it, while a firm holding a model id keeps that choice
forever, so writing an id on the firm's behalf would silently convert "follow the platform" into
"pinned to today's occupant of it". That control wants a setting that can express the tier.

**The seam is asserted, not assumed.** The test that matters is the last one: the two gates this
screen writes are read back through `resolveMagnusFirmGates`, in all three of its states. A settings
screen that wrote keys the resolver did not read would look exactly like a working one and do nothing,
and that failure is invisible from either side alone.

**One shared registry change.** `SettingKind` gains `number` — a bounded integer field for the
assistant's daily question ceiling — and its bounds are **required** rather than optional, checked by
`apps/web/test/settings-mode-purity.test.ts`: a numeric field with no stated ceiling renders as one
that will take anything and be refused by the server, which teaches the wrong thing about what a firm
may choose. `SettingValue` widens to carry a number rather than stringly typing one, so no staging
boundary compares `"500"` against `500`.

title: A session can be ended, on this device and on the others
entry:
**You can sign out — and sign out of your other devices.**

`Sign out` in the profile menu was the last control left over from before accounts existed: a session could be started and never ended. It ends the real session now, and it leaves by loading a fresh page rather than navigating within the application, so nothing the session had read stays behind in the tab for the next person at that computer. A sign-out that does not go through says so and keeps you where you are — the one thing worse than not signing out is believing you did.

**Account → Active Sessions** is a new section beside Profile and Security: every computer and phone signed in as you, one row each — the device, when it signed in, the address it signed in from, and when it expires — with the one you are reading on marked and left alone. Sign out of any of them, or **Sign out everywhere else** in one go, which is the right move when you cannot tell which row is the intruder. The screen states the one thing that would otherwise be discovered the hard way: a device signed out here can take up to five minutes to be turned away, so somebody who thinks their account is compromised is told to change their password as well.

Two facts the screen deliberately refuses to state. It shows no "last used" time — the record knows when a session STARTED and not when it was last active, and a stamp that read as the second while meaning the first would have people clearing rows that were in use. And a browser it cannot identify is listed as unrecognised rather than guessed at.

Under it: `logout` and `session.revoked` join the control-plane audit trail, decided by the endpoint the session was deleted under rather than by the deletion itself — sweeping an expired session and the rotation that happens when a second factor is enabled both delete a session row, and neither is somebody leaving. And Better Auth's session-freshness dial is turned off, because in the pinned version it gates the listing and none of the writes: left at its default it would have hidden the signed-in-devices screen from anybody signed in longer than a day, which is exactly the long-lived session the screen exists to let somebody find and end.

title: The Upload panel asks one question fewer, and reads before it sends
entry:
**The Upload panel, after the owner's 2026-09-08 round, plus the diagnosis behind it.**

The Add menu becomes one press (files; the folder ask rides a chevron on the same control, because
no engine offers a picker taking both). Where the File System Access pickers exist they replace the
hidden `<input>`s, so choosing a folder no longer makes Chrome raise its own "Upload N files to this
site?" over the panel. The batch-wide document type is gone: it is a column on the source table set
on the selected rows, so `UploadBatchPlan` carries `documentTypeIds` keyed by intake key rather than
one id. "On Arrival" is a folded **Advanced Settings** accordion holding the dating basis and a new
`checkDuplicates` setting. `DataTable.ClearFilters` joins the panel's control row, which is the one
table companion the source table lacked.

Hashing moves out of the upload lane into a new register, `upload-digests.svelte.ts`: reads start
when a file is CHOSEN, run one behind another (there is one worker), are memoized per intake key,
and report to a caller that arrives mid-read from wherever the read has got to.
`UploadQueueDependencies.hash(file, …)` is therefore replaced by `digest(entry, …)` — the seam any
stand-in for the queue's network implements. The pace line beside the progress bar takes a fixed
measure from the new `size.transfer-pace` token, so a changing byte count no longer resizes the bar.

The failed upload in the owner's log was the CORS signature from §15 of the operations runbook — a
201 reservation, no part calls, an abort seven to nine seconds later (the retry ladder), and no
Worker-side error at all, because the refusal happens between the browser and the bucket. That
signature is now written into the runbook, and a transport failure on the byte write says the
storage did not answer rather than the flat "nothing answered" that sent readers to check their own
connection.

title: Every date is typed into the same field, and the wrong-day bug's second spelling
entry:
**Six more surfaces named the wrong day, and the gate that missed them now reads the argument rather than the operation.** "Opened", "Closed" and "On hold since" on the matter overview; "Created" and a credit note's "Opened" on the invoice window; "On hold since" on the matter status dialog.

All six passed a stored instant to `formatDate` — with no slice anywhere, which is why the rule written last round did not see them. `formatDate` pins to UTC deliberately, because a recorded day must not move under the reader; hand it a moment and that pinning is exactly what makes the wrong answer silent rather than loud. `matter.openedAt` is written as `openedAt: now` beside `createdAt: now` from the same clock, so the matter overview named the following day for every matter opened after late afternoon in an American office.

The lesson is the rule's, not the six sites'. Slicing was only ever one _spelling_ of "take the day of an instant"; the rule now keys on the argument's name — the `At` suffix this codebase uses consistently enough that the schema's column scan relies on the same convention — and deliberately says nothing about `validFrom`/`validTo`, which are dual-shape by design, or anything ending `AtTime`, which is a wall clock.

**And the seam that made all ten possible is now one.** Seven print sheets each declared their own formatting context, with the date parameter named `isoDate` in five and `civilDate` in two. That disagreement was a record of nobody being sure what the function took. `apps/web/src/lib/print-sheet/` declares the pair once — `date` for a day the firm wrote down, `instantDate` for the day a moment fell on — and a supplier calls `printSheetDates()` instead of wiring two closures, so it cannot wire them to the wrong pair. Nine suppliers collapsed to that one call.

The calendar entry sheet keeps its own `date`, because it prints "Tuesday, September 15, 2026" and that is a genuine per-sheet choice; it takes `instantDate` from the shared set like everything else.

**Every date on the platform is now entered through one control.** Sixteen surfaces held a native `<Input type="date">`; all sixteen are the design system's `DatePicker`, and `pnpm run lint:date-handling` fails a native date field wherever it is written — the design system included. There is no allowance list any more: it is empty and a test asserts it stays empty.

It had been recorded rather than failed, because whether the native control was good enough for some fields looked like a design question with real trade-offs. It was not one. The design system's own notes had already called the native date types "a thin interim", and only the component can carry a firm-configured week start or a locale-aware week — the native `type="week"` is hard-locked to ISO 8601, Monday-start, not configurable. Two controls also meant two behaviours on the same screen, and the split was quietly growing: it reached sixteen entries on a merge while the gate stayed green.

Three things had to exist first. The picker gained the Input's own `size` scale, imported rather than redeclared, so a date field and the text field beside it can be set to one row height — that is what let a column's date-range filter, two boxes inside a menu, keep its compact geometry. It gained an `aria-label` that reaches the segment group: the property spread goes to a root element that renders no DOM, so an `aria-label` written the obvious way disappeared without a warning and left the field unnamed. And the conversion between the picker's value and the `YYYY-MM-DD` text a record holds moved to sit beside the picker, because a design-system component cannot import an app; screens still reach it at the same import path.

One thing was given up, recorded here so it is not rediscovered as a defect: the invitation screen's birthdate field carried `autocomplete="bday"`, and a browser fills a birthday only into a native date input it recognises as one. The picker has no `name` or `autocomplete` to pass through, so that date is typed now, like every other one.

Two smaller repairs came with it. `startOfCivilMonth` joins `endOfCivilMonth` in `@magna-carta/civil-time`, so the draft-bill dialog's billing period starts from the month's parts instead of `` `${today.slice(0, 8)}01` `` — correct, unreadable, and one edit from being a day out. And the `FieldRow` catalog specimen now holds a real date field, which makes it the specimen for the one thing the two label recipes have to agree on: they must measure the same, or a date field starts a few pixels below the fields beside it.

title: Retire the call log's third-review-round note
The notification centre and the live bell, over the read API that had no caller
entry:
**The notification centre and the live bell** — the two screens that were still `awaiting-screen`
over a read API that had shipped with no caller.

`apps/web/src/routes/(app)/notifications/+page.svelte` replaces the stub with the real feed: cursor
paged through the shared `PagedList`, narrowed by state and category as QUERY parameters so a
filtered read is cheaper rather than merely shorter, settling a row on follow and dismissing
separately, and reporting what the retention sweep took while unread. The top-bar bell became
`$lib/notifications/notification-tray.svelte` beside the download and upload trays, over a shared
count (`$lib/notifications/unread-count.svelte.ts`) polled slowly and on focus, paused while the page
is hidden, and never cleared by a failed read. The preference matrix at `settings/notifications` landed
from the settings stream while this was in flight and stands as it is; what this branch does there
is give its vocabulary and its transport one home each (`category-vocabulary.ts`,
`preferences-api.ts`) rather than the second copy this branch had grown independently.

A notification row carries no sentence, so the card is composed on the client from the kind and the
declared facts (`$lib/notifications/notification-presentation.ts`). A kind that module has no entry
for renders as its category's own noun rather than being dropped: a client that shipped before a type
did must not swallow a notification somebody was meant to see.
`apps/web/test/notification-presentation.test.ts` scans the server's registry as text — apps/web does
not depend on `@magna-carta/notifications` and should not start — and fails when a registered kind has
no words here.

**One contract gap closed.** `POST /api/v1/notifications/read-all` requires a `throughCursor` naming
the newest row the member saw, and no route handed one out: `nextCursor` names the page's OLDEST row
and is null exactly when a member's whole backlog fits on one page. The subsystem's own test minted
the cursor by hand, which is why nothing had noticed. The feed page now reports `readThroughCursor`
beside `nextCursor`, and that test uses it, so the encoding stays in the one module that owns it.

title: One window records a call and reads one, and every call carries a number
entry:
**Recording a call and reading one are the same window, because there is no reason for two.** A call
was recorded in an action dialog and read in a record window. Both rendered the same fields through
the same component, and both disagreed about everything around those fields: one had tabs and the
other did not, one printed and the other did not, one called its commit Save under a heading and the
other under an action bar. Two surfaces for one record is two things for a reader to learn and two
places for the next field to be added to only one of. There is one now, and the only difference
between its states is whether it opened with a record in it — a new one opens straight into the
fields, asks where it belongs, and carries the number it is about to be given.

**A call's length is typed, and it is allowed to disagree with the clock.** The round before this one
worked the duration out from a start and an end, which is right until somebody is put on hold: an
hour on the line and twenty minutes of call are two true facts about one call, and computing either
from the other asserts they are the same number. `communication.ended_at` is now stored beside
`duration_seconds`; the length is typed and reads `20`, `45m`, `1h 5m` or `1:20`; and an end fills an
EMPTY length and never overwrites one somebody wrote. Where the two differ, the form and the record
say both, so the gap reads as the hold it is.

**Every call and text carries a number a person can say out loud, and it exists before the record
does.** `2026-09-08-0042` — the day it happened, and that day's own sequence. A handle is what the
platform joins on; it is not something a receptionist can write on a message slip or read back down a
telephone, and a call is quoted out loud more often than any other record a firm keeps, because the
person on the other end of it is still on the line. So the window shows the number the next record
for that day WOULD draw, before anything is saved, and says that it is a preview rather than a
reservation; the record's own number replaces it the moment there is a record. The migration that
adds the column numbers every row already on the table, so the log has no rows without one.

The sequence is the shared counter idiom (`@magna-carta/sequence-numbering`) with one departure worth
naming: it has **no allocation table**. The general warning that a unique index on a rendered number
cannot stand in for one is about schemes carrying a segment that varies within a counter scope, and
this scheme carries none — the day IS the scope key — so two draws that observed the same value in
one day render byte-identical strings and the partial unique index aborts the loser exactly as an
allocation primary key would.

**The description is the row's second line rather than a column.** It is prose, and usually longer
than every other fact on the row put together, so as a column it was either truncated to a few words
— which is not a description — or wide enough to push the facts off the screen. It has the row's full
width underneath the facts now, through the one table's own row-detail, which is the same mechanism
the time sheet's description already sat in.

**Digits past the end of a phone number are an extension, not a formatting failure.** `AsYouType`
stops formatting silently once the digits exceed what a country's numbers hold, so typing a direct
dial onto the end of a number turned `(312) 555-0148` into a run of fourteen digits under the cursor.
The overflow now rolls into an extension the shared phone field owns, and the split is the longest
prefix libphonenumber calls possible rather than the country's digit count — so a North American
number typed with its trunk 1 is not cut a digit short. The two halves store as one string,
`+13125550148x4102`, which the formatter reads back into both. The Directory's contact rows had built
their own extension input beside the shared field; they use the field's own now, which is the last
half of that pair that was still built twice.

**And an intake starts from the form, not only from a record.** Save And Start An Intake records the
call first and hands the saved row up — an intake with no account of the call that caused it is what
the control exists to prevent. The provenance tab is a History rail, in the shape every other record
window uses.

title: Reports has a screen: two screens over one registry, the trust-compliance pack wired, its three questions decided
entry:
**The report screen, as two screens over one registry.** `/reports` lists every report the platform
declares, grouped by family, from `apps/web/src/lib/reports/report-registry.ts`; `/reports/<id>`
draws a report's controls from its declaration (a period on every report, a knowledge instant on a
bitemporal one, a trust account where the report is about one, the report's own options), reads
through the declaration's port when the scope is complete, and renders the answer as titled sections
of tables whose shape is the tabular export document's, so the export menu takes every report with
no per-report code. The scope rides the address. The trust-compliance pack is the first report wired;
the financial, productivity and operational families are declared at stage `soon`, visible and
disabled in the catalogue with what each waits on. A presenter computes nothing, and its test says
so. Adds `GET /api/v1/trust/accounts` (cursor-paged, `trust:read`), the one listing of a firm's
trust accounts, which the trust ledger's `account` gap has been waiting on; the ledger's wiring is
left to its own stream. Design: `docs/specs/2026-09-07-report-screen-design.md`. Sidebar row flipped
to shipped.

**The three questions the screen flagged, decided and built in the same stream.** The account
picker names `trust:read` in the refusal sentence when a member holding only the report key hits
it. The knowledge instant is the end of the chosen day in the zone of the office that holds the
account (the trust listing now carries `timeZone`, resolved through `timeZoneForLocation`), and
changing the account keeps the day and moves the instant. What the pack lists is a firm policy:
`firm:manageReportPolicy` (seeded to Owner/Admin), `GET`/`PATCH /api/v1/firm/reports/policy`
(audited), the pack route defaulting from it, Settings › Practice › Reports over the calendar
settings page's server-backed draft pattern, and the two selects gone from the run screen.

title: A failing migration names itself and the statement that failed
entry:
A migration that fails now says which migration and which statement, instead of only what SQLite thought of it.

Two outages ran on one sentence — `FOREIGN KEY constraint failed` — and that sentence is identical for every migration in the lineage and every statement inside each one, so it locates nothing. The runner had both facts in hand at the moment it threw and discarded them with the error it re-raised. A failure now reads `<tag> statement 5/9 [DROP TABLE matter] FOREIGN KEY constraint failed`, with the identity first so it survives the bounded field it surfaces through, and the statement collapsed to its opening keywords, which is what tells `DROP TABLE` apart from an `INSERT INTO role_permission`.

The health read's fault line is bounded longer than a logged message head to match. `MESSAGE_HEAD_LENGTH` is sized for a log line, where the same fault repeats across entries and the tail is recoverable from any of them; this is one line on screen for a fault a reader cannot get at any other way, and 120 characters cut it off before the part that identifies anything.

title: Retire the messaging stream note
Messaging is calls and texts — and the visibility gate a caller could neutralize is fixed at its source
entry:
**The sidebar's Messaging row is calls and texts, and the four things wearing that name are down to
one.** The row had an id meaning the whole three-channel Communications layer (`communications`), a
label meaning one channel (Messaging), and a description meaning two ("Client and portal messages") —
while the matter section wearing the same label described a fourth thing again, the client portal's
`comment`/`message` grant capability. Nothing in the tree agreed, and every future reader of either
registry would have had to guess. The owner settled it on 2026-09-07: **Messaging is voice and
SMS/MMS** — the two channels ADR-0047 already decided and neither of which has a line of code — for
logging what occurs, routed through the carrier so the logging happens by itself, with recording and
transcription over the voice half.

**Email is refused from the row on purpose, and the refusal is argued rather than assumed.** The case
for folding it in is real: captured mail that routes to no matter lands unrouted today —
`apps/api-worker/src/emails/capture-consumer.ts` says so outright — and **no screen anywhere in the
product shows those**, so mail is being captured into a place nobody can look at. It loses anyway,
twice. Email already has a home the platform deliberately does not replace: the whole posture is
_file from the mailbox into the matter_ — the add-in's pane, the forward/CC capture address, the
auto-file rules — so a row that opens a mail list competes with the client the member already has
open. And calls and texts have no other home at all; there is no mailbox for the firm's SMS number,
and a phone call leaves no artifact unless the platform makes one. The verbs are different —
_route what exists_ against _cause a record to exist_ — and one row cannot carry both. The unrouted
mail gap survives as an open question rather than being quietly absorbed.

**The design names the log as the durable thing and the carrier as a producer into it**, which is
what takes the surface off the vendor's critical path. One `communication` record — channel,
direction, counterparty, member, nullable matter, instant, duration, body, attachments in per-firm
R2 — written by three producers in the order they can be built: a member logging a call by hand, the
Telnyx adapter writing the same row from a signed webhook, and transcription enriching a row that has
a recording. A2P 10DLC registration is weeks of procurement lead time by ADR-0047's own account and
gates only the second of those, so the record model and both screens are blocked on nothing.

**The global row and the matter section are split by one sentence: the global row holds the
unassigned and the cross-matter, the section holds the assigned and the case-bound.** An inbound text
from an unrecognised number belongs to no matter, which makes filing a conversation onto a matter an
act that exists only globally; inside a matter the reverse act exists (unlink, as filed mail already
has) but routing from scratch does not. The gate is where they actually diverge: a section inherits
the matter's own access, while the global screen must narrow routed rows to matters the member may
see before anything hydrates — the email add-in's suggestion ranking is the precedent to reuse — and
unrouted rows, having no matter, fall through every matter-based gate and need a permission of their
own rather than "any member may read the firm's inbound traffic."

**Recording is sequenced last for a legal reason, not a technical one.** ADR-0047 gates call-recording
consent on the jurisdiction-profile machinery — roughly a dozen states require all-party consent where
Nevada requires one — and that machinery is still in design. Text logging, manual call logging and
carrier call _metadata_ carry no such gate; the audio does.

**And it is built, not only designed.** One per-firm `communication` row behind
`@magna-carta/communications` and seven operations; the firm-wide `/communications` screen and the
matter's Messaging section over ONE listing component, so the section cannot drift from the log it is
a view of; the section off `soon` with a search source, a timeline source and a create noun, which
answers all three coverage lints rather than deferring them; the destination flipped to `shipped` at
`alpha` in the same commit as the screen, per the registry's own rule. The audit log carries
identifiers, enums and instants and never the words or the number, asserted by a test rather than
trusted. 45 tests.

**Building the gate found a real hole in it.** `readRoutableMatter` selected from an unaliased
`matter`, and the visible-matter predicate composes as `EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM matter WHERE matter.id
= <expression> …)` — so the subquery's table shadowed the outer one, the correlation degenerated to
`matter.id = matter.id`, which is true of every row, and the anchor check silently passed **every
matter in the firm**, the platform-owned custody holding matter included. The outer table is now
aliased `anchor`, and the test that caught it is kept beside the one that proves an unrouted row is
unreachable by id without the capability. Anything else composing this predicate over `matter` itself
is exposed the same way.

Five open questions for the owner remain, including where portal secure messaging now lives and where
the unrouted **email** queue does — the one part of the cross-channel argument that survives the
refusal above, and still the one screen the product does not have.

**The firm's matter-visibility gate could be silently neutralized by the caller's own table names, and
the fitness functions that exist to guarantee it could never have caught that.**

The predicate every matter-scoped read composes is an `EXISTS` over `matter`, correlated to an
expression the caller supplies. Written against the bare table name, the correlation dies whenever
the CALLER's query also has an unaliased `matter` in scope: inside the subquery `matter` resolves to
the subquery's own copy, the correlation degenerates to `matter.id = matter.id` — true of every row —
and the `EXISTS` is satisfied by any visible matter in the firm rather than by the one being checked.
The gate reads exactly like a working gate and checks nothing.

**It shipped.** The call and text log's anchor check selected from `matter` and composed the
predicate over its own id, so it accepted every matter in the firm, the platform-owned custody
holding matter included. It was caught by a behavioural test asserting that holding matter is
unreachable — not by anything looking at the SQL, and not by any of the three fitness functions whose
whole purpose is this predicate. They assert the predicate's MARKER appears in the built statement,
and it did: the predicate was composed, it was composed uselessly, and a test looking for evidence of
composition cannot tell those two apart.

**Fixed at the source rather than at the call site: the subquery now aliases its own table.** A
caller's `matter` can no longer be shadowed, so an expression naming `matter.id` correlates to the
caller's row — which is what every author writing one intends. The failure becomes unwritable rather
than merely tested for. The narrowed variant gets the same treatment, and there it matters more: that
is the shape an ethical-wall overlay takes when it is built, where a dead correlation would exclude
the wrong rows rather than merely fail open.

**Swept, and this was the only instance.** All 56 call sites of the predicate were checked against
the two conditions the bug needs — the predicate composed, and an unaliased `matter` in the caller's
own FROM or JOIN. No timeline or search source is exposed: none passes `matter` as its `from`. Two
hand-written `EXISTS` clauses over `matter` exist, in the task list and the notification feed, and
both correlate against a different table, so both are sound.

Three regression tests, each verified to fail against the old predicate, including one that reads
real rows and watches the holding matter leak. The calendar's schema-name scanner now knows the
alias, with the reason attached, so nobody removes it to quiet the scan.

title: Production stack frames name the source file, line and function
entry: **Production stack frames name the source file, line and function.** The web build now emits source maps without the source text (`sourcemapExcludeSources`) and stops renaming identifiers (`mangle: false`, compression and whitespace removal kept), on both the page build and the Web Worker build in `apps/web/vite.config.ts`. The sign-in crash was diagnosed from `De.get (naXSyiPE.js:5:816)`, which says nothing; the minifier's map does not record the original of a renamed identifier, so a map alone left the `De`. `magna-carta-web` is an assets-only Worker, so the `.map` files are public assets: carrying mappings and paths but no text, a fetched map gives away no code and no comment. Measured cost on the day's build: 897 KB to 1.12 MB gzipped over the whole app, a fraction of that per chunk.

title: Retire the page-inset stream
The one page inset, held by a gate; and the task list searches through ScreenSearch
entry:
**Three screens drew a second page inset inside the App Shell's own.** Tasks, Time and Magnus each
wrapped themselves in `p-24` while `<main>` already carries it, so all three sat 48px from the chrome
where every other screen sits 24px. Each was written from a copy of the last, which is how one
mistake became three. The wrappers now match the rest of the app (`flex h-full min-h-0 flex-col
gap-16`), and Tasks and Magnus trade a `flex-1` that did nothing under a block container for the
`h-full` their lists need to hold their vertical space.

**`pnpm run lint:page-inset` now holds the line.** A fitness function over the route tree: for every
screen that renders into the App Shell's `<main>`, no top-level element may carry a uniform padding
(`p-*`, or a whole axis as `px-*`/`py-*`) or an inert `flex-1`. It derives both premises from the
shell's own markup rather than hardcoding them — that `<main>` pads itself, and that it lays out no
children — and fails on the premise if either stops holding, so it can never go on enforcing a rule
whose ground has moved. A one-sided padding is deliberately left alone: the home screen's closing
quote takes `pt-12` off its own `border-t`, which is spacing between the things on a screen and not
an inset. It reads the markup with a scanner rather than a pattern, because the time sheet declares a
snippet as `{#snippet cell({ row }: GridCellContext<TimeEntrySummary>)}` and a pattern reads that
type argument as an opening tag that never closes — which made the first draft of this scan report
the page clean. The rule is recorded under _Spacing and rhythm_ in
`docs/conventions/design-corrections.md`.

**The task list searched its own way.** It carried a hand-rolled `Input` with a leading Lucide
`Search` icon, a labelled box permanently occupying the control row, and a private 250ms debounce —
the exact defect `ScreenSearch` was built to end, and the reason its own header says a screen that
hand-rolls a search box is one. It now uses `ScreenSearch` with `searchOn="pause"`, which brings the
rest of the standing rules with it: the control rests as an icon and costs the row no vertical space,
opens focused into the field, keeps an accent hairline and an X while a query is live, and answers
Escape. The control row follows the ruling that the search and the create control travel together,
search first — search, New Task, then the clear-narrowing control as a `FunnelX` icon carrying a
summary of what it will undo, in place of the old text "Clear" button. Both surfaces on the shared
list move together: the member's own work list and the matter's Tasks section.

title: One heading for all three sections, and pills that count
entry:
The version panel's three carets are one component, and a shut heading says what it hides.

The three sections each computed their own collapsed badge, and the differences had stopped being decisions. Deployment carried a count of Workers without a version and dropped the sync read entirely — so folding it hid whether the two Workers serving the app agree, which is the one fact a reader opens that section for. Workers carried the same warning with no sense of how many Workers were behind the fold. Database carried a mood, "Needs attention" or "Not working", with no count at all, so one bad row out of four and four bad rows read identically. And all three said nothing whatever when healthy, which looks exactly like a section that never loaded.

The heading is now one component every fold renders through, and all three hand it the same shape from the model: a **count** of what the fold hides, always, then a **status** pill only where there is something to say beyond the count. A count present when things are fine is what makes a quiet heading meaningful — "13 Workers" with nothing beside it is a section reporting health, where an empty heading was a section reporting nothing.

The wording changed with it. "Without a version" named the missing field rather than the condition, and reads now as "2 not reporting" — a reader wants to know the Worker did not answer, not which column is blank. The database mood becomes "1 not working" or "2 needs attention" against a "4 checks" count. Deployment's shut heading carries the sync read it used to lose: "3 parts · In sync".

`collapsedHealthBadge` and `summarizeSilentWorkers` are gone, superseded by the pill builders, along with the dead worst-reading derived they fed.

title: Foreign keys come off where SQLite honours the pragma
entry:
Table-rebuild migrations only believed they had disabled foreign keys, and a firm's database paid for it.

`PRAGMA foreign_keys` is a no-op inside a transaction — SQLite honours it only when no transaction is open, and reports success either way. Every rebuild migration writes `PRAGMA foreign_keys=OFF` in its own text, and the runner executes that text inside `transactionSync`, so enforcement was never actually off. A rebuild drops the old table, `DROP TABLE` on a parent with enforcement live fires a violation for every child row, and the migration failed with `FOREIGN KEY constraint failed` — taking the firm's whole database with it, because the per-firm lineage is applied in the durable object's constructor ahead of any read it serves.

It passed everywhere it was tested. A database with no rows has no children to orphan, and the test harness applied migrations in a bare loop with no transaction and no enforcement at all — so the one condition that triggers this could not arise. A harness that applies migrations differently from production is not testing the migrations, and it now applies them the same way: enforcement on, each migration in a transaction, the pragma toggled outside it.

The pragma moves to where SQLite honours it, in the migration target either side of the transaction, and is restored in a `finally` so a failed migration cannot leave enforcement off for the reads that follow. What that owes back is paid inside the transaction: `PRAGMA foreign_key_check` runs before the ledger row commits, so a migration that genuinely orphans a row now aborts and rolls back rather than committing a dangling reference for a later read to trip over. That is a stronger guarantee than the one the migrations thought they had.

The copy control also carries a faulted row's reason now, not just its status — a report that said "Firm database: Not answering" and stopped handed over the symptom with the diagnosis stripped out of it.

title: Retire the Magnus interface stream
Magnus gets its interface: one transcript surface, two homes
entry:
**The assistant's interface is designed, and the list endpoint can finally be asked for one matter's
conversations.**

Two places were reserved for Magnus and both were stubs: an announced sidebar destination at
`/magnus`, and a `soon` section on the matter strip. The reservation said where, and never what makes
them two places rather than the same page rendered twice. That is now written down in
[`docs/specs/2026-09-07-magnus-interface-design.md`](docs/specs/2026-09-07-magnus-interface-design.md),
and the answer is short: **the sidebar destination is a place, the matter section is a section of a
record.** The first is the member's own workspace across everything, where a new conversation starts
on no matter; the second is one matter's file of transcripts, where a new conversation starts on that
matter and the screen offers no picker. Both compose one conversation surface, on the Tasks precedent
— one component, two routes, neither knowing the other exists.

The difference is deliberately **not** a difference in what the assistant can see. The matter link
scopes the record and not the prompt, so a conversation filed on a matter puts none of that matter's
content into anything the assistant is sent. Standing inside a matter is exactly the context that
makes a reader assume the opposite, so the section states it in one line above the composer, and that
line goes away when context grants ship and not before.

`GET /api/v1/magnus/conversations` takes an optional `matterId`. Without it the matter's own surface
could not ask for its own conversations — the column has been there, indexed and populated, since the
record was built, and nothing could filter on it. It narrows; it never becomes a default, and absent
still means every conversation the other conditions allow rather than the ones on no matter.

**Magnus has an interface, in both of the homes it was always going to need.**

The assistant's backend has been complete and unreachable since it landed: the conversation record,
both fail-closed consent gates, the queue-dispatched path to an answer, the audit and the metering.
There was no way in. There are now two, and they are two on purpose.

**The sidebar's Magnus is a place** — the member's own workspace, every conversation they have had
across everything, newest first, each citing the matter its transcript is kept on when it is kept on
one. A conversation started here belongs to no matter.

**A matter's Magnus is a section of that record** — the conversations kept on that matter's file and
no others, where a new one is filed on the matter without the screen asking. It draws no header and
no way back, because the matter's own masthead and section strip are already on screen.

Both are one component read through two routes, on the Tasks precedent: a conversation looks and
behaves the same wherever it is opened, and neither screen knows the other exists. What differs is
what the place IS, not what it can do.

**The one thing the matter section says that the workspace does not** sits above its composer:
_Magnus reads only what you type in this conversation. Keeping the conversation on this matter's file
does not let Magnus read the matter: not its documents, not its calendar, not its parties._ Standing
inside a matter is exactly the context that makes a reader assume the opposite, and the matter link
scopes the record rather than the request. That line goes away when the assistant can genuinely be
given a matter to read, and not a day before.

**A member accepts a disclosure before their first question**, and it says the things a member — not
an administrator — needs told: what leaves the platform, that the assistant sees only what they type,
that it can do nothing but answer, that the transcript is a firm record readable inside the firm and
never by a client, and that it can be wrong, is not legal advice, and is theirs to verify. The
version accepted is recorded, so a change to what the assistant can see or do asks everybody again.

**Every state the record can actually reach is on screen.** The two firm-closed screens name which
consent is missing and who can change it, rather than offering a control the reader cannot use. A
question in flight shows its pending answer. Each of the five ways an answer can fail is said in
words a member can act on — the model was unavailable, the firm switched the assistant off while the
question waited, the day's allowance is spent, the message was too long, it was cancelled — and none
of them reads "something went wrong". An answer built from a shortened conversation says so, because
only the member can tell whether the dropped part mattered.

**The transcript reads as a record, not a chat window.** The new `Conversation` component in the
design system draws a speaker label over a body, hairline-separated, in the register the rest of the
