platform reads its records in — no bubbles, no avatars, no coloured alignment, no motion. It holds
no copy of its own.

Magnus stays **off until a firm turns it on**, and turning it on still takes the settings write path:
the firm-administrator enablement screen is the next piece. Until then every firm's Magnus renders
its closed state and names the gate.

title: The sign-in screen no longer crashes on its version chip, and a render crash draws the failure screen
entry:
**A render boundary in the root layout** (`apps/web/src/lib/diagnostics/render-boundary.svelte`): a throw while a route's components render now draws the standard failure screen with a client-minted Error ID, the breadcrumb, and the Reload and Report controls, instead of a blank page and a line in the console. SvelteKit's `+error.svelte` answers a failure inside `load` only; a render throw escaped the app's start as an unhandled rejection, which is how the sign-in screen's tooltip crash was found in the inspector rather than on the page. The hook and the boundary share `crash.ts` (the handle, the breadcrumb, the one development console line, the remedy steps), so the two crash screens cannot drift. The web test config gains what mounting the failure screen needs: bits-ui and its Svelte helpers inlined, the build identity defined, and `$app/state` aliased to a stub.

**The `Tooltip.Provider` moved from the app shell to the root layout**, so every route group sits beneath it. The version chip reached the signed-out surfaces on 2026-09-02 and brought a tooltip with it; a `Tooltip.Root` with no Provider above it throws (`Context "Tooltip.Provider" not found`) rather than rendering bare, and the only Provider lived inside the app shell, which the sign-in, password-reset and joining screens never mount. Clearing cookies and reloading therefore crashed the sign-in screen before it drew. The shell's own Provider is gone (one, at the root, is the design system's stated placement), and `apps/web/test/root-layout-tooltip-provider.test.ts` pins that a bare tooltip throws and the same tooltip renders beneath the root layout.

title: A document opens in its editor: one Open gesture, a new tab, and a text editor beside the Collabora frame
entry:
**The one Open gesture opens a document's editor, in a new tab.** The file manager's ruling that
"Open" is one gesture whose meaning is decided by the file has been built: `activate()` in
`file-manager.svelte` reads `openDestinationOf` (`apps/web/src/lib/documents/editable-documents.ts`)
and a word-processing or plain-text document with clean, committed bytes opens
`/documents/{fileId}/edit` through the `session` reason of the one new-tab gate; everything else
previews as before, and a withheld file previews the withholding. The screen behind that address is
new: for office formats it opens the editing session and loads the Collabora frame the way a WOPI
host must, by form-posting `access_token` and `access_token_ttl` into the iframe (the old unused
detail panel set the frame's `src` with no token and could never have rendered; it is deleted); for
plain text it reads the current version through the audited download path into an in-app editor
and saves through the upload ceremony as the next version (`text-document.ts`). The office frame
still fills only where the `magna-carta-edit` worker is deployed, which the screen states in
development; the text editor runs everywhere.

title: Retire the 2026-09-06 walk's stream note
The panel says why the database is not answering, copies the whole diagnosis, and Workers stands on its own
entry:
The database panel names the fault instead of only the symptom, and the docket stops rendering `[object Object]`.

A firm database bricked by a failing migration read as "Firm database: Not answering" and nothing more. The cause was in hand the whole time — the durable object throws a specific error, and the health read was catching it in a bare `catch` and discarding it — so a reader went to the logs for a fact the panel already held. The firm-database check now carries that message, scrubbed and bounded to the same length the error pipeline gives any `messageHead`, because a constraint failure names the constraint but a UNIQUE violation can carry the offending value out with it. Where the database gave no reason at all, the row says that plainly rather than implying none exists.

Separately, the docket's failure branch interpolated the failure RECORD into its Alert, so a reader got `[object Object]` where the sentence belonged — and no Error ID, which is the one thing that makes a report actionable. It goes through the standard failure surface now, which reads the problem's own detail, keeps this screen's words for when the server sent none, and carries both the correlation handle and the retry.

The version panel copies the whole diagnosis, from a control at the top, and Workers is a section rather than a drawer.

Copy sat at the FOOT of the Database section and put four health rows on the clipboard. A member reporting a fault therefore pasted the database's state and nothing about which build was serving it — the one fact that says whether a fix has even shipped yet — and copying part of the diagnosis reads exactly like copying all of it. The control is now at the top, where a reader reaches for it before scrolling past everything they wanted copied, and it takes the whole panel: this page's build, the API, every Worker the read named, and the database line. Multi-line, because a dozen facts on one line is a paste people summarize from memory instead. A Worker that reported nothing says so rather than going missing, since "absent from the paste" and "reported nothing" are different faults.

Workers has left Deployment and become a caret of its own, beside Deployment and Database. Nesting it made the fleet something a reader reached THROUGH the deployment, when in practice the two are asked about separately: "what build is live" and "is anything not answering" are different questions, and one of them was two folds deep. Each shut heading now counts only the Workers its own fold hides — one count across the whole read would have both headings claiming the same silent Worker.

Three source assertions that pinned the old shape were rewritten to the rules they were actually guarding, rather than to the layout that happened to satisfy them: section order is asserted over the markup instead of the whole file, and the refresh rule is that every gesture a person makes probes fresh rather than that there are exactly two such gestures. One of them required a hand-written `aria-busy` on the refresh control, which the later ruling that every loading state runs through one region forbids outright — the two rules contradicted each other, and the test was the older one.

title: The sidebar's utility tray has two ends
A colour scheme is not a colour: paint the root, and set the scheme before the stylesheet arrives
entry:
**The white flash between screens, the last two steps.** The document base landed the colour scheme and the root ink; this carries the same rule to the two places a flash survived it.

**A colour scheme is not a colour.** `color-scheme` buys the browser's own generic canvas for the mode, not the surface the product is drawn on — and against a 99% warm surface the light one reads as a flash to pure white, which is how the defect was reported. Every shell paints its background on an element inside the Svelte tree, so the canvas is what shows wherever that tree does not cover the viewport: the boot of a hard load, the frame where leaving the workspace for Account or sign-in swaps one shell for another, an overscroll, the scrollbar gutter. The root now takes `background-color` from `--mc-surface-default`, and a background on the root propagates to the canvas, so no unpainted layer is left to show through.

**A stylesheet cannot reach the window before it arrives.** `applyThemeToDocument` writes `color-scheme` as an inline style, mirrored in the boot script — the same fact `base.css` declares, written where a separate request has not landed yet. With `ssr = false` behind an `index.html` fallback the served document has an empty body until the application mounts, so that window is the entire boot, and the longest of the flashes.

Both are pinned: the root's paint joins the two facts already asserted in `document-base.test.ts`, the inline write joins the boot-script mirror, and `theme-preference.test.ts` holds it to moving with the dark class in both directions.

title: Downloads and Uploads move to the sidebar's footer utility tray
entry:
**Downloads and Uploads left the Workspace group for the sidebar's footer utility tray.** The
owner's ruling of 2026-09-07: the two transfer registers describe what the application is doing —
often both at once, since a download and an upload can run together — rather than naming a place in
the firm's work, so they belong beside Settings and Customize at the rail's foot and not among the
destination rows.

The mechanism is the registry's existing `footerPinned` tier, which until now held Settings alone:
`sidebarGroups()` and `sidebarEditingGroups()` already skip it, so marking the two entries takes
them out of the scrolling groups AND out of Customize mode in one move, with each row keeping
exactly one home. Both are `pinned` as well, so they are fixtures rather than stars — there is
nowhere else for them to be, and nothing to hide them from. A member who had arranged or unstarred
either one keeps a stale id in stored preferences, which `mergeGroupOrder` has always filtered
against the visible set, so no migration was needed.

The shell renders the tray from the registry rather than hand-listing icons, but states the ORDER
itself — Settings, Downloads, Uploads, then Customize — because Settings must lead: the collapsed
rail shows the tray's first icon and hides the rest, and the registry orders by where a destination
sits in the app, not by which icon survives a collapse.

The top-bar trays are unchanged, and the two levels are deliberately distinct: the tray beside the
timer is a summary with quick actions, the footer icon opens the full surface.

title: The owner's 2026-09-06 walk: the file manager's second search, the create verb, the header's hovers, the custody rail — and the colour scheme the document never had
entry:
**Three corrections from a walk of the deployed app.**

**The calendar makes things with New, like everything else.** The firm calendar's primary action was a hand-built dropdown reading "Record" — the product's one create control, re-implemented under a different verb — and it is `CreateControl` now, reading the bare "New" over "New Event", "New Deadline" and "New Firm Event". The matter's own calendar section had the same mislabel from the other side: it read "New Event" over a menu that also records a deadline. A control that opens a menu reads the bare "New" and the items carry the nouns; the section registry says which sections those are (`CREATE_SEVERAL_KINDS`), so the label does not change under the reader as the page mounts. Each kind wears the glyph it already wears wherever it is named — a calendar, a clock, a building — rather than a second choice made per menu. The gate that refuses a rival create button never walked the calendar's routes, which is how the hand-built one survived; it walks them now.

**The header's controls name themselves on hover.** Notifications, Time Sheet, Downloads, Build Information — one name each, through the design system's Tooltip. Three of the four had no hover text at all and the fourth explained what pressing it would do, so four controls in one band read as four kinds of thing. Where the control is already a popover's trigger the two share one button: `Tooltip.Trigger` now takes bits' `child` snippet, which app code could not reach before because bits-ui is importable only inside the design system.

**The custody register is one table at the full width.** The container tree down its left side is gone. It narrowed to a whole branch — a subtree read no column filter over loaded rows can express — and that did not pay for making this register read as a different kind of table from every other one; Location was already a set-filtered column, narrowed from its own header the way Status is. The server's subtree read stays in the API, and the holdings-by-location report stays with it, for the custody reports.

**Five corrections against the deployed file manager, one of which was never the file manager's.**

The toolbar's own search field is gone. The matter is searched from the matter header and nowhere else; this surface had a second field, and the ruling that put the search in the header predates the header having one. What reaches the file manager's Search Results view now is the query in the address (`?q=`), read the same way `?entry=` already hands a section a record, so a search still opens the view, losing it still leaves, and a search survives a reload.

The rail's "No folders yet" sentence is gone — the root row and the control that makes a folder had already said it. The table header menu's display settings moved out of the Columns submenu into the menu's own root: Columns holds columns, and a setting filed under a noun that does not name it is a setting nobody finds. The icon view's settings control moved to the LEFT of the list-or-icons swapper, so the swapper stops sliding sideways every time a reader changes view.

**The breadcrumb reading black in dark mode was a document-wide defect wearing a file manager costume.** The app declared no `color-scheme` and gave the root no text colour, so the browser painted its own light-mode system colours underneath every dark theme, and any element written without a colour took `canvastext` — black — however dark the band behind it was. The tokens were correct the whole time, which is why it looked like one screen's bug. `packages/design-system/src/lib/styles/base.css` declares both, in the `base` layer, imported by the app entry and the catalog preview alike; it also hands the browser the dark canvas behind an overscroll, dark scrollbars and dark form controls, none of which a token reaches. Measured before and after on the running app: an uncoloured element computed `rgb(0, 0, 0)` without it and the theme's ink with it.

title: A pull request opens with the questions its review asks
entry: **A pull request now opens with the questions its review asks.** `.github/pull_request_template.md` pre-fills every new pull request with the sections the conventions already require and previously left to memory: what and why, the Conventional Commits type, what reaches production at merge (migration, contract, binding), the documentation lanes with the exact fragment path each one takes, the local `pnpm test` result the 2026-09-03 ruling asks every description to state, and the golden rules a review most often catches late. The template links to `docs/conventions/documentation.md` and `documentation-style.md` for the standards rather than restating them, so it stays a layout and those files stay the home.

title: A matter still spelled `prospective` took its firm's whole database offline, and the reads that would have said so went with it
entry:
A matter still spelled `prospective` stopped its firm's database from migrating, and took every read and write in the firm down with it.

The matter status rename widened `matter_status_check` to the new vocabulary — `intake`, `consultation`, `open`, `closed` — and copied `status` into the rebuilt table verbatim, on the reasoning that no firm held a matter yet and nothing could still carry the old spelling. A deployed firm held one. The replacement's CHECK rejected the row, the copy threw, and the migration rolled back — cleanly, and then again on the next request, forever.

The blast radius is the part worth recording. The per-firm lineage is applied in the FirmDatabase durable object's constructor, under `blockConcurrencyWhile`, ahead of any read or write it serves. A migration that cannot complete therefore does not degrade a screen; it makes the firm's whole database unreachable. The reported symptom was an unrelated `GET /api/v1/meta/versions` failing, because by then every firm-scoped route was failing.

The copy now maps `prospective` to `consultation` — the same rung under its new name — and leaves every other status alone. The correction had to go into the migration itself: the runner stops at the first failure, so no later migration is ever reached, and the durable object cannot be opened out of band to repair the row by hand. It is safe to correct in place because the applied ledger is keyed by tag with no content hash, so a database that already applied the migration skips it and never re-reads the file.

The regression test seeds the old vocabulary and runs the lineage over it, which is the case that was never covered: the chain always did apply to an empty database, and that is exactly why the fault reached production.

The version and database-health reads no longer go dark when the firm database is the thing that is broken.

Both are firm-scoped, and the chokepoint resolves a firm by checking that the session's member row is active — a read against the firm's own database. When that database cannot be reached at all, the check does not answer, it throws, and every firm-scoped route answers 500. That includes the two routes whose entire subject is whether the firm database can be reached. An unreachable database took out the panel built to say the database is unreachable, and the reported symptom became an unrelated version read failing.

`RouteMeta` gains `firmDatabaseOutage`, defaulting to `"reject"` so every route that has not thought about it still fails closed: membership could not be verified, so no firm data is served. A route declaring `"tolerate"` is admitted with the context the control plane alone could build, and no permissions. Registration refuses that declaration alongside a named capability — permissions are read from the same unreachable database, so a route claiming one could not be honoured — which makes the misconfiguration a startup failure rather than a discovery during the outage it was written for.

Nothing is relaxed while the database is up: the member-active check runs exactly as before and a deactivated member is still absent. Nothing leaks while it is down: the reads that would carry firm data are the reads that cannot complete. The health handler already caught every probe and reported `unreachable` per check — it simply never got to run.

title: Time becomes a place you can go: the period ledger and the listing it needed
entry:
**The period ledger at `/time`, and the cross-matter listing that had to exist first.** The sidebar's Time row was an announced Soon stub for a structural reason rather than a cosmetic one: `GET /api/v1/time-entries` answered one timekeeper on one day, or one matter entire, and returned an empty list for anything else. The top bar's firm-wide Time Sheet was therefore reading nothing at all, and flipping `shipped` would have linked to a screen with no read behind it.

The third listing shape closes that: a `from`/`to` span of work dates across every matter, narrowable to one timekeeper, matter or status, cursor-paged on the same `(work_date, id)` key the per-matter read walks so a cursor means one thing on both. `listTimeEntriesInRange` in `packages/timekeeping/src/queries.ts`; one added index (`time_entry_work_date_index`), because the unnarrowed span had no work-date-leading index to ride.

A period naming no timekeeper asks for the firm's whole record and is gated on `time:viewFirm`; naming somebody else is gated identically. Defaulting an ungated caller to themselves was considered and rejected — a listing that silently answers a narrower question than it was asked is the defect the per-matter status default already was. A span that reads backwards is refused rather than swapped.

The screen reuses what the matter's Time tab already had: the one grid, the entry record window, the status register, and the scope arithmetic the Time Sheet uses (which gains last-week and the two month spans — one function, two menus). It adds a Matter column, resolved client-side against the firm's matters rather than denormalized onto the row, and the period totals. Deliberately no free-text search: the period pages, and a box covering only the loaded rows would report a word missing from a month it never read.

title: Retire the screen-header consolidation's stream note
Every main screen says its name the same way
entry:
**Every main screen states its name the same way, and the sidebar agrees with it.** The screens had
drifted into four ways of introducing themselves: Home greeted the reader with the time of day,
Notifications titled itself "Notification Center" while the sidebar row opening it said
Notifications, Downloads and Notifications each carried an eyebrow repeating their own title back,
and Conflicts Check, Tools, WHOIS Lookup and Assemble a document each carried a sentence under the
title restating what the title said. Matters, Directory and Custodian carried a title and nothing
else, because the ruling that got them there reached the list screens in 2026-08 and stopped.

Every main screen now takes the Matters shape — `ScreenHeader` with the destination's own name from
`navigation/destinations.ts`, no `eyebrow`, no descriptive `meta`. The rule is not new ("a heading
carries no explanatory sub-text"); it had only ever bound lists, and now binds every archetype,
recorded under a new "Screen headers" heading in
[`docs/conventions/design-corrections.md`](docs/conventions/design-corrections.md) and restated
on `screen-header.svelte` itself so the next author meets it at the call site. A meta line still
carries facts — Home's date, a room's kind and seat count, the speed test's run time, Assemble a
document's alpha badge — because the test is unchanged: removing the line must lose a fact.

**The `my-work` destination becomes `tasks`.** A matter's own section was already Tasks, so the
registry and the matter used two names for one noun. That screen also had no page heading at all —
its name was a `FieldLabel as="h2"` inside `TaskList`, so the route rendered no `h1` — and it now
carries a real `ScreenHeader`. `TaskList`'s `heading` turns optional for exactly that reason: a
matter's Tasks section still names itself, because the matter's masthead carries the matter's name,
while the firm-wide list lets the page's own header speak. `mergeGroupOrder` skips stored ids it no
longer knows, so a member who had dragged the old row to a custom sidebar position finds Tasks at
its canonical position and keeps the rest of their arrangement.

**What a header gives up, the page takes back.** Neither line that carried a real fact was deleted;
each moved to where the fact is used. The safe website viewer's isolation notice now renders in
`WebsiteShell`'s new `note` band, at the address bar beside the control it qualifies, yielding to
`invalidHint` because a fault with the address in hand outranks a standing fact. The seventeen
settings pages give up their masthead descriptor the same way: `SettingsMasthead` no longer takes a
`meta`, and the sentence renders through `settings-description.svelte` as the first line of the
page's own scroll area, so it travels with the plates it describes. `SettingsPage` still takes
`meta` and passes it there, so a standard settings page is unchanged at its call site.

**And the rule becomes a gate.** `pnpm run lint:screen-headers` (`tooling/lint-screen-headers/`,
nineteen unit tests) refuses an eyebrow on any screen, a destination screen titled something
`destinations.ts` does not call it, and a meta line that is fixed prose rather than a read value.
It earned itself immediately: the uploads screen landed on `main` mid-consolidation carrying
`eyebrow="Uploads"` over `title="Uploads"`, and the file workbench was found stating three fixed
sentences under its title — including the same "Runs outside any matter" removed from Tools — from a
header in `lib/` that the route-level pass never saw. Its privacy consequence now reads full width
under the header, where the narrow file rail could not have held it. Membership derives from the
`lint:*` scripts, so the scan joins both the inner loop and CI's governance job with no further
wiring.

The `tasks.my-work-*` load-profile measurement names are left alone — recorded measurements, not
user-facing text.

title: Matter file upload: the failing PUT fixed, the dialog rebuilt, hash-first dedupe, and the pace read as it goes
entry:
**Every production upload failed at the storage write, and a failed upload left an empty file on the
matter.** The reservation answered two spellings of one header — `Content-Type` beside the
presigner's own `content-type` — and the browser's `Headers` merges those into a single doubled value
(`application/pdf, application/pdf`), which is not the value the signature covers, so R2 refused the
PUT with a signature mismatch. The same-origin development route never checks the signature, so the
test pool passed throughout. `routes/uploads.ts` and the check-in route now pass the presigner's set
through untouched, the development presigner spells the same set, `putUploadBytes` collapses any
duplicate that slips through, and a route test asserts the set through `Headers` itself. A
reservation whose bytes never land is now given back: `uploadIntoFolder` and the document loop's
client abort the session on a failed PUT or complete (and on the refused oversize case), which
abandons the pending version and drops the row that used to sit in the list with no size.

**The Upload dialog is rebuilt as intake beside source.** The left pane is the intake — the
destination matter (a searchable picker defaulting to the matter on screen, `upload-matter-picker.svelte`),
the folder, how the files are dated (the file's own date, or the upload date) and the document type
they carry; the right pane is the source — the chosen files as the product's one grid
(`DataTable.Grid`), nested the way they sit on disk with folders that fold, filterable from the
header (a filter flattens to the matching files with a Folder column, the search-results rule), and
a Status column that carries each file's stage once the transfer runs. One **Add** control offers
files or a folder; the whole pane takes a drop; several folders can be chosen at once. Nothing moves
when Upload is pressed: every control stays and is disabled, and the header line over the table
turns from the chosen count into the running tally. The grid gained an `orderRows` option and a
`gridRowComparator` export so a hierarchy sorts siblings by the grid's own rule
(`upload-intake.ts` holds the row model, tested without a browser).

**Progress is bytes, and large files upload in parts.** The storage write moved from `fetch` to
XMLHttpRequest, the one browser transport that reports upload progress (`putUploadBytes` takes
`onProgress`, an `AbortSignal`, and answers the ETag), so a sending row reads "Sending · 42%" and
the bars measure bytes. Above the firm's mode threshold (100 MB by default) `uploadIntoFolder` now
runs the multipart leg the host already tracked: fixed 16 MiB parts, three in flight, each signed
through `GET /uploads/{id}/parts/{n}`, sent, and retried on its own with backoff; the ETags go back
as the completion manifest. The single-shot PUT is retried the same way.

**A file the firm already holds is not sent, and the pace is read as it goes.** The browser hashes
each file first (`upload-hash.ts`: an incremental SHA-256 from `@noble/hashes` fed a chunk at a time
in a Web Worker, so a file of any size is read with nothing held past the chunk in hand, and the row
reads "Reading · 42%" while it goes) and asks `POST /uploads/matches` what the firm holds by digest
and size (a new index on `file_version.content_sha256` serves it). A live file on
the matter with those bytes reads Already here and nothing is sent; one elsewhere in the firm is made
into a new file on the matter through `POST /uploads/duplicates` (`duplicateVersionIntoMatter`, a
server-side bucket copy restamped for the target matter, the gate's verdict carried across). So a
folder re-sent after a failed batch sends only what did not land. A pace sampler in the queue
(`upload-pace.ts`) reads the rate and the time left over a trailing window; a stall is called only
once the whole window has seen nothing move, and a file the matter already held adds nothing to the
rate. The counts (`batchCountsText`) head the panel, the tray and the new `/uploads` page alike, and
the bytes and pace (`batchPaceText`) sit beside each bar, where a header line would cut them short.
The page lays out every batch this tab is running through the one source table component
(`upload-source-table.svelte`), which the dialog now uses too.

**A transfer outlives its panel.** Upload hands the batch to the upload queue
(`upload-queue.svelte.ts`, module state, three files at a time, one folder creation per path however
many files wait on it), the panel stays to report it and Close leaves it running, a top-bar
**upload tray** (`upload-tray.svelte`, seated ahead of the download tray) shows every batch with its
tally, a Retry Failed that resends only what failed into the same folders, and Open folder
(`/matters/{id}/files?folder=`), and the file list re-reads when a batch on its matter finishes.
Closing the tab while bytes move asks first; navigating away from the screen with files chosen and
not yet sent asks first. **Cancel Upload** stops a running batch (what landed stays, what is being
sent is given back, the rest reads Not sent and can be sent afterwards). `file_version.source_modified_at` records the device's last-modified
instant for every uploaded version, and the reservation's `createdAtBasis` dates a new file by it
when asked, clamped to now; the inspector shows it as **File's Own Date**.

title: The intake desk, the intake and hold rungs, New beside every person field, and the numbering framework
entry:
**The matter lifecycle gains its first rung and a hold, and the intake desk stands on it.** A
matter now passes through `intake`, `consultation` (the status formerly stored as `prospective`,
renamed as spelled because no firm holds a matter yet; a reviewed rebuild of `matter` widens the
CHECK), `open`, `hold` and `closed`. A hold is an open matter the firm has stopped working without
closing it, for a recorded reason: `holdMatter` behind `POST /api/v1/matters/{id}/hold` (the reason
in the body) and `releaseMatter` behind `.../release`, guarded in the batch, drawing and surrendering
nothing, carrying `held_at` and `hold_reason` on the row (a second reviewed rebuild), and audited as
`matter.held` and `matter.released`, which the matter timeline, the activity section and the
responsible member's notifications all read. One permission, `matters:hold`, both ways, seeded to
Owner/Admin and Attorney. The docket keeps held matters under their own status; the conflicts corpus
and auto-file rules treat them as live; reopen returns a matter closed on hold to its hold. An intake draws no number of any kind; `graduateMatter` behind
`POST /api/v1/matters/{id}/graduate` (and its readiness read) runs the intake procedure as its gate
and draws the consultation number; `openMatter` requires a consultation and runs no intake gate;
reopen returns a matter to the rung it left. The docket excludes both unnumbered rungs. The sidebar's
Intake destination lists every intake and consultation in flight, starts one, completes it, and
schedules the consultation. The desk is a reading of the firm's matters rather than a register of its own: `readIntakeDesk`
in `@magna-carta/intake` behind `GET /api/v1/intake/consultations` (firm-wide, `intake:read`,
cursor-paged, capped at fifty because each row's standing is derived on read) joins the matters
listing to the client party, the member and matter-type names, the next scheduled event, and one
checklist read per row. The New Matter window gains an intake purpose (Intake, Start Intake,
no money block) and offers Intake among its statuses; the calendar's event window takes a seeded title and participants; the sidebar row
flips to alpha. The step-kind vocabulary gains `client-forms` and `payment` on the procedure's
own principle — a member's record ahead of the portal and the payments port — through a same-
transaction rebuild of `intake_procedure_step`. The design system's `EntityPicker` gains a
top-level New control and a per-kind add row (`onCreate` now carries the kind, and `createRefusal`
keeps the control present when the reader may not create); `directory-entity-picker.svelte` wraps
it with the Directory's own New Person and New Organization windows, seeded from what was typed,
and every surface that picks a person or an organization takes the wrapper.

**The numbering scheme has an editor, and a matter's number can be set by hand.** Settings ·
Matter Numbering replaces its Soon stub with two editors over the routes that already existed
(`GET`/`PUT /api/v1/numbering-scheme`, `POST /api/v1/numbering-scheme/preview`): one for the matter
number and one for the consultation sequence, each an ordered list of parts (text, the one counter,
year, date opened, office code, practice-area code, client code, attorney initials, client name)
with the scoping flag drawn as "restarts the count", starters for the common shapes, and a live
preview rendered by the server against a sample matter whose values are printed beside it. The
model lives in `apps/web/src/lib/matters/numbering-scheme.ts`; the editor in
`numbering-scheme-editor.svelte`. The matter's status window gains a Number block with Set Number
(Change Number where one stands) behind `matters:renumber`, over `POST /api/v1/matters/{id}/renumber`,
offered only where the matter has been active; `renumberMatter` now refuses an intake or a
consultation (`matter-not-open`), since no matter number exists before a matter is active.

title: The loading region holds a read's whole state set, states a stall, announces its finish and measures every settle
entry:
**The loading region holds a read's whole state set, states a stall, announces its finish and measures every settle.** `LoadingRegion` gains `failed` with a `failure` snippet (rendered first, whatever else is true, so the failure-exit ruling is structural), `empty` with an `emptyState` snippet, `refreshing` for a re-read that keeps the content on screen while marking the region busy, and `onRetry`. Past fifteen seconds in flight the region says "Still reading …. This is taking longer than it should." above the shape and offers Retry, so a permanent skeleton cannot happen by construction. One status line carries the sentence and then says the read finished. Every settle writes a User Timing measure and dispatches `mc-loading-settled`; the app shell records it as a `loading` breadcrumb, so a report says which reads a member waited on and for how long. The four-branch chain around every region in `apps/web` folds into the region, and the Refresh control and the directory's duplicate check use `refreshing` in place of hand-written busy marks.

**Every fixture's words come from one invented vocabulary.** `@magna-carta/design-system/loading-fixtures` supplies people, organizations, matters, dates, amounts and a sentence by index, plausible in length and provably not a client's; the story, the gallery and every surface draw from it.

**Two more gates.** `silent-loading` fails a null-sentinel branch that renders nothing or a bare "Reading…" sentence, the gap the first rule could not see; `fixture-shape` fails a fixture that renders a component its region's children never do, with `{@render}` expanded to the snippet it names. Both are proved against known-bad input. The developer-console gallery adds the state set, and a fitness test measures the bone's contrast on every surface in every theme and mode (1.16:1 to 1.59:1 today, against a 3:1 non-text target the owner has yet to rule on) and pins a floor under it.

**And the round after it.** A fourth rule, `loading-label`, holds a region's label to the house voice (a capitalised gerund, never "Loading", no terminal punctuation), since the finished and stalled sentences are derived from it. The callers the migration left short now supply what their regions can use: Retry on the conflicts posture panel and the matter search, a failed versions read carried into the file inspector instead of collapsing to "no versions yet", a guard against a second concurrent integrity check, and one announcement per region on the version chip. Every fixture date is on the vocabulary in the shape its column needs. The developer console's performance module lists the reads the tab waited on, from the User Timing measures the regions write.

title: Undo, redo and reversal: one history stack, the table's own controls, and reversibility as route metadata
entry:
**Both surfaces that had their own undo now render the design system's, and both old stacks are
gone.** `apps/web/src/lib/file-manager/move-history.ts` and
`apps/web/src/lib/time/time-sheet-history.svelte.ts` are deleted; the file manager's footer and the
Time Sheet's toolbar each render `UndoRedoControls` over a `HistoryStack`, and the four hand-built
split controls become one. What a surface still varies is the register — quiet ghost buttons in a
counts footer, bordered secondary ones in a toolbar of secondary buttons — because that is a fact
about the chrome the pair sits in rather than about undo.

**The file manager's recorded move became the first inverse command.** Each key goes back to where
IT came from, which is exactly what the old `RecordedMove` already held and what a snapshot of the
surface could never have said. A write that refuses now throws, so the stack keeps the step and the
reader gets another attempt at the same move rather than the one beneath it; the refusal goes to the
same band every other refused act on that surface uses. The revision counter the controls needed in
order to re-derive is gone with it: the shared stack's steps are reactive, so there is nothing to
bump and nothing to forget to bump.

**The Time Sheet's snapshot became a pair of field writes, and that is where its two defects were.**
An undo now writes **the row the step changed** — the snapshot could not say which field moved, so
putting one back meant writing every row on the sheet, over rows the step never touched and over
whatever somebody had changed in another window meanwhile. And the announcement now waits for the
write: `runUndo` used to say "Undid {label}" the instant the stack popped while
`#writeBackEverySavedRow` was unawaited, so a reader was told the entry went back before the record
agreed, and heard nothing when it then refused.

**An inverse whose entry has left draft refuses rather than writing.** The void, the submission or
the approval is the newer fact, and putting a value back on an entry somebody voided in between
would be a second act wearing the first one's name. The step stays on the stack and the walk says
which act it stopped at. Two existing tests already pinned the behaviour through the snapshot model;
they now pin the refusal, and assert that the walk reports it.

Two new tests cover what the port is for: that an undo writes the row the step changed and no other
row on the sheet, and that a walk answers only once the write has answered. The design system gains
leaf export paths — `@magna-carta/design-system/history-stack` and `/history-shortcuts` — because a
module with no Svelte in it must not pull the control's component tree in; doing so fails as
`Unknown file extension ".svelte"` deep inside bits-ui, which reads like anything but the import
that caused it.

And the defect the shared control was built with: all four undo and redo dropdowns rendered
`DropdownMenu.GroupHeading` with no `DropdownMenu.Group`, which throws when the caret is pressed. It
went with the markup that carried it.

**Reversibility becomes route metadata, and the first census it produced answers a question the
platform could not answer before: of the thirty-three things it deletes, what puts each one back?**
`RouteMeta` carries `reversal` — one of `inverse`, `compensating` or `none`, the first two naming
the operation involved (a route that reverses itself names itself) and `none` obliged to carry the
reason nothing does. An arm earns its place by changing what a SURFACE does, which is why there are
three and not five. `defineOpenAPIRoute` refuses a DELETE that declares nothing, and a conformance fitness
function checks the cross-references over the emitted document: a declaration reading "files.restore
puts it back" is worth exactly as much as `files.restore` existing, and a surface rendering that
sentence has no way to find out that it does not.

**Twenty of the thirty-three are `inverse`, which nobody expected.** More than half of what the
platform calls deletion is not deletion — it is detaching, unlinking, revoking, clearing: a statement
about a relationship, fully reversible by the route that made it, and in several cases already worded
that way in the route's own description. None of those needs a confirmation dialog, and several have
one.

**Twelve are `none`, and reading their reasons sorts them into three groups.** Irreversible by design
and correctly so (the assistant's erasure instrument, a revoked auto-file rule kept so every message
it placed can still name it, a terminal recovery job). Irreversible because there is nothing to
restore (the two custom-field hard deletes, which refuse to run unless the field holds no values).
And **irreversible by omission** — `notes.deleteNote`, whose own design rules that no hard delete
should exist; `tasks.deleteTask`; `custody.deactivateItemType`; `emails.unlink`;
`templates.deleteFieldMapping`; `downloads.remove`; and the sharpest of them,
`matterAssets.deleteAsset`, whose route description says "a firm that removed a house by mistake this
morning wants it back this afternoon" and whose schema keeps the row — with no route that clears the
flag, so the sentence is aspirational.

That third group was a suspicion and is now a list.

**The gate starts at DELETE rather than at every mutating method**, deliberately: 349 mutating
operations declared in one pass would be 349 guesses, and deletion is where the question is asked
most and was answered least — thirty-three deletions against five reversals of any kind. Widening it
is its own slice, and the two that most want declaring next are the void family
(`timeEntries.void` → `timeEntries.unvoid` is an inverse the platform already has) and the
ledger's compensating pairs, which is where that arm earns its place.

The declaration is emitted as `x-mc-reversal` and carried into the generated client, because the
point is that a dialog's recoverability line stops being a string in a Svelte file and becomes the
rendering of the route's own declaration — so "It moves out of the list and stays recoverable" cannot
drift from what delete actually does.

**The design system gains the undo and redo the product had twice and had never agreed on.**
`HistoryStack`, `UndoRedoControls` and `historyShortcuts` live at
`packages/design-system/src/lib/components/history/`, and all three are in `lint:one-ui`'s
one-implementation registry — so the third undo stack is now a gate failure rather than something
somebody notices a year later. There were two before this: the Time Sheet's snapshot stack and the
file manager's inverse-command stack, built weeks apart, bounded differently, labelled differently,
each carrying its own copy of the split-control markup.

**A step is a command with an inverse, never a snapshot.** A snapshot restores a screen; an inverse
restores the record, which is what a reader means by undo. The difference is not academic — a
snapshot cannot know which fields moved, which is why the Time Sheet's undo writes back **every** row
on the sheet rather than the ones the step changed, over rows the step never touched and over
whatever somebody changed in another window meanwhile.

**The outcome follows the inverse, never the pop.** `undo` answers once the writes have answered, and
a failure leaves the step where it was: on the stack, still offered, with the failing act named. The
Time Sheet announces "Undid {label}" the instant the stack pops while its write-through is unawaited,
so a reader is told the record went back before it has; the shared contract cannot do that. The
control hands the outcome back through `onOutcome` and says nothing itself, because the live region
belongs to the surface and a control that spoke would be a second voice on the same strip.

**And the sentence for what undo cannot reach.** `irreversibleAnnouncement` states both halves — that
undo does not reach this act, and where the repair that does reach it lives — because a surface that
offers a step and then announces a reversal that never ran is the worse failure, and "undo does not
reach this" is only half an answer when the other half exists.

**Building it found a live defect in what shipped: all four undo and redo dropdowns on the product
throw when they are opened.** Each renders `DropdownMenu.GroupHeading` with no `DropdownMenu.Group`
above it, and bits answers `Context "Menu.Group | Menu.RadioGroup" not found`. The throw happens on
the press rather than on render, so nothing showed it — two surfaces, built weeks apart, copied the
same markup. The shared control has the group, and the story that opens the menu is what pins it.

Also settled here: a walk in flight refuses the next one rather than interleaving two sequences of
inverses; only `push` grows the stack, so walking back and forth cannot drop the step at the far end;
and the keys are a handler the surface attaches to its own element rather than a window listener, so
two surfaces with stacks cannot receive each other's presses. They reach inside text fields by
default — on a rapid-entry grid the cell is not the surface — with yielding as the seam for a surface
that is one long field, which corrects the design document's stricter first claim.

Thirty-two unit tests and four story tests, the latter running as browser behaviour tests with their
own axe pass. The two ports are deliberately not in this change: those files belong to the streams
that own them, and each port picks up the missing group for free.

**The controls a table's control row and counts strip are made of are now table components, and the
count of hand-built copies they replace is the argument.** The clear-filters control was built
**seven times in three shapes**; the labelled figures strip **five times**, one of them already
reading in the opposite order; the load-more control **three times in two places**, one of them
below the strip entirely where it read as an act on the page rather than on the list. All twelve
grid consumers assembled the footer's trailing area through the one escape hatch it had.

**`DataTable.GridFigures`** owns the arrangement and never the formatting: label first, figure
second, tabular, `·` between, and "In view:" before the first one under a filter — because a total
that silently changed meaning when a column was filtered is the most quietly wrong thing a footer
can do. The value arrives as text, since money, durations and counts each format through their own
home and a strip that took minor units and a currency would have to learn all three. The Bills
register's reversed label/figure order is corrected in the move.

**`DataTable.ClearFilters` is two acts and says which.** Column filters alone read "Clear Filters";
a surface whose own search or scope is also holding rows back reads "Show Everything", because
clearing a search under a button labelled Clear Filters is a lie about what the press will do.
Neither is configured — both are derived from what is actually narrowing the view. Its `grid` is
optional, since a surface can be narrowed before its grid exists.

**`DataTable.LoadMore` says the noun** — "Load more matters", not "Load more" — and leaves when
there is nothing more, on the same rule every control that undoes a state follows: absence is the
answer, never a disabled control.

**Two owner placements, recorded as rulings.** The clear control lives in the control row above the
table, where the filters were set (`L42b`, revising L42's footer placement; `TB2c` for the time
surfaces, where TT2 had already put it there). The undo and redo pair lives in the footer on every
surface that has a stack (`A15c`, `TS9`) — the Time Sheet's toolbar pair moved down to join the
worked / billed / value figures. The footer's inline "Show all" stays: it is part of the tally
sentence, not a control in a control row, and the two are different things.

What is left in a surface's own hands is what genuinely belongs to it: the file manager's scale
control and File Analysis's own acts still ride the footer's `extras` slot, which is the slot
working as designed — one escape hatch at the end of a declared order, rather than a declared order
that exists nowhere.

**Undo, redo and reversal are designed as one contract, and the inventory that forced it is the
finding.** The platform ships **seven** distinct ways to take something back — two independent
client-side undo stacks, soft delete and restore, the discovery journal's exact compensation, void
and unvoid, the ledger's compensating entry, and two shapes of hard delete — and nothing joins them.
The emitted contract carries **thirty-three DELETE operations and five reversal operations of any
kind**. The per-firm schema carries **thirteen `deleted_at` columns and exactly one `deleted_by`**, so
twelve of the platform's thirteen soft-deleting tables cannot answer the first question a deleted view
is asked.

**Three things are called undo and only one of them is.** A surface stack reverses gestures inside a
session; a record's reversibility is a property of an operation, independent of who is looking; and
deletion's lifecycle is a third question that ADR-0049 has settled for files and nowhere else. Every
defect found is a boundary crossing between those three. The file manager's stack covers movement and
stops, its module explaining that a delete is already recoverable through Deleted Files — a Layer-A
stack deferring to Layer B correctly, by hand, and only there. The Time Sheet refuses a step for a
void for the same reason and has to say so in a hand-written sentence naming two other surfaces.

**The proposal is that reversibility becomes route metadata.** `RouteMeta` already carries
`operationId`, `permission`, `audited` and `idempotency`, emitted as `x-mc-*` and gated by conformance
fitness functions; a `reversal` field joins them, as a discriminated union over what the platform can
actually do — `inverse`, `compensating`, `none` — required on every
mutating route, with a `none` obliged to carry the sentence that says why. The count of irreversible
operations becomes a number CI knows. The dialog's recoverability line stops being a string in a
Svelte file and becomes the rendering of the declaration, so "It moves out of the list and stays
recoverable" cannot drift from what delete does.

**Three defects verified in the source, each a consequence of the same conflation.** The Time Sheet
announces "Undid {label}" the instant the stack pops while the write-through is unawaited, so a reader
is told the record went back before it has. The same undo writes back **every** row on the sheet
rather than the ones the step changed, because a snapshot cannot know which fields moved — which also
writes over a row somebody changed elsewhere. And `notes.deleteNote` hard-deletes a note whose own
design rules that there is no hard delete in the product and that retraction is a state.

Also proposed: one `HistoryStack` and one `UndoRedoControls` in the design system, taking the inverse-
command model from `MoveHistory` and the bounding, labels and announcement helper from `SheetHistory`,
so the split control exists once instead of twice; a named deletion vocabulary separating soft delete,
detach, deactivate, tombstoned hard delete and unrecorded hard delete, with soft delete as the default
for anything a member authored; the deleted view as a pattern rather than a screen; and the ruling
with the widest reach — that an acknowledgement dialog is offered **only** where the declaration is
`none`, which is the Nielsen Norman Group posture the product already follows by instinct with one
alert dialog in the entire application.

A generic undo journal was considered and rejected on two independent grounds: it would hold prior
values of privileged content, which `audit_log.metadata` is redacted by construction to exclude, and a
generic backward replay cannot know that unvoiding a cost-converted time entry is forbidden or that a
coding act's undo must be exact to the rows it wrote. Those are domain rules and the subsystems
already express them as routes; the declaration points at those routes rather than replacing them.

No code, no schema, no migration, no route. Eight owner decisions, five build slices, and one
deliberate omission — the implementation plan waits, because slice 1's census changes what the later
slices contain.

title: Every loading state runs through one region, and the placeholder is the component itself
entry:
**Every loading state in the app runs through one region, and the placeholder is the component itself.** `LoadingRegion` (`@magna-carta/design-system/loading-region`) renders a surface's real markup over a fixture snippet while its data has not arrived, and one recipe turns the text, media and controls into bones while the frame, the headings, the labels and the column heads stay real. The region takes `loading` and a `label` sentence, is `inert` and `aria-busy` while loading, and owns the rest by having no prop for it. Eighty-nine hand-placed `Skeleton` boxes across thirty-seven files, three loading sentences and two static spinner glyphs are gone; the `./skeleton` export is gone with them, and the box stays only inside the six design-system components that render placeholder rows of their own shape, under one count prop name, `placeholderCount`.

The research behind it ([`docs/research/2026-09-05-skeleton-loading-framework.md`](docs/research/2026-09-05-skeleton-loading-framework.md)) surveyed the libraries that derive a skeleton from the finished component and found that every one of them, runtime or build-time, needs representative content before it can measure anything, and that once a fixture exists the measurement is the part worth dropping. The design is [`docs/specs/2026-09-05-loading-region-design.md`](docs/specs/2026-09-05-loading-region-design.md).

It cannot stray: `lint:one-ui` carries a `hand-placed-loading` rule that fails the Skeleton import or tag, the recipe class, `aria-busy`, a pulsing utility or a loader glyph anywhere in the app, and the same signals inside the design system outside the homes the registry declares; the rule is proved against known-bad input, the region's story asserts the announcement and the inert fixture, and `/developer-console/loading-states` shows every shape beside its settled state.

title: A directory record is one window wherever it opens; the tabbed record screen is gone
entry: **A directory record opens in one window, wherever it is reached, and the tabbed record screen is gone.** `apps/web/src/lib/directory/entity-window.svelte` is the entity window: the action dialog's reading kind at record width, the record's sections as a rail on the left in the New Person screen's arrangement, the chosen section's pane beside it, and on the right what stands about the record — the roles a matter knows it holds there (`apps/web/src/lib/matters/party-standing.ts`) above the record's own facts. The directory list, a matter's parties tab, the client fact on the overview and the conflicts hit window all host it; a related record opened from inside it swaps the subject. `entityRecordHref` now builds `/directory?record=<id>`, the list opens the window from that address and mirrors swaps and closes back into it, and the old `/directory/<id>` route redirects there so earlier links still land. The path that made a screen's way back lead somewhere the reader had not come from is gone, so the registry-named way back stays true on every remaining screen; `lint:back-navigation` carries the redirect route as its one stated exemption.

title: The calendar's fifth round: the interface taken apart along its own rules
entry: **The calendar's fifth round: the interface taken apart along its own rules.** A modularity review of `apps/web/src/lib/calendar/` found the entry window at 2,150 lines deciding what the module's conventions say a pure module decides, and one host reading what the shared context already held. This round is behaviour-preserving. The window's decisions are pure modules with tests: `entry-verbs.ts` (which verbs a record's state allows, and the tab counts), `entry-updates.ts` (a correction never re-sends participants), `continue-draft.ts` (the fourth draft), `entry-links.ts` (which end of a link is the other one, and what may still be related), `calendar-permission.ts` (the one wording of the calendar-manage refusal, used by the window, the firm screen, the matter section and the three settings catalogs), and `draft-text.ts` (the trim-to-null, wall-clock and civil-date readings the four drafts and three forms each carried a copy of). The Links and Rooms tabs are their own components owning their reads, forms and failures (`entry-links-tab.svelte`, `entry-rooms-tab.svelte`); the window's event, firm-event and continuance panes render `record-timing-fields.svelte` and the new `event-type-select.svelte` instead of six hand-written copies of the same fields, which also ends the drift between "End date" and "End Date". The matter section's List view moves into the module as `matter-calendar-list.svelte`, and the page reads through the shared context, by the owner's ruling. The view's per-scope sentences and addresses move down into `calendar-scope.ts`, `calendar-window.ts` and `calendar-reads.ts`; the untested pure modules gain tests. The window is under 1,300 lines and every question it used to answer inline is asserted without a browser.

title: Keep every windowed modal off the edges of the screen
entry: **Where a modal panel sits on the screen is now one module, and it keeps every panel off the screen's edges.** `styles/recipes/modal-stage.css` holds every placement rule: `mc-modal-stage`, the viewport pulled in by the new `size.modal-gutter` token (32px), centring its panel with flex and capping it there by flex shrinking; and `mc-modal-panel`, what makes any panel its child, so the panel recipes keep only their look and carry no `max-h-*` utility any more. `internal/modal-stage.svelte` is the stage's one piece of markup, rendered by `Dialog.Content` and `AlertDialog.Content`. `internal/modal-placement.ts` is the closed placement axis (`centered | anchored`), stamped on every panel and taken by `Dialog.Content` as `placement`; the command palette says `anchored` instead of reaching for a utility. `modal-geometry/` is the diagnostic: a Playwright sweep that measures every modal specimen at every screen size in its matrix, screenshots it, and fails an edge nearer than the gutter. Pinned in `test/modal-stage.test.ts` and `test/modal-geometry.test.ts`; ruled in `docs/conventions/design-corrections.md`.

title: Retire the table-hover stream note
An empty table stops answering the pointer, and a table says when there is more to the side
entry:
**An empty table no longer lights up under the pointer, and a table says when there is more to the side.** Two findings from one owner walk over the tables.

The first was reported as "the hover does not extend down the entire table, it stops about halfway", and the table it was reported on was an EMPTY one. The empty, filtered-empty and loading placeholders sit inside the table so the frame holds its height, which makes each of them a `<tr class="mc-table-row">` in the same body as the records — and the row hover found them there. Hovering an empty register painted a grey band exactly as tall as its message (measured at 70% and 78% of two frames on the table-states page, and about half of a taller one) with the rest of the frame left white: a hover that appears to give out partway down the table. The ruling against this was issued on 2026-08-30 and only half carried out — marking the placeholder's CELL does nothing, because the treatment being withheld belongs to the ROW. The row now carries `data-placeholder="true"`, and the shared recipe passes it over for the hover fill and for the `cursor: pointer` that promised a click there was nothing to click. Records are untouched. The story tests hold the cursor half of the treatment on both sides — a record offers itself, a placeholder does not — because the fill answers only to a real pointer, which the browser-mode driver does not supply.

The second is the gilt scroll-edge hint, which existed only inside the sidebar: a thin gold rule that DRAWS in at the edge of a scroll area while more content lies that way, the affordance the rail's hidden scrollbar gave up. It is now `ScrollEdgeHint` in the design system, taking the scrollport as a prop (the consumer keeps their own element, classes and handlers) and watching it through its scroll event plus a ResizeObserver over both the scrollport and its content, so a table gaining rows or a column being widened moves the rule without a scroll event. `Sidebar.Content` moves onto it unchanged, and `DataTable.Grid` now wears its inline pair: a table whose columns run past the frame says so on the side it runs off, and the rule swaps to the leading edge once the reader reaches the far one. The block pair is deliberately not drawn on the grid — its vertical scrollbar is visible and already says that much.

title: One surface for the five money sections, wearing the file manager's frame; Trust takes its first screen
entry:
**The five money sections render inside one surface, `MoneySurface` (`apps/web/src/lib/money/`), wearing the file manager's frame.** Time, Fees, Costs, Billing and Trust each hand the surface their grid, cells, figures, acts and details panel; the surface draws the toolbar flush under the section strip (a coins glyph, the five sub-parts as quiet links with the current one marked, Clear Filters while a filter is on, a ledger's own acts, the density and layout switches), the notices band, the list, an optional line above the footer (where Time and Costs now keep Load more), and the counts strip with the pane toggle last. Two reader preferences are shared by every money section under one key each: the layout (`flush`, the default, or `framed`, the previous rounded-card look) and the row density. Four copies of the frame, the Clear Filters control and the pane toggle became one.

**Trust takes its first surface.** `apps/web/src/lib/trust/` holds the client (`readMatterTrustLedger` over the matter ledger read), the column set, the figures (Balance, Held, Available), the gap register and the ledger, built whole against the trust movement record. The one dependency is named where the fee ledger names its own: the matter ledger is read against a trust account, and no route lists the firm's trust accounts yet, so the list stands empty with the Soon line and the header's New Deposit is disabled with that reason. The trust activity contribution moved out of `awaiting/` and beside the surface it belongs to.

**An empty table no longer lights up under the pointer.** The shared grid's row hover and pointer cursor (`packages/design-system/src/lib/components/data-table/data-table.css`) now exclude the placeholder row, which the standing ruling on placeholder rows already required and which the flush layout made visible: with the grid's own frame gone, a tinted placeholder read as a band of a different surface.

title: The intake procedure: per-matter-type steps answered by the subsystems that own them, and the opening gate
entry:
**The intake procedure: what a kind of matter must clear before it opens, as a firm-authored list
whose steps are answered by the subsystems that own the facts.** `@magna-carta/intake` adds
`intake_procedure` (bound to a matter type or every type), `intake_procedure_step` (eight kinds held
by a CHECK) and `matter_intake_step_record` (append-and-flip, one live record per step per matter),
four permissions seeded on the tasks split, twelve routes, and a reader seam per kind registered by
the composition root: the conflicts posture, the billing arrangement, document assembly, the trust
position and custom-field values answer today; identity verification and acknowledgement are a
member's record until a subsystem exists. `@magna-carta/matters` gained `openPreconditions`
mirroring the close hook, threaded through `openMatter` before the draw, and
`GET /api/v1/matters/{id}/open-readiness`. Surfaces: Settings · Intake Procedures, the matter's
Intake section, and Requirements To Open in the status window. The platform seeds no procedure.

title: The pane toggle ends the counts strip, on every surface that has a pane
entry:
`icon-sm` — the Button's square at the small control height.

The icon size is a square at the medium height, which is right for a toolbar and four points too tall for a band that already holds one line at the small scale: a table's counts strip, a card's own header. A glyph control joining such a band had to either grow it or be styled off the recipe. This is the size that lets it join without doing either.

The control that shows and hides a side pane now ends the counts strip, on every surface that has one.

It used to sit above the table. On Time, Fees, Costs and Billing that meant a row whose only occupant, most of the time, was one glyph — 41 points taken off a table already fighting for them, spent on something that is not an act on the records at all. Those rows now render only when something has to be in them: the way out of a filter, and Costs' Review where the firm runs review. An unfiltered ledger draws no row and its table starts at the top of the screen.

The strip is not free either, and does not need to be: it grows from 32 points to 41 to seat the control. Against the row's 41, that is a net 32 points back to the table and one less band between the reader and the records.

The file manager's two toggles came down as well, though it never had the complaint — theirs ended a toolbar the screen draws anyway. They moved because the answer has to be in one place: a reader should not have to remember that it is at the top of one screen and the bottom of four others. The folder tree keeps its toggle for now.

The five details-panel toggles render through `DetailsPanel.Toggle`, which is what stops four ledgers drawing it four different ways. The folder tree's stays written out in the file manager's footer: one surface has a folder tree, and a component shared by a single caller is indirection rather than reuse. Every glyph control in that footer stepped down to the small square with them, so one band wears one chrome and the strip is four points shorter than it was.

A review surface for where the show-and-hide-a-pane control belongs: `/developer-console/pane-toggle-placements`.

Time, Fees, Costs and Billing each draw a row above their table whose only occupant, most of the time, is one glyph. The row costs a control's height plus the stack gap, taken off a table already fighting for it, and it is spent on a control that is not an act on the records at all. The glyph came from the file manager, where it ends a toolbar the screen draws anyway — the ledgers copied the button without copying the band it stood in.

Every candidate home is rendered from the shipping components over one fixture, at one fixed height, so what each costs the table is the visible difference between two specimens: the row as it is today, the counts strip's inline end, the pane's own edge, the matter's header band, and no toggle at all with the selection opening the pane. Files gets the same treatment — it carries two of these toggles, and is the only screen in the product that lets a reader close its own folder tree, so one specimen simply takes that toggle away.

Nothing has moved yet. The surface exists so the choice is made by looking rather than by describing.

title: Retire the database-health stream note
The header chip says whether your firm's database is reachable, and both its sections fold
entry:
**The header chip now answers "can I reach my firm's records", not only "what version am I on" —
and both of its sections fold.**

A newly created firm produced screens that all refused with the same sentence — "Your role does not
grant this action in this firm" — for a reason that had nothing to do with roles: the owner's member
record had not yet been mirrored from the control plane into the firm's own database, so their
effective permission set was empty. That state was invisible from the interface, indistinguishable
from a role somebody had forgotten to grant, and self-clearing within minutes, which is the worst
combination a diagnosis can have.

- **A new read, `GET /api/v1/meta/database-health`.** It reports five facts separately: a timed
  round trip to the firm's own database, the control plane's answer and whether the firm's storage
  is allocated, the applied migration lineage against the one this build expects, the session's own
  member row with the roles on it and the permission count they resolve to, and any
  `member.provision` message for the firm still pending or dead-lettered. Every check reports a
  state rather than prose, a check that could not run says "unknown" instead of reporting health,
  and one failing check never fails the reply — the route has to be readable during the outage it
  is describing. It carries `permission: null` deliberately: a gated version of it would refuse
  exactly the session it exists to explain.
- **A Database section in the Build Versions panel** renders that read as four rows, each with the
  remedy its own state implies — a wait, an administrator's grant, a broken seeding, a connection
  fault — plus a Provisioning line when a member mirror is still on its way or has been given up on,
  and a Copy diagnosis control that puts the whole reading on the clipboard.
- **Deployment and Database each sit behind a caret now**, remembered per browser and open by
  default, with the fleet keeping its own fold inside Deployment. All three render through one
  disclosure snippet, and a shut heading carries what folding it hides: the count of Workers without
  a version, or the worst reading among the health rows.
- **Neither read fires until the panel is opened**, so the chip costs a page load nothing, and the
  panel's one Refresh control now re-asks both.

title: Retire the component-consolidation stream note
Component consolidation: one details panel, one display vocabulary, one caps register, and four gates
entry:
The four financial ledgers' details panels become one shell, and a refused control says what it would have done.

Time, Costs, Fees and Billing each carried their own details panel, and the four were the same panel: the same three faces, the same header, the same ruled runs of facts, down to identical class strings. `$lib/details-panel` is the shell they now compose — Root, Header, Title, Subtitle, Close, Body, Section, Facts, Fact — and what stays in each surface is what only that surface knows. `DetailsPanel.Toggle` takes the pane control with it: four ledgers had written that out identically, copied comment included.

The shell keeps two deliberate seams rather than pretending they do not exist. `Fact` takes a snippet where a value is a mark rather than a figure, because the fee panel's standing badge is neither tabular nor right-aligned; and it takes a class where one figure has to carry a warning the column does not, because a bill past its due date is that case.

A refused control was explained in two competing sentences: seventeen call sites naming the act and the permission, and seven more naming only the permission. `permissionRefusal(act, permission)` is the one home. The seven that said only "This account does not hold the billing:credit capability" now also name the act, which is the half a reader can take to whoever administers their account — so those seven tooltips read differently than they did. One more said "capability" where the other twenty-four said "permission", and now says "permission" too.

The display vocabulary and the caps label each become one thing, and the registry starts naming the surfaces it had been leaving out.

Money, counts and civil dates were presented from inside the table's typed columns, which is where a column author found them and nowhere a details panel would think to look. They move to `packages/design-system/src/lib/formatters/`, beside the answers for how long, when, who and which version, and the table re-exports them so every existing import still resolves. The move is not a bug fix and the note in `money.ts` says so: the float path only starts disagreeing with an exact minor-unit sum once a single row passes roughly a trillion of the major unit, which was measured rather than assumed. Two of the four answers to "how long" — `hoursFromMinutes` and `decimalHoursText` — turned out to have no callers at all outside one test, and are gone.

The caps field label existed 101 times, hand-written, in two tones that disagreed: the invoice window alone used both. Worse, 77 of those sites reached for an inline `letter-spacing` style to put back the tracking every design-system recipe already carries, which is raw CSS in a codebase that forbids it. `FieldLabel` takes the register the masthead eyebrow and the eyebrow link already agreed on and stops it being retyped; it renders whichever element the caller's document structure needs, because the alternative is the callers that need a `dt` or a heading carrying on by hand.

`Badge` gains `caps` for the same reason. Six badges that label a standing rather than count something — a matter's status seal, the "View" marker on a settings section — were each written as `class="uppercase"` plus an inline letter-spacing style; uppercase without the tracking is wrong, and the tracking is not expressible as a utility, so every one of them reached for raw CSS. One more inline style, on a table header, was restating tracking `.mc-table-head` already sets. The app carried 77 of these; it now carries 2, both in surfaces whose colour varies with state and which are somebody else's stream to touch.

Eight shared surfaces the one-implementation registry had never named — `DataTable`, `Masthead`, `TopBar`, `EmptyState`, `LabelledField`, `FieldRow`, `StatusMark` and the new `FieldLabel` — now have entries. The registry's promise is that no second file claims the name; it had not been making that promise about the components most likely to be forked.

Four new rules in `lint:one-ui`, so the consolidations cannot drift back one surface at a time.

A consolidation that is only a cleanup is a cleanup that gets undone: the next screen copies the nearest example, and the nearest example is whatever was written last. Each of these rules names one thing the platform has agreed to have once, and each was proved against a deliberately reintroduced violation before it landed.

- **`caps-register`** — the letterspaced small-caps voice built out of utilities, or finished by hand with an inline `letter-spacing`. The remedy is `FieldLabel`, or the `caps` option on the component being dressed.
- **`money-presentation`** — `style: "currency"` outside the two files allowed to print an amount. Date presentation is deliberately NOT gated and the runner says so: `Intl.DateTimeFormat` has twenty legitimate callers here doing time-zone arithmetic rather than display, and a rule that cried wolf over those is a rule somebody switches off.
- **`permission-refusal`** — the refusal sentence written out rather than taken from `permissionRefusal`. Both wordings are matched, and neither loosely: a dev-console note about somebody who "does not hold the address" is not a refusal, and the rule has a test saying so.
- **`details-panel`** — the panel's frame or scrolling body written out instead of composed from the shell.

Turning them on found four sites the hand migration had missed — an inline letter-spacing that had survived inside a converted component, two refusals written in full, and the false positive above, which is why the rule is now narrower than it started.

The last residuals went with them. The three `Card.Title`s in the invoice window that were field labels wearing a card title's name are `FieldLabel`s; the workbench's absence heading and the version chip's fleet label, both of which took their colour from `class:` directives and so slipped the first pass, are too. The app now writes the caps voice by hand nowhere and reaches for an inline `letter-spacing` nowhere.

One allowance is recorded rather than fixed: a Combobox group heading is a label, and the shared sentence is a sentence — ninety characters in a slot whose other branch reads "Add to the Firm's Practice Areas". It keeps the first clause of the shared wording verbatim so the two cannot disagree about the same permission.

`clockText` is gone. It was the last real second answer to "how long": a hand-derived `H:MM` beside the sheet, with a seconds mode the shared formatter lacked and no sign handling the shared one has. `formatClock(seconds, { toTheSecond })` is now the one clock, `formatDuration` reports it rather than deriving its own, and the equivalence was checked across 4001 quarter-minute probes before the old one was deleted. Its test moved to the formatter and gained the cases the sheet's copy never made.

title: The calendar's fourth round: the event-type catalog and related links in the entry window
entry: **The calendar's fourth round: the event-type catalog and related links.** Settings › Practice › Event Types is the catalog on the Rooms and Resources pattern: a platform type is recategorized or retired (its name and code are the shared vocabulary), a firm type is added, renamed or retired; retiring asks first and is one way, as the contract is. Two reads join the API, `GET /api/v1/events/{eventId}/links` and `/firm-events/{firmEventId}/links`, over the package's existing `readLinksTouchingEvent`, recorded as bounded by construction; the entry window's Links tab lists the settings related by hand with the other end's title (read on that end's own path, under its own visibility), and gains Relate (a setting on the same matter, or a firm event within six months, with a note) and Remove. The plan's Timeline view on the Calendar section was not built: the matter's Activity section, which landed meanwhile, is that read's one screen.

title: New Person on the side rail: every section reachable at creation, contact in four kinds, identifiers as shapes
entry:
`POST /api/v1/directory/persons` takes the whole draft (other names, pronouns, dates, emails, phones, addresses, identifiers, organizations) and `createPersonRecord` writes it in one effect batch, each part composed by the module that owns it (`compose*` functions on person, name-history, contact-email/phone/address, edges, identifiers). The sections under `apps/web/src/lib/directory/sections/` are data-blind components used by the dialog to draft and by the Contact and Identifiers panes to persist. The organization keeps a one-section dialog beside the same duplicate gate.
