**An identifier is a shape, checked before it is sealed.** `packages/directory/src/identifier-shape.ts` declares what each kind is made of — SSN nine digits, EIN nine in two groups, licence region + number, bar number jurisdiction + number, account held-with + number + username + secret — and `checkIdentifier` refuses a value that does not fit with the sentence the screen shows beside the field; the API runs the same check on `AddIdentifierRequest` (now `type`, `label`, `number`, `username`, `secret`) and on every identifier in a create. `directory_identifier` gains a nullable plaintext `label` (migration `20260903T090000_directory-identifier-label`) so the enumeration can say what a sealed value is of. An account's sealed value is the JSON of its three parts; its blind index normalizes the number alone, so the username and secret never reach an index; the reveal route hands the parts back apart.

**The `dob` kind is gone.** A date of birth is a date on the person, in the clear, beside the date of death; a sealed birthday could be neither shown nor used to tell two people apart. The sealed `client.dateOfBirth` merge field went with it — a plain field from the person's date column is a document-assembly follow-up.

**Email and phone rules are shared.** `packages/directory/src/email-address.ts` is the one email check, used by the API's `prepareAddress` and the screen's live refusal. The web app takes `libphonenumber-js` (already in the lockfile through `class-validator`) for dial codes, as-you-type national formatting and E.164 submission; the server's own parser is unchanged and receives the international form with the region beside it.

title: Nothing is sent until Upload is pressed, and a new firm's bucket takes browser uploads
entry:
**A newly provisioned firm's bucket accepts browser uploads.** The first production upload failed with "Nothing answered while sending the bytes to storage": the browser PUTs bytes straight to a presigned URL on the firm's own bucket, which is a cross-origin request, and the bucket carried no CORS policy — so the preflight was refused before a byte moved, and the app could only report that nothing answered. Provisioning had never configured CORS; the runbook step that applies it was written for the shared platform bucket, and a firm bucket minted by `firm-provisioner.ts` got neither. `firm-resource-provider.ts` now carries `configureBucketCors`, run unconditionally on every provisioning run that reaches the bucket step alongside the notifications and expiry rules, translating the rule set (now a module beside the code that reads it, `apps/api-worker/src/files/browser-upload-cors.ts`, replacing the checked-in JSON artifact, and naming the `workers.dev` serving origins too) into the REST API's shape and folding in the deployment's `APP_BASE_URL`; `pnpm run emit-r2-cors` prints it as the dashboard's JSON for the by-hand path. Buckets that existed before the step — the platform bucket and the one production firm — still take the policy by hand; the runbook's section 15 now says so, and names the read that tells whether a bucket has one.

**The file manager's Upload dialog comes first, and nothing is sent until Upload is pressed.** `apps/web/src/lib/file-manager/upload-dialog.svelte` replaces the destination dialog: it opens on Upload, on a drop onto the list and on the empty folder's button, holds the file, files or whole folder chosen in it (the design-system Dropzone gained `onEntries`, which walks a dropped folder through the entry API instead of handing the consumer a zero-byte stub named after it), asks the Upload Location beside them, and starts the transfer only on its commit — "Upload", not "Save". A folder is recreated under the location, level by level, before its files go in. The running commentary is gone with the early transfer: no "each is uploading now" subtitle and no "closing keeps what has already landed" line, which read as something saved behind the reader's back. A file that did not go reads "Upload failed", with the stage and Error ID as before. A download that fails on the Downloads page or in the top-bar tray now states so on its own row with a Retry beside it, instead of a toast that vanished.

title: The conflicts read surface, and the search corrections from its first walk
entry:
**A conflicts hit names the party it is about.** The candidate list carried an entity handle and
nothing else, and the column that should have named the party said "Not served" on every row: the
check read put `entity_id` on the wire unresolved, and naming each row from the browser would have
been one request per row.

The read that fixes it already existed. `readSubjectFactsBatch` resolves a set of entity ids in one
query per node table per hundred ids, chunked at D1's bound-parameter cap, and it had been on the
WRITE path all along, seeding the matcher. `readEntityDisplayNames` beside it does the same for a
reader — a person's stored display name falling back to the name parts, an organization's to its
legal name — and `GET /api/v1/conflicts/checks/{checkId}` now carries a `party` on every hit.

It is resolved on the READ rather than copied onto the log. The log is append-only and records the
entity by reference, so a reviewer deciding today sees the name the firm holds today; a hit whose
entity no longer resolves at all — a merge after the check, which the append-only rule makes
reachable — reports an unresolved party and never an absent one, because a conflicts hit with no
party would invert what the row means.

**Two N+1 reads went with it.** The handler was resolving dispositions with a per-hit
`readCurrentDisposition` inside a `Promise.all` — the exact shape `readHitDispositionStates` was
written to replace, and whose own comment names it as the mistake the posture read cannot afford.
The checks screen was separately spending one Directory read per hit a reviewer opened. The handler
now makes two set-valued reads and the screen makes none: only a waiver's consenting party, which is
a different entity, is still read one at a time.

A general "name these entity ids" endpoint was deliberately NOT built. It would have been a
Directory batch read reachable with `conflicts:read`, which is a wider grant than this surface needs.

**A hit carries what the firm already said about the same party — as context, and nothing more.**
The sixth and last read of the conflicts read surface, built under the owner's ruling of 2026-09-02.

`readPriorConclusions` matches on the ENTITY alone, across every check but the one in hand, and the
check response carries the result as `previouslyAnswered` — a field deliberately separate from
`disposition`, so a hit with an earlier answer about the same party is still **unanswered**.

The case that settled the rule, and the reason a narrower key would not be safer: a company cleared
in March under Rule 1.9 as a FORMER client re-surfaces in September through the graph, as the
subsidiary of a CURRENT client. That is a Rule 1.7 question on a materially higher bar. Same entity,
different question. Matching on the entity and presenting the March clearance as the September hit's
answer would carry a judgment across two conflicts that are not the same conflict.

Both narrower keys were rejected on that same case rather than a different one. Adding the source
class would hide the September hit precisely BECAUSE it arrived through the graph; adding the
evidence tier would make a firm turning on the over-inclusive band look like a new conflict. Neither
makes the judgment safer — they only move where it is wrong.

It needed a second index. `conflicts_hit` carried only `(check_id)`, so matching a party across
earlier checks scanned a table that is append-only and only grows;
`conflicts_hit_entity_created_index` on `(entity_id, created_at)` holds it, with a plan probe beside
the two check-history probes.

`conflicts-gaps.ts` is now down to one entry — the assembled report document, which is its own work.

**A conflicts hit shows every answer recorded against it, not just the last one.** The conflicts log
is append-only precisely so that a reviewer who clears a hit and later reverses leaves both acts
standing — a reversal is a second row, never an edit — and until now nothing read that back. The hit
window showed the reviewer's latest word and a line saying the earlier ones were on the record and
unreadable.

`GET /api/v1/conflicts/hits/{hitId}/dispositions` serves the trail on `conflicts:read`, oldest
first, each entry carrying its own rationale, its reviewer, and for a waiver its own waiver record
and what that record is short of. `readDispositionTrail` uses the same `created_at`/`rowid`
tie-break `readCurrentDisposition` does, so the two reads can never disagree about which answer is
the latest — the pair that most needs a stable order is an answer and its reversal.

The hit's existence IS checked, unlike the matter posture read and for the opposite reason: "no such
hit" is not a state with a meaning of its own, so an empty trail must mean "nobody has answered this
hit" and nothing else. Conflating them would let a mistyped handle read as an unanswered candidate.

**The conformance gate caught a real contract bug on the first emit.** Reusing `DispositionDetail`
in the new response registered one component name under two schema shapes — the check response uses
it as `.nullable()`, and zod-to-openapi carries the component name onto the nullable schema, which
that library resolves first-write-wins. A trail entry is now its own component, which is also the
honest reading: on the check response `disposition` is the latest word and null means unanswered; on
the trail every entry is an act that happened and there is no null to express.

**A matter can be re-checked on demand, and the firm's floor is readable.** Reads 3 and 4 of the
conflicts read surface, and both were routes the machinery was already waiting for.

`POST /api/v1/matters/{matterId}/conflicts-rechecks` on `conflicts:run` takes **no scope**, and that
is why it exists beside the general check route rather than being a call to it. "Re-check this
matter" has no scope for a caller to state, and a scope field would invite a screen to compose a
narrower search than the firm requires. It names no subjects either: `runConflictsCheck` reads the
matter's own live parties, so a party added since the last check is searched without anybody listing
them — which is the staleness a re-check exists to answer.

It is recorded as a MANUAL run naming the member who asked, and carries no cause. A cause is a
corpus change the platform noticed; a person asking now is not one. It also neither reads nor
satisfies the automatic re-check ledger — an open cause stays open, because the interval between a
cause and the check that answered it is evidence about the firm's procedure, and a manual run did
not answer it.

`GET /api/v1/firm/conflicts-policy` is `readConflictsPolicy` behind a route, on `conflicts:read` —
every member who can read a check is held to the floor, so a reviewer looking at a check that fell
short of it has to be able to see what it is. The check runner now states the floor instead of
marking it unreadable.

The route declares 409 among its responses because the shared conflicts error mapper can return the
idempotency chokepoint's refusal, and the typechecker caught the omission: a response a route can
produce but does not declare is a contract that lies about what a caller may receive.

**A firm can read the checks it has run.** `GET /api/v1/conflicts/checks` pages them newest first
over the uniform `{ data, nextCursor }` envelope, optionally narrowed to one matter. Each line names
what set the run going, who asked where anybody did, the strictness and depth it ran at, whether the
firm's floor raised the scope above what was requested, and how many candidates surfaced — never a
conclusion about them, which is a reviewer's act recorded as a disposition.

**The load-profile plan probe was right, and it was right in advance.** The design said the
unfiltered listing would plan a full table scan because `conflicts_check`'s only index leads with
`subject_matter_id` — which serves one matter's own history and cannot serve a listing across every
matter. The probe measured exactly that on the first run. `conflicts_check_created_id_index` on
`(created_at, id)` landed in the same change rather than as a note to revisit, and both shapes of the
read are now probed separately because they plan differently.

That index is not a micro-optimization. The conflicts log is append-only by design, with
`RAISE(ABORT)` triggers refusing UPDATE and DELETE, so a scan there is not a fixed cost — it rises
every week a firm operates.

The row is deliberately narrow: the whole check, its recorded scope, its statement and its hits are
one identifier away, and a listing carrying all of it would read every check's `inputs_json` for a
surface that shows none of it. The hit count comes from a correlated subquery served by the
`(check_id)` index rather than a `GROUP BY` join, which would have to de-duplicate the check row per
hit before the limit could apply.

**The screen search clears, closes, and goes somewhere.** Four corrections from the owner's first
walk of the matter search, all made in the one shared control so every list screen inherits them.

A live query now carries an **X** at the field's trailing edge. Escape always cleared the field, but
Escape is a key and nothing on screen said so — a person reaching for a pointer had to select the
text and delete it. Both paths now run the same code.

**Clicking away closes an empty search.** It did not before: focus landing on the page's background
was read as focus going nowhere, so the field stayed open behind whatever you did next. A search
with something in it still stays open, because a narrowed list has to carry its reason on screen.

**Enter opens the full results**, flushing whatever you typed last so it never opens a search one
keystroke behind the field.

**The panel opens with the field** rather than with your first keystroke, so the scope and the way
through to the full search are reachable before you have typed anything — including going straight
to the full search page with nothing typed at all.

**A matter search finds folders.** Searching a matter for a folder by name answered nothing while
the folder sat in the tree: the Files source only ever matched file names, and consulted folders
only to say which one a file was in. Folder names are now matched alongside file names, in the same
Files group, each labelled so a folder and a file of the same name are told apart.

**The control opens in two directions, and the downward one is now a seam on the component.** The
icon opens to the inline start into the field (writing the query) and downward into a `panel` snippet
(aiming it, and reading what came back). That panel renders INSIDE ScreenSearch's own root, which is
load-bearing rather than tidy: the collapse watches measure against that root, so a panel rendered
beside the control is read as "outside" and shuts the field on the first click into it. The matter
search's scope moved out of the `scope` seam and into that panel — the seam seats a control inside
the field's leading edge, and "Everything on this matter" spelled out there took most of the field's
width on a header line.

The results page follows the same arrangement, through the same component. `MatterSearchSettings`
is the scope, the deleted toggle and a trailing slot, rendered by the header control inside its
panel and by the results page as the row under its field — two seats, one object. It holds no state:
both surfaces already keep the scope somewhere authoritative and disagree about where (the control
on its `MatterSearch`, the page in the address), so a third copy could only be right when neither of
theirs was.

One fitness rule was widened to allow it, deliberately and narrowly: a percentage on a logical
`inset-*` property means "this element's own extent", which `styles/animations.css` already
establishes cannot be a token. Only bare percentages, only on the four inset properties.

title: The matter's Activity section as a contract every subsystem fulfils, and the note that opens in the window every other record opens in
entry:
Matter notes: a note is written, read, changed and deleted in the shared record window, its date and time sit on one line, and a document can be attached before the note exists.

The owner's first review round on the section, and one report that did not reproduce.

**The composer is gone; the record window took its place.** Writing a note was a form that unfolded inside the list it would join — a second place to learn where a note's fields live, and a list that lost its own shape while somebody was typing. A note now opens in the same two-pane window a time entry and a cost open in: the record on the left, its Attachments tab on the right, one action bar underneath. Creating one is that window with nothing in it and its fields already open, which is what makes starting a note a modal act rather than an inline one. The primary action reads **New Note**, the occurrence field is labelled **Date** with **Time** beside it on the same line, and the shared window brings a printable sheet with it — a note states both of the times it carries, so a reader years later can see how long after the call it was written down.

**A document is attached while the note is still a draft.** The picker offers the matter's own files from the first keystroke; the choices are held in the window and written the moment the note is. Nothing is uploaded and nothing is copied, exactly as before. Where a note is written but one of its documents does not attach, the list says which one and why rather than reporting a failure to save — the note exists, and somebody told otherwise would write it twice. Notes have no upload path of their own, so the shared attachments tab now withholds its dropzone from any record that cannot take one, rather than rendering a control that swallows a file in silence.

**On the report that the section never stopped loading:** it did not reproduce. The section was driven end to end against a real Worker — an empty matter, a matter with notes, a note written through the window, a document attached before saving — and the list settled every time; so does the route's empty-page envelope, now pinned by its own tests. What the rebuild changed is the shape that made a permanent skeleton possible at all. The notes read is an effect of its own, so nothing else the screen wants (who is signed in, the roster, the matter's files) can abort it before the read is even asked for, and a failed read settles the list with a stated reason and a Retry instead of leaving the skeleton standing. A section sitting on a skeleton is indistinguishable from a firm whose record cannot be read, which is why that is now structurally unreachable rather than merely unobserved.

Two things found on the way. A size utility off the generated spacing scale (`w-160`, `w-192`) compiles to no rule at all and no gate says so, which had left a search field and a date field full-bleed where both were meant to be narrow; the trap is recorded in the UI conventions. And `apps/web/e2e/login.spec.ts` no longer matches the shipped sign-in screen — the suite is not wired into CI, so it rotted unnoticed, and one of its assertions now contradicts shipped behaviour rather than merely naming a stale selector.

The matter's Activity section: fifteen subsystems' worth of history, in order, on one screen, each row named by the subsystem that owns it.

The federated timeline has been built, tested and served since the calendar slice — `GET /api/v1/matters/{matterId}/timeline`, fifteen declared sources read in place under one sort key, one cursor and one visibility contract, with nothing projected or copied. **Nothing in the web app called it.** The matter's story was scattered across the sections that each hold a piece of it, and the read that puts it back together answered to no screen.

**A consolidation view cannot know what its rows are, so it does not try.** Only the file manager knows what a file is; only the calendar knows what a hearing is called. The Activity section names no source and switches on none. Each subsystem declares its own half on both tiers:

- On the server, every timeline source now declares the read capability a description of its rows sits behind (`permission`), and a source whose rows have names declares a `describe` — one statement through `describeSelect`, which binds the matter, the page's row ids, the visibility predicate and the LIMIT, projecting a title, the subsystem's own word for what the row is, and that subsystem's own facts as one JSON object. The matter-scoped route asks for it after the merge, at most one statement per source present on the page, so the cost scales with the registry and never with the rows. The firm-wide read is never described, and a test asserts it: the no-label discipline on the projection is unchanged.
- On the client, an `ActivityContribution` per source lives beside the owning subsystem's own code (`$lib/file-manager/activity-contribution.ts`, `$lib/time/activity-contribution.ts`, and so on) and is registered once in `$lib/activity/contributions.ts`: the section word, the noun, the sentence for an undescribed row, the glyph, the Type word and the facts read out of the description in that subsystem's own vocabulary, how a row opens, and how one is made. `apps/web/test/activity-contributions.test.ts` scans the calendar package's own declarations and fails until every source has one; `pnpm run lint:matter-timeline-coverage` fails until every source is owned by a matter section's new `timelineSources` or declared ownerless in `sections.ts` with a reason.

**The permission gates the words, never the row.** A member who may not read notes still sees that a note was written on the matter, when and by whom — the entry carries no content — and does not see what it said. Six sources describe their rows today: a document by its name with its size, version and safety standing; a note by its opening line with when it happened and how many documents it points at; a time entry by its narrative with the hours; a cost by its description with the amount; an event by its title with its time and place; a deadline by its title with whether it is overdue, computed where the reader is. The rest keep the platform's own sentence, and adding one is a describe on the source and a contribution beside the subsystem.

**A file's type is what the file manager says it is.** The first cut took a name suffix for that. The new `$lib/file-manager/file-identity.ts` is the one place a file becomes words — the document type where the firm set one, else the label of the identification the design-system FileIcon resolves from the content type and the name ("PDF document", "Archive"), its size, and its safety standing out of the status register — and the Activity section draws the file manager's own glyph over the same inputs. Section and Type are two columns with two set filters: which part of the matter a row belongs to, and what it is in its own subsystem's words; one column doing both jobs had mixed "Deadline" with "pdf" in one list.

**It is the product's table, and its column controls are the column's own.** `DataTable.Grid` with Date (anchored), Time, Section, Type, Name, Details and Who; right-clicking a column heading opens the shared head menu for that column's filter, hide, pin and the roster of columns. There is no filter bar and no Columns button.

**It can make a record.** "+ New Note" opens the note window on the Activity section — the same window the Notes section opens, hosted by the new `NoteWindowHost` so the section knows nothing about notes beyond the fact that they have a window — and the row appears when it saves. A subsystem with a window of its own adds a create verb to its contribution and the control grows into a menu.

**Every section honours the entry an Activity row hands it.** Every deep link the timeline builds is `/matters/{id}/{section}?entry={rowId}`, and until now no section read it — a row opened onto a list. Now the Notes section opens the note in its window, read by its id through the new `GET /api/v1/notes/{noteId}` (so a note older than the first page opens all the same); the Time and Costs sections open the entry or cost in their windows, from the loaded page or by id; the Files section opens the file's folder, selects it and shows it in the inspector; the Calendar marks and scrolls to the row; the Custodian section opens the packet — the custody sources' deep links now carry the packet id through a `link_id` on the timeline projection, on matter-search's precedent, because the movement is the row and the packet is the door. A note row on Activity itself opens in the note window in place, through the same window host "+ New Note" uses.

**What happened to a document after it arrived is on the chronology.** A sixteenth source, `fileHistory`, admits the File History view's own events — renamed, moved, deleted, restored, a new version, an earlier version restored, the document type set, held by the safety check — through the one join that confines the audit log's polymorphic subject to a matter, exactly as the History view reads them. A first version's commit stays out, because a document's arrival is already the row that says it was added. Each row is named by the file as it is called now, typed by the History view's own action word through the same `historyActionLabel`, and opens onto the file.

**One register, two homes.** The Activity section's body is now `$lib/activity/activity-register.svelte`, and the Overview's "Recent activity" placeholder tile is that same register with a row budget of eight, the glance-level columns, and "See all activity" one step away — so what the Overview shows is what the Activity section shows, never a second summary of it. A firm-wide feed on the Home dashboard is the third home, and waits on the one design question it raises: whether a page spanning the member's matters may be described row by row, which the timeline's label discipline was written to refuse.

**Nothing says a document was "filed".** To a lawyer, filing means filing with a court, and this platform files nothing with a court: a document is added to the matter, an email is saved to it. The source keys stay `documentFiled` and `emailFiled` because they are wire contracts — which is exactly why the words a person reads are decided in the contributions and not taken from them.

Three deep links were repaired on the way. `emailFiled` pointed at a matter section spelled `email` and the three custody sources at `custody`; the app routes `emails` and `custodian`. A conflicts check has no matter section at all, so its rows state what happened and offer nowhere to go — the section registry says why, and the coverage lint keeps the answer current.

title: Every screen entered from another screen has a way back, and a gate says so
entry:
**Every screen's title now comes from one component, and a screen entered from another names where it came from.** The two are the same change: the reason three detail screens shipped with no way back is that there was no one place a header rule could live. Twenty screens assembled the design-system Masthead by hand in eight different combinations of its parts; four more hand-rolled an `h1` over a letterspaced `p` outside the design system entirely; and three area wrappers (settings, account, matter) had each partially centralized it for themselves, duplicating the same framing verbatim. Nothing was wrong with any one of them — the problem was that "what does a screen header look like here" had twenty-four answers.

`apps/web/src/lib/screen/screen-header.svelte` is now the one answer: the way back, the eyebrow, the title, the citation line, the actions, and a `trailing` column for a band that shares its height with something else. The Masthead recipe stays the primitive underneath — the register, the display serif, the density step — and this is the one assembly of it. Twenty-four call sites became one; `Masthead.Root` now appears exactly once in the application.

**The way back is named, not drawn** (owner's direction, 2026-09-03). A screen passes a destination **id** — `back="directory"` — and the href, the user-facing label and the glyph all come from the sidebar's own registry, so a back link cannot point at a screen that does not exist, cannot call it something the sidebar calls something else, and cannot go stale when a path moves. `DestinationId` is a literal union derived from the registry, so a typo is a type error rather than a link that renders and goes nowhere. The arrow shows the destination **in miniature** — its own sidebar mark beside its own name — because the point is to learn where the link lands, not merely that there is a way out. A screen outside the sidebar (the developer console) passes a spelled-out target instead, deliberately more work to write than an id.

The matter band takes the one shape too, which costs it a row it had spent two rounds saving: its way back was an unlabelled arrow inside the citation line, which cost no height but said only "back". It now leads the band, named and marked, in the same place as on every other screen.

`pnpm run lint:back-navigation` answers three questions from the route tree and the registry rather than from a list: every route whose nearest ancestor route renders a page passes a `back`; the destination it names resolves to that ancestor's own path; and nothing in the application assembles `Masthead.Root` itself or builds its own back link out of `EyebrowLink` and an arrow icon. The third is what keeps the first true — a screen with a hand-made header is free to grow its own idea of the way back, or none. It runs in the inner loop and in CI by derivation (every `lint:*` script in the root manifest is repo-wide), and its nineteen tests feed it deliberately broken route trees, including the one that would make the whole gate pass vacuously: a component walk that followed the import into the shared header and found the back link every screen's answer flows through.

**Moving between a matter's sections threw, because the create control treated an ordinary navigation as a defect.** The header's control checks that the claim behind it answers for the section the reader is standing on — a real guarantee, since the label comes from the address and the behaviour from the page, and a mismatch would mean the label says one thing and the press does another. It enforced that by throwing.

Leaving a section updates the address _before_ the outgoing page's effect cleanup releases its claim, so for one flush every ordinary navigation holds a claim for the section just left. The check fired on that window, inside a `$derived`, which crashed the screen: `The create control is claimed for "files" but the reader is on "parties"`, on every pair of tabs.

The decision moved into `honouredClaim` in `create-action.svelte.ts`, which ignores a claim belonging to another section rather than throwing. The guarantee is unchanged — an unhonoured claim is not pressable — and the control falls back to disabled carrying the line it already shows in the moment before a section claims. A genuine mismatch, a page answering for a section it does not render, now surfaces as a control that never becomes pressable instead of a white screen. Four tests pin the predicate, including the navigation window itself.

The slot's other rule is untouched: a second claimant while a first still holds the control is still refused loudly, because that one really is two parts of a screen believing they own the same action.

**The load-profile snapshot tests stop failing on a busy runner.** Every test in `packages/fixtures/test/load-profile-snapshot.test.ts` seeds a real SQLite snapshot — the version-bump case seeds two — and all six ran under Vitest's five-second default, which is sized for tests that compute rather than tests that do a second or more of genuine work. On a loaded node shard that is not enough: the version-bump case timed out twice on one pull request, and it passes in 1.36 s on an idle machine, so what failed was a measurement of the runner rather than anything about the code.

The five seeding tests now carry an explicit `60_000`, matching `load-profile-smoke.test.ts` beside them, which was given the same treatment for the same reason and is why the pattern was already in the file next door. The sixth test seeds nothing and stays on the default, which is honest — it really is a unit test. Sixty seconds is deliberately generous: nothing here measures how fast the seeding is, so a timeout that trips on a slow machine only ever reports the machine.

Nothing about what the tests assert changed. The timeout is the clock, not the claim.

title: The calendar interface: one component, the firm screen, the entry window, the record forms, the firm's week start, layers and cards, and rooms
entry:
**The calendar's third round: the room grid, bookings on an event, and the resource catalog.** `CalendarView` gains the `resource` scope: `/calendar/rooms` is the one component over `GET /api/v1/calendar/resources/{id}/availability`, a week at a time, with a picker that names the room and mirrors it into the address. A booking paints as the event it belongs to (the availability read carries a type name and never a title), takes the danger register with a "Double-booked" line where the read pre-paired it with another booking, and opens that event's window. Two small reads join the API, `GET /api/v1/events/{eventId}/bookings` and `GET /api/v1/firm-events/{firmEventId}/bookings`, over the package's existing `readBookingsForEvent`, so an event's window can list what it booked; the entry window gains a Rooms tab, a Book a Room verb (the booking takes the event's own window, lands even when it double-books, and says so) and Release per row. Settings › Practice › Rooms and Resources is the catalog: add, change, retire and restore, each an `ActionDialog` committing at once, gated on the session's `calendar:manage`.

**The calendar's second round: layers, a colleague, a settled filter, and two cards.** The firm calendar can be widened to the timeline's date-bearing sources through a LAYER (`CALENDAR_LAYERS` in `apps/web/src/lib/calendar/calendar-vocabulary.ts`): custody dates first, the due-backs and review dates the safe custody register already federates, each painting its custody number and opening the register. Only sources whose rows fall due qualify; the timeline's history sources stay in the timeline rather than flooding a month. A colleague picker seats after Mine and Everyone and reads one colleague's calendar through the same member filter, under the reader's own visibility. The agenda gains "Hide settled", which leaves out cancelled settings and satisfied, vacated or superseded deadlines and says how many it left out; the month and the week always paint them struck (owner flag C5). Every refinement is mirrored into the address.

The firm-wide read now says a setting was called off: the `matterEvent` source emits `cancelledEvent` as its own kind (a closed word, never the reason a person typed), so the firm grid strikes a vacated hearing exactly as the matter section does, and the settled filter can leave it out. Before this the federated row carried no status and a cancelled hearing painted on the firm calendar as if it were still on.

`CalendarView` takes `agendaDays` and `limit`, and two hosts embed it: Home's Today card (the reader's own scope, today and tomorrow, six rows, a line to the rest) and the matter overview's Coming up card (the matter's next thirty days, six rows, a line to the Calendar section). Neither writes a read of its own.

**The calendar is reachable, and it is one component.** Slices 6·1 and 6·2 had been the largest built-but-unreachable surface in the program: thirty-three routes, a federated read, firm events, resources, links and continuance, and one matter tab that read two tables. `docs/specs/2026-09-02-calendar-interface-design.md` plans the interface and this lands its first slice.

Two homes, on the EventRail division. `@magna-carta/design-system/calendar-grid` is the domain-free presentation: `CalendarGrid.Month`, `.Week` and `.Agenda` take entries with a civil day, a label, a detail line, a caller-formatted time, a subtle-register tone and a strike, and never learn what a hearing is. `apps/web/src/lib/calendar/` holds `CalendarView`, the one calendar every surface embeds with a scope (`firm`, `mine`, `matter`); it owns the window arithmetic on `CalendarDate` (a month is the full weeks it spans, never more than six, inside the read's cap), the read plan per scope, the projection through one vocabulary, the view state mirrored into the address, and the entry window. Both are registered in `tooling/lint-one-ui/registry.json`, so a second month grid or a second calendar composition fails the gate.

The firm grid paints kinds and matter numbers, never titles: the federated read declares non-privileged labels by design, and the title is fetched for the one row somebody opened. Deadlines paint from their own access-gated read with titles and the read-time overdue flag; the federated read is narrowed to the event kind so nothing is painted twice; firm events paint from the firm's own listing. The three reads fail independently and the notice names which one did; each walk has a page ceiling and says when it hit it.

`/calendar` is the firm screen (Mine / Everyone, month / week / agenda, a Record menu); `/calendar/firm-events?entry=` is the deep link the federated read already emitted. The matter's Calendar section keeps its two tables as the List view and gains Month and Agenda over the same component, and its two record controls go live: the earlier deferral to a participant picker is answered by building the picker (a firm member, a directory entity, or somebody who is neither). The entry window is a `RecordWindow` with in-place editing and the verbs the record allows; every form is an `ActionDialog` over a pure draft model, asserted without a browser. The sidebar's Calendar row flips to shipped.

**The day the week begins on is a firm setting.** The owner's ruling on the calendar's first slice: the week is the unit a firm plans in, so which day it begins on is the firm's decision, never a personal preference. `packages/calendar/src/settings.ts` holds it over the per-firm setting table (`calendar.weekStartsOn`, Sunday by default); `GET /api/v1/calendar/settings` reads it for every member who can read the calendar and `PATCH` moves it under `calendar:manage`, audited and idempotent, with the contract and the client regenerated. `CalendarView` reads it once with the rest of its context and hands it to every grid, so no surface picks a week start of its own.

Settings › Practice › Calendar is the page, and it is the first settings page with a server behind it: a draft that keeps the shape the shared rows and footer already understand but answers from the firm's own read and saves through the route, never through local storage. It shows no per-browser history, because a ledger in one browser would misstate a firm-wide fact; the record is the audit row. The standing rule is in `docs/conventions/design-corrections.md`.

**The gate's test battery runs only when asked for.** The node shards, the Miniflare shards and the story suite are the bulk of the Actions bill and the whole of a pull request's wall-clock, and the node shards outgrew the 1-vCPU runner's fifteen-minute cap twice in one day. By the owner's ruling a pull request now runs them only under the `run-tests` label (attaching it re-runs the gate with the battery); a manual dispatch asks with its `test_battery` input; a queued merge always asks. The checks stay on every pull request. The branch's own full `pnpm test` is the standing merge bar, stated in the pull request. The node battery is also six shards rather than four. `docs/conventions/build-performance.md` carries the ruling and the trade.

title: One create control, at one width, on every screen: New moves up beside the search
entry:
**One create control, at one width, on every screen — and on a matter it sits beside the search.** Every matter section carried its own create button in its own action row, a different distance down the screen on every tab and a different width on every one of them: "New Fee", "Record a Cost", "Log Time", "Write Note", a bare "New". The owner's ruling on 2026-09-03 moves the affordance up into the matter header beside the search, as ONE control that reflects the section it is on without ever changing size.

`CreateControl` is a design-system component: a primary Button held at a token width (`size.create-control`), reading "New" and one noun, pressing straight through or opening a menu in the same footprint, and rendering disabled with its reason rather than leaving the row. The noun grammar (`create-label.ts`) refuses a phrase or a noun the width cannot hold, so the truncation the recipe carries is theoretical.

On a matter the control is answered from two places. `sections.ts` gains a required `createNoun` — a noun, or `null` with a `createWaitingOn` line — so the label is settled by the address before the section has mounted and never flickers between tabs. The section's page claims the behaviour through `claimMatterCreate` (`create-action.svelte.ts`) while it is mounted: a ledger exports `openNew()` and the page hands it over; Files hands over a three-item menu; Calendar states the refusal it used to draw as two disabled buttons. The slot refuses a second claimant, and a mount test pins the assumption that refusal rests on — a page swap releases the leaving claim before the arriving one lands.

The docket, the directory and the firm's custody register render the same component in their mastheads, and the custody register gains the register search beside it, so the pair reads the same way everywhere. Empty states no longer carry a second create button; each names the control at the top instead.

`pnpm run lint:matter-create-control` is the gate: every section answers, every noun fits, and no `<Button>` or menu trigger wearing the plus glyph — or reading as a create verb — survives on a screen that carries the control.

title: Retire the arrangement-move stream note
The fee arrangement lives behind the status seal, and names its signed agreement
entry: **The fee arrangement moves from the Fees screen into the matter status window, and a version can name its signed agreement.** `matter-status-dialog.svelte` reads the arrangement on open and shows an Engagement section (agreement on file, billed as, terms, in force since, folded history) with Amend seated beside it; `fee-ledger.svelte` and `fee-details-panel.svelte` lose the strip, View and Amend, and `arrangement-dialog.svelte` is deleted with its allowance. `matter_billing_arrangement` gains a nullable `agreement_file_id` (a matter file, the conflicts waiver's precedent), carried through `setBillingArrangement`, the route contract and the client; the amend dialog gains a document picker, now the shared `matter-document-picker.svelte`.

title: The time fields stop apologising, and a void stops being permanent
entry:
A draft's rate can be set, and its amount now follows every input it is computed from.

The rate chain has always ranked a per-entry override above every stored tier, and capture has always accepted one. What was missing was a way to SAY it — the record window showed the rate as a fact rather than a field — and a way to say it on an entry the firm already holds. **`PATCH /api/v1/time-entries/{id}` now takes `overrideRateE4`**: a number prices this entry, null hands it back to the chain, and absent leaves the rate exactly where it stands.

This does not weaken the rate snapshot. That rule says a rate card edited LATER never re-rates a standing entry, and it still holds; what changed is somebody's deliberate answer for one entry, not a card's answer for all of them.

**Two defects surfaced while building it, and are fixed with it.** Both are about the same thing — an entry's money columns are DERIVED, and the route was not re-deriving them:

- **Changing the time worked left the entry billed at the old figure.** The patch wrote `raw_duration_minutes` and left `duration_minutes` and `amount_minor` untouched, so an entry corrected from one hour to two was still billed as one hour and still priced as one hour. The worked time is now re-rounded on the firm's own increment and the amount recomputed. This could not be left alone alongside the change above: a settable rate whose amount is computed against a stale duration is a worse field than no field at all.
- **Correcting an entry's work date silently threw away its rate.** The date change re-asked the chain without the entry's own override, so a correction to one field put the card's answer back and quietly changed what the client is charged. A standing override now carries through.

**`GET /api/v1/time-entries/rounding-policy`** serves the increment and direction in force for a matter and a member, resolved through the same scope chain the capture uses. A screen cannot otherwise state what an entry will actually be billed at, and a screen that guesses records the wrong amount of time.

Two pieces of chrome every surface inherits: a full-screen panel squares its corners, and a table's totals sit on the bottom of its frame.

**A modal filling the screen has square corners.** A radius says the panel is a sheet lying on top of something; at full size there is nothing underneath it, and the curve reads as four notches of desktop showing through the corners of the application. Fixed on the shared modal frame rather than in the record window, so any shell that grows an expand gesture inherits it.

**A totals strip sits on the bottom edge of its frame, not under the last row.** A ledger fills the height it is given, so the ordinary case is a table with room beneath it — and the strip is held down by stickiness, which does nothing while there is nothing below it to scroll past. The totals of a four-row ledger were coming to rest halfway up the screen with a band of empty surface below them. The table now asks for its frame's full height and a scenery row takes the difference, so the records keep the one line each the density gives them.

Table layout does not behave the way it reads, and that row's placement was settled by measuring a real browser rather than by reasoning: in the table's foot, or as a percentage on the cell rather than the row, it is given nothing at all and the surplus is handed to the last record, which stretches to fill; with a zero-height body the records keep their height but are pushed to the bottom, putting the gap above them. As the last row of the body it takes the whole surplus and everything else stays put.

**A date field's label sits its control on the same baseline as the fields beside it.** It was omitting the line-height every other field label sets, so a date field started a few pixels below its neighbours and a row of three read as two fields and a mistake.

A voided time entry can be put back.

Voiding is how a mistaken entry is retired, and it has always been one-way. That is right for the act and wrong for the accident: people void the wrong row, void on a colleague's say-so that turns out to be mistaken, and void an afternoon's work when they meant to void one line of it. Until now the only repair was to type the whole entry again, which loses its number, its internal memo, its codes, its attached documents and its history — exactly the loss that made a misfiled entry worth moving rather than re-typing.

**`POST /api/v1/time-entries/{id}/unvoid` returns it to draft** with all of that intact. It restores to DRAFT and never to submitted or approved: those were somebody's judgement about an entry that has since been withdrawn, and they have to be given again. The restore is recorded as its own event, so a reader of the entry's history sees both acts.

**It is not a lifecycle transition, deliberately.** The state machine still says nothing leaves a terminal state, because every other record kind in the product reads that same table and none of them has been designed for a backward move. This is its own guarded act with its own refusals, the way refiling a misfiled entry is its own statement rather than a field on the update.

**The one void that must stay a void is an entry converted into a cost.** That conversion moves the entry's value onto a cost record and voids the time in the same batch, precisely so the firm cannot count the work twice; restoring the time afterwards would undo the half of that act that was protecting the client. The conversion is recorded in the audit trail and nowhere else — no column on either row names the other — so that is what the route asks before it will restore anything.

On screen it is the verb in the place the opposite verb lives: the ledger's own menu turns Void into Unvoid on a voided row, and the record window offers it on the action bar, which is where somebody lands when they open an entry to find out what happened to it.

Several fields on the time and cost windows stop explaining themselves and start working.

- **Every code field carries a `(None)` row, for every firm.** A firm that does not code its time is the commonest configuration in the product, and it was getting two paragraphs apologising that it had no codes turned on, under two fields it could not use. `(None)` is also what the field READS at rest rather than a blank: an empty box says nobody has filled this in, and `(None)` says the entry carries no code. The explanatory line survives for the two states that really are inabilities — this account may not read the catalogue, or the read failed.
- **The internal memo moved under the description and lost its badge.** They are one act of writing that differs only in who reads it; down beside the arithmetic the memo was a stranded field a reader met after they had finished with the entry. The "Internal" chip beside the label said in a second voice what the word Internal in the label had already said.
- **The Billing dropdown lost "No charge, on the bill at nothing".** It is non-billable under a longer name — both mean the client is charged nothing and the entry carries no value, and the only difference anybody could name is whether the line prints, which is a question about a bill rather than about this entry. Two rows for one disposition make a member choose between them, and there is no right answer to that choice.
- **A document can be attached before the entry is saved.** "Save the entry first" is a true statement about the route and a wrong one about the work: the person writing up an afternoon has the document open in front of them. The picks are held and applied the moment the entry is written.
- **The cost window writes the same pair in the same shape** — Description then Internal Memo, stacked and full width — and commits with the same words, "Save & Close". A cost and a time entry are recorded minutes apart by the same person, and the fields they share should not move between them.
- **Voided, never struck.** One word for the act, across the history rail, the sheet, the ledger and the record window.

Time is entered in hours, in units, or as the span between two clock times.

Three ways of saying the same thing, because firms are three. **Hours** — "1:30", "1.5", "90m" — is what everybody understands and is always available. **Units** counts the firm's own billing increment: a practice that bills in tenths thinks in tenths, and asking that person to convert six units into 0.6 hours is asking them to do arithmetic the product already knows how to do. **A span** is the two clock times the work happened between, which is how somebody who was in a meeting from nine to half past ten actually remembers it.

All three are live at once and each is a view of the same minutes: type in any of them and the others follow.

**A unit is whatever the firm bills in, and is asked rather than assumed.** Six minutes is the prevailing default and a firm on quarter hours means two and a half times as much work by "two units" — so the increment is read from the firm's own setting, scoped to the matter and the member, and never guessed.

**How many of the three are on screen is the reader's own setting**, in the record window's menu. All three show by default, because a capability nobody can see is a capability nobody has; a member who only ever thinks in one of them can put the other two away. The last one standing cannot be turned off — a window with no way to state how long the work took cannot record time — so the control refuses rather than obeys, and says so.

A span that ends earlier than it starts is read as crossing midnight, because that is a real evening.

title: The governance-advisories stream retires its note
The queue cannot be clicked here, and the node tests stop hitting the runner's cap
entry:
**The merge queue is not on offer here, and the conventions stop promising it.** GitHub offers merge queues only in organization-owned repositories (public, or private on Enterprise Cloud); this repository is private and user-owned, so the setting that #488 documented does not exist for it. The owner declined the transfer that would make it available (2026-09-03), so the deploy-queue entry now records why it cannot be clicked, the decision, and the habit that stands in — one merge at a time, the next branch synced onto the `main` the last merge produced — with the up-to-date-before-merge ruleset option deliberately left off because it spends a full battery per open stream per merge. `build-performance.md`, `operations.md` and `CLAUDE.md` describe the pull-request tier as the only run between a merge and production, which is what is true; the `merge_group` tier stays wired for the day the ownership changes. Recorded as a decision.

**And the node test job stops running into the runner's cap.** On #488's battery the second of two node shards was cancelled at fifteen minutes with every test it had reached passing: the slim runner caps a job at fifteen minutes regardless of the job's own timeout, and the suite has grown to where two shards sit on that line. The job now runs four shards, each well under the cap for the same test minutes.

**And the column-filter story stops racing the menu it opens.** The grid's ColumnFilters story failed about one run in six under the suite's load, with focus on the header menu's panel instead of the filter field being typed into: the menu takes focus on open on the next animation frame, not with its mount, and a step that reached the field first had that frame land afterwards. The story now waits for focus to be inside the menu before opening the submenu, and sends the filter keys to the field directly since the rule it asserts is the keyboard one. Six consecutive full-suite runs pass.

title: Slice 6·3 — Tasks: the record, matter plans, the time link, and the seam an addon writes through
entry:
**Matter plans — `matter_plan_template`, `matter_plan_task_template`, eleven routes, and the two
provenance columns `matter_task` was deliberately left without.**

A plan is firm-authored configuration, never a record: rows come only from the createPlan route
behind `tasks:managePlans`, which is why both list reads are claimed bounded-by-construction rather
than paged. The platform seeds none, and the migration inserts none.

`proposeMatterPlan` is a PURE read — it computes the dates and resolves the roles and commits
nothing. `acceptMatterPlan` writes the kept subset in one batch, because a matter carrying six of
eleven steps after a half-failed batch is worse than one carrying none. The proposal is a GET and
acceptance is the POST, which is how the surface says out loud which one writes.

The anchor vocabulary is `matter_opened` and `none`, held by a CHECK so a third value is a reviewed
migration; every candidate beyond it is the front half of a docketing rule. `addCalendarDays` is the
one piece of date arithmetic in the package, and `test/no-arithmetic.test.ts` now pins that function's
uniqueness rather than the absence of arithmetic — an exception has to be visible to stay one.

Provenance is not a live link: a test edits every field of a template and asserts the accepted task
comes back byte-identical. Three more pin what the review exists to catch — an offset landing on a
Sunday, a role resolving to nobody and arriving NAMED rather than blank, and a kept step whose
predecessor was dropped waiting on nothing rather than on a task never created.

`opened_at` holds a civil date on some paths and an instant on others, so the anchor read cuts ten
characters rather than parsing — the same cut the note ordering already makes.

The offer is rendered on the matter's Tasks section rather than the new-matter screen: a matter
opened before its plan existed can still take it, and somebody who declined can come back.

**Tasks — `@magna-carta/tasks`, the `matter_task` record, eleven routes, and two screens.**

`matter_task` holds what to do, whose it is, when it is due, whether it is still owed, the one task
it waits on, and the matter's files it points at; `matter_task_document` links those on the
`matter_note_document` model. Three permission keys (`tasks:read`, `tasks:write`, `tasks:assign`)
seeded to the seats that do firm work, Billing included.

**`matter_id` is nullable**, which is the opposite of the call `firm_event` made against
`matter_event`, and both table comments now say why. The calendar split its tables because a firm
event and a matter event are read on two different surfaces; tasks have one surface either way, so
splitting would mean unioning back together on the read every member makes most often. The
does-not-apply branch the calendar warned about is answered by confinement: `taskVisibilityFragment`
is the whole population of "may this member see this task", and every read composes it.

Nothing derives a date and no overdue column exists — the calendar's date-arithmetic source scan runs
over this package, and a schema scan asserts the absence. Cancellation and deletion are both real,
held apart by two CHECK constraints so each terminal state carries its own evidence.

Notifications raise four topics for two acts, split by whether the task is on a matter — the
`calendar.firmEvent.*` split, forced by the registry's two matter-anchoring fitness rules. The
assignee needed a sixth audience: the design routed assignment to `designated`, which is the firm's
trust-compliance designation and resolves to nobody when unconfigured, so as specified every task
assignment would have delivered to no one, silently. `named-recipient` reads the member from the
payload, so the person told is whoever was named at the write. `tasks` joins the category vocabulary
and `matterTask` the subject kinds — two CHECKs, so two table rebuilds.

Open tasks register a close advisory and never a precondition. The matter's Tasks section and My Work
at `/tasks` are one component reading two routes.

**Tasks gain the four things an outside system needs and none of the things a vendor does.**

The platform still integrates with nothing. It ships no adapter, schedules no sync, resolves no
conflict and maps no vocabulary — every one of those is a decision about somebody else's product and
belongs to the addon that knows it, on `@magna-carta/integrations` where the credential and
capability machinery already lives. What ships is the part the platform cannot delegate, and each
piece is here because it is impossible to add afterwards:

`matter_task_external_link` records that a task IS some object over there. `system` is open text with
a non-empty CHECK — the `directory_edge.edge_type` discipline — so a second system is an addon
rather than a reviewed migration, and nothing in the schema names a vendor. **Two uniqueness rules,
and they are different claims:** one remote object maps to at most one task, or two tasks fight over
one mirror and each wins half the time; one task holds at most one identity per system, or a change
here has two places to go and no way to choose. Both are INDEXES rather than service checks, because
a race between two syncs is exactly the case a pre-check loses — a test composes two colliding links
before committing either and asserts the loser aborts.

`matter_task_deletion` is the tombstone, written in the **same batch** as the delete. A row that is
gone cannot be enumerated afterwards, so a mirror learns of a deletion there or never, and one that
never learns keeps the work alive somewhere the firm has stopped looking. It carries identifiers and
nothing else: a tombstone preserving the title would defeat the delete it records. A deleted task's
external links go with it, so its remote object is free to be linked to a real task again.

`matter_task.updated_by` is echo suppression. A two-way sync must tell its own writes from a
person's, or it pushes back everything it just pulled and the two sides oscillate. Every write path
stamps it — including the cascade that clears a successor's blocker, because that successor really
did change. It is required rather than optional in the statement signatures, which is what made the
compiler name all six call sites.

`readTaskChanges` answers "what moved since I last looked" as two keyset streams with
**INDEPENDENT POSITIONS**. One shared cursor looks sufficient and is wrong in a way that would never
surface in testing: the cursor's id half comes from whichever stream produced the last row, and a
`matterTaskDeletion_` handle applied as the tie-break against `matter_task.id` silently excludes
every live task sorting below it at that same instant — a change lost permanently, at a page
boundary, under a clock collision nobody can reproduce on demand. A test walks five tasks written at
one instant a page at a time and asserts nothing is skipped or repeated.

Visibility is not relaxed for any of it. The feed composes `taskVisibilityFragment` like every other
task read, so an addon connected as a member syncs exactly what that member can see, and the
external-id lookup returns the same null for "no such correspondence" and "you cannot see the task it
names" so it cannot be used to probe.

Five routes, the external links folded into the page read beside the attachments and the time, and
the adapter-author contract written where an adapter author will look: `packages/tasks/CLAUDE.md`.

**A time entry names the task it was worked on — one nullable `task_id` on `time_entry`, with the
minutes read back grouped over a whole page of tasks.**

The scope study's flag **T2** answered its own way: ONE task per entry, never a set. An entry split
across two tasks needs an allocation of its minutes between them, and an allocation is a second
ledger with its own rounding and its own disputes; the honest encoding of "this block served two
tasks" is two entries, which the capture surface already supports. A join table is an additive
migration over this column's data if many-to-many is ever wanted; the reverse is not.

`assertTaskOnMatter` is the whole enforcement of the one rule the schema cannot hold — SQLite cannot
express the cross-table condition without a trigger. It refuses three shapes under one code, on the
`file-not-on-matter` model, because the caller's remedy is the same for all three: a task that does
not exist, a task on another matter (which would let one matter's time point at work another matter
is paying for), and a task on NO matter, which is the firm's own work and has nothing to bill it to.
A null `matter_id` on the task is a refusal, never a wildcard.

`readTaskTimeSummaries` is minutes and never money: what a task COST is a billing question with a
different audience and a different permission, and a summary carrying both would be gated by the
stricter everywhere it is read. Void is excluded and every other status counts. It is **batched by
construction** — a set of task identifiers in, a map out — because its caller is a paged list, and
it rides `pageFrom` beside the attachments read rather than a route of its own, so nothing was left
uncalled. The scope travels WITH the totals rather than once per page: the same two numbers mean
"what the task cost the firm" under `firm` and "what I put into it" under `own`, and a consumer must
not be able to render one without the other.

Setting the link is a field in the time record window offering that matter's open tasks. The load
profile gained a task volume — the deep list, the firm's own matterless work, and the linked time —
and the harness earned its keep on the first run: `tasks.my-work-page-1` scans, which is structural
(the firm-wide read names no matter and no assignee, and its visibility fragment is an OR spanning
the presence of `matter_id` itself), and it is recorded by name with the number to revisit it
against rather than waved through. Two pre-existing firm-window scans, `matterNote` and `matterTask`,
were sitting unallowlisted and are now named with the same reason as the other eight.

title: The one-table ruling is now a gate: raw-table and table-machinery in lint:one-ui
entry:
`pnpm run lint:one-ui` now holds the one-table ruling, which until today was a header comment on `DataTable.Grid` and a row in the port plan's table of rules nobody had built.

Two rules. `raw-table` fails a `<table>`, `<thead>`, `<tr>`, `<th>`, `<td>` or a table ARIA role written anywhere outside the design system's data-table home, on both sides of the app/design-system line, one problem per file at its first element. `table-machinery` fails the half that rule cannot see: a screen that composes the presentational primitives correctly and then writes what the Grid already carries — a sortable header (`aria-sort`, the `mc-table-sort` recipe), the headless engine composed by hand (`createSvelteTable`, a direct `@tanstack/table-core` import) or the adapter's toolbar parts. That is the shape the ruling calls a defect by definition: a second answer to "what does clicking a header do", with the recipe on it so it reads fine in review.

The audit that preceded the rule: twelve surfaces render through `DataTable.Grid`, eighteen compose the primitives for a plain grid of facts, one page wrote a raw `<table>` (the speed test's sample list, now on the primitives) and one wrote its own sort (the firm-usage By Location table, recorded as an allowance that names the port it needs). Every rule is proved against known-bad input in the tool's own test file, and the allowance fails the run the day its violation is gone.

title: One way to name a person anywhere: the directory-linking family, the matter's parties and client, and the record finished
entry:
**Opening a new tab is one gated pattern.** Fifteen call sites opened beside the reader in three
spellings (`target="_blank"` anchors, `window.open`, `globalThis.open`) and no stated rule. They now
go through `apps/web/src/lib/navigation/open-beside.ts`, naming why the destination cannot open in
place from a closed set of reasons — `external`, `file`, `session`, `unsaved-work` — and a source
scan (`apps/web/test/open-beside.test.ts`) refuses any `_blank` that did not come through it. The
owner's ruling: a new tab is unusual here, and where it happens it follows one repeatable process
rather than a screen's own judgement.

**The conflicts check, the waiver disposition and the cost record pick people through the one
picker.** `subject-party-picker.svelte` and `cost-payee-picker.svelte` are deleted; the check runner
uses `EntityPicker` in multiple mode, the disposition dialog and the cost record window in single
mode, all over `directoryPickerSearch`. A source scan (`apps/web/test/entity-picker-gate.test.ts`)
refuses any other caller of `searchDirectory` outside `$lib/directory`, naming the one standing copy
— the custodian's `owner-picker.svelte` — with the reason it stands: the custodian-refinements
stream rewrites that file and its dialog, and folds it when it lands. The allowance fails the scan
the day the copy is gone.

**The directory-linking family, and the matter's parties built on it.** Three design-system
components: `EntityIdentity`, the one mark for a person or an organization wherever one is named;
`EntityPicker`, the one field one is chosen in, which takes a `search` and never fetches (the
settle, the floor, the abort of a superseded question and the three states live in
`picker-search.ts`, tested on their own); and `RecordParties`, the tab a record shows its people
in, the counterpart of `RecordAttachments`, with its confirmation on `ActionDialog` from the first
commit. `apps/web/src/lib/directory/directory-picker-source.ts` is the one adapter from the
directory's ranked search to the picker. The matter Parties page moves onto the tab and gains
`linkMatterParty`; its hand-composed removal dialog and its allowance go. The conflicts, custodian
and cost pickers still carry their own combobox over `searchDirectory` and fold onto `EntityPicker`
in a later slice; the one-implementation registry refuses a fourth copy meanwhile. The Directory's
route is renamed from `/contacts` to `/directory`.

**The matter calendar's Soon line names its real dependency.** It said recording waited on the
participant picker; the picker exists now, and what recording waits on is the event and deadline
forms, which the calendar stream builds. When it does, `participantKind: "entity"` is an
`EntityPicker` pick and an event opened in a record window shows its people on `RecordParties`; a
judge stays an `external` participant by default, as the calendar design rules.

**The client is a party from the moment a matter exists.** `CreateMatterRequest` gains
`clientEntityId`; `packages/matters` `createMatter` writes the `client` `matter_party` row in the
same batch as the matter (`clientPartyStatements`), so billing, trust, document assembly and the
conflicts engine, which all derive the client from that link, find one from the first read.
`MatterDetail` and `MatterSummary` carry `clientEntityId` (one batched read per page, never per
row). The intake's client field is the design-system `EntityPicker` over the directory; the draft
refuses to create a matter of either status without a chosen client; `client-picker.svelte` and
`knownClientNames` are gone. "Open Client Record" is a real link, and "Run Conflict Check" runs a
preliminary check against the chosen client before the matter exists, reporting the hit count with
a link to the report. The overview's Client fact opens the directory record. The never-called
`client-migration.ts` backfill is deleted with the owner's ruling that there is nothing to back
fill; `client_display_name` keeps being written as the docket's caption, and the contract step that
drops it is not this change.

**The directory record's remaining gaps close.** `EDGE_TYPES` gains the membership family
(`officer_of`, `director_of`, `partner_of`, `trustee_of`, `personal_representative_of`, `agent_of`,
`employment`, `member_of`, `shareholder_of`, `beneficiary_of`, `guardian_of`,
`point_of_contact_for`); `affiliation` stays for the rows already recorded and is no longer offered.
Every new type is classed in `packages/conflicts/src/edge-classes.ts` — the constituent types under
`control` for now, the over-inclusive direction, because the tighter fifth class waits for the
conflicts pass. `createDirectoryEdge` and `createDirectoryCategory` join the web client. The
relationships pane is one `edges-pane.svelte` registered three times: Relationships on both kinds,
People on an organization, Organizations on a person, each recording an edge through `EntityPicker`
with the type narrowed by the record's kind and the direction decided by the type
(`edge-draft.ts`, tested). `new-entity-dialog.svelte` and `merge-dialog.svelte` move onto
`ActionDialog` and their allowances go; the categories pane creates a category through the add row.

title: A firm provisioned at 2 a.m. is readable at 2 a.m.
entry:
A firm whose bucket is not the one bound to this Worker can be read and written again.

Provisioning has minted a bucket per firm since the beginning; the Worker binds one. R2 bindings are static configuration and no runtime API turns a bucket name into a handle, so the resolver refused rather than write a firm's bytes where no read path could reach them — which took uploads and the download shelf down for every provisioned firm, not just the one in the log.

`resolveFirmBucket` now returns an S3-API-backed handle for a bucket the Worker has no binding to, signed with the account-scoped credential that already reaches every bucket in the account. The bound bucket still resolves to its binding, so the common path pays no signing round trip and no network hop. Firm creation stays off the release path: a firm provisioned at 2 a.m. is readable at 2 a.m., with no config commit and no deploy.

The adapter is written to the surface its callers use and refuses the rest out loud rather than quietly. Where the S3 API cannot answer what the binding would — a listing carries no user metadata — it does the extra work instead of returning a plausible wrong answer, because the sweep that reads metadata off a listing decides from it whether a firm's whole bucket needs rewriting.

Provisioning also applies the firm bucket's expiry rules now: bundles at seven days, conversion results at twenty-four hours, and abandoned multipart uploads at twenty-four hours. Firm buckets previously got none of them, so every artifact a firm had ever downloaded or converted accumulated, metered, forever.

A download or conversion result is checked for in the same bucket the URL handed back addresses.

`files/firm-bucket.ts` resolves a firm's storage as a pair — the name a presigned URL addresses, and the handle the Worker reads through — because presigning against one bucket while reading through another is silent data loss. Five call sites took the name and then reached for the bound binding anyway, which is the exact split the seam exists to prevent.

The bundle and conversion progress resolvers took a bare `bucketName`, signed a URL against it, and asked the bound binding whether the artifact was still there. So did the ZIP download route, for both its cached-artifact fast paths and the inline stream, and the bundle build consumer for the bytes it reads and the artifact it writes. Today the guard's refusal hides this, because a firm whose bucket is not the bound one cannot get that far. Once a firm resolves to its own bucket, the same code would report a live artifact `expired`, or hand back a signed URL for an object it had confirmed in a different bucket.

All five now take the pair, and the two job coordinators resolve it through the same seam rather than reading the binding off their own `env`. The name a URL is signed against and the handle its bytes come from are one decision again.

Every read and write of a firm's objects resolves the firm's bucket through one seam.

`src/files/firm-bucket.ts` is the one home for "which bucket holds this firm's bytes", and it answers as a pair: the name a presigned URL addresses, and the handle the Worker reads through. Twenty-one modules reached the bound binding directly instead, past that resolver. Eight of them were genuinely a firm's bytes — the email capture consumer, preview delivery, the search index consumer and its compaction sweep, the natural-language feed, the storage tiering sweep, the WOPI host, and the document editing session — and now resolve through the seam.

Several already had the answer and did not use it. The capture consumer carried the bucket name on its own message and passed it to attachment extraction while reading through the binding. The preview delivery token has carried a `bucket` field all along, with a comment calling it a forward seam. The tiering sweep's comment described this exact change as future work.

The seam grew a second entry point for callers holding only a firm id — a queue consumer whose message predates any bucket field — so nothing needed a new message field to be correct.

Four modules keep the binding because their bytes belong to the platform or to local development: the status reachability probe, the development presigner's staging objects, the development upload leg, and the development seeder. `pnpm run lint:firm-bucket-seam` fails any new direct use, and fails a stale allow-list entry too, so an exemption cannot outlive its reason.

title: The three full-screen surfaces come onto the shells
entry:
The three surfaces excluded as "full-screen" open in `ActionDialog`, now that the frame owns expand.

The time sheet is a reading panel that opens filling the screen, its toolbar the first row of the pane and its identity the frame's header; the flag, the two icons and the three utilities it had rebuilt by hand are gone, and the frame's corner control shrinks it back to the record width. The safe-browse screenshot viewer is a reading panel opened expanded. The cost review was never full-screen: it is a reading panel whose three answers — Skip, Kick Back, Approve — sit under the facts they decide, and it walks on rather than closing.

Three allowances leave the registry; three remain, every one a named exclusion: the command palette (a launcher), the settings ledger (a Sheet), and the fee-arrangement window (a record's shape, and a layout the owner is rethinking).

title: Filling the screen is the frame's, not one shell's
entry:
Filling the screen is the frame's, not one shell's.

The record window's expand — the corner control, the session memory, the geometry that drops the width cap — moves beneath both modal shells as `internal/frame-expansion.svelte.ts`, and `ActionDialog` gains the same control on its Dialog kinds (`form`, `reading`; never on a question) with its own session memory, kept apart from the record window's: a reader who filled the screen with one form has said nothing about the next question they are asked. Both shells take a bindable `expanded`, which is how a panel opens expanded by design. The record window's four frame-bearing stories are byte-identical before and after.

The one panel that had rebuilt all of this by hand — the time sheet's own flag, icons and utilities inside a raw dialog — migrates with the other two full-screen surfaces in the pass that follows.

title: The queue tests the tree that lands, and the conventions say what is true
entry:
**The gate is ready for a merge queue, and the conventions say what is true again.** Every red check the first full battery found on 2026-09-02 was two branches merged minutes apart and never tested together, which the pull-request tier cannot see by construction. The `merge_group` tier now resolves its diff base from the queue's own payload, and while the austerity holds it defers the fan-out sinks exactly as the pull request does (the sink lint alone is a 2-core runner for twenty-six minutes per merge). The setting that turns the queue on is a repository ruleset, so `docs/deploy-queue.md` carries it as its first entry, with the values to pick and why; it replaces the billing-block entry, which cleared on 2026-09-01.

The conventions stop describing a blocked gate: `build-performance.md`'s austerity section records what happened in August and what the revert is now a decision against, `operations.md`'s quality-gates section names the jobs the gate actually has and the tiers that actually run, and `CLAUDE.md` no longer says the gate of record is blocked.

Two things found on the way.
