The generated OpenAPI client was behind the committed snapshot for the third time (#445, #459, and now #486 each regenerated the snapshot and left the client), and is regenerated; a queued merge runs the drift check on the tree that lands, which is what stops a fourth. And `check:scoped`'s format step refused a change whose every script file the formatter ignores, which is exactly what a client regeneration looks like; it now carries `--no-error-on-unmatched-pattern` as its lint-only sibling already did, with a test pinning that shape.

And one real regression, found because this change runs the full battery: #477's grid publishes the frame's visible width to CSS from a resize observer, and it wrote the property inside the observer's own callback on every notification. Under the story suite's load that churn made the column-filter field lose focus to its menu while a word was being typed. The write now lands on the next frame and only when the width changed; the full story suite passes.

title: The five dialogs the directory panes were hiding open in the one shell
entry:
Five more panels open in `ActionDialog`: the ones the four directory panes compose.

The panes had been excluded from the migration as "panes inside a surface, not modals," a reason that described the files rather than the hits; each pane holds a real form dialog. Assign A Category, Record A Way To Reach Them, Record An Identifier, Change The Name On The Record and Record Another Name are now on the shell, on `LabelledField` and `FieldRow` where they had hand-minted ids, each refusing its commit with a reason where it used to disable silently, and each asking before a stray Escape throws typed work away (the change dialog compares against the name it was seeded with, so an untouched seed asks nothing).

Four allowances leave the registry; six remain, every one a named exclusion. The design records the correction: an allowance's reason should name the panel it excuses, not the file that holds it.

title: Finish what the refile route left red on main
Retire the modal migration's stream note
The last two panels: the document flow, and trust funds with commitSoon
entry:
Add a Document opens in `ActionDialog`, and with it every panel in the migration's scope is on one of the two shells.

Its two paths — from a file, from a template — share the shell's one commit, whose verb follows the open path ("Add Document", "Build Document") and refuses with the reason until that path has what it needs. A document that landed, whether created, rejected by the scan, or still being checked, leaves the panel `done` with the outcome in place of the form; a request that never reached the server, or a problem the server stated, is a refusal with the reason in the notice band and the form still in hand.

Apply Trust Funds, excluded while the Soon affordance lived in the app, is a plain form with `commitSoon` now that the shell carries the affordance; its dependency reads on the commit's hover and to a screen reader rather than as a line beneath it.

Twenty-seven panels migrated across six pull requests. Ten `hand-composed-modal` allowances remain in `tooling/lint-one-ui/registry.json`, every one a named exclusion: the command palette (a launcher), the four directory panes (panes, not modals), the settings ledger (a Sheet), the three full-screen surfaces (a separate design), and the fee-arrangement window (`RecordWindow`'s shape).

title: The send panels stay to show their reference
entry:
The three send panels open in `ActionDialog`, and each stays on `done` to show what it came to.

Report an Issue and Report a Problem file through the firm's pipeline and then stay open with the reference the report was recorded under, the bar ending at Close; their Copy control moves out of the bar and sits beside the diagnostics it copies, since the bar holds one commit. Request a Change hands the shell `commitSoon` for the filing that is not wired yet, seats Copy beside the request it copies, and asks the shell not to restore focus to its row trigger on close — `restoreFocus={false}`, a new closed seam for the one trigger shape (revealed on focus) that a restored focus keeps latched open. The issue report and the change request keep their drafts across an ordinary close by design, so both tell the shell there is nothing to lose. All three lay their fields out with `LabelledField`.

Three allowances leave the registry; twelve remain, eleven of them named exclusions. Two wording changes: "Request a change" is "Request a Change", and the copy controls lost their bar seat, not their icons.

title: The four forms open in the one shell
entry:
Four more panels open in `ActionDialog`, and two of them are the first callers of the seams the shell just gained.

Move to Another Ledger hands the shell `commitSoon` with the dependency the move waits on, so the shell wraps its own commit in the Soon affordance and the panel no longer composes one around a commit of its own. New Person / New Organization lays its fields out with `LabelledField` and `FieldRow`, which mint the ids and wire the labels; its "Checking the firm's record" hint moves from the bar into the body. Fold One Record Into The Other is a `destructive` kind — the alertdialog role, no incidental dismiss, the commit in the colour of an act that takes something away — and states why its commit is refused until the acknowledgement is ticked, where it used to be silently disabled. Answer This Hit puts its rationale and the waiver's pickers in labelled fields and its "recorded as a new row" line in the body.

Four allowances leave the registry; fifteen remain, eleven of them named exclusions. Two wording changes: "Record the answer" is "Record the Answer", and the commit icons (the arrows, the merge glyph) are gone, as they went from billing.

title: Seven confirmations open in the one shell, and a commit may stay
entry:
Seven more panels open in `ActionDialog`, and the shell gained the outcome one of them needed.

The file manager's three (delete a folder, restore a file, the upload destination), the note and party removals, the settings recap before a save, and the attachment detach inside `RecordAttachments` — the last a design-system component that composed its own `AlertDialog` while registered. The file-manager panels stop taking a `running` flag from their host: the host returns the outcome and the shell owns the busy state; their host-worded failures render in the notice slot. The upload panel's report column becomes the context pane beside its decision, and its bar hint moves into the body.

`ActionOutcome` gained `"done"`: the panel stays open with nothing left to ask — the commit leaves the bar, the dismissal reads Close, the guard stands down — and `fields`/`context` are handed `done`. The upload panel saves its destination and stays to show the batch landing; the two send panels still to migrate will use it the same way. Seven allowances leave `tooling/lint-one-ui/registry.json`; nineteen remain, eleven of them named exclusions.

title: A misfiled entry moves rather than being struck and typed again
entry:
A time entry filed on the wrong matter can be moved to the right one.

Time gets recorded against the wrong matter — a person is on two of them in one afternoon, the picker was left where it was, the timer was bound before anybody had decided. Until now the only remedy was to strike the entry and type it again, which loses its number, its internal memo, its codes, its attached files and its whole history, and leaves a struck row standing on a matter the work was never really on.

**`POST /api/v1/time-entries/{id}/refile` moves it instead.** Its own route rather than a `matterId` on the update, and deliberately: this is a cross-matter write. Two ledgers change, two matters' totals move, and the rate the entry froze was resolved against the matter it is leaving. A patch field would let anything that can edit a narrative also move money between matters without meaning to.

**What carries, and what is re-asked.** The entry number carries — a reference that changes is a reference that lies, and anything that cited it has to keep resolving. The consequence is stated rather than hidden: the number's own shape names the matter the entry was FIRST written on, so after a move that prefix is provenance and not a claim about where the entry lives now. The description, the memo, the codes, the attachments and the history all carry untouched.

The **rate and the rounding increment are re-resolved** against the destination, on the entry's own work date. Both are matter-scoped — the rate chain reads matter, then client, then timekeeper; the increment resolves matter, then client, then user — so carrying one client's answers to another is how a firm bills at the wrong rate. This is not the rate-snapshot invariant bending: that rule says a rate card edited later never re-rates a standing entry, and it still holds. What changed here is the question, not somebody's later edit to the answer. The acknowledgement reports what the entry now carries, so a screen that assumed only the matter moved is not left showing the wrong money.

**What it refuses, and why.** Anything past draft, anything on a bill, anything a draft invoice has claimed, a matter this firm does not have, and the matter the entry is already on. Past draft the entry is evidence somebody is relying on — an approved entry is a reviewer's decision about a matter, a billed one a line on a finalized invoice — and the answer to both is a void and a fresh record, never a move nobody can see. Refusing the no-op move rather than reporting success keeps the act's meaning.

**Every move is on the record**, as one audit event naming both matters, so a reader of the entry's history can see where it came from and when it moved.

On screen, the Matter field is now settable on every draft — in the Time Sheet's Matter cell and in the record window. On a row not yet written it is still the choice that lets the row be written at all; on one the firm holds, picking another matter moves the entry. The one thing a move cannot do is take a written entry off a matter altogether: the record has to be somewhere.

title: The shell takes the seams its first fifteen callers repeated
entry:
**Enter commits in every `ActionDialog`.** The primary pane is a `<form>` and the commit in the bar is its submit button by `form` attribute, so the platform's implicit submission does the work and a disabled commit stops it; Ctrl+Enter or Cmd+Enter commits from a textarea via the form's keydown listener. No caller changed.

`ActionDialog` gained the seams its first fifteen callers were writing by hand, and the design system gained the maturity family and two field primitives.

The primary pane is a real `<form>` and the commit is its submit button by id, so Enter commits in every panel and a disabled commit stops it; Ctrl+Enter or Cmd+Enter commits from a textarea. `subtitle` takes a string (twelve of fourteen were plain text; the eight that could be are now one attribute). `commitSoon: { reason }` renders the commit inside the Soon affordance for an act not served yet — the shell wraps its own control, so the bar still holds one commit in its source and `footer-set` is unchanged.

`apps/web/src/lib/maturity/` moved whole into `@magna-carta/design-system/maturity` — the stage model, `MaturityBadge`, `MaturityDot`, `SoonAffordance` and its wording — because the shell cannot import the app; thirty-five files changed an import path, the two tests moved with the module, and `SoonAffordance` is registered in `lint:one-ui`'s one-implementation registry with three stories in the catalog.

`LabelledField` (label, control, hint, error; the id minted, the description joined, an error marked invalid, the control's attributes handed over as `props` to spread) and `FieldRow` (two or three across) replace the column written fifty-six times and the row written sixteen. The field's gap is the panels' space-8 where the superforms-bound `Form.Field` uses space-4; the recipe says so rather than picking for the owner.

title: Three tests that were red on main learn what landed
entry:
**Three node-shard tests that were red on `main` are green again.** Each is a fitness function or an exact-list assertion that a recent merge outran while the gate ran nothing on `main`: the permission registry test did not know the `reports:export` key the download register added; the document-assembly purity test rejected the tabular composer's import of the platform's one renderable document model, which is now an allowed external with its reason; and the load-profile smoke caught the matter-note timeline source scanning at the firm-window scope. That source orders on `COALESCE(occurred_on, created_at's date)`, an expression no plain index serves, so it joins the calendar scan allowlist on the same terms as the eight sources already there rather than gaining an expression index for one read.

The worker shards had five more of the same kind. Two `/api/v1/me` expectations still listed `notes:retract`, which the edit-and-delete model removed, and did not list `search:matter`, which the consolidated matter search added. Two `resolveFirmBucket` tests matched the old one-line fault messages after the failure surface rewrote them into sentences a person can act on; they match the new wording. And the sweep that fires a credential-less request at every declared-authenticated operation, five hundred and counting, is sized to that work instead of a 40-second guess that held on a quiet box and not on the gate.

title: Take out the status window's allowance, which outlived its violation
The gate runs what the change can reach, and restores what main already built
entry:
**The gate runs the test substrates a change can reach, restores its WASM artefacts from `main`, and is sectioned by tier.** The first month of real gate runs showed where the bill goes: `test-worker` (two to four 2-core shards of eight to ten minutes each) was the largest single item on every pull request, and every branch's first run paid a ~7-minute cold Docker build of the WASM packages because nothing had saved that cache on `main` since the push-to-main tier was suspended — a pull request can only restore what its own branch or `main` saved.

Three changes in `.github/workflows/gate.yml` and beside it:

- **Substrate gating.** `classify` (the job formerly called `changes`) now emits whether the Miniflare suites (`apps/api-worker`, `apps/status-worker`) and the Storybook suite (`packages/design-system`) are reachable from the change, read off the same undeferred dependent closure the lint scope already uses; `test-worker` and `test-stories` are skipped when they are not. A UI-only change never boots a Workers runtime and an api-only change never boots Chromium. The reading is fail-safe: `ALL` and `NONE` (a crate, a container, a workflow) both run everything, and only a concrete package list that omits the substrate's package skips it. `lint` is likewise skipped at the job level on a `NONE` scope instead of paying a 2-core runner to print that.
- **`seed-caches.yml`.** On every push to `main`, restore-or-build the WASM artefacts under the gate's own cache key, so a branch's first run hits. `pnpm run lint:cache-keys` (`tooling/lint-cache-keys`) holds the two key expressions identical, because a seed under a different key warms nothing.
- **Named and sectioned.** Jobs are grouped under banners by tier — classify, always-on guards, WASM artefacts, consumers, Rust and containers, aggregate — and named for what they do (`classify`, `build-wasm`). The four-step preamble every consumer repeated (checkout, setup, download the artefact, untar it) is now `./.github/actions/setup` with `wasm: "true"`, so each job's steps are what that job checks.

`assemble-docs.yml` moves to the 1-vCPU runner and installs the workspace only once the dependency-free assemblers have produced something to format; its second run per merge, which finds nothing, now costs a checkout. Standard: `docs/conventions/build-performance.md`.

One gate-reliability fix rides along: the worker suites' `beforeAll` hooks apply the control-plane migrations and, in the heavier files, seed several firms through the real registration flow, which on a loaded 2-core runner overran Vitest's 10-second default twice in one afternoon while every test in the file would have passed. `apps/api-worker/vitest.config.ts` sizes `hookTimeout` to that work; the per-test timeout is unchanged.

title: The four ledgers share one frame, and the time screens stop refusing what the server sends
entry:
The four financial ledgers — Time, Fees, Costs and Billing — now hold their chrome in common, and an empty table centres in what the reader can see.

**They take the screen and keep it.** Each ledger capped its table at the viewport height and then grew past it, so the counts footer walked off the bottom as entries arrived. They now sit in one `FullHeightSection`, the frame the file manager already used: the table scrolls inside itself, the footer stays on the bottom edge, and a page never reflows because a row landed. The panes below it are one `LedgerPanes` component rather than four copies of the same geometry — a difference between two of these tables was already a defect by the one-table ruling, and the frame around the table is the same argument one level out.

**The empty state stops running off the right.** A placeholder row spans every column, so its cell is as wide as the TABLE — wider than the frame whenever the columns are, and far wider once anybody has widened one. Centred in that cell, the empty state's watermark and heading landed off past the inline end with the sentence trailing after them: measured in a 660-pixel frame, the heading sat entirely past its right edge, centred at 691 where the frame ended at 680. The grid now measures its own visible width and the placeholder's content sits in a block stuck to the frame's leading edge and sized to it, so the state centres in the visible width and holds its place when the table is scrolled sideways. Two rules had to be beaten for that to land, and both were found by measurement rather than by eye: the cell's own inline padding, and the transparent border every row's first cell reserves for the selection rail — two pixels of silent offset on a row that is not a row and is never selected.

**One pane toggle, the file manager's.** All four wore a bordered secondary button; they now wear the same quiet chrome affordance the file manager does, last in the row on every ledger. The divider between the panes loses its centred grip handle — resizing is unchanged, and the whole edge always dragged.

**The Time tab drops its Time Sheet button.** The sheet opens from the top bar on every screen including this one, so a second door here took a reader somewhere they were already standing. Its handle in the top bar also loses the border that made it read as a different kind of control from the download tray and the bell beside it.

**The Fees toolbar is one row.** View, Amend, New Fee and the pane toggle sat across two lines with the arrangement's facts; they are now one row, and the second line is back.

The time surfaces stop saying "not recorded yet" about eight things the server had been serving all along.

The Time Sheet, the matter Time tab and the shared record window were built whole against a record fuller than the listing answered, and every field the contract could not fill was rendered honestly as a gap — the right call, and each one was written down in a register. What nobody re-asked is whether the contract had caught up. It had, in the same commit that built the Time Sheet. So the entry number, the entered date and who entered it, the resolved rate, both UTBMS codes, the internal memo, the attachment relation and the per-entry event history were all being served while three screens went on refusing them. The web type declared 12 of the 28 fields the server sends, which is what let it last: a type naming a subset is not a smaller truth, it is a screen that cannot see what arrived.

**What is now real.** The **entry number** on the ledger column, the sheet's Time Code cell, the record window's subtitle, the details panel and the printed sheet — and an entry captured before the sequence existed says it has none rather than being given an invented one. **Both dates and both people**, on every row rather than only the delegated ones. The **resolved rate**, read and not typed, naming where in the chain it came from: an entry keeps the rate in force on its work date for ever, so this states a fact rather than offering a change. **Category and Activity** as typable comboboxes over the firm's own UTBMS catalogue, one component rendered twice; a catalogue this account may not read costs the picker and not the field, because the entry's own code and label ride the listing. The **internal memo**, written and saved on the sheet's third row line and in the record window, and shown on a read-only record too — internal is not the same as hidden. Its exclusion from the printed sheet is now proved against a real rendering holding a real memo, not asserted in a comment. **Attachments**: what an entry points at, attaching one of the matter's own documents, detaching without deleting. And the **History tab** reads the served events, translating the audit's own names into a reader's words, reading an unknown event back rather than dropping it, and quoting only a reason somebody actually wrote — the audit's metadata is a field list by construction, and a field list is not prose.

**What is still a gap, and still rendered as one:** moving a written entry to another matter, recording one member's work under another's hand, the review gate as a served setting, unsubmit, delete-draft, billing disposition beyond the boolean, the rounding increment, capture before an entry has a description and a duration, the non-billable category, and the invoice's own number beside its identifier.

The register that got this wrong now says what it is for: a list of gaps is only honest while somebody re-asks it against the contract, and unasked it states the opposite. A test holds the retired eight out of it.

title: Retire the reading-kind stream note
A reading kind for ActionDialog, and the matter-status window opens in it
entry:
`ActionDialog` has a fourth kind, `reading`, and the matter-status window is its first caller.

A reading panel states a fact and seats any step it offers beside that fact — Close Matter, Reopen — rather than in the action bar, whose one control says "Close" because nothing was begun. The props are now a discriminated union on `kind`: the acting kinds require a commit exactly as they did, and the reading kind forbids one, so neither arm got weaker to admit the other. The kind table gained a row (`commitVariant: null`) and the bar renders its commit only when there is a variant to render it in.

The status window had merged composing `Dialog.Content` by hand — the shape the `hand-composed-modal` rule refuses — and left `main` red on `lint:one-ui`, because nothing before merge ran the rule. It migrates rather than taking an allowance: it postdates the shell. Two visible changes on that window: "Done" reads "Close", and the control is no longer disabled while a step is in flight, since the shell owns the dismissal.

title: Five HIGH advisories leave the governance gate: one bump, and one mock server nobody ran
entry:
**Four tests that were red on `main` are green again, and two of them found real gaps.** All four had passed through unseen because the gate ran nothing on `main` for a month, and each is a seam between two branches that merged in quick succession.

- When the column controls moved into each header's right-click menu, the trailing-pinned column's held pin did not come with them: the grid model already refused to toggle a `pinnedEnd` column, but the menu offered "Pin Status" as if it could, and the Time Sheet story still clicked a Columns button that no longer existed. The menu now shows a trailing-pinned column as pinned and disabled, titled "always keeps its place at the trailing edge", and the story asserts that through the header menu.
- The masthead's "Compact density" story rendered two page banners for comparison, which axe rejects; the comparison masthead now sits inside a labelled section, where a header is that section's header rather than a second banner.
- The conformance suite's committed operation list still named the four notes operations the edit-and-delete model replaced; it names the four that replaced them.
- The export-snapshot write on a member's shelf (`recordExportSnapshot`) put its object into the firm bucket with no dimensions, which the R2 dimension scan exists to catch: an object nothing can scope. It now carries the new firm-scoped class `export-snapshot` (`@magna-carta/object-dimensions`), on the same footing as `download-bundle`, since its figures may span matters and the shelf is the member's.

One more collision of the same day is recorded rather than fixed here: the matter-status window (#473) composes its own `Dialog.Content`, which the one-shell lint (#466) rejects. It stands as an allowance in `tooling/lint-one-ui/registry.json`, on the reading that it is a record window's shape, and the migration is owed to the stream that owns the screen.

**Five HIGH advisories that turned the governance job red on every branch are cleared, one by a bump and four by removing a carrier.** On 2026-09-02 osv-scanner began reporting four advisories on fast-uri 3.1.5 (host confusion and server-side request forgery through URI normalization, CVSS 7.5 each) and one on @faker-js/faker 5.5.3 (`helpers.fake` code execution, CVSS 7.8) against a lockfile identical to `main`'s, so no pull request could merge past a failure none of them caused.

fast-uri is fixed in 3.1.6; the override in `pnpm-workspace.yaml` moves to 3.1.7. It reaches the tree only through ajv, whose declared range already admits that line, so nothing else resolves differently.

faker had a wall. Its sole carrier, postman-collection, hard-pins 5.5.3 through its newest release and reads the v5 API at module load, so forcing the fixed line (10.5.0, a different major) makes the package throw on require. postman-collection reached the lockfile only through the Prism mock server's HTTP layer, and nothing in the repository ran Prism: no script, tool, test, plugin or workflow, and the "Prism mock smoke" the API conventions described lived in a workflow file that does not exist. So `@stoplight/prism-cli` leaves `apps/api-worker`, and with it postman-collection, faker 5.5.3, and uuid, whose override existed only for that carrier. The mock server stays available on demand (`pnpm dlx @stoplight/prism-cli mock …`, documented in `docs/conventions/api.md`) without living in the audited tree. The lodash override remains as a floor. Spectral, the contract lint the gate actually runs, is untouched.

title: Dropdown menus open as the pointer rests on them
entry: **Dropdown menus open on hover.** `DropdownMenu.Root` now owns a hover controller (`packages/design-system/src/lib/components/dropdown-menu/hover-open.ts`), shared with Trigger, Content, and SubContent through context: a mouse pointer resting on the Trigger for 120 ms opens the menu, the menu follows the pointer between the three, and it closes 250 ms after the pointer has left them all. A press, a key, or a tap opens the menu exactly as before and a menu opened that way is not hover's to close; a press on a hover-opened trigger keeps the menu rather than toggling it shut; a hover-opened menu leaves focus where it was unless focus has entered the panel; and hover-opening one menu closes another hover had opened, so Money and Record on the matter strip never overlap. On for every menu, `openOnHover={false}` keeps one click-only. Select and Combobox are unchanged: a form control that opened as the pointer crossed a form would fight the reader.

title: Retire the modal-frame stream note
One frame under both modal shells: the pane system, extracted and lent
entry:
Opening a matter happens in `ActionDialog`, with the client and the clearance in the context pane beside the entry.

The window used to build the record window's frame by hand — a header band, a separator, a body that scrolled alone, a two-pane grid — because there was no frame to reach for. It was the evidence that one was needed, and it is the first caller of the one that was built: 647 lines to 622, the hand-built bands and grid gone.

It gains what every panel on the shell has. Escape, the corner dismiss and a press outside ask before throwing away a half-entered matter. The reason the commit is refused is rendered beside it rather than only reachable by hover. And a matter that opened with somebody left unstaffed now refuses its commit for the rest of the panel's life, naming who was missed — pressing it again used to open a second matter against the same draft.

The proposal that this window move onto `RecordWindow` with editing raised is withdrawn: it is not a record being read, it is an act with context beside it, and the file's own head comment says so.

The pane system moves out of the record window into a frame both modal shells sit on.

The record window's frame — the header band and its quiet controls, the body, the primary pane that stops at its measure beside a context pane that takes the rest, the action bar of fixed geometry, and the fit-first/cap-second rule they all obey — is now `styles/recipes/modal-frame.css`, an internal recipe rather than a component. The record window keeps every class name as a hook and every pixel as it was: its four frame-bearing stories were screenshotted from the static catalog before and after, and all four are byte-identical.

Extracted because the alternative was measured. The largest panel in the app had rebuilt every one of these rules from utilities in 647 lines, quoting the record window's own doctrine in its comments, because there was nothing to reach for. A pane system that lives in one shell is a pane system every other panel rebuilds.

`ActionDialog` moves onto the same frame and gains a `context` pane — the record window's right pane, lent to a form. A context pane implies the record width whatever `width` asked for; a primary pane with no context beside it fills the frame. The notice band now sits outside the scroll, directly above the action bar, where the reader is looking when a commit comes back refused. Focus lands on the first field rather than the header's own dismiss.

title: Matter status: the seal is the control, and the program answers what closing requires
entry:
**The matter status seal is the control that changes it, and the program answers what closing requires.** Pressing the seal on a matter's masthead opens the status window; the lifecycle action left the overflow menu, which held nothing else and is gone with it. The window is short by design: the status, what closing requires with each requirement already answered, where the firm's paper file is kept, and the one step the status allows. One step per status, never a status picker, because none of the three operations takes a status on the wire.

`GET /api/v1/matters/{id}/close-readiness` is new. The close hook's rules are pure reads with a separate commit guard, so running them read-only is the same question the close asks and none of the write — which means the window can list what closing requires with each one marked met or unmet, rather than handing somebody boxes to tick or a button to press to find out. One reply answers every requirement, because the route runs every rule and reports every failure, so a rule it does not name is a rule that passed; a refusal naming a rule this build has never heard of becomes its own unmet row rather than disappearing. An unmet requirement disables the press, per the rule that a control does not offer a press whose refusal is predictable — but an unanswered one never does, because nothing has been predicted there and the close is the authority either way. The route reports an already-closed matter as not closable with that as its blocker, so one definition of the word survives. A close refused at the last moment answers in the same shape and re-answers the requirements already on screen rather than arriving beside them. Those sentences reach the screen through a new `errors` array on the shared problem envelope, which until now dropped everything a refusal said beyond its one summary line.

**The step is seated on the status, not at the foot of the window.** Somebody may open this window to read where the file is kept, and one whose bottom-right corner offers Close Matter puts the act they did not come for exactly where a hand goes by habit. The corner offers only Done; the step is a quiet secondary control beside the fact it changes, with the requirements that gate it directly beneath, where they read as the reason it is disabled.

**The window is the firm's wide working window, and it has two sides.** The left is bounded and always will be: a status and the one step it offers. The right is a panel that grows into a real physical-file register, so it is sized for the work it will hold rather than for today's three empty rows — the structure that will hold results renders at rest. The division is the point. Left: the status and the step it offers. Right: the firm's own paper file. They are apart because the paper file is a STANDING fact and not a consequence of the step — a firm keeps a matter's folder in a box, commonly with other matters' folders and commonly at a remote store, and closing the matter moves none of that. Laid out under the requirements it would read as what closing does to the file, which is the one thing it must not say, so the panel says the opposite in as many words.

**Location**, **Held in** and **Destroy after** render, each holding nothing and marked Soon. There is deliberately no sentence under them naming the dependency: a row that reads "Not recorded" beside the Soon mark has said it is not built, and a paragraph repeating that under three rows was the loudest copy on a window whose whole point is to be short. The middle row deliberately does not say "Box": firms keep files in boxes, in cabinet drawers, in safes, on shelves, and a row that named one of them would decide the medium for every firm. What holds a file will be a record carrying its own kind, which a matter points at — for the same reason it is not part of the location, since one container holds several matters' folders. That system needs its own design work and the ledger node says so. None of it is modelled: the platform has no register of the firm's OWN paper files, and no retention policy anywhere to derive a destruction date from — the custody register is explicit that it runs no timer at all, destroying an original on a written basis by two people rather than because a date arrived. Custodian is client property left with the firm to guard, which outlives the matter that brought it in, and is not the firm's file for a matter; conflating them would put a client's will where a paper file belongs. The gap is now a ledger node (`matters.physical-file`) rather than an absence.

**`StatusMark` is a new design-system component** (`@magna-carta/design-system/status-mark`): the affirmative mark, a disc filled in the success tone with the check knocked out of it. It existed as a recipe class three surfaces reached for with their own icon import, and they had already drifted onto two different Lucide glyphs — `circle-check` in the file manager, the larger-tick `circle-check-big` in the catalog and the record-window gallery. One mark that reads the same everywhere is the whole point of a register, so the glyph is decided in one place now and `statusMarkClasses()` is retired; a met requirement in the status window looks exactly like a clean file in the file manager, because it is the same component. It carries an accessible name by default and takes `decorative` where words beside it already say the word.

The masthead also gained the way back, as a bare arrow at the head of the ledger line — the labelled `BackLink` rule earns its label above a masthead, where "back" is ambiguous; on a matter's own ledger line the docket is the only place up.

title: One search that answers a whole matter, and the build context the search image never had
entry:
**A matter can be searched from one box, and the read layer behind it is a registry rather than a screen.** A matter is fourteen sections holding one case and nothing could ask that case a question: five sections had a hand-rolled search box, nine had nothing, and no query reached more than one of them.

`@magna-carta/matter-search` takes the federated timeline's architecture rather than inventing one, because it is the structurally identical problem — many subsystems, one federated read, one visibility seam, a bounded fan-out. A source declares where its rows live, which capability gates them, whether its answer is a listing or a ranked one, what it matches on, and whether it has a non-privileged snippet or declares that it has none. It is never a write-path obligation and there is no second copy of anything, so the answer cannot drift from the section a hit links into.

The shared statement builder is where the guarantees live rather than in anyone's diligence: it composes the matter binding itself, so a source cannot search across matters; it composes the visible-matter predicate before the `LIMIT`; it reads one row past the limit, so "there is more" is measured rather than estimated; and it names an `ESCAPE` on every `LIKE`. `test/source-fitness.test.ts` asserts all four over the SQL each source actually builds, plus the rule that is about disclosure rather than correctness — no registered source may name a discovery review table, because a review set is its own corpus precisely so a matter search cannot reach it.

`GET /api/v1/matters/{matterId}/search` carries two permission gates and the finer one runs first. `search:matter` gates the surface; then every source whose capability the member lacks is dropped **before a statement is built**, never post-filtered, and reported rather than returned empty. `in` narrows the registry before anything is built, which is what makes the default scope — the section the reader is standing on — the cheapest query rather than the most expensive.

`ScreenSearch` gains its first production consumer for the `scope` seam it shipped with, unchanged. The control renders from the matter **layout**, so every section inherits it and none can mount a second one; `sections.ts` now carries a required `searchSource` — a key, or `null` with the line saying what it waits on — and `pnpm run lint:matter-search-coverage` refuses a section that answers neither way, which is what makes the growth mechanical rather than remembered.

Nine sources ship — files by name, time narratives, cost descriptions, parties, notes, custody, billing lines, calendar titles and asset descriptions — and five sections decline with a reason. Notes composes `packages/notes`'s own model rather than restating it — one row, edited in place, ordered by the day the note is ABOUT rather than the day it was typed, so a hit sits where the Notes tab itself would put it. Two incidental fixes: the transport seam takes an `AbortSignal`, and the api-worker conformance suite was already red on this branch's base — the notes routes had landed without their six operation ids or a `notes` namespace binding.

title: Retire the billing-migration stream note
Billing and costs open in the one shell
entry:
Ten more panels — eight in billing, two in costs — open in `ActionDialog`.

Write off a balance, issue a credit note, draft a bill, finalize one, edit a line, record a delivery, void a draft, amend an agreement, kick back a cost, void a cost. Each lost its own open flag, its own busy flag, its own hand-built footer and its own `$effect` that reset the fields; each gained the guard that asks before Escape throws away a half-written correction.

Two of the twelve turned out not to belong here, and naming them is the point. `arrangement-dialog` reads a record — the fee arrangement in force, its terms and its version history — and its one act opens a different panel; that is `RecordWindow`'s shape, not this one's. `apply-trust-funds-dialog` is an act whose commit is not served yet: its control is wrapped in `SoonAffordance`, the product's own primitive for a designed-but-unbuilt capability, and it becomes a plain `ActionDialog` the day a route hands out a trust account. Both keep an allowance, but the allowance now names which shell they belong to and when rather than recording them as debt.

The commit's icon is gone from the eight that carried one. `RecordWindow`'s commit has always been text, and a glyph beside "Write Off" under a heading that already reads "Write Off a Balance" was decoration the two shells disagreed about. Where a footer carried an explanatory line — what opening a draft actually does, which permission finalizing needs — it moved into the body: the action bar is the shell's, and a sentence is content rather than a control.

title: The matter strip groups by meaning, and the band loses a menu that held nothing
entry:
The matter's section strip is grouped, the header's overflow (`...`) control and the Other section
are gone, and Magnus takes a section.

The control held exactly one item — the status's lifecycle action, shipped disabled and marked Soon
— so a member had to open it to discover there was nothing in it to press. That is a control's width
of chrome returning nothing, and it also quietly broke the standing rule it was built to honour: a
designed-but-unwired capability ships VISIBLE, and a seam in a drawer is not visible. The lifecycle
action comes back as a named control on the row when it is wired. Until then the band carries no
actions at all, and its inline-end column is the section strip and nothing else.

The Other section leaves both the registry and the route tree. It was the only tab whose label named
no place: it stood for whatever the other thirteen
did not cover, which is a bin rather than a destination, and its stub had to be written in the
abstract because nothing concrete was ever going to land there first. Content with no home yet waits
for the section that will own it.

In its place, **Magnus gets a matter section** — a `soon` stub for now, at the head of the non-core
group so it is visible on a wide canvas and the last of that group to fold. The assistant reads a
matter rather than recording anything on it, so it does not hold a core record section's width; it
now has both of the homes it was always going to need, the always-reachable sidebar destination and
the conversation already scoped to one matter.

**The strip stopped folding by measurement and started grouping by meaning.** Fourteen sections fit
no canvas: at 1440 the measured fold left seven on the row and put the other seven behind More, and
which seven was decided by pixel arithmetic — Trust and Calendar were buried for sitting late in a
list, not for being less used. The row now carries seven entries, five of them sections and two
named neighbourhoods that open a menu:

**Overview · Files · Money ⌄ · Parties · Calendar · Record ⌄ · Magnus**

Money is Time, Fees, Costs, Billing and Trust; Record is Notes, Emails, Messaging and Custodian.
Only what a member can afford to reach through a menu is grouped: a matter's dates are checked too
often for that, so Calendar stays on the row and Parties with it. The arrangement's order is also
the fold order, so the tail is the cheapest thing to reach through a menu — Magnus, then Record,
then the dates and the people, with Money holding the row longest because all five of its sections
are live.

Measured after building, all seven hold the row at 1440. The measured fold stays underneath as a
backstop for anything narrower, and an entry that reaches it folds as a GROUP — its name becomes a
menu heading over its own sections, so the two routes to one destination never disagree about what
it belongs to.

`sections.ts` now carries two lists with one home: every section that exists, and the arrangement
the strip reads them in, declared by slug. A section nobody placed, a slug naming no section, a
section placed twice, and a group of one are all module-load failures, so the strip cannot silently
stop offering a section that exists. The `core` flag is gone with the flat strip that used it.

All three generalizations are in `docs/conventions/design-corrections.md`, and the Record Detail
archetype carries the grouping rule and no longer lists a `⋯` in its header.

title: Retire the modal-shell stream note
Two shells and never a third: the panel an act is asked for in
entry:
`lint:one-ui` now recognizes a modal panel built outside the shells.

The expensive shape was never the crude one. A raw `<dialog>` and a scrim in a `<style>` block were already caught; what passed every gate was a screen importing the design system's own `Dialog.Root` and `Dialog.Content` and composing a panel by hand. It renders correctly, it typechecks, it lints, and it reads fine in review — it simply does not share the answers the shells settle.

Three source signals, because a modal built outside the system arrives as any of them: a composed `Dialog`/`AlertDialog`/`Sheet` panel outside a declared shell's home, a scrim written as utilities (`fixed inset-0` at the modal layer, which the style-block rule cannot see and which is the shape this repository actually writes), and a reach for the platform's own modal. Both shells also stamp `data-modal-shell` on the panel they render, which is the half that reads behaviour rather than source — a marker a rendered-DOM check can require of anything carrying the `dialog` or `alertdialog` role, and the only thing that catches a panel whose parts were aliased on import or chosen at runtime.

Which homes may compose a panel is **declared**, in `registry.json` beside the component register, rather than listed inside the rule — so adding a shell is a reviewed edit to the file that already answers "what is in the system". Being a registered component is deliberately not enough on its own: `RecordAttachments` is registered and still holds a confirmation that should be an `ActionDialog`, so it carries an allowance rather than an exemption.

A second rule, `footer-set`, asserts the action bar the way the header set has always been asserted against the record window: exactly the dismissal then the commit, in that order. A reader who has learned where the commit sits has learned it in every panel in the product, and a third control would un-learn that everywhere in one edit.

The thirty-seven panels that predate all this are carried as printed allowances with a reason each. They are debt, not exemptions: an allowance that outlives its violation is itself a failure, so the list can only shrink.

The custodian's three panels — logging a packet, describing an item, filing a copy — are the first screens to open in `ActionDialog`.

They landed the same week the shell did, each carrying the scaffold by hand: its own open flag, its own busy flag, its own footer, and no guard on the way out. `lint:one-ui` caught all three the moment the two branches met, which is what the rule is for. They are migrated rather than allowanced: an allowance records debt that predates a rule, and these postdate it.

Being real callers changed the shell twice, which is what first adopters are for. A commit now takes a second word for the same verb — "Logging" beside "Log Packet" — because thirteen panels across the product already changed their label in flight and losing that would have been a visible regression. And the reason a commit is refused is now **rendered** at the weak end of the action bar rather than only hovered: a `title` is not discoverable by anyone who is not already hunting for it, and the reader who most needs it is the one looking at a control that will not press.

All three gain the guard they never had: Escape, the corner dismiss and a press outside now ask before throwing away a half-described will.

`ActionDialog` — the one panel an act is asked for in, and `RecordWindow`'s modal peer.

Thirty-four files in `apps/web` composed a modal panel by hand, and each re-derived the same seven mechanics: the open flag, the reset when it opens, the busy flag, the commit, the failure band, the refusal that disables the commit, and the footer. They had already drifted in every way drift was available — thirteen said "Cancel" where five said "Close" for the identical gesture, eighteen suppressed the corner dismiss where twelve kept it. **And not one of the thirty `Dialog` panels asked before it discarded**, so a stray Escape threw away a half-written write-off, credit note or new matter in silence. `RecordWindow` was given a guard for exactly that and could not lend it.

The shell owns what no caller may re-derive, and owns it by having no prop for it: the footer's geometry and the order of its two controls, the dismissal's word, the busy state, whether the corner dismiss shows, which primitive renders the panel, and the one close path every exit runs through. A caller differs on a closed set — a `fields` snippet, a `notice` slot the app puts its failure band in, `kind`, `width`, and a commit that reports `committed` or `refused`. `kind` is the line that carries the most weight: a form is a `Dialog`, a question is an `AlertDialog` with the role and the dismissal behaviour that implies. Four panels reached `AlertDialog` before this and thirty did not, with no rule behind the split.

The unsaved-work guard moved out of `record-window.svelte` into an internal both shells consume, so the product asks that question in one voice rather than in one window.

title: The Custodian register can be written to, and an item has a history of its own
entry:
**One item's chain of custody is now readable.** The ledger has always recorded item-scoped rows — `custody_movement.item_id` is nullable precisely so that withdrawing one instrument, superseding it, or holding it alone is recordable against the item rather than the envelope — and nothing could read them back at that scope. A packet's history was the only history, and an item's rows sat inside it unmarked, so a `withdrawn` entry did not say which of a packet's five instruments left.

`GET /api/v1/custody/packets/{packetId}/movements` takes an optional `itemId`. **The filter is deliberately not `item_id = ?`**: an item inside a packet goes wherever the packet goes, so the scope is the item's own rows PLUS the packet-wide ones. A read that returned only the rows naming the item would answer "Contents described" over a decade of moves and check-outs and present that as a chain of custody, which is the failure worth guarding — `apps/api-worker/test/custody-routes.test.ts` pins it, including that the OTHER item's rows stay out.

Every row already carried `itemId`, so which of the two kinds an entry is never has to be inferred. `movementDetailLines` takes a scope: reading a packet's history an item row names its item ("About Item 1: Original will"), and reading one item's history the packet-wide rows say "The whole packet". Neither says anything in the list where it is the ordinary case, so no history repeats itself on every line.

In the packet window each item in Contents opens onto its own rail, and opening is what reads the ledger — a packet with nine items draws a list rather than nine histories nobody asked for.

**The Custodian register gained its entry paths, and lost three tabs.** The whole `custody.*` write surface already existed and no screen reached any of it, so the register could be read and never begun: `apps/web/src/lib/custodian/custody-api.ts` had no POST at all and the primary action was a `SoonAffordance`.

Three modals over the existing endpoints, with `packet-draft.ts` holding the readiness and request assembly for all three so what is sent, and what stops a submit, is pure and tested rather than living in a component nobody can exercise without driving a dialog. An untouched optional field is absent from the body rather than sent empty, which is the difference between "nobody was asked" and "the firm was told the depositor is nobody" on an append-only record.

The screen is now one table: the By Owner, Holds and Due tab strip and its four panels are deleted, the status select above the rows is gone (Status is a column with its own filter, per the matters docket ruling), and the local search box is gone ahead of the centralized search component, with the server's `search` filter left plumbed for it. `packet-register.svelte` lends its grid back to the surface so the show/hide-columns and clear-filters controls sit in the screen's one action row.

Two shared-surface changes ride along. The data-table recipe's placeholder cell now sets `white-space: normal`: it inherited the grid's `nowrap`, so a wordy empty state was one unbreakable line that widened the table past its own frame and dragged the empty state off the inline end, on any surface, not only this one. And custody `out` renders as "On loan" rather than "Out": the two states in which property is off the shelf are `out` and `released`, they are opposites, and neither "Out" nor a first pass at "Checked out" separated them — both only say it left the building. "On loan" carries the return, and is the ledger's own noun for it (the row records a `borrower` and a `due_back_on`). `released`'s hover now states that custody has ended. The movement label is untouched: the act is still "Checked out" in a packet's history.

title: One place a failure lands, and one paste that explains it
entry:
`apps/web` had no client error boundary. A throw inside an event handler, an effect, or a promise
nobody awaited left a screen that silently stopped working, no Error ID, and nothing to report;
`+error.svelte` only ever caught a failure while loading or rendering a route. `hooks.client.ts` now
mints a handle for every one of them — prefixed `client_` rather than the platform's `error_`,
because it resolves to no server-side trace and a handle that looks like it should resolve costs
somebody a search — and installs the `onerror` and `unhandledrejection` handlers, which record the
exception's kind and where it was thrown and never its message.

Nothing files automatically. A crash offers Report a problem and does not send one, holding the
Off/strict default the diagnostics setting already defines.

**Every failure in `apps/web` renders from one record through one component family.** The client
kept four of the twelve fields an RFC 9457 problem carries; it now reads all of them, and
`requestAccess` / `stepUpRequired` — emitted at six places in the API worker and previously read at
none — become the control the member presses instead of another apology. Four private copies of the
problem parser collapse into `lib/api/problem.ts`; `PagedList` holds the failure rather than a
string, which is what made nine surfaces structurally unable to show an Error ID; and
`failure-state` / `failure-band` / `failure-details` in the design system are extracted from the
costs and billing pair rather than invented. The copy path assembles the whole trace once
(`lib/diagnostics/failure-trace.ts`), states absent facts rather than dropping them, and falls back
to a selection copy where the async clipboard is refused. `lint:failure-surface` is the fitness
function that keeps it.

title: The file manager's writes land, the Time Sheet takes the screen, and a consultation gets a number
entry:
**A consultation is numbered from the moment it is recorded.** A prospective matter carried no number at all, so every surface that prints a matter number printed the word "Consultation" instead — a category, not a name, and nothing a person can quote on an intake sheet, a conflicts check, or a bill for the consultation itself. Consultations now draw a tentative number from their own sequence at creation (`matter.consultation_number`, migration `20260901T130001_consultation-number`).

It is a SEPARATE run from the matter number, not a preview of it. A consultation that never becomes a matter must consume no matter number — a gap in that run reads as a lost file — so the two never share a counter, and opening a matter ADDS its permanent number rather than replacing the tentative one, which stays on the record so anything filed under it still resolves. Both draws ride the same `matter_number_counter` / `matter_number_allocation` mechanism (and the same allocation-key backstop against a losing concurrent draw), separated by a `consultation/` scope-key prefix that no rendered matter scope key can forge — every segment value is folded into the URL-safe set, which contains no `/`.

`numbering_scheme` rows now carry a `purpose` (`matter` or `consultation`), with one active scheme per purpose; `GET`/`PUT /api/v1/numbering-scheme` take it and default to `matter`, so a caller that says nothing means what it always meant. A firm that has configured no consultation scheme renders from the built-in default (`C2026-0001` — a leading C, the year, and a per-year counter), and the GET says so with `usingDefault`, so the settings screen shows what is actually in force rather than an empty box beside numbers people can already see. The matter sequence deliberately keeps no default: there is no defensible shape to invent for a number that is then frozen, so a draw with no scheme still refuses.

`consultationNumber` is served on the matter summary, the matter detail, the consultations list, and the create acknowledgement, and the docket's search matches it alongside the matter number — for a file that is still a consultation it is the only number anyone has.

**The time entry is served as a record, not a row.** The listing and detail reads carried eleven fields against a table that stores twice that, so the Time Sheet redesign had nothing to render where the design puts a rate, a code, an enterer or an invoice. `timeEntries.list` and `timeEntries.get` now serve the whole record through one shared read (`readTimeEntryRecord` / the listing queries in `@magna-carta/timekeeping`): the frozen rate snapshot (`rateE4`, `rateSource`, `rateCardId`), the UTBMS task and activity codes with their ids, codes and labels resolved, `source`, `invoiceId`, `createdAt` (the entered date, distinct from the work date), `createdByUserId` + `createdByName` (the enterer, resolved through the member mirror like the timekeeper's name, null where the member row is gone), `timekeeperName` on every read, and `attachmentCount`. Four new surfaces beside it, all per-firm-migrated (`20260901T130000_time-entry-record-surfaces`):

- **Internal memo** — a nullable `memo` column, settable on create and PATCH (null clears), served everywhere the entry is. It is the firm's own note and never client-facing; the audit trail records which fields an edit touched, never the text.
- **Entry number** — an immutable matter-scoped reference minted at capture through `@magna-carta/sequence-numbering` (counter per matter + allocation-key backstop): the matter's number, a dot, a zero-padded sequence (`2026-0147.0042`). Every capture path draws one (create, grid batch, timer stop-commit); existing entries stay honestly null. Served as `entryNumber` and echoed on the capture acks.
- **History** — `GET /api/v1/time-entries/{id}/events` serves the entry's recorded audit events oldest first (actor id + resolved name, redacted detail), the file-history shape; capture now records its source and an update the field names it touched, so the rail can say what happened.
- **Attachments** — a `time_entry_attachment` relation linking an entry to files already in its matter, with list/attach/detach routes. Attach refuses a file on another matter; detach removes the link and never the file; both acts are audited.

`POST /api/v1/time-entries/{id}/convert-to-cost` converts a mis-recorded charge: one idempotent act captures the cost (matter, narrative as description, the entry's amount, work date as incurred date) and voids the time entry so the value is never counted twice, with cross-referencing audit events on both records. It refuses an entry that is billed, void, claimed by a draft invoice, or carrying no amount, and requires `costs:track` on top of `time:track`. Convert-to-fee is deliberately not built: the fee work-in-progress store does not exist yet, and a fee route against invoice lines would bill a charge no one recorded.

title: Retire the matter-chrome stream note
The matter's identity block stops spending three rows on itself
entry:
The matter's header band goes from 111px to 76px, and `Masthead.Root` learns a `density`.

The section strip already shared the band. What was left was the identity block, which spent three rows on itself: the ledger line, the title, the citation. Now it spends two — the matter number and its status seal lead the citation rather than holding a row above the title — and the title takes the Masthead recipe's new `compact` density, 2rem down to 1.5rem. The step lives in the recipe because the masthead is the one door to the display serif, and a screen that can set `text-2xl` on the Title has taken that door off its hinges.

The change that actually moved the number was on the other side. Six settings were measured, and three that look nothing alike came out at exactly 90px: the inline-end column was the overflow control stacked over the strip — 40px + 8px + 41px = 89px — and it floored the band however short the identity got. Putting the whole identity on one line bought nothing at all. Moving the control onto the strip's own row makes that column 41px, and the identity block sets the height again.

152px of matter chrome at the start of this work, 111px after the strip moved off its own row, 76px now, at every canvas width. A third density step was built, measured and dropped: at 1.25rem the display face is close enough to the citation that the register's scale contrast nearly goes, and it bought nothing over the structural saving.

title: Where a file lands is one seam
entry:
**A central save target.** Every download in the app already passed through one `saveExport` call, so
where files land became a single decision rather than four. `$lib/export/save-target.ts` writes into a
folder the member chose where the browser can do that, and hands the file to the browser exactly as
before where it cannot.

The state of the web decides the shape, and it is progressive enhancement rather than a capability
claimed everywhere: only the File System Access API lets a page choose a folder, and today Chromium
implements it while Firefox and Safari ship only the sandboxed Origin Private File System. What
Firefox and Safari DO have is the browser's own "always ask where to save" — a real local-disk picker,
just one the person turns on rather than one a page opens. `Settings · Downloads` shows a working
picker where the browser can, and names that browser setting where it cannot, rather than rendering a
control that does nothing.

Two properties the module holds, both stated in it. **It never fails a download**: a lapsed
permission, a folder that moved or was deleted, a picker that throws — each falls back to the
ordinary download rather than costing the member the file. **The folder never leaves the machine**: a
directory handle cannot be serialized to a server, so it lives in this browser's IndexedDB, which is
exactly why the folder is per browser while save-immediately is per member.

**Also fixed, and a consequence of the new default:** when the shelf refuses an export, the default
path had produced nothing at all — no file and no item, which is worse than the behavior it replaced.
It now falls back to downloading the file and says plainly that it was not kept.

title: A note is edited and deleted, and says when the thing happened
entry:
Matter notes: edit and delete replace correction-by-revision and withdrawal, a note records when the thing it describes happened, and a note can point at the matter's documents.

Three changes on the owner's direction, hours after the note primitive first shipped.

**The model collapses to one row.** The first cut held an identity row plus a chain of revisions, with three `RAISE(ABORT)` triggers making a stored body unrewritable and withdrawal as a state rather than a delete. An edit now overwrites and a delete removes the row. The owner's reason: replacing a note with another note every time somebody fixes a word accumulates without end. What it costs is stated rather than buried — there is no record of what a note said before, and nothing survives a deletion but an audit row carrying identifiers — and the superseded reasoning is kept in `docs/decisions/pending/` rather than deleted, because the position was really taken. The migration is a reviewed rebuild that carries every standing note across with its current text; `notes:retract` retires and deleting rides `notes:write`.

**A note carries two times and stops conflating them.** `created_at` is when somebody typed it; the new `occurred_on` / `occurred_at_time` / `time_zone` are when the thing it describes happened, on the calendar's model — a civil date, an optional wall clock, and a zone required whenever there is a clock. Every read orders by the occurrence falling back to the written day, and so does the federated timeline source, whose `timeColumnShape` moves from `instant` to `civilDate`. That puts a note about Tuesday's call beside Tuesday's hearing, which is how `matterEvent`, `matterDeadline` and `timeEntry` are already ordered; the one source that orders by when the row was written is the audit log, and that is named as its weakness rather than copied.

**A note can point at the matter's documents.** `matter_note_document` is a many-to-many link on the `matter_asset_document` model, and it links a handle rather than moving bytes: upload stays the File Manager's presigned-upload and quarantine chokepoint, so an attached document keeps its versions, its holds and its reachability from discovery. Deleting a note detaches its documents and deletes none of them. The merge-field fitness function now refuses the link table too, since a resolver reaching it would be one join from the bodies of every note discussing the document being assembled.

The composer shows every field the note will carry before anything is typed, generated ones included: the matter, the writer's name and the instant it will be stamped with.

title: Retire the matter-chrome stream note
The matter's section tabs move into the header's empty half
entry:
The matter's section tabs move into the empty half of its header, and the Alpha pillboxes come off the product.

A matter spent two rows before any content: the masthead, whose inline-end half carried one overflow control and otherwise nothing, and then the section strip on a row of its own. Those are now one band. The actions sit on the title's row, the strip sits beneath them packed to the same end, and both share the band's bottom rule — so the gold active bar still lands on a rule rather than floating. The masthead keeps everything it had: the serif title at masthead scale, the ledger line, the citation. 152px of chrome becomes 111px.

Four arrangements were built and measured before this one was chosen, which is the only reason it holds up. An even split of the band was measured against a capped identity block and both against a wrapping one: wrapping the title at a 1024 canvas costs 27px, turning a 42px saving into a net loss, and capping the identity block starved the strip to a single tab. The shipped split truncates the title and the citation instead, so the band is 111px at 1600 and 111px at 1024 rather than growing as the window narrows. The citation became one joined string in the same change, because a flex row of separate entries cannot ellipsis and truncating each entry to its share gives four stubs and no citation.

Separately, `alpha` and `beta` stopped rendering a maturity mark anywhere — the matter tabs, the sidebar destinations, the tools listing, the contacts sections. A surface a member can open does not announce how finished it is, and the pill cost each tab about as much width as its own label. `soon` still marks, because it says there is nothing behind this yet. The stages are unchanged and still decide whether a destination is a live link or a stub.

title: Exporting gathers rather than scatters
entry:
Exporting no longer saves a file. It GENERATES the item onto the member's download shelf, so several
can be gathered over a morning and taken together — the owner's direction, and the reason the shelf
existed in the first place. The format menu stays on the export control, because the format is what
the item is made for and what its download defaults to; that choice is kept on the new
`download_item.requested_format` column, distinct from `downloaded_formats_json`, since "what this
was made for" and "what has actually left the platform" answer different questions and are both true
at once.

The register learns the difference: `POST /api/v1/downloads/snapshots` takes `taken`, defaulting to
false, so a format asked for is not recorded as a format downloaded. Claiming otherwise would tell a
member they already hold a file that was never made.

**Multi-select and one archive.** `/downloads` gains row selection and a bulk action that appears
only while a selection is in play. Snapshots render and travel in a single `client-zip` archive
rather than firing a download each — several simultaneous downloads make the browser prompt and then
scatter the files, which is the mess the gathering exists to avoid. An artifact cannot join the
archive and that is structural, not an omission: its bytes reach the member over a presigned URL the
browser downloads directly, and pulling them through the tab to repack them is what
`network-resilience.md` rule 2 forbids. Those open on their own, and a partial result is always
reported as partial.

**`Settings · Downloads`** carries the one preference: save a file as soon as I export. A user-tier
scoped setting, so it follows the member between machines, audited on the
`notificationPreferences.update` precedent, and written to the member's own tier and nothing else.

Where a file LANDS is deliberately absent, and stays absent: a page cannot choose the folder, the
local-disk pickers are Chromium-only, and they could never apply to a bundle whose bytes never pass
through the page. The browser's own "ask where to save each file" already covers every download; the
platform-side answer belongs to the desktop app.

Also repaired, and not from this stream: the matter-notes routes landed without their conformance
entries, so `main` was failing two fitness assertions — the six `notes.*` operations are added to the
committed operation list and the `notes:` namespace bound to the matter resource.

title: A firm can be renamed, so its name is never served from the row cache
entry:
**A renamed firm is named correctly again.** The per-isolate firm-row cache carried the firm's
display name, on the stated assumption that nothing renames a firm after provisioning — which is
wrong: a firm can be renamed, so for up to a minute every request served the old name. The name is
now resolved on demand (`FirmContext.readFirmName`) and the cache holds only what a rename cannot
falsify — that the firm exists, and its bucket. Two routes ask for the name, and both are ones where
a stale answer is wrong rather than untidy: the session bootstrap that puts it in the app shell, and
the file-integrity receipt, a document a firm relies on. `firm-absence-gate.test.ts` renames a firm
between two reads through one cached minute and asserts the second reports the new name; it was
confirmed to fail against the cached-name version first.

Also fixes five stale expectations in `me.test.ts` — `downloads:shelf`, `reports:export` and the
three `notes:*` keys reached the role seeds without updating the list, leaving that suite red on
`main` where the blocked CI gate could not report it.

title: A refused export looked exactly like one that never arrived
entry:
An export could be downloaded successfully and never appear on the download shelf, with nothing
anywhere saying why. Two defects, and the second is the one that mattered.

**The register's schema requires a finite number on a two-faced cell, and rejects the WHOLE document
otherwise** — so a single unmeasured figure cost the member the entire shelf item. The same class of
defect the spreadsheet renderer already guards against in `cellPlan`, arriving one layer along:
`storedFromExport` now falls back to the printed text face when the number is not real, which loses
nothing a reader can see. `packages/export-document` gains a test pinning what the schema accepts,
and the client pins the fallback.

**The failure was silent by construction, which is why it went unnoticed.** `keepExportOnShelf`
swallowed every outcome so that a shelf failure could never cost a member the download they already
had. That reasoning holds — it still never throws and never blocks — but swallowing made a refused
document indistinguishable from one that simply never arrived, with no Error ID and nothing to act
on. It now returns the outcome, and the export menu reports a refusal with the server's own words
and its Error ID.

title: Colour-code the API/web sync in the Build Versions panel, stop it resizing on you
entry:
**The Build Versions panel reads the pair that serves you at a glance, and stops resizing itself
while you watch.** The fixed sentence explaining that `magna-carta-web` and `magna-carta` deploy
separately and may report different builds is gone. In its place, the leading pair carries a
colour-coded badge: green **In sync** once they match, amber **Web behind** when the web build is
the one that has fallen behind (the one case actually worth reloading for), or a calm **Different
builds** for any other gap — shown only once both sides have a real version to compare. Separately,
the "Checking services" / "Services checked … ago" line under the header no longer appears and
disappears as a read moves from in flight to freshly answered to aged; it now holds its place at a
constant height, so the panel's size never depends on which sentence happens to be showing.

title: The workbench's stream note retires with the work it tracked
A note is corrected by revision and withdrawn, never deleted
entry:
Matter notes: the Notes section on a matter is real, and a note is a record rather than a text field.

Until now the platform had no note anywhere. What it had were scalar `note` columns on a dozen individual records, each one nullable free text on one row, attributable to nobody, editable in place, with no history and no reader but that row's own detail view. The matter's Notes section had promised "dated, attributed, and searchable" since the shell was built.

A note is dated and attributed when it is written, and those never move. Correcting one appends a version and keeps the old one, so the history is every body the note has ever had, each with its own author and instant; a colleague correcting a partner's note is recorded as having corrected it. Nothing is edited in place, because what makes a note worth having is that it was written then, by that person, saying that.

Withdrawing is the answer to text that should never have been typed: another client's privileged material, somebody's medical information, a note filed against the wrong matter. The words stop being shown everywhere, including the matter's activity history and search, while the record that the note existed, who wrote it and who withdrew it stays, with a required reason standing where the text was. There is no delete anywhere in the feature: no button, no route, no capability. The one case where bytes must genuinely leave is a legal question that reaches a person through the erasure report.

Reading, writing and withdrawing are three separate permissions, seeded to the seats that work matters and not to Billing or Read-only. A note joins the matter's activity history as one more entry carrying its author and its date and never a word of its text, on the same discipline that keeps an email's subject line off that read. No merge field can resolve to a note, so work product cannot be assembled into a letter under the firm's letterhead, and notes stay outside discovery collection: producing one means exporting it as a document first, which gives it a version, a hash and a custodian of record.

Search finds notes on the matter you are on, and matches the current text only. A note corrected to take out a name stops being findable by that name, which is usually why somebody corrected it.

title: The download tray sits beside the Time Keeper
entry:
The download tray: a Download control in the top-bar actions cluster, seated beside the Time Keeper
on the owner's direction, whose panel gives the overview of what the platform has made for this
member and links to the full register at the bottom. The register shipped as a sidebar destination
only, which was the wrong reach for it — a download is something you look up for, not something you
go looking through the rail for.

It is deliberately NOT a transfer manager and must not become one: bytes move over a presigned URL
that the browser's own download manager drives
([`network-resilience.md`](docs/conventions/network-resilience.md) rules 1 and 2), so there is no
progress for this component to show and no transfer for it to own.

Its dot is real state rather than decoration — the shelf holds something that arrived since this
browser last opened the tray, kept per browser in `localStorage` and read defensively so a private
window degrades to "nothing is new" rather than throwing. One 16px corner holds one mark, so while
something is new the arrival dot takes the slot from the maturity dot; the stage stays stated on the
sidebar row. A shared revision signal (`download-shelf-signal.svelte.ts`) is what makes a download
appear in the tray at once instead of at the next page load — the export menu and the tray never
meet, since one is rendered by whichever screen is exporting and the other is seated once in the
shell. The Downloads destination moves to `alpha`.

title: One workbench for a file nobody has filed yet
entry:
The **File Workbench** — one Tools screen where a file that belongs to no matter is dropped once and read every way at once, instead of ten screens each asking for the same bytes.

Type, Hash, Malware Scan, Metadata, Email, Convert, Repair, Text Recognition, Unlock and AI Text are all capabilities of one surface. Two of them are real in the browser today with no backend at all: what the file actually is, read from its leading bytes against what its name claims, and its SHA-256 and SHA-1. The other eight render their own control, disabled, naming what they wait on.

A flagged file still gets everything. The scan verdict is reported on the file's row and in its Overview and gates nothing, because a file somebody does not trust is precisely what this surface is for and the readings a gate would withhold are the ones that answer whether to trust it. A fitness test holds it: every capability is evaluated against the same file under each verdict, and the answers have to be identical.

Conversion acts on the whole selection, and offers only the formats every selected file can reach — a production of sixty scans is one gesture, and a target half the selection cannot become is not offered at all rather than failing partway.
